Because I am untouched by conceptualization, like space; because I cannot be shaken by anyone, like Mount Meru—I am immovable. Thus, through constant contemplation, the mind becomes free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa); by that—
The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished what was to be done. || 20–23 ||
Through the practice of yoga, there is the direct realization of Brahman;
by practicing that, having restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
one should rest the hands between the scrotum and the anus and take refuge [in that state].
Gently pressing the tongue with the teeth so that it protrudes only the measure of a barley grain.
Having fixed his gaze on the tip of his nose like a single bean, and likewise upon the ground, he should not attend to sounds through the ears, nor to the nature of odors through the nostrils. (25)
Now, that state which is Śaiva is Brahman; it is the supreme Brahman.
It may be attained through its practice by one whose self has been purified through the merits acquired in previous births.
If knowledge does not arise in this way, then by means of yoga practice, having unified the prāṇa and apāna,
and having awakened the kuṇḍalinī through the "six-faced" method,
one should pierce the six centers consisting of the three knots and realize Brahman in the thousand-petaled lotus.
He says that one should do so "by its practice.

By the practice of yoga, preceded by the restraint of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one should pierce the *suṣumnā* with the *kuṇḍalinī*; regarding this, he says "the testicles," indicating that the mantras to be mentioned hereafter are applicable. [The phrase] "between the testicles and the *apāna*" refers to the middle space between them.

Having pressed [the hands] together with both hands, preceded by the binding of the tongue and preceded by focusing on a target the size of a *māṣa* bean, one should fix the gaze upon the space of the ears, the earth, and the two feet;
[this constitutes] the grasping of the scent of the ear-nose.

This is for the purpose of indicating the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) and their five respective objects. The meaning is that one should not allow the connection between the sense organs and their objects, nor the connection between the mind and its volitions (*saṃkalpa*).
When this is done, the unification of *prāṇa* and *apāna* occurs; thereafter, Kuṇḍalinī pierces the *suṣumnā*, and then—

Having entered the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāracakra*), it dissolves. Along with that, the senses, the ego, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) also dissolve into that very place where the state of Śiva shines forth. That substratum of dissolution is Brahman alone; [the text says] "it dissolves into that" because it is the locus of that dissolution.
Thus, he states that practice becomes fruitful: "by the practice of that. This which...

The yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) was previously described; by one whose self (*ātman*)—meaning his own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—was acquired and practiced in a prior birth, that self acquired in the previous birth, through its repeated practice, leads to the attainment of the higher and lower Brahman in accordance with the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the host of yogis. In that regard, the knower of the non-dual (*nirviśeṣajñānin*), at the very moment of his own realization, becomes Brahman itself.
Thus it has been stated: "it comes to be. (24–26)
For one possessing specialized knowledge, there is gradual liberation.
Having caused the vital breaths to resound through the heart, austerity is said [to be performed];
then, having pierced the crown of the head, he departs from the body toward the imperishable.
But those people who, having reached the summit of their own body, have attained the supreme goal and know the higher and the lower, do not return again. (28)
Now, he describes the gradual liberation for one who possesses knowledge with attributes (saviśeṣajñānin), beginning with the words "by those that have come into being" (saṃbhūtaiḥ).

Those which come into being perfectly are the external and internal organs (bāhyāntaḥkaraṇa). That which, together with them, is heated—that is, ignited and made manifest—by the fire of knowledge with attributes is called *tapa* (heat/austerity). Having entered the heart, [it heats] the air located there...
Having been informed that the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is capable of piercing the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*),

and having mastered that breath, one passes upward from the body through the door of the *suṣumnā*, pierces the crown of the head, and attains that very same imperishable Supreme Brahman. Regarding the statement that "having reached that, they do not return," [it is as follows]:

"Those people who know the higher and the lower return"—this refers to the worshippers of the *śabala* (differentiated) Brahman; having pierced the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) by way of the *suṣumnā* channel, they enter the world of Brahmā through the gateway of the sun, and dwelling there until the dissolution of all beings (*yāvadābhūtasaṃplavam*), they continue their search for the non-differentiated Brahman. Then...
The meaning is that, through the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā), having attained absolute liberation (kaivalya) along with Brahman, they never return again.
For those who know Brahman as devoid of distinctions, there is liberation;
the attributes of the witnessed do not touch the Witness, which is distinct,
changeless, and indifferent— just as the duties of a householder do not affect a lamp.
Whether rolling in water or on land, this inert thing may wallow as it will; I am not defiled by its qualities, just as the sky is not affected by the qualities of a jar.
I am actionless, I am changeless, I am partless, I am formless;
I am free from conceptual construction, I am eternal, I am without support, and I am non-dual. || 31 ||
I am the self of all, I am everything, I am beyond all, I am non-dual;
I am absolute, indivisible consciousness, I am uninterrupted self-bliss.
Seeing only myself everywhere, considering myself as non-dual,
and experiencing my own bliss, I become free from conceptual construction. (33)
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or otherwise, the wise sage who delights in the Self may always dwell according to his own will. (34)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Regarding the statement that some, having known Brahman as devoid of distinctions right here, become fulfilled in their purpose—it is said that even if there appears to be any mental construction (*kalanā*) of something other than oneself, then by becoming the witness (*sākṣin*) of that, they become liberated. [The text says: "No."
Regarding the word *sākṣiṇam*:

the meaning is that by abandoning the notion of "self" and "mine" with respect to one's own body and everything else, and by means of uninterrupted contemplation of Brahman, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done and attains liberation beyond the body (*videhamukta*). Thus ends the word *upaniṣat*.
This marks the conclusion of the Kuṇḍikopaniṣad. || 29–34 ||
This commentary on the Kuṇḍikopaniṣad, which brings about the awakening of one's own self, has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
It is recorded that the total extent of this commentary on the Kuṇḍikopaniṣad consists of one hundred verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kuṇḍikopaniṣad, completing the seventy-fourth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the venerable Īśa.
Jābāla Upaniṣad “Pūrṇam adaḥ”— thus the peace invocation.
First Section: Meditation on Avimukta.
Bṛhaspati said to Yājñavalkya: "That which is Kurukṣetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods..."

For all beings, the abode of Brahman is Avimukta, indeed Kurukṣetra, the place of sacrifice for the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings. Therefore, wherever one goes, one should consider that very place to be so. (In place of "iti," [the reading is] "iti ityasya sthāne").

It is seen as being indeed never-forsaken. This, verily, is Kurukṣetra, the sacrificial ground of the gods, the abode of Brahman for all beings. For here, when the vital breaths of a living being are departing, Rudra explains the saving Brahman (*tārakaṃ brahma*), by which he becomes immortal and attains liberation.
"One should practice only that which is not liberated from darkness; one should not abandon that which is not liberated.
"Just so, Yājñavalkya; just so, O Venerable One," [he said]. "Indeed, Yājñavalkya," [the other replied]. || 1 ||
That which is the domain of the knowledge of renunciation as proclaimed in the Jābāla Upaniṣad is, in reality, the three-footed Brahman; nothing but one's own Self remains.

Within the Jābāla recension belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda, there exist three sections (kāṇḍas), beginning with the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa). Among these, those possessing desire attain the world of the moon through the performance of the ritual section; for those free from desire, [the attainment comes] through ritual and meditation—

Through the performance of the combined sections (*kāṇḍa-samuccaya*), one attains the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). For those who are detached from the meaning of both sections and are endowed with the means consisting of the recitation of the *Śatarudrīya* and the renunciation of all actions (*sarvakarma-saṃnyāsa*), which are the causes for attaining Brahman alone—
This Jābāla-upaniṣad, consisting of the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), serves as a means for attaining the state of Brahman alone;

it is intended for the purpose of praising that knowledge. Having defeated the Brāhmaṇas through debate at the edge of a grove near Mithilā, and having awakened Janaka with his own knowledge of the inner and outer Brahman, Yājñavalkya, together with his circle of disciples—

Furthermore, he dwelt for some time in the grove of Mithilā. Bṛhaspati, desiring to know the extent of Avimukta, spoke to Yājñavalkya—who was nearly omniscient—concerning that which is more renowned than all other sacred fields:
"Kuru" is so called because one who performs despicable or sinful deeds (*pāpa-karman*) cries out there; [it is] preceded by the casting away (*kṣepaṇa*) of such a person.

It is called Kurukṣetra because it protects its own people (*svagata-jana-trāṇāt*). Alternatively: *ku* is the earth; that which cries out (*rauti*) or makes sound upon it is *kuru*, namely the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The body, which is the cause for the abiding of that [breath], is *kurukṣetra*.
Therein lies the sacrifice (*yajana*) of the deity—the inwardly conscious essence (*pratyak-cid-dhātu*)—which is the instrumental cause for the activity of the deities, that is, the sense organs.
[The cause of worship: the performance of worship. For here, the senses [are worshipped] by means of offerings of their respective appropriate objects.

"The abode of Brahman" (*brahmasadana*) is the place for attaining Brahman. Just as Kurukṣetra is the means for performing sacrifices to the gods, so too is this internal Kurukṣetra, distinguished by the two aforementioned qualifications; this is in accordance with the question of Bṛhaspati.

The Sage said: "Unliberated" (avimuktam). That essential nature which is liberated from one's own ignorance, desire, and karma is the unliberated Brahman; where that is perceived, that very place—the wheel of command (ājñācakra) situated between the eyebrows—is Kurukṣetra. The meaning of the words beginning with "of the gods" (devānām) has already been explained.

Since this is so, therefore, one should think and know that wherever one goes—whether to places such as the Gaṅgā or Prayāga, or even elsewhere—that very place is Avimukta (the Unreleased). "In this manner" means by this method. "This indeed is the Brahman attained by me. The meaning of "Kurukṣetra" and so forth has already been explained. This is because the generality of all fields (kṣetra) is conceptually constructed by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever apart from that. Here, when Brahman is realized as Kurukṣetra in its unmanifest form (*avimukta-rūpa*), then— in accordance with that realization— for every living being (*jantu*) at the moment their vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are departing, Rudra— the Supreme Lord who dissolves (*drāvayati*) and destroys the affliction of one's own ignorance— is the savior from *saṃsāra*.

It explains—that is, declares—the nature of Brahman as being Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). By means of such instruction as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi), this individual soul (jīva) becomes immortal and is liberated from the delusion of being separate from itself;
it remains as nothing but Brahman alone, which is established through the negation of all that is other than itself and is devoid of any counter-correlate.

Since this is so, therefore, prior to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman alone, one should cultivate the unliberated liṅga of light situated between the eyebrows; one should practice the contemplation: "I am the liṅga of light."
(41) "The ascetic should always meditate eternally on the *jyotir-liṅga* between the eyebrows," according to the Śruti.
Until the knowledge of Brahman alone arises, [one remains within] the unliberated [phenomenal world].
"One should not abandon the inner self or the Lord. When Yājñavalkya had spoken thus, Bṛhaspati accepted what was said; this is expressed by the words "evam eva" (it is exactly so). || 1 ||
Thus ends the first section.
The Second Section:
Inquiry into the Nature of Avimukta. Then Atri questioned Yājñavalkya: "That which is this infinite, unmanifest Self—"
"How may I understand this? Yājñavalkya said to him: "That which is to be meditated upon is the Unreleased; that which is infinite and unmanifest Self is established in the Unreleased. || 1 ||

But how can that which is unliberated be worshipped, given its unmanifest nature? Thus, immediately after resolving Bṛhaspati’s question regarding the true nature of liberation, Atri, the son of Brahmā, questioned Yājñavalkya.
What was the question? It was this: "That which is called Tāraka-Brahman—this infinite one, devoid of the three limitations—is unmanifest."
"How may I know—that is, how may I understand—the Self characterized as described above?

To this question, Yājñavalkya spoke in reply to Bṛhaspati: "That which has been declared as the 'Savior' (tāraka) is to be meditated upon as non-different from the inner self (pratyak), namely the Unreleased (Avimukta). The reason for this is that which was asked by you..."

This infinite, unmanifest Self has been explained. It is established in the Lord-with-attributes (sopādhikeśvara) at Avimukta; because that [Lord] is free from obscuration, the unmanifest, infinite Self is perceived therein. || 1 ||
That which is the means for attaining non-liberation is itself non-liberated. In what is it established? It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī.
What indeed is the Varaṇā and what is the Nāsī? [They are] all those things produced by the senses.
Because it wards off faults, it is called *varaṇā*. Because it destroys all evils committed by the sense faculties, it is called *nāsī*. And what is its location?
"That which is the junction between the eyebrows and the nose is the junction of this world and the world beyond.
This junction, indeed, the knowers of Brahman worship as the *saṃdhyā*. That is what is to be worshipped as the Unreleased (*avimukta*).
He truly explains the knowledge of the Unreleased who knows it thus. (2)
He asks about the location of its perception: "Wherein is this Avimukta established?
Being asked where this Lord (Īśvara) is situated, he gives the answer: "It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī. The meaning is that it is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī.
The *Śruti* will explain the regions of the *varaṇā* and *nāsī*; therefore, they have not been explained here.
He asks about the nature of the *varaṇā* and *nāsī*: "What indeed is the *varaṇā*, and what is the *nāsī*?
In that regard, he explains the meaning of the word *varaṇā*: "All..."—all those [actions] performed by the organs of knowledge and action.

It wards off and restrains faults; therefore, it is called *varaṇā*. It destroys all evils committed by the senses; therefore, it is called *nāsī*, meaning "the destroyer. The letter *sa* has the sense of the letter *śa*. By the statement that [it] is established between the *varaṇā* and the *nāsī*, the junction of the nose and the eyebrows is indicated. Nevertheless...
He asks about that location: "And what is its place?
This means [the place] of this one who is not yet liberated. The word "iti" everywhere serves to mark the completion of the question.
That which is well-known as the junction between the eyebrows and the nose—that is this well-known [place].

There is a junction between the world of heaven, which corresponds to the skull of Brahmā, and the other world of earth, which corresponds to the region ending at the chin. The word "ca" (and) serves to combine these two worlds. "This indeed"—that is, this very [Self]—is the junction (*sandhi*);
it is called *sandhi* because one is joined (*saṃdhīyate*) in this, namely, the Unliberated (*avimukta*). That junction is one's own Self (*svātman*). That junction, one's own Self...

The knowers of Brahman worship the *saṃdhyā* at the junction of the eyebrows and the nose; they become intent on meditating upon the *jyotir-liṅga* located there. It has been explained that this is the *Avimukta* which is to be worshipped. He states the fruit of that knowledge: "He who indeed...
He who, being wise, knows the true nature of *Avimukta*, having set aside the portion to be discarded therein, [realizes] the attributeless Self.
That wise one knows it; having himself attained the state of the Lord, he teaches the knowledge that is the cause for the direct realization of that Avimukta. (p. 43)
At the final stage of his disciple's course of devotion, he imparts the instruction regarding the knowledge of the Star (the Tāraka-jñāna);
the meaning is that [the teacher] himself becomes none other than the undifferentiated Brahman. || 1 ||
Thus ends the second section.
The Third Section:
The Means of Knowledge of the Unliberated.
Then the students said to him: "Tell us, by reciting what may immortality be attained? He replied:
Yājñavalkya said: "By means of the Śatarudrīya. These indeed are the names of immortality; by these one indeed becomes immortal. || 1 ||
He says that the *brahmacārins* ask for the means to the knowledge of the true nature of liberation—beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*).
Now, after the resolution of Atri’s question, his disciples, the *brahmacārins*, indeed said this to Yājñavalkya: "By what recitation (*japya*) does one attain immortality? By what?"

"Through recitation (*japya*), the knowledge that is the means to attain immortality arises; tell us that, O Blessed One. Thus questioned by them, Yājñavalkya said: "What [is it]? [They replied: "By the *Pañcarudra* beginning with *Kaivalya*, or by the *Rudrādhyāya*, the knowledge that is the means to attain immortality arises; from that, immortality [is attained]. These are the names of the *Śatarudrīya*.

The names of Rudra are of the nature of nectar (amṛta). By means of these recitations of the Śatarudrīya, through the knowledge attained via the purification of the mind, the sage who recites the Śatarudra becomes immortal. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of this section. || 1 ||
Thus ends the third section.
The Fourth Section:
Inquiry into Knowledge and Renunciation of All Actions.
Now Janaka of Videha, having approached Yājñavalkya, said: "Venerable Sir,"
"Explain renunciation to me," he said. Yājñavalkya replied: "Having completed the period of student life (brahmacarya)...

One should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the stage of studenthood, or from the home, or from the forest. Furthermore, whether one has not taken vows or has taken vows, whether one is a graduate (*snātaka*) or not a graduate, whether one's sacred fires have been extinguished or one maintains them—one should renounce on the very day one becomes dispassionate.

With the intention of inquiring about the knowledge of the renunciation of all actions (*sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa*), he introduces the narrative with the word "Now" (*atha*): "Now, after the question of the religious student, Janaka by name, the King of Videha, approached Yājñavalkya and said. What did he say?

When he said, "O Blessed One, please explain the renunciation of all actions," Yājñavalkya replied: "What [should be done]? He stated the arrangement of the stages of life (*āśrama*) from the perspective of one who has not yet attained dispassion, beginning with "Brahmacarya. If one is not dispassionate, then one should spend that time in *brahmacarya* for the purpose of acquiring knowledge. If one is indeed not dispassionate, then it is so.

Having completed [the student stage], one should become a householder. There, one should spend time performing virtuous deeds (*satkarma*) according to one's capacity with a desireless mind (*niṣkāma-buddhi*).

If detachment (*virakti*) arises there, then, having left the household for the forest-dwelling stage (*vānaprastha*), either with or without the sacred fires (*sāgni* or *niragni*), one should spend time in that very state. If, however, the conviction of sufficiency (*alam-buddhi*) arises, then one should renounce and enter the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*).

Thus, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) should be performed in this sequence and not otherwise; therefore, he says "yadi vā" (or else). "Yadi vā" indicates an alternative option. When an even more intense dispassion (vairāgya) arises, then the learned one who has studied the Vedānta may renounce from the very first stage of life, the student's order (brahmacarya), and proceed to the order of the wandering mendicant (pāramahaṃsya).

If it is argued that one should undertake the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) after completing the student stage (*brahmacarya*) by following the sequence beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*, we say no;

for that sequence is intended for those whose dispassion (*virāga*) is weak. The meaning is that when dispassion is complete, one is able to embrace the state of the supreme mendicant (*pāramahaṃsya*) directly. If detachment arises while in the householder stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*), then one may renounce from the home.

Or [he may renounce] from the forest; the meaning is that because renunciation has detachment (*vairāgya*) as its cause, there is no requirement for a specific sequence. He says, "Now" (*atha*), in the sense of immediate succession to detachment, to show that when detachment arises, renunciation (*nyāsa*) is appropriate even during the interval between the three stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, even upon the completion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of one dwelling in the forest, renunciation does not [occur] due to some particular cause.
At that time, its maintenance is obtained in two ways: recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). That indeed is his vow (*vrata*).

One who possesses that is a "vow-possessor" (*vratī*). Whether he is not a vow-possessor or a vow-possessor—meaning either one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*) as a *snātaka*, or one who has studied some portion of the Veda but is not a *snātaka*—even a householder becomes a non-ascetic (*anāśramī*) in two ways.
One who has formally adopted the sacred fires (*svīkṛtāgni*); one whose fires have been extinguished due to the death of his wife even though she is still living;

one who is without fire (*niragni*) because he has not yet performed the initiatory rites (*asaṃskṛtatvāt*), meaning he has not taken up the fires; or one who is without fire (*anagnika*) because dispassion (*virakti*) has arisen—this applies to all cases, as it is understood that "he should go forth as a wandering mendicant" (*parivrajet*). What need is there for further elaboration?

(45) He states that there is no restriction regarding time in this matter: "When... etc. On whichever very day one might become detached—that is, attain dispassion—on that very day one should go forth, i.e., renounce. || 1 ||
The procedure for the renunciation of one who has maintained the sacred fires:

regarding this, some perform only the *prājāpatya* sacrifice; however, one should not do so. One should perform only the *āgneyī* sacrifice, for Agni is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of this [sacrifice], one thereby establishes the vital breath. One should perform only the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice; by this very [sacrifice]—
There are three qualities, namely: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
This is your seasonal source from which, once born, you shone forth;
knowing that, O Agni, ascend it and then increase our wealth for us.
With this mantra he should smell the fire. "This indeed is the womb of Agni, which is the vital breath (prāṇa). By saying "Go to the vital breath, svāhā," he says exactly this. || 2 ||

When one who has maintained the sacred fires renounces them, he describes a specific sacrifice for that occasion with the word "that" (*tad*). Regarding this, some teachers perform a sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati, known as the *Prājāpatyā* sacrifice;
however, even though it is mentioned by them, one should not perform it. What then should be done? In this regard, one should perform only the *Āgneyī* sacrifice, which has Agni as its deity.
In this regard, the reasoning is as follows: for breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed fire (*agni*), because fire is the essence of the deities and thus possesses the nature of a thread (*sūtra*).

Since this is so, one should perform this sacrifice dedicated to Agni (*āgneyī iṣṭi*) which effects the very breath; thereafter, one should perform the *Traidhātavīyā* sacrifice, which is well-known among practitioners of ritual as having Indra as its deity.

The proof for this is as follows: by means of this very sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), the three elements are [manifested], namely: the fiery, which is the triad of forms—*sattva* being white, *rajas* red, and *tamas* black. The word "iti" serves to mark the conclusion of the statement.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the scripture and in the manner previously described, one performs the smelling of the fire with this mantra.

He says that one should do so: "This," etc. O Agni, this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is your womb (*yoni*), because the principal vital breath has the Virāj as its source. It is seasonal (*ṛtviya*), because it is a constituent part of the seasons which are themselves the self of the year; from that Sūtra, having been born, you have shone forth (*arocathāḥ*), that is, you have produced light. Knowing that Self who is your cause, ascend.
The meaning is: "become merely the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which has become its own cause.
46) Then, after entering its own cause, [grant] our *rayi* (wealth).

Increase the wealth of the knowledge of your own Self. At the conclusion of the mantra, there is the word *iti*. With this mantra, one should smell the fire. The Śruti reiterates the meaning of the mantra: "This, indeed, is the womb of Agni, which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
This is clear. Go to the vital breath, which is your own cause. The word *svāhā* [signifies the offering].
It indicates the identity of cause and effect; indeed, the mantra also says exactly this. || 2 ||

The procedure for the fireless renunciation (*niragnika-saṃnyāsa*): Having brought fire from a village, one should have [the disciple] smell the fire as before. If one should not find fire, one should offer oblations into water;
for "Water indeed is all the deities. Having offered with the formula, "I offer to all the deities, svāhā," and having drawn out [the remains]:

One should eat the sacrificial oblation with clarified butter for the sake of health; thus one should obtain the mantra of liberation. "This is Brahman; this is to be meditated upon. "That is Brahman; that is to be meditated upon.
"It is even so, O Venerable One," said Yājñavalkya. 3.

Now he describes the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for those who maintain no sacred fire (*niragnika*), beginning with the words "from the village": Having fetched fire from the house of a *śrotriya* in the village,
one should perform the oblations as before— excluding the *iṣṭi* sacrifice— using the *Virajā-homa* mantras and the *Puruṣasūkta*, up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

With the mantra "This is for you," the officiating priest (adhvaryu) of the renunciation ceremony should cause the fire to be extinguished. As for the alternative case: if one should not find fire, one should offer oblations into water. The reasoning for this is: "Water indeed is all the deities.
One should offer with this mantra: "I offer to all the deities originating from the syllable Om; Svāhā!"
Having offered the oblation and drawn out the remainder, one should consume the food mixed with clarified butter, which is free from disease.
Because the food remaining from the offering is the cause of freedom from ailment, that which is to be chanted at that time is now stated:

it is the *praṇava* mantra, the cause of liberation from one's own ignorance, since it embodies the three Vedas (*trayī*). One should know thus: "I am that which is the nature of the meaning of the *praṇava*."

That which is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth—that Brahman is to be meditated upon as the meaning of the *praṇava*. Janaka accepted what Yājñavalkya had thus stated. How so? "It is exactly so, O Venerable One," he said, "O Yājñavalkya. In the reading "eṣa" (this), it refers to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). || 3 ||
Thus ends the fourth section.
The fifth section.
A Brāhmaṇa has the qualification for renunciation.
Then Atri questioned Yājñavalkya: "I ask you, Yājñavalkya, how can one be a Brāhmaṇa without the sacred thread? Yājñavalkya replied:
The self alone is his sacrificial thread. Having sipped water and sipped again, this is the rule for those who have gone forth [i.e., the wandering mendicants]. 1.
The Śruti states that Atri questioned Yājñavalkya with the permission of Janaka regarding what ought to be asked by Janaka—beginning with the word "atha" (now).

Now, after the questions of Janaka, Atri, urged by Janaka, questioned this Yājñavalkya. What was it? "O Yājñavalkya, I ask you. [For] a Brāhmaṇa is one who wears the sacrificial thread as an auxiliary to ritual action.

Such is the common worldly understanding. But when asked, "How can this man, who does not wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), be a Brāhmaṇa?", Yājñavalkya replied: "This very knowledge of Brahman is the sacrificial thread of this renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), because it leads him to Viṣṇu, whose form is sacrifice; for he has ascertained: 'I am He, the Self that is self-luminous.'"

By the statement "having consumed water," the rule for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is declared. How so? Immediately after the formal command (praiṣa), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times while reciting the mantra: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! preceded by the casting of the topknot (śikhā) and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) into the water. This is the rule for wandering mendicants (parivrājins). || 1 ||
The determination of the duties for those who are not qualified for formal renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is as follows:
either on the path of heroes (*vīrādhvāna*), or by fasting unto death (*anāśaka*), or by entering the waters, or by entering the fire, or by the great journey (*mahāprasthāna*).
Now, the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) wears discolored garments, is shaven-headed, possesses no belongings, is pure, and is free from malice; [he subsists on alms].
"By begging for alms, one becomes fit for becoming Brahman. If he should be afflicted by illness, he may renounce through thought or speech.
This is the path discovered by Brahman; by it goes the renouncer who knows Brahman. "It is even so, O Blessed One," said Yājñavalkya. || 2 ||

(48) Since those of the *kṣatriya* caste and others lack the qualification for the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), [the author] states "Vīra" [in the verse], implying that for those who have fallen from their stage of life (*āśrama-bhraṣṭa*), there is no remedy for their condition—just as there is no cure for incurable diseases. Or rather, it refers to the path of heroes (*vīrādhvāna*), which is the path of those heroes who do not retreat from battle. On that path...

For one who possesses food, that is "anāśaka" (fasting); or in that state of fasting, or upon entering the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, or upon entering a blazing fire, or by traveling on the Great Journey (*mahāprasthāna*) until the fall of the body—in all these five modes, it should be applied thus: "one should abandon the body. If this person is qualified for hearing (*śravaṇa*), then:

Wearing white or other ochre-colored robes, he is "shaven" (muṇḍa) because he is devoid of the top-knot of hair and facial hair. He is "without possessions" (aparigraha), meaning he has no acquisitions beyond what is necessary for maintaining the body alone.
Being pure through external and internal cleanliness, he is non-violent toward all living beings in his actions of mind, speech, and body.
Seeking alms for the sake of sustaining life, he becomes fit for becoming Brahman—that is, for the direct realization of Brahman.

This is another alternative, because one who is overcome by thieves, tigers, disease, and the like is unable to perform the rites that are ancillary to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). If such a person is capable of speaking, he should do so with speech joined to the mind.

One should renounce preceded by the utterance of the formal injunctions (*praiṣa*). If one is incapable even of that, then one should renounce or form the resolve through the mind alone. This is the path leading to knowledge, discovered and attained by Brahmā, the qualified seeker;
by that path spoken of as "the path of the knower of Brahman," the renunciant goes to Brahman in accordance with his own realized awakening.
"If one possesses knowledge free from distinctions, then one attains liberation while in the body (videha-kaivalya)," as stated by the Sage;
Atri accepted this, saying, "It is exactly so, O Blessed One," and Yājñavalkya replied, "So it is. || 2 ||
Thus ends the fifth section.
The sixth section:
The supreme excellence of the order of Paramahaṃsas.
Among them, those known as Paramahaṃsas—such as Saṃvartaka, Āruṇi, Śvetaketu, Durvāsas, Ṛbhu, Nidāgha, and others—conduct themselves like madmen. || 1 ||

Now, the sage Yājñavalkya, in order to increase the faith of the listeners, even though unasked, reveals the supreme excellence of the multitude of duties belonging to the stage of the Paramahaṃsa, due to its being resorted to by the great; he does so with the words "Therein" (*tatra*). Therein, among those such as the Kuṭīcaka and others mentioned in the Śruti, [he speaks of] those who practice the fourth division of the fourth stage of life.
Those known as *paramahaṃsas* are indeed well-known, as will be described hereafter.
To the question "Who are they?", [the answer is] the nine individuals beginning with Saṃvartaka and Raivataka, who are recited in the Śruti.
The passage from "avyaktaliṅgāḥ" to "ācarantaḥ" is an epithet of Saṃvartaka and the others.

Those who do not possess the outward marks (*liṅga*) of those observing vows (*vratin*), such as matted hair or bark garments, are "those with unmanifested marks" (*avyaktaliṅga*). Those whose conduct is not perceived by the world are "those of unmanifested conduct" (*avyaktācāra*). They are "not insane" (*anunmatta*).
Because they are free from the delusion that causes madness, they act like those who are mad; yet, because their minds have been transformed into the form of Brahman,
they are awakened by others, and whatever they appear to do is seen as nothing other than a means for the cessation of the world's madness.
Being awakened by those standing at their side, the virtuous perform the conduct handed down through the sequence of ancient tradition,
just like those who have risen from sleep after being awakened.
Thus says the Śruti. || 1 ||

Having cast into the waters with the mantra "Bhūḥ Svāhā" all these— the triple staff, water-pot, sling, alms-bowl, water-strainer, topknot, and sacred thread— which are the characteristics of the Sāmbara Paramahaṃsa, he should seek the Self.

Previously, the state of a paramahaṃsa was described as being absolute. Now, he reveals the state of a paramahaṃsa following the renunciation of the emblems such as those of the *kuṭīcaka* and others—beginning with the words "the triple staff" (*tridaṇḍam*). [This refers to] the triple bamboo staff, the water-pot made of clay, wood, or gourd, the sling made of muñja grass and other materials, and the alms-bowl for collecting food.

He made a water-purifier (*jalapavitra*) from a modification of wood such as *dāru*, measuring one span (*vitasti*), as well as a crest-lock (*śikhā*) and a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the renunciation of all other duties. Having cast all this—the five mudrās, the *gāyatrī*, and so forth—into the water with the mantra "Bhūḥ Svāhā," he approached the Preceptor (*deśika*).
One should seek the Self through the hearing of the Vedanta and other such means. || 2 ||
The characteristics of a Digambara Paramahaṃsa are as follows:
wearing his natural form, free from dualities, without bonds, and without possessions;
perfectly established on the path of Brahman—the reality of that very Brahman; and pure in mind.
For the sake of sustaining life, at the prescribed time, being free from attachment and practicing alms-gathering with his belly as his bowl—
remaining equanimous toward gain and loss—
he stays in empty houses or temples.

(p. 50) Devoted to white meditation (*śukladhyāna*), established in the inner self (*adhyātmaniṣṭha*), and intent on uprooting both auspicious and inauspicious karma, he dwells in places such as grass huts, anthills, the roots of trees, potter’s workshops, fire-sanctuaries, riverbanks, and mountain caves.
He who effects the abandonment of the body through renunciation is called a Paramahaṃsa. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 3.

Having described the characteristics of the *sāmbara-paramahaṃsa*, he states the characteristics of the *digambara-paramahaṃsa* with the words "yathā" (as follows): "As one who wears the natural form (*yathājātarūpadhara*), who is sky-clad (*digambara*), free from dualities (*nirdvandva*), whose intellect is equanimous toward cold, heat, and so forth, and who possesses no acquisitions other than the means for maintaining the body— namely, the loincloth, covering, alms, and shelter."
The path that leads to that is the knowledge of it; one who has become perfectly perfected in that path of reality, Brahman—that is to say, one who is established in it—is meant here.

Regarding that, he states the means: "one whose mind is pure. Because of being free from volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*), there is merely the maintenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during the aforementioned times characterized by the absence of smoke and so forth.

The meaning is that, liberated from one's own ignorance and its effects, one should pass the time by practicing mendicancy with a stomach as one's bowl according to what is appropriate, opening the mouth [only for food], remaining equanimous toward the gain or loss of alms and the like, and not giving way to joy or dejection. Now, he describes the places where such a person should dwell:
By the words "in an empty house" and so forth: an empty house devoid of people; the temple of a deity such as Viṣṇu;

a heap of grass arisen from some cause; an anthill constructed by ants and the like; the root of a tree such as the banyan or the holy fig; or a potter’s workshop where unbaked earthenware vessels are kept.

A place with three or five *agnihotra* sheds; a sandy bank on the shore of a great river; a dense area overgrown with bamboo and other vegetation on a mountain; a mountain cleft; a mountain cave or plateau; a ravine; the hollow interior of a tree;
a hollow in the trunk (*koṭara*); a region where water flows; a waterfall (*nirjhara*); a pure stretch of ground; and an open, unobstructed sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
From empty houses to sacred ground (sthaṇḍila), he dwells in those places as appropriate; he is a homeless wanderer,

making no effort regarding various kinds of requisites, free from the sense of "mine" toward things other than himself, having reached the conclusion that the pure radiance of Brahman is his own non-dual self alone, and is thus devoted to pure meditation (śukladhyāna).
According to the Vedic scripture, "Brahman consists of pure luster. With reference to the Self alone, there arises this knowledge of the Self (*adhyātma*);

one who is established in that knowledge and renounces all actions—whether with desire or without desire—that lead to auspicious or inauspicious states, thinking "I renounce," and who effects the abandonment of identification with that body, is this wise person, the *paramahaṃsa*.

"It is certain that the one called the Supreme Self (paramātman) is capable of sustaining the distinction between the internal and the external. These two words "iti" and "upaniṣat" signify the completion of the scripture. || 3 ||
Thus ends the sixth section (p. 51),
composed by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the Jābāla Upaniṣad has been clearly written;
the Jābāla Upaniṣad exposition is recorded as being slightly less than two hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Jābāla Upaniṣad, completing the thirteenth in the series of commentaries on the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
The Turīyātītāvadhūtopaniṣad. Peace: "That is full. (p. 53)
The culmination of the conduct of the *avadhūta* who has transcended the fourth state (*turīyātītāvadhūta*).

Now, having approached his father, the Lord Ādinārāyaṇa—the Grandfather of all the worlds—he asked: "What is this path of those who have transcended the fourth state? What is their way of life? To him, the Lord said:

Nārāyaṇa: This one who stands on the path of the *avadhūta* is rarer in the world than even the rarest, yet he is not common; if there be even one such person, he alone is eternally pure, he alone is the embodiment of dispassion, he alone is the form of knowledge, and he alone is the Person of the Veda—thus do the wise consider him. He is a Great Being whose mind abides in Me alone.
And I remained in that very state. Thus, he first gradually attained the stage of a *kuṭīcaka*, then reached that of a *bahūdaka*;
having become a *bahūdaka*, he took up the state of a *haṃsa*, and becoming a *paramahaṃsa*, through the contemplation of his own true nature, he realized the entire phenomenal world as it truly is.

Having cast into the waters everything— the staff, the water-pot, the waist-string, the loincloth, the covering garment, and all rituals prescribed by his own rule— and having become naked, he should even abandon the possession of discolored, worn-out bark garments or deerskins; thereafter, acting without mantras and avoiding shaving, oiling, bathing, the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and so forth.
Having withdrawn even that which is both Vedic and worldly, being at all times (p.
54) devoid of merit and demerit, and having abandoned both knowledge and ignorance—

Having conquered cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, preceded by the three-fold latent impressions (vāsanās) regarding the body and so forth— namely, blame and praise, pride and envy, hypocrisy and arrogance, desire and aversion, lust, anger, greed, and delusion— and seeing [all things] as equal, one should, without effort and without fixed rules, treat gain and loss as the same, following the "cow-like" way of life (govṛtti).
Sustaining his life merely by whatever was obtained, free from craving,

he reduced the elaborate display of scholarship in all sciences to ashes; concealing his true nature, he abandoned the distinctions of seniority and juniority, and established the non-duality of being the supreme excellence and the self of all.
Reflecting that there is no other being distinct from himself,
he internalizes within himself the wealth of the gods' treasures and the like; thus, he is neither agitated by suffering nor delighted by pleasure,
is free from longing for passion, and is without attachment to anything, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
With all his senses stilled, he does not follow the authority of the duties, knowledge, or conduct pertaining to the stages of life previously entered;

always wandering, with nothing but his body remaining, carrying a water-pot as if on land or water, ever free from madness, wandering alone like a child, a madman, or a ghost, he is intent on remaining silent.

By means of meditation on one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), having taken hold of the objectless (*nirālamba*) state, and by being favorable toward abiding in the Self (*svātmaniṣṭhā*), he forgets everything;

transcending the fourth state (*turīyātīta*), devoted to the non-dual state (*advaitaniṣṭhā*) in the guise of an Avadhūta, he who casts off the body as being of the nature of the *praṇava*—he is an Avadhūta, and he has accomplished all that was to be done. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. || 1 ||
I meditate daily upon that which is to be known through the Upaniṣad called Turyātīta— the supreme imperishable, the pure consciousness beyond the fourth state, and my own true nature alone.

Herein indeed unfolds this *Turīyātītāvadhūtopaniṣad*, which is a division of the Śukla-Yajurveda; it is intent upon revealing the secondary and primary modes of the life of the Avadhūta, and culminates in Brahman alone. A commentary on this [Upaniṣad], based on its very brief text, is now commenced. [The dialogue between] the disciple and the teacher—

55) This narrative is intended for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*). He introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now). Those who follow the conduct of the *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa* as distinguished within the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*)...
Having understood this as it truly is, those who have transcended that state which completes the uncountable stages of the paramahaṃsa, and have gone beyond even the turyātīta,
are those who, having leaped over the stages of life (āśramas) and the social classes (varṇas), always abide in the Self alone.
The yogi who transcends the castes and stages of life is called an Avadhūta.
Because he is imperishable, because he is most excellent, because he has shaken off the bonds of saṃsāra,
and because he is characterized by such [mahāvākya]s as "That thou art," he is called an *avadhūta*.

Thus, there are the secondary and primary *avadhūtas*, as well as the *turiyātītāvadhūtas*. By the phrase "what is this path of those great-souled ones," their conduct (*caryā*) to be practiced is understood; and by the phrase "what is the state? (*kā sthitiḥ*), their final realization (*niṣṭhā*) is also to be known. Having accepted that question, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke to him. What was that?

In this context, because that path is exceedingly difficult to attain, He first praises those [who have reached it] with the words "He who... Since he remains in Me, which is eternally pure, having attained My own state, those possessed of knowledge who have entered My state consider him so;
for this very reason, he is a *mahāpuruṣa* (Great Person). How does he possess the status of a Great Person? To this, [the Lord says]: "Because..."

His mind abides in Me alone because of the absence of thoughts exceeding Me. To the question "Where do you abide?", [the answer is] "I abide in that very same place. The duties of the *kuṭīcaka* and other orders have been fully explained in the *Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad*. Among them, this one is the *paramahaṃsa*.

"Brahman, established through the negation of everything, is one's own self alone, devoid of any counterpart. By means of the contemplation of one's true nature, having realized through the "not this, not this" (neti neti) that the entire phenomenal world is nothing other than oneself, one should, with the realization that the insignia of the highest asceticism (pāramahaṃsya-liṅga) must be abandoned at the very moment of that knowledge, renounce even those.
The meaning is that its renunciation is logically established through the realization of the nature of saṃsāra.

Thereafter—that is, after the renunciation of the stage of the paramahaṃsa—since there is no longer any duty to be performed, one acts like one without mantras (amantravat), having no need for mantras regarding the movements of the body and so forth. This...

Having abandoned shaving and other such acts by the desire that "this must be done," and likewise having withdrawn both Vedic and worldly activities because they share the common nature of being mental fluctuations; and having abandoned even knowledge and ignorance, having conquered cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor through the relinquishing of identification with the body; and having [abandoned] the ego-sense preceded by the three-fold latent impressions (vāsanās) of the body and so forth—*ahaṃ*...

Having concealed his own nature and character by not revealing that he was "of such a kind," and by denying the status of elder and younger through saying "this one is my elder" or "he is my younger," he meditated upon non-duality,
thinking that there is no duality apart from Advaita; that very meditation is [the meaning of] *devaguhyāt*, the secret of the gods.
Because it is to be consumed by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman alone,
even the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman is "fuel"; having withdrawn that as well into the Self through the cognition of the Self alone—

If, however, suffering and so forth should arise from relying on appearances that seem distinct from oneself, one should not be agitated by that suffering—this is the sense. "Prābhavam" means power or majesty. Recalling that the fruit of the knowledge known to me culminates in this very state, in reality even that [recollection] need not be mentally pursued. By oneself, [one should perform] such acts as washing the feet...

The meaning is that the comparison with a water-basin on land is indeed appropriate. One who is intent on not conversing with anyone at all, having forgotten the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as something apart from oneself, becomes devoted to non-duality (*advaita*), taking refuge in the non-dual Self; [realizing] that every object denoted by words is of the nature of the *praṇava*.

By means of the nature of the *praṇava* established by the scriptures, as the self of the fourth-of-the-fourth (*turyāturya*), which is the meaning of the *praṇava*, he effects the abandonment of the body;

he effects the renunciation and the sublation of the mental constructs beginning with waking-waking (*jāgraj-jāgrat*)—which are accomplished by that body—up to the final state of the "single flavor of permission" (*anujñaikarasa*). Of him...

For a mendicant (*yati*) adorned with the dharma of the state of a *paramahaṃsa*, the delusion that there exists even in appearance anything to be removed other than his own Self— that is the state of a "secondary" (*gauṇa*) *avadhūta*. On the other hand,
for one who possesses the knowledge that Brahman alone is without a counterpart and that there is no object to be negated apart from it—
He for whom something to be accomplished appears as distinct from his own self becomes a secondary Avadhūta, due to the delusion that there exists anything other than himself.
He for whom the impossibility of anything other than Brahman arises through the realization that only Brahman exists, is a primary Avadhūta; that sage remains as his own Self alone.
Thus, according to the Smṛti; the word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the Upaniṣad under discussion. || 1 ||

This clear commentary on the *Turyātīta* has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra. The collection of texts concerning the *Turyātīta* is said to consist of forty [chapters].
Thus ends the commentary on the *Turīyātītāvadhūtopaniṣad*, completing the sixty-fourth [text] in the venerable exposition of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the *Īśā*.
The Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad.
"May there be well-being through our ears"— thus [ends] the Peace Invocation.
The First Instruction:
The Question of Śaunaka and Others Regarding Nārada.
Now, on one occasion, Nārada, adorned with the marks of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), while wandering through all the worlds, beheld something unprecedented—

Peaceful and self-controlled, having attained detachment from all things and having reflected upon the contemplation of his own true nature, he beheld the sacred site of the Naimiṣa forest— a place frequented by sages, characterized by a specific joy of self-restraint, and resonant with the notes known as sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, and ni, which inspire dispassion and awakening.

With specific melodies turned away from worldly things, with conversations concerning the stories of Hari, and with specific forms of devotion to the Lord manifested in all things moving and stationary— whether humans, animals, kinnaras,
or gods— [the sages], having beheld Nārada, were endowed with the study and mastery of the Vedas as they stood ready for the twelve-year sacrificial session.

The great sages, Śaunaka and others— all of whom were omniscient, devoted to asceticism, and endowed with knowledge and dispassion— rose from their seats, bowed, and after being offered appropriate hospitality,
they all sat down and said: "O Blessed One, O Son of Brahmā, what is the means to liberation for us?"
It must be stated. || 1 ||
I take refuge in that Rāma, by whose awakening the multitude of those adorned with the dharma of wandering mendicancy attains the goal signified by the ten *praṇavas*.

Herein begins the exposition of the *Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad*, which is indeed a division of the Atharvaveda; it commences with a detailed description of the conduct pertaining to one's own stages of life (*āśrama*), beginning with the *vratya* and others, and proceeds to the classification of the *kuṭīcaka*, *bahūdaka*, *haṃsa*, and *paramahaṃsa* ascetics, following the dialogue between Śaunaka and the assembly of sages on one side and Nārada and his grandfather on the other.
The scripture introduces the narrative with the words "atha" and so forth. The word "atha" signifies a beginning.

Once, Nārada, the crest-jewel of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), while traveling through all the worlds, was sanctifying holy places and sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*) by the mere placement of his feet.

Having perceived the entire multitude of the phenomenal world as something other than himself to be false, and having thereby attained purity of mind, he becomes free from enmity through the contemplation of the oneness of the Self in all; he is tranquil regarding mental fluctuations such as volition and self-controlled regarding external activities;
and having attained detachment and dispassion toward everything everywhere.

Having reflected upon the contemplation of his own true nature and beheld the Naimiṣa forest characterized by the aforementioned attributes, [he did so] with conversations concerning the stories of Hari— conversations imbued with devotion and love for the Lord— which, through the tinkling of the ornaments on his own hands and the sound of his lute, awakened external dispassion in those who heard them at the time of his arrival.
Seeing Nārada— who had arrived bewildering them with his manifold manifestations as humans, deer, and other beings—

the great sages Śaunaka and the others rose from their seats and performed honors such as rising to greet him; having seated him upon a divine throne, they all spontaneously realized the supreme reality of the ultimate truth simply by the sight of him, even though it had already been taught to them.

He says that they ask him for the sake of favoring the world: "O Blessed One! [The question is: "O son of Brahmā, how may liberation from the delusion of the existence of anything other than our own Self occur for us who have taken refuge in the Blessed One?
Or what is the means for attaining that? Thus it must be told. || 1 ||

Having stated, "This is the instruction on the means for attaining liberation while bodiless (videhamukti)," Nārada spoke to them as follows: "One who is born of a noble family, initiated according to the proper rites of initiation,
endowed with the forty sacraments (saṃskāras), and having completed the study of his own Vedic branch in the presence of a single teacher of his own choice— "
Twelve years of celibacy preceded by service, twenty-five years of the householder stage, and twenty-five years of the forest-dweller stage.

Having duly accomplished the fourfold student life (*brahmacarya*) in its proper sequence, having correctly practiced the sixfold duties of the householder (*gārhasthya*), and the fourfold duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and having performed all the appropriate actions for those stages,

one who is endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) should remain above the entire cycle of transmigration through the actions of mind, speech, and body, just as a lotus leaf remains untouched by water.

By means of the stage of the Paramahaṃsa and through meditation on one's own true nature without faltering, one effects the abandonment of the body; he becomes liberated, he becomes liberated. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 2.

Thus questioned by them, the celestial sage said: "It was said thus. That is, having been addressed in this manner by Śaunaka and the others, Nārada spoke. What was that? He said: "He who is born in a noble family"—any twice-born person whatsoever who is born of a noble lineage, who has been initiated according to the rules, and who is endowed with the forty sacraments (*saṃskāras*). The forty sacraments are as follows: [list omitted].
Regarding the question of what these are like, it is recorded in the Gautama Dharma-sūtra as follows:

namely— the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *niṣkramaṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *cūḍākaraṇa*, *upanayana*, the *vedavratas*, the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), and union with the partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*)— these are the five.
The performance of sacrifices consists of these five: [sacrifices] for the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman.
The seven forms of *pākayajña* are: the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *caitrī*, and the *āśvayujī*.

[The seven forms of *haviryajña* are: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*).
The four-month sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the *sautrāmaṇī*—these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*.
The *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*—these are the seven forms of the *soma* sacrifice.
Thus, these constitute the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, there are the eight qualities of the self, beginning with compassion toward all beings.

Forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, compassion, and lack of possessiveness— whosoever lacks these forty refinements as well as the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with or residence in the same world as Brahman. However, for whosoever possesses even a portion of these refinements along with the eight qualities of the self, [he attains that state].
Then, having become endowed with the aforementioned purificatory rites (saṃskāra) by which one attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahmā,

he should, in accordance with such scriptural injunctions as "the teacher should be perfected in the Vedas, devoted to Viṣṇu, free from envy," and so forth, first approach his chosen single Guru who is characterized by the stated qualifications.
Having studied all branches of knowledge preceded by the study of one's own Vedic school, having performed service for twelve years [to the teacher],
and having practiced the duties appropriate to the householder stage of life until the age of twenty-five,
then likewise five—

(p. 60) Having duly and sequentially fulfilled the entire range of duties appropriate for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life up to the age of twenty, he should then renounce [the world] after seventy; this is the meaning.
To the question of how many kinds of dharmas such as *brahmacarya* there are, he says: "The fourfold *brahmacarya*.

In this regard, the *Kāṇvāyana-smṛti* is cited according to its meaning: "The *gāyatra*, the *brāhma*, the *prājāpatya*, and the *bṛhat*—thus the student (*brahmacārin*) is of four kinds. The meaning of this is as follows:
Among these, he who, after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), studies the *Gāyatrī* for three nights while consuming food that is neither pungent nor salty is called a *Gāyatra*.

He who practices student-life (*brahmacarya*) until he has mastered the Veda is called a *Brāhma*. One who observes the Vedic vows for a year is a *Prājāpatya*. One who dwells in the teacher’s house until death is called a *Naiṣṭhika*, the "Great" one.

To the question "How many kinds of householdership are there?", he says: "Householdership is sixfold. Thus, householders are also of six types. They are as follows: the Vārtāka, the Śālīna, the Yāyāvara, the Ghorasaṃnyāsika, the Uñchavṛtti, and the Ayācita. Among these, [the first] is defined by the performance of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth.

One who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya and is devoted to such activities as agriculture is a *vārtāvṛtti*. A *śālīna*, however, is devoted to the six duties (*ṣaṭkarma*) and subsists through officiating at sacrifices and other such means. A *yāyāvara*, on the other hand, collects small amounts of rice from the houses of the learned for the purpose of maintaining his own family. A *ghorasaṃnyāsika*, however—

Performing his duties day by day with water that has been drawn up and purified, he should obtain rice from among cultured people (*śiṣṭa*). "Gleaning" (*uñcha*) refers to the livelihood of gathering ears of grain; "unasked for" (*ayācita*) refers to one who subsists on what is obtained by chance.
To the question of how many types of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) there are, he says: "There is a fourfold division. Those who dwell in the forest are also of four kinds.

They are as follows: the Vaikhānasa, the Audumbara, the Vālakhilya, and the Phenapa. Among them, one who performs the *agnihotra* and other rites using uncultivated herbs grown outside the village is called a Vaikhānasa. As for the Audumbara, he is one who, having risen in the morning, [subsists on] the *udumbara* fruits found in whichever direction he looks.

One who earns his livelihood for eight months, takes food only during the four-month rainy season, and renounces all flowers and fruits on the full moon of Kārttika is a *vālakhilya*. However, the *phenapas* subsist on withered leaves and fruits; dwelling anywhere at all, they are devoted solely to ritual action.

Having thus fulfilled the entire range of duties beginning with studenthood (*brahmacarya*) and ending with forest-dwelling (*vānaprastha*), and having become endowed with the fourfold means of accomplishment (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) such as the sense of permanence (*nityatva*), one should renounce the latent impressions of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti-vāsanā*) and the three types of desire (*eṣaṇā-traya*).

One who is freed from the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta). The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. The word "Upaniṣad" indicates the conclusion of the first instruction. || 2 ||
Thus ends the first instruction;
the second instruction is the sequence for wandering mendicancy.

Then all the disciples of Śaunaka and others questioned the venerable Nārada, saying, "O Blessed One, tell us the procedure for renunciation. Observing them, Nārada said, "It is proper to learn the entire nature of this matter from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā) himself," and thereafter, following the completion of the sacrificial session (*satrayāga*), he [proceeded] together with them.

Having gone to Satyaloka, Nārada duly bowed to and praised the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who is devoted to Brahman, according to the prescribed rites. Then, having sat down with them as was appropriate by his command, he spoke to the Grandfather (Pitāmaha): "You are my teacher, you are my father; you are the knower of the secrets of all sciences and you are omniscient. Therefore, [please reveal] one secret that is dear to me."

It must be said: who else besides you is capable of speaking the secret doctrine desired by me? If it is asked why, [the answer is that] when requested by Nārada, "Tell us the sequence of the nature of the wandering mendicant's life," Parameṣṭhin, having surveyed everything from all sides and remained for a moment established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [described] the suffering of worldly existence—

O my son, the secret taught by the Virāṭ Puruṣa— who assumes an unsurpassed form that reveals the mystery of the Puruṣasūkta Upaniṣad— is now explained to you in detail. Listen with great attention to that most profound sequence.

O Nārada, first according to the prescribed rule, after his initiation (*upanayana*), one born of a noble family, obedient to his father and mother, and situated elsewhere than in his father’s presence, [should approach] one who stands within a true tradition, who is endowed with faith, and born of a noble family.
Having approached a true guru— one learned in the Vedas, affectionate toward the scriptures, virtuous, and straightforward— and having bowed to him,
one should request one's desired goal after first serving him according to his needs.

Having practiced all branches of knowledge preceded by twelve years of service, and having married a desired bride suitable for his own family with the teacher's permission, he dwelt in the teacher’s house for twenty-five years;
then, with the teacher's permission, performing the duties appropriate for a householder, he attained freedom from the state of being a mere nominal Brahmin.

Desiring the increase of his own lineage, having obtained an only son, he should spend twenty-five years suitable for taking up the duties of a householder; thereafter, for a period of twenty-five years,
he should perform the three daily ablutions preceded by contact with water.
Taking food only once at the fourth meal-time, becoming a forest-dweller alone,

abandoning his former wandering through cities and villages, performing the duties appropriate for his station free from all attachments, and attaining freedom from craving for the objects of sight and hearing, he was endowed with the forty refinements.
Having become detached from everything and attained purity of mind, and having burnt away hope, envy, jealousy, and egoism, one should practice the means of realization.

Thus instructed by Nārada, the sages headed by Śaunaka again questioned Nārada out of a desire for further specific knowledge. He [Nārada] replied: "That which has been asked by you was [already told] by the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā)."

Having said, "It must be known," Nārada went with them to Satyaloka after the completion of the sacrifice currently under discussion; having approached the Grandfather (Brahmā) according to the prescribed rites, he asked about the dharma of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*).
This is stated with the word "atha" [in the text]: [He asked about] that which is supreme in the state of Brahman, established through the negation of everything other than itself.
The continuous contemplation that Brahman is one's own non-dual self alone is itself the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*).

That which is intent upon that and established in that is [Brahman]; because he stands in that supreme state, he is the "Supreme Lord" (*parameṣṭhin*). Nārada said to the Grandfather (Brahmā): "What is it? [He replied: "You are the teacher of all, including myself. Thus was it said by Nārada.

Being questioned, Parameṣṭhin, having understood the purpose of that arrival through divine knowledge, said: "That which was asked by you has been taught to me by Virāṭpuruṣa; that is now being stated. Listen to this," he said, addressing Nārada with the words "O Nārada! and so forth, in order to draw him toward himself. As for what that was, [he spoke] to him in sequence.

He says "bho" (O! while teaching the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). "Established in the tradition of the virtuous" and so forth are qualifiers of the teacher (*ācārya*). "A *śrotriya*" is one who has studied the Veda along with its limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), as well as their meaning.
Having lived in the teacher’s house for twenty-five years together with his wife, [and having performed] the three daily ablutions...
"According to the Śruti: 'One who touches water [for purification] should eat his meal at the fourth time [of the day]. Regarding the term *nikiravirahita*:
where there is *nikira*, that is, the sowing of seeds (*nitarāṃ kiraṃ bījāvāpanam*), such as wheat, rice, millet, and so forth, it is *nikira*."

Free from that [desire], he is devoid of longing for worldly and otherworldly enjoyments—such as the rites appropriate to the actions dependent on wild rice, grass, grain, and so forth, including offerings to gods and ancestors (havya and kavya) performed with visible worldly aims or invisible transcendental goals; this is "freedom from thirst" (vaitṛṣṇya). He is endowed with the forty sacraments (saṃskāras).

The meaning of what has been stated beginning with these words is as explained. The remainder is clear. The word "iti" (thus) at the end of the Upanishad indicates the conclusion of the second instruction. || 1 ||
Thus ends the second instruction.
The third instruction concerns the eligibility for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
Then Nārada questioned the Grandfather (Brahmā): "O Blessed One, by what [qualification] is there renunciation, and who is eligible for renunciation?

Having thus first defined the one eligible for renunciation, the procedure for renunciation will be stated afterwards. Listen attentively. Now, one who is impotent, fallen, physically disabled, or effeminate...

One who is deaf, a child, mute, a heretic, one bearing the discus (Cakrin), one bearing the linga (Lingin), a forest-dweller (Vaikhānasa), a Brahmin who has twice married, one who teaches for a fee, one with skin disease (Śipiviṣṭa), and one who maintains no sacred fires—even if they possess dispassion, these are not eligible for renunciation.
Even if they have already renounced, they are not qualified for instruction in the Great Sayings (Mahāvākya). [This applies except for] one who was previously a renunciant.
The qualified candidate for the Paramahaṃsa stage. || 1 ||
"He attains fearlessness through another for himself, and likewise through himself for another; he is a wandering mendicant (parivrāj)," so says the Smṛti.

A eunuch, one who is deformed, a blind man, a child, an outcast, one who has fallen from his caste, one who frequents the wives of others, as well as a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) and a student (brahmacārin)—these are the twice-born who [should not be invited]. (3)

One who possesses a wheel-mark, one who bears the sectarian mark (liṅgin), a heretic, one who has Shiva as his deity (śipiviṣṭa), one who maintains no sacred fire, one who has renounced twice or thrice, a hired servant, and even a mere sustainer—
these do not deserve renunciation without following the prescribed sequence. || 4 ||
(On page 64:
Having been thus instructed by his father that one endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) is qualified to renounce (*saṃnyastum arhati*), Nārada,
desiring to discern the true nature of renunciation and the nature of its qualified practitioner, addressed his father [with the words] "this must be known."

"He asked," he says, with the word "atha" (now). "What is this renunciation, or who is qualified for renunciation?"—the answer to these questions is given by the word "evam" (thus). First, he defines those who are not qualified for renunciation with the word "atha. "Śipiviṣṭa" means one whose penis is exposed. By the opposite of what has been stated, one who grants fearlessness to all beings [is qualified].

He states that one to whom all beings will grant fearlessness is the one qualified for renunciation (saṃnyāsa), beginning with the words "pūrva... [18.42]. To the question "What is this Smṛti? he says:
"He who, unattached to the fruit of action, performs the action that ought to be done... [18.66].
He is both a renunciant and a yogi, yet he is neither one who maintains no sacred fires nor one who performs no actions.

Thus, according to the Smṛti, a twice-born who, preceded by the renunciation of the desire for results and the means to achieve them, performs action without desire (niṣkāma-karma), is a former renunciant (pūrva-saṃnyāsī). He alone is qualified for the stage of the Paramahaṃsa. However, it is also heard in the two Mandras that even one who is the opposite of this—lacking such qualification—is [eligible].
"The eunuch," [sūtra] 1.4.
Regarding the renunciation of the sick (*āturasannyāsa*): how is the time of illness approved by the Noble Ones?
The period immediately preceding the departure of the vital breath is designated as "the time of illness."
No other time is so intent upon setting forth the path to liberation. || 5 ||

Having raised the objection as to how the renunciation of the sick (āturasannyāsa) can be considered acceptable by the wise, he states that it is indeed so accepted—provided there is no performance of the eight śrāddhas and other rites—at which point he says: "At the time of the sick. This means the time when the departure of the vital breath is imminent;
that is, the period immediately preceding the departure of the vital breath. || 5 ||
Regarding the procedure for renunciation in the case of the sick:
even in the case of renunciation by one who is ill, the wise person should renounce according to the rules, preceded by the respective mantras and having performed the repetition of those mantras.
Even in the case of the sick and in the sequence of rites, there is nowhere any difference in the injunctions;
for a mantra devoid of ritual action does not depend upon action, nor does action depend upon a mantra.
(65) Ritual action devoid of mantra is not [valid]; therefore, one should not abandon the mantra.
If one performs ritual action without a mantra, it would be like an oblation poured into ashes. || 8 ||
Renunciation due to illness is said to be that which results from the abrupt abandonment of actions prescribed by injunction;
therefore, O Sage, there is no rule for the repetition of mantras in the case of renunciation due to illness.

He explains the procedure for renunciation in the case of one who is afflicted by illness with the words, "Even in the case of the afflicted. Since there might be a difference in the formal instruction (*praiṣa*) between one who is healthy and one who is afflicted by illness, he says, "Even in the case of the afflicted. He states that ritual action is dependent upon mantras and that action devoid of mantras is fruitless with the words, "Not without a mantra. Regarding the phrase "not without a mantra," it means [not] without the mantra.

There is an inversion of case endings. He says that where there is an omission of ritual action due solely to the predominance of the mantra, that is this "sannyāsa for the sick" (*āturasannyāsa*), by the words "stated in the injunction" (*vidhyukta*). Because it is thus, therefore [the conclusion follows]. (6–9)
The procedure for renunciation for one who has maintained the sacred fires while residing in another country:
"If one who has maintained the sacred fires becomes dispassionate while traveling in another country, he should perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice in the waters themselves and then renounce. (10)

Whether by means of the mind, or through the repetition of mantras prescribed by the Vedas, or in water, or by way of the path of Vedic practice, or indeed by the performance of ritual action— having completed these, the wise man should renounce; otherwise, he shall incur a fall from his status.

If one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) becomes dispassionate and goes to a distant land, how should he perform renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)? In response to this inquiry, it is said: "The one who has maintained the fires" (*āhitāgni*). Having performed the *prājāpatya* sacrifice in water through mind, speech, or action, he should indeed renounce; otherwise, he becomes fallen (*patita*), even if he has gone to another country.
If that were so, [then... || 10-11 ||

For one who possesses craving, there is the attainment of hell through both renunciation and acceptance. When detachment toward all things has arisen in the mind, then they desire renunciation; otherwise, one would be fallen.
The wise man, being dispassionate, should go forth into the homeless life; but one who is still possessed of passion should remain at home.
For that lowest of the twice-born who goes forth while still full of passion goes to hell. (13)

Dispassion toward objects other than one's own Self is the cause for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). He states that if one who is still possessed of craving for anything whatsoever should renounce, he would fall into hell—beginning with the verse "yadā" (12–13).
Freedom from craving alone is the cause for undertaking renunciation.
He whose tongue, genitals, stomach, and hands are well-guarded—such a Brahmin, remaining celibate and unmarried, may renounce. (14)

Having seen that cyclic existence itself is devoid of essence, and desiring to see the essence, they go forth into homelessness, having taken refuge in supreme dispassion and not yet having raised their arms [in worldly activity]. || 15 ||
Action is characterized by engagement, while knowledge is characterized by renunciation;
therefore, having placed knowledge foremost, a wise person should renounce in this world.

He whose tongue and other senses are under his own control, for whom a supreme sense of "enough" arises regarding this world, and whose knowledge becomes the means for liberation—he, whether a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller, should renounce;
thus he says, "yasya" (of whom). Since this is so, therefore [he should renounce]. (14–16)
Regarding the renunciation of the knower (vidvatsaṃnyāsa):
