"But when the reality, the supreme, eternal Brahman, has been known, then, having taken up the single staff along with the sacred thread, one should discard the topknot. (17)
He who is attached to the Supreme Self and detached from that which is not the Supreme Self, being entirely liberated from all desires, is worthy to partake of alms. 18.
Just as he would become well-pleased when honored and saluted, so too does he become [well-pleased] when being struck; then he becomes a consumer of alms.
When one’s conviction becomes firm that "I alone am the non-dual Imperishable Brahman known as Vāsudeva," then he may subsist on alms. (20)

In that [stage] where there is peace, tranquility, purity, truthfulness, contentment, straightforwardness, possessionlessness, and freedom from pride—he shall abide in the hermitage of liberation (kaivalyāśrama). || 21 ||
When one does not harbor an evil disposition toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one becomes a true mendicant.
Having practiced the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedāntas according to the injunctions, the twice-born man, freed from his debts, should renounce.
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
He who does not reminisce about past enjoyments, nor likewise about those yet to come,
and who does not rejoice in those already attained— he shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalyāśrama).
He who is always able to keep the senses, which reside within, inside, and the objects, which exist outside, outside, shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalya-āśrama). || 26 ||
Just as when the vital breath has departed, the body no longer experiences pleasure or pain.
If that were so, then even one endowed with vital breaths might dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalya-āśrama). || 27 ||

He describes the renunciation of the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) with the words "When... and so forth. He states that one who possesses innate self-devotion, detachment from what is other than the Self, equanimity, and the like, is fit for the state of a *yati* (ascetic), using the passage beginning with "In the Supreme Self... and so on. "Possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) means that whose mind does not conceive of anything existing as separate from itself. Furthermore, he says "When... and so forth.

Furthermore, renunciation for the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) is described by way of another method—beginning with the word "ten": "free from debt" (*anṛṇaḥ*), [meaning] having paid one's debt to the sages through the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
"By sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors—this one indeed is free from debt," so says the Śruti.
The Śruti itself explains the portion concerning "dharma consisting of ten characteristics" with the word "fortitude" (dhṛti).
It states that one who has no desire for enjoyment delimited by the three periods of time, such as the past and so forth, should dwell in the stage of life dedicated to liberation (mokṣāśrama).

Regarding the word "past" (*atītān*): he says "within" (*antar*) to indicate that one should dwell in the stage of liberation (*mokṣāśrama*), having restrained both internal and external mental fluctuations.
What more need be said? It is simply "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*). (Verses 17–27)

There is sin in possessing anything not sanctioned by law; for a Paramahaṃsa ascetic, the permitted possessions are a pair of loincloths, a patched garment, and a single staff—nothing more is ordained. (28)
Or if, out of passion, he takes possession of what belongs to another, he goes to the Raurava hell and is born among the animal wombs. || 29 ||
Having sewn together tattered and pure pieces of cloth,
he should wear an outer garment dyed with ochre as a patched robe (kanthā).
Clad in a single garment or without any clothing, possessing a single vision and free from greed, he should always wander alone; however, during the rainy season, he may dwell in one place.
Having completely renounced family, wife, and children, as well as the Vedāṅgas,
sacrifice, and the sacred thread, the ascetic should wander in secret.

For an ascetic (*yati*), there is no rule for possession other than that which is necessary for maintaining the body and for proper conduct. If he were to possess anything else, he would incur sin; thus it is said: "only a loincloth," and so forth. If he is afraid of cold, then [he may wear] tattered garments. Whether clothed or naked—if he is one whose engagement in hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) has become sparse—then [this applies].
Then he says that for them, traveling through a village for only one night is prescribed: "One," etc. (28–32).
The qualities of wandering mendicants are desire, anger, as well as pride, greed, delusion, and so forth;
having abandoned those defects, a wandering mendicant should be free from the sense of "mine."

One whose self is free from passion and hatred, who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, who has desisted from harming living beings, and who is devoid of longing for everything— such a person is a sage (muni). (34)
Freed from hypocrisy and egoism, avoiding violence and backbiting,
and endowed with the quality of self-knowledge, the ascetic shall attain liberation.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of the objects of desire;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. 37.
That man who, having heard, touched, eaten, seen, or smelled [objects of sense],
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison, and he should always long for dishonor as if it were nectar. (40)
For he who is held in contempt sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness;
he moves about happily in this world, while the one who insults perishes. 41.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, relying upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone. 42.
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent, and free from desires,
one who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred, and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. (45)
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (46)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is beset by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (47)
If a fool feels attachment toward this body— a mere collection of flesh, blood, pus, excrement, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones— he will find delight even in hell.

That which is the path of the Kālasūtra hell, that which is the snare of the Mahāvīci hell, and that which is the row of sword-leaf forests—all these are the state of identifying with the body as "I. (49)
She must be abandoned with every effort, even when total ruin is imminent;
she should not be touched by a noble man, any more than a Pulkasī woman carrying dog-meat.
Having cast off both good deeds toward those dear to him and evil deeds toward those not dear, through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman. 51.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments and being liberated from all dualities, he remains established in Brahman alone.
One should always wander alone without companions for the sake of accomplishment;
for seeing that accomplishment belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned. (53)

He sets forth the duties of a wandering mendicant with the words beginning "kāma" (desire), etc. The meaning is that one should be free from the sense of "mine," such that one does not harbor the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding one's own body or anything other than it. A *muni* is one whose nature is contemplation. He states that bondage and liberation arise through the contact or non-contact of the senses with their objects: The wise person, having abandoned all desires, should wander about alone. Free from the sense of "mine," silent, and self-restrained, he should not form attachments anywhere. For by contact with the objects of the senses, both bondage and liberation occur for the sage. Therefore, he should avoid the touch of the objects of the senses, as if avoiding fire. Desiring liberation, he should not touch them even with his mind. Regarding the phrase "of the senses": [the opponent might argue] that the pacification of desire would come about through the enjoyment of desires; therefore, he says "no. If this were so, one might ask how the state of having conquered the senses is achieved; to this, he says—

When [the senses] are properly guarded and have attained a state of attenuation, the ascetic, disregarding honor, should desire only contempt; thus it is said: "From honor... Furthermore, he should endure "excessive words," that is, insults uttered by others.
He should not despise anyone through the knowledge of his own Self. For there are indeed seven vital breaths (prāṇas) located in the head.

One should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates; rather, one who always delights in the inner self (adhyātma) should [speak] that which constitutes the seventh gate. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of the senses": having abandoned the ego-intellect (ahaṃdhī), which is rooted in the body under its own superintendence and brings about one's own ruin, one should fix the intellect upon Brahman as the Self. Thus he says: "The bones," etc.
That which arises from the union of semen and blood is the "rajasvala" (the impure body). He specifies the defect regarding what is considered the abode of the elements with the word "māṃsa" (flesh).
The meaning is that one should direct the notion of "I" residing in the body toward Brahman alone, thinking "I am Brahman.
Thus, even for one intent on the contemplation of Brahman, there remain the good and evil deeds produced by the connection with the body—

The meaning is that because his merit and demerit—which are obstacles to the attainment of Brahman—have been taken away by pleasant and unpleasant people, he attains Brahman, which is devoid of all opposites, through the thought of his own self alone; thus, even regarding the pleasant and unpleasant, it is "by this [means]. 33.
The conduct of the ascetic (yaticaryā) and its fruit.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, tattered garments, lack of companionship, and equanimity toward all things—these are the characteristics of one who is liberated. (54)
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot,
delighting in solitude, he should wander forth as a mendicant and enter a village only for the sake of alms.
One monk is as described; two are considered a pair; three are declared to be a village, while more than that becomes like a city. (56)
A city, a village, or likewise a household should not be established by him;
for a renunciant who undertakes these three falls away from his own duty.
Among them, talk of kings and the like may arise, as well as gossip regarding alms;
through close proximity, affection, backbiting, and envy will undoubtedly occur. (58)
(72) A mendicant should remain alone and free from desire; indeed, he should not converse with anyone.
He should always give the reply "Nārāyaṇa" alone. 59.
Alone, one should contemplate Brahman through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
nor should one welcome death or life in any way whatsoever.
One should simply await one's time until the end of life is reached;
one should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life.
One should wait for the appointed time, just as a servant awaits his command. || 61 ||
One who is tongueless, a eunuch, lame, blind, deaf, and even one who is mentally dull—a monk liberated by these six has no doubt [of liberation]. 62.
Furthermore, he describes the practice of asceticism (*yaticaryā*) and its fruit with the words beginning "the skull" (*kapāla*).
He who disciplines his speech, body, and mind through the means of silence, eating little, and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the great ascetic, the *tridaṇḍin*.
The staff of speech, the staff of body, and the staff of mind—these three are his;
he whose staffs are thus restrained is a great ascetic, a *tridaṇḍin*.

Thus says the Śruti. He is "delighting in the One" (ekārāma) because he rejoices everywhere by virtue of the fact that everything remains as the one Brahman. How is that? [It is] through the affairs of kings and so forth. Because it is thus, he is called "alone" (ekākī). To the question, "What should one who is alone do?", he says: "Alone, he should reflect. He states that the ascetic (yati), possessing the state of being tongueless and so forth, is liberated from the delusion of anything other than himself: ... [the verse] ... || 10 || He is "tongueless" (ajihva) because he does not praise others; he is "handless" (ahasta) because he does not perform service for others; he is "footless" (apāda) because he does not go to the houses of others; he is "mindless" (amanaska) because he does not think of anything else; he is "earless" (akarṇa) because he does not listen to the talk of others; he is "eyeless" (acakṣuḥ) because he does not look at the faces of others. Thus, having abandoned the six organs of action, he is liberated from the delusion of duality. || 10 || He is "tongueless" because he does not speak of the faults of others; he is "handless" because he does not grasp the objects of the senses; he is "footless" because he does not wander among villages and towns; he is "mindless" because he does not contemplate the world; he is "earless" because he does not hear the rumors of the world; he is "eyeless" because he does not see the faces of men and women. Thus, having abandoned the six organs of action, he is liberated from the delusion of duality. || 10 || He is "tongueless" because he does not speak of the faults of others; he is "handless" because he does not grasp the objects of the senses; he is "footless" because he does not wander among villages and towns; he is "mindless" because he does not contemplate the world; he is "earless" because he does not hear the rumors of the world; he is "eyeless" because he does not see the faces of men and women. The characteristic of the tongueless one (ajihva) is this: even while eating, he is not attached to the thought "this is delicious" or "this is not";
he speaks what is beneficial, true, and measured—him they call tongueless. (63)
He who, upon seeing a woman born today, one sixteen years of age,
and one a hundred years old, remains free from any change of state, is a eunuch.
He who wanders for the sake of alms and for the discharge of excrement and urine does not travel more than a *yojana*; in every respect, he is truly like one who is lame. (65)
Whether standing or walking, he whose vision does not reach far beyond the earth of the four ages is called a blind wanderer.
Having heard words that are beneficial or harmful, pleasing to the mind or bringing grief, he who does not listen as if he had not heard at all is proclaimed to be deaf.
He who, though capable and possessing unimpaired senses when objects are present,
always behaves as if asleep— that mendicant is called "dormant" (mugdha).

The scripture itself explains, in due order, the statement that serves as the aphorism (*sūtra*). Therein, it states the meaning of the word "tongueless" (*ajihva*)—namely, "for the sake of alms. It states the meaning of the word "blind" (*andha*)—namely, "standing [there]. It explains the word "deaf" (*badhira*)—namely, "beneficial [words]. It clarifies the meaning of the word "deluded" (*mugdha*)—namely, "in the presence [of others]. (63)
Those things to be avoided by ascetics are:
watching actors and the like, gambling, women, friends, as well as food to be chewed and food to be eaten, and a woman in her courses; these six one should never look upon.
A disciplined ascetic should never, even in thought, harbor these six—passion, hatred, pride, deceit, malice, and delusion—toward others or toward himself. (70)
A couch, white clothing, talk of women, indulgence in sensual pleasures, sleeping during the day, and riding in vehicles—these are the six transgressions for ascetics. 71.
One who is mindful of the self should avoid long journeys with great effort.
By the verse beginning with "naṭādi" (69), he demonstrates one portion of that which must be renounced by ascetics.
Ascetics should always practice the knowledge of the Upaniṣads, which is the cause of liberation.
An ascetic should not be one who constantly frequents holy bathing places, nor should he be intent on fasting;
he should not be habitually devoted to Vedic study, nor should he be intent on giving expositions.
One should always practice a conduct that is free from evil, free from deceit, and straightforward;
having withdrawn the senses from all sides, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs. (74)
With the functions of the senses and the mind extinguished, free from desire and without possessions, beyond dualities, offering no salutations, and likewise uttering no *svadhā* calls. (75)
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, indifferent, and without expectations, one who is devoted to a secluded place is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said].
He states what is to be practiced: "Always," etc. "Sinless" means free from both sin and merit, as well as their fruits;
"honest" means that which is to be cultivated by virtuous people and pertains to Brahman; "tongueless" means silence—this is the meaning.
The word "iti" marks the completion of the mantra. (72–76)

In accordance with the stages of life (*āśrama*), one who is vigilant, endowed with ritual action, devotion, and knowledge, and having attained independence and dispassion— whether he be a student (*brahmacārī*),
a householder (*gṛhī*), or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)— if he follows the primary path, he should complete his studentship and become a householder.

Having lived as a householder, one should go forth into the forest; or otherwise, one may go forth directly from the stage of studentship, or from the household, or from the forest. Furthermore, whether one has not observed vows or has observed them, whether one is a graduate (*snātaka*) or not a graduate, whether one’s sacred fires have been extinguished or one is without fires—if on any day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth. Regarding this, some say:
They perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice; or rather, they should not perform it; they should perform only the Āgneyī sacrifice, for Agni is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
By this [verse], one indeed establishes the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, one should perform only the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice. These are the three elements (*dhātu*), namely:
goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*).
"This is your womb, born of the seasons, from which once born you shone forth."
Knowing that, O Agni, ascend [the altar], and then increase our wealth.

With this mantra he should smell the fire: "This indeed is the womb of Agni, which is the breath; go to the breath, go to your own womb, svāhā!"—thus he says this. Having brought fire from the Āhavanīya, he should smell the fire as before. If he should not find fire, he should offer oblations in water; for water is indeed all the deities.

Having offered with "I offer to all the deities, svāhā," and having drawn out that water, he should drink it— this oblation, accompanied by clarified butter, is health-giving and bestows liberation. Having renounced the topknot, the sacred thread, father, son, wife,
ritual action, study, and other mantras, the knower of the Self indeed goes forth as a wandering mendicant.
One should obtain it through the liberating mantras belonging to the three realms; that is Brahman, that is to be worshipped. "It is exactly so," [he said]. || 78 ||

On whatever day the cessation of the phenomenal world—which is other than oneself—arises, like the vomiting of food or the voiding of urine and excrement, for one whose conduct and so forth are characterized as previously described, on that very day he should renounce. If, however, his renunciation is weak, then he should renounce in accordance with the sequence of the stages of life (*āśrama*); thus it is said: "being vigilant" (*apramatta*). If...

If, while maintaining one's own stage of life with a mild degree of detachment, one’s primary inclination toward that state remains, then after completing the student life (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder. Or, if otherwise, if an even more intense renunciation arises, then one should renounce the world from the very stage of the student. One would become detached; that is, one would possess an intensely fervent dispassion. Because this is so, therefore: having completed the student life...

Beginning with these words and ending with "that Brahman is to be meditated upon," this passage from the fourth section of the Jābāla Upaniṣad, in the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya, has been explained almost word for word. || 77-78 ||
76) Nārada again asked the Grandfather (Brahmā): "How can one who does not wear the sacrificial thread be a Brāhmaṇa? He replied to him:
The Grandfather. || 79 ||
Having shaved his head including the top-knot, the wise man should discard the external thread;
he should maintain that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman as his [true] thread.
They say it is called a "sūtra" because it provides instruction; the sūtra is indeed the supreme state.
He by whom that sūtra is known is a true brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
The yogi who perceives the reality of yoga should maintain that thread by which all this is strung together, like clusters of jewels upon a string. 82.
The wise man, established in the supreme yoga, should discard the external thread;
that conscious person who wears this thread of the nature of Brahman shall,
by wearing that thread, be neither impure from food remnants nor defiled.
Those for whom the Sūtra is internal, who wear the sacred thread of knowledge—
they alone in this world truly know the Sūtra, and they alone are the ones who wear the sacred thread.
For those whose crest is knowledge, who are established in knowledge, and for whom the sacred thread is knowledge—knowledge alone is their supreme purifier; it is called knowledge.
He whose crest consists of knowledge, like the flame of a fire, is called a "crested one" (śikhin)—the wise man—and not others who merely wear hair. || 86 ||
But those Brahmins and others who are authorized for Vedic ritual action—by them this Sūtra must be worn, for it is indeed remembered as an auxiliary to that ritual action. (87)
"Those who know Brahman understand that he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread is likewise composed of it possesses the entirety of true Brahminhood. (88)
Thus [it is said].

The Śruti states that Nārada asks the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) how this man deserves the title of "Brāhmaṇa," given that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is preceded by the abandonment of the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). To him, the Grandfather says: "With the topknot" (*saśikham*), and so forth.
The section ending with "those who know Brahman know" has been explained word by word in the *Brahmopaniṣad* [verses 79–88].
The acceptance [of the status] of a Paramahaṃsa or of the Avadhūta stage of life—
having understood this, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce the world; as a wandering mendicant (parivrāj), he should wear a single garment, keep his head shaven, remain without possessions,
and if he is unable to endure bodily hardships, he may, according to the rule, become a wearer of the "natural gold" (jātarūpadhara).

Having renounced his own sons, friends, wife, relatives, kinsmen, and so forth, as well as his Vedic study and meritorious deeds— and having abandoned this entire universe, along with his loincloth, staff, and clothing—
he endures the pairs of opposites, experiencing neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor pain, nor sleep.

Free from honor and dishonor, and devoid of the six waves— censure, egoism, envy, pride, hypocrisy, and jealousy— one should regard everything internal and external as being like a corpse, distinct from oneself; without offering salutation to anyone, one should neither utter *svāhā* nor *svadhā*, and remaining free from blame or praise, one should live according to chance.

Content with whatever comes by chance, he should not take possession of gold or other such things. There is no invocation, no dismissal, no mantra, no non-mantra, no meditation, no worship, no object of focus, nothing separate, nothing non-separate, and nothing else; homeless, steady-minded, he dwells in empty houses, at the roots of trees, or in temples.
—on the plateaus of mountain caves and waterfalls, or in the forest, like Śvetaketu, Ṛbhu, Nidāgha, Ṛṣabha, and Durvāsas. (p. 78)
With his external marks unmanifest like those of Saṃvartaka, Dattātreya, or Raivataka, and with his conduct unmanifest,

behaving like a child, a madman, or a ghost— though not actually insane or mad— he should cast away the triple staff, the sling, the bowl, the water-pot, the waist-thread, and the loincloth, all of them into the water, saying: "Bhūḥ Svāhā."
Having cast away his waist-thread, loincloth, staff, garment, and water-pot into the waters, he should then wander about wearing only the form of gold (naked).

One should seek the Self. Wearing the appearance of one just born, free from dualities, without possessions, and devoted to the reality of Brahman, at the prescribed times, taking food that has not been solicited— either with the hollow of his hands or by other means— regarding gain and loss as equal,
free from the sense of "mine," intent upon pure meditation, and established in the inner self.
Devoted to uprooting both auspicious and inauspicious karma, having renounced [all worldly ties], and being solely established in the realization of perfect bliss—that Brahman alone is the Self.
Having cast off the three bodies through renunciation itself, he abandons the body; he becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 91.
Having understood that true Brahminhood belongs primarily to the ascetic alone, one should renounce the world and become an avadhūta who has attained the state of the paramahaṃsa.

One should perform such virtuous acts as listening to the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; endure the dualities of cold and heat; and transcend the six waves of worldly existence, such as hunger and thirst.
Through the contemplation that Brahman is indeed the inner and non-external Self, one should abandon all else—whether internal or external—as being distinct from oneself.
"By chance" (yādṛcchika) means he should wander alone with independence;

"satisfied with whatever is obtained by chance" because he lacks any personal purpose. The accusative case is used for the nominative—meaning neither with a mantra nor without a mantra—referring to the absence of mantras for invocation and dismissal, as well as the absence of meditation and worship beyond himself.

Sthiramati: Since the *avadhūta* has accomplished all that was to be done, there is no further obligation for him to engage in hearing [the teachings] and so forth; therefore, it is appropriate for him to possess a steady mind while remaining without a fixed abode.

This is the meaning. He states their place of residence: "in a deserted [place]. He specifies the name of the excellent group of *avadhūtas*: "Śvetaketu," and so forth. Whoever has unmanifested signs (*avyaktaliṅga*) and whose own true nature remains unswerving—then, if he is a *tridaṇḍin*, he carries a triple staff; if he is a *paramahaṃsa*, then he carries a waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*). What follows from this?

In this regard, one should seek the Self in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "All this is merely the Self; there is nothing whatsoever other than the Self. On the path of reality and Brahman—that is, on the way of knowledge which leads to its attainment—one should subsist by means of food obtained from the hand, from another vessel, or from the mouth; that is to say, taking food that has not been solicited, even in that case.

Having become equanimous toward gain and loss, free from the sense of "mine," and devoted to pure meditation in accordance with the Vedic scripture stating that Brahman consists of pure light, he is established in the inner self; having renounced the world-appearance as something separate from himself, he is the singular consciousness of perfect bliss.

Remembering the Brahman-Praṇava as "I am that Brahman," which is established through the negation of the fourteen and fifteen divisions beginning with the waking-of-the-waking state, and casting off the identification of self and mine regarding the three bodies and their designations— according to the analogy of the worm in the bee-hive— he who has abandoned the delusion of the existence of anything other than himself [attains liberation].
The word "iti" and the term "Upaniṣad" signify the conclusion of the third instruction. || 89-91 ||
Thus ends the third instruction;
the fourth instruction is the presentation of the duties of ascetics and their fruit.
Having abandoned the worlds, the Vedas, sense objects, and the senses, he who abides in the Self alone attains the supreme goal. || 1 ||
A true ascetic should never proclaim his name, lineage, and so forth, nor his country, time, learning, family, age, conduct, vows, or character.
One should not converse with any woman, nor should one recall one previously seen; one should avoid talk concerning them and should not look even at their likeness in a painting. (3)
If an ascetic practices these four things out of delusion toward women, his mind will inevitably undergo transformation; through that transformation, he perishes.
Thirst, anger, falsehood, deceit, greed, delusion, the pleasant and the unpleasant, craftsmanship, exposition, yoga, desire, passion, and possessiveness. || 5 ||
Egoism, the sense of "mine," medical treatment, violence toward the Dharma, expiation, exile, and blessings accompanied by mantras and medicinal herbs—
these are forbidden; one who practices them shall go downward.
"Come," "go," "stay," "welcome"— even to a friend,
a sage devoted to liberation should not utter such words of social courtesy.
A monk should never accept a gift, nor cause another to give one,
nor incite others to do so, even in a dream.
Having heard of or seen the good and bad fortune of his wife, brothers, sons, and other kinsmen, the ascetic should not tremble; he should abandon grief and delusion.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness;
lack of arrogance, absence of dejection, serenity, steadfastness, and straightforwardness. (10)
Affection, service to the guru, faith, patience, self-restraint, tranquility, equanimity, fortitude, sweetness, endurance, and likewise compassion. || 11 ||
Modesty, as well as knowledge and discernment, yoga, moderation in eating, and fortitude—this is proclaimed as the specific duty of ascetics who have restrained their selves. 12.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, seeing with equanimity everywhere—
the ascetic is the fourth state, the supreme *haṃsa*, Nārāyaṇa himself in visible form. (13)
One should dwell in a village for one night and in a town for five nights;
except during the rainy season, one should dwell for four months in the rains.
A monk should not dwell in a village for two nights; if he should dwell there, then passion and other defilements would ensnare him, and by that he would become a denizen of hell. || 15 ||
With his mind restrained and without a fixed dwelling, he should wander like an insect upon the earth in lonely places at the edge of a village; during the rainy season, he should stay in one place.
Clad in a single garment or without clothing, possessing a single vision and free from greed, he should wander the earth engaged in meditation, without defiling the path of the virtuous. (17)
In a clean place, the mendicant, always observing his own duty,
should wander as a yogi, constantly surveying the surface of the earth.
Neither at night nor at midday, nor during the two twilights, nor while wandering about; neither in a deserted place nor in a difficult terrain, nor where there is danger to living beings.
A mendicant should stay for one night in a village, three days in a town,
two days in a city, and five nights in a capital.
During the rainy season, one should stay in a single place at a location surrounded by sacred waters.
Beholding all beings as his own self, a mendicant should wander the earth like one who is blind,
like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is deaf, insane, or mute.
It is prescribed that those who dwell in the bahūdaka and vanastha stages perform the three daily ablutions;
for the haṃsa, however, it should be performed only once, while for the paramahaṃsa, no such rite exists.
(82) Silence, the yogic posture, yoga, endurance, solitude, virtuous conduct, desirelessness, and equanimity— these seven belong to the Ekadaṇḍins. (23)

For one established in the stage of the *parahaṃsa*, due to the absence of prescribed rules for bathing and other such acts, he should practice solely the renunciation of all mental fluctuations. (24)
What difference is there between worms delighting in a mass of skin, flesh, blood, sinews, marrow, fat, and bones, and those delighting in feces, urine, and pus? 25.
Where is this body, a vast accumulation of phlegm and other humors without exception; and where are qualities such as the beauty of the limbs, good fortune, and loveliness? (26)
If one feels attachment toward this body— a mere collection of flesh, blood, pus, excrement, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones— that fool will find delight even in hell.
Although there is no difference between the private parts of women and a moist wound in a vein, people are generally deceived by the difference in their mental perceptions. 28.
Homage to those who take delight in a piece of hide split in two, fuming with the upward breath of excrement; what greater act of audacity could there be than this?
For that wise one, there exists neither duty nor outward mark;
he is free from possessiveness, fearless, tranquil, beyond dualities, and eats food without regard for its appearance.
The sage, clad in a loincloth or naked, should be intent on meditation;
thus, the yogi devoted to knowledge is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Even though this subtle body (liṅga) exists, knowledge alone is indeed the cause for the liberation of beings in this world; the collection of the subtle body is useless [for that purpose]. || 32 ||
He whom no one knows as existent or non-existent, as unlearned or deeply learned, as well-conducted or ill-conducted— that man is a Brāhmaṇa. (33)
Therefore, the knower of dharma who is without marks, observing the vow of Brahman as his own vow,
being a wise man who has taken refuge in the hidden dharma, should conduct himself with the behavior of one who is ignorant.
Free from doubt regarding all beings and devoid of the distinctions of caste and stage of life, he should wander the earth like one who is blind, dull-witted, and mute. (35)
Seeing him with a tranquil mind, the denizens of heaven yearn for him;
yet, because of the absence of marks, he attains absolute liberation—such is the instruction of Brahmā.
Thus [it is said].

By the end [of this passage], it is stated that [the seeker] must first renounce the collection of dharmas that are causes for the existence of anything other than Brahman, and then cultivate those dharmas that are causes for the realization of Brahman alone. Furthermore, at no time and by no means should an ascetic (*yati*) choose a name, lineage, or the like for himself; nor, being driven by passion (*rāga*), should he engage in conversation with women, recollect them, discuss them, or look at paintings of women—any of which would serve as a cause for his own downfall.

He says it should be abandoned with the word "no. Furthermore, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) such as "may this be mine" or "may this not be mine"; deceit (*māyā*), which is the act of deluding others; and the practice of explaining non-self-scriptures (*anātma-śāstra*). [One should not say] regarding gardens, dwellings, and so forth: "Come near to me! One should never accept gifts (*pratigraha*). If ever...

Having heard or seen the good or bad fortune of his wife and others, he should not tremble; the ascetic should abandon grief and delusion regarding those objects. He states the ascetic’s own duty as follows: non-violence, patience—which is forbearance—and eating light food according to one's whim. Having thus been refined by this collection of duties, the yogi becomes Nārāyaṇa; so he says:
Regarding the term "free from dualities" (*nirdvandva*): if he has ceased from activities such as hearing and meditating, then [the rule is] "one night";

even when staying for one night in a village, it is considered "within a village. To show that a *paramahaṃsa* or an *avadhūta*, though acting according to his own will, should not defile the path of the righteous, he says: "clad in a single garment" (*ekavāsā*).

"Free from greed," meaning devoid of longing in all respects; "looking about for the sake of not harming living beings"—by this he states the time and place for the prohibition against wandering. "In an empty [place]," meaning in a place devoid of people. Regarding the time for staying in a village or similar location, he says: "for one night. After the four-month retreat (*cāturmāsya*), [he should stay] "like himself," just as [he would stay]...

The meaning is that, just as one who is blind and so forth does not perceive the distinctions of form and other objects, [the ascetic likewise does not perceive them]. Regarding the rule for bathing for forest-dwellers and others, he says: "Bathing. As to what the dharma to be practiced by the Paramahaṃsa is, [it is stated] here:

"Mauna" and so forth: silence (*mauna*) is simply the absence of activity in the organs of speech and the rest. Regarding "parahaṃsa," it is conducive to yoga; for the scripture states, "Bathing is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind. He describes the equality of the body to a worm through the phrase "of women" and so forth. [He establishes] the primacy of knowledge over gender and other such factors, and the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) for the wise one.

And it says: "Not for him. Because one who perceives only Brahman does not perceive the distinctions of caste and stage of life such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, he should practice begging for alms among all castes, preceded by the avoidance of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their status; for thus says the Śruti. [This applies to] one who is without external marks (aliṅga).

He explains what constitutes being a *brāhmaṇa*: "whom"—that is, a certain person in the world who does not know that sage by his goodness or lack of goodness, by his learning or lack of learning, or by his good conduct or bad conduct. By the observation of such signs of unknowability, he is a *brāhmaṇa*. Or alternatively, it refers to whichever yogi [knows] this Self.

That sage knows him who exists as the self of the three bodies yet does not exist as a limited individual form— never heard of nor widely renowned from the perspective of one's own ignorance, neither of good conduct nor of evil conduct due to the absence of an internal organ (antahkarana) that causes the manifestation of behavior; he knows him through the realization of his own non-dual nature alone, established by the total negation of all else.
The meaning is that at the very moment of realization, the Brāhmaṇa, being the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, becomes Brahman itself.
And so says the Śruti: "He who knows it thus as seedless becomes indeed seedless;
having abandoned both seeing and not-seeing, he exists by himself in his absolute form."
O tiger among monkeys, he who sits there is not himself a knower of Brahman.
Thus.

Since the state of being a true Brahmin is declared for one who is signless (aliṅga) and has abandoned the perception of the phenomenal world as something separate from oneself, therefore the gods long for such a person, thinking, "When shall we become like him, whose mind is stilled by the cessation of all notions of anything apart from itself? It is precisely when the sign of the existence of anything separate from oneself no longer appears that this occurs.
The meaning is that Brahmā instructs Nārada thus: "This is isolation (kaivalya). || 1.36 ||
The Exposition of the Method of Gradual Renunciation:
Now Nārada asked the Grandfather (Brahmā), "Please tell us the method of renunciation.
The Grandfather, having consented by saying "So be it," [spoke] regarding the undertaking of the fourth stage of life, whether in a state of illness or through the gradual process.
85) One should perform the eight śrāddhas preceded by the penance of *kṛcchra*;

one should perform the eight śrāddhas for the gods (*deva*), sages (*ṛṣi*), celestial beings (*divya*), humans (*manuṣya*), spirits (*bhūta*), ancestors (*pitṛ*), mother (*mātṛ*), and oneself (*ātman*).
First, one should invoke the Viśvedevas known as Satya and Vasu in the *deva-śrāddha*;

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*; the divine sages (*devarṣis*), royal sages (*kṣatriyarṣis*), and human sages (*manuṣyarṣis*) in the *divya-śrāddha*; and those in the form of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas in the *mānuṣa-śrāddha*.

In the *bhūtaśrāddha*, one offers to Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, and Sanatsujāta, as well as to the five elements beginning with earth; in the *mātuḥśrāddha*, to the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother;
and in the *ātmaśrāddha*, to oneself, one’s father, and paternal grandfather—if one’s father is living, then excluding the father.
[He should worship] the self, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. In all cases, he should honor the Brahmins by arranging them in pairs.

Whether following the single-sacrifice (ekādhvara) system or the eight-sacrifice (aṣṭādhvara) system, he should perform the eight Śrāddhas over eight days or on a single day, using the mantras prescribed in his own Vedic branch, according to the procedure stated for the Pitṛyajña.

Having honored the Brahmins, having completed the ritual meal according to the rules, having performed the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), having satisfied the Brahmins with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and betel leaves, and having dismissed them, the twice-born man, for the sake of completing the remaining rites, should cut off seven hairs; or, for the sake of completing the remaining rites, he should shorten seven or eight hairs.

He should have his hair, beard, and nails shaved; having preserved the seven locks of hair (*saptakeśa*), and having first undergone a shave excluding the armpits and the private parts, he should bathe, perform the evening *saṃdhyā* worship, recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra one thousand times, complete the *brahmayajña*, and having attended upon the fire under his own control, [he should study] his own Vedic branch...

Having completed the procedure for the oblations, having consumed barley meal three times with [the mantras] beginning with "ātman," and having protected the fire after performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he himself stands to the north of the fire upon a black antelope skin and keeps watch while listening to the Purāṇas; then, at the end of the fourth watch, having bathed, [he performs the rite] in that same fire.
Having cooked the *caru* and offered sixteen oblations of food with the *Puruṣasūkta*, and having performed the *virajā-homa*,
he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), give a garment, gold, a vessel, and a cow as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and thus complete the rite.
Having performed the dismissal of the Brahman,
may the Maruts sprinkle me, may Indra sprinkle me, may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me;
may this Agni sprinkle me with long life, with wealth, and with strength, and may he make me possessed of long life.
Thus, O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice— come here, ascend it, yourself by yourself;
bestowing upon us many noble riches.
Becoming the sacrifice, enter the sacrifice as your own womb; O Jātavedas, being born from the earth, come to your dwelling place.

Having thus superimposed the fire upon oneself and meditated on the fire, and having performed circumambulation and prostration preceded by [these acts], one should sit in water reaching the navel; then, having performed the dismissal of Gāyatrī preceded by the *arghya* offerings to the eight guardians of the directions, and having caused Sāvitrī to enter the *vyāhṛtis*, [one recites]: "I am the tree..."

"Like a river, like the fame of a mountain; with the purifier above, like a swift steed, I am my own nectar—wealthful, radiant, wise, immortal, and imperishable. Thus was the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku:
"He who is the bull among the meters, possessing all forms, who arose from the meters and from the nectar—he..."

May Mena, with wisdom, protect me. O God, may I become a sustainer of immortality. May my body be most discerning; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears. You are the treasury of sacred knowledge (*brahman*), covered by wisdom. Protect what I have heard.
I have renounced the desire for wife, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds. Oṃ bhūḥ, I have renounced; oṃ bhuvaḥ, I have renounced; oṃ suvaḥ, I have renounced; oṃ.

Having mentally or vocally uttered "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, this has been renounced by me," with soft, medium, and high-pitched tones, and having consumed water while reciting "Fearlessness to all beings; everything proceeds from me,
Svāhā," he should cast a full handful of water toward the eastern direction and pluck out his topknot while saying "Oṃ Svāhā."

The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the supreme purifier, which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning—put on this foremost, auspicious thread that bestows long life; may it be strength and splendor for you.
Do not dwell outside as the sacred thread; having entered within, abide eternally in the center.
Bestow supreme purity, glory, strength, knowledge, dispassion, and intelligence.

Having thus cut the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should offer it into the water together with a handful of water, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, go to the ocean, svāhā. Then, having recited three times—"Oṃ bhūḥ, it has been renounced by me; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, it has been renounced by me; Oṃ suvaḥ, it has been renounced by me"—and having consecrated that water three times, one should drink it and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Saying "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā," he should cast away both his garment and his waist-thread into the water; then, recollecting "I am the one who has brought all ritual actions to an end," and assuming the state of nakedness (jātarūpadhara), he should go toward the north with arms raised, preceded by the contemplation of his own true nature (svarūpa). || 37 ||

As before, if he is a renunciant by knowledge (*vidvatsaṃnyāsī*), having received from his guru the instruction on the *praṇava* and the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), he may wander at ease, subsisting on fruits, leaves, and water in mountains, forests, and the abodes of deities, thinking, "There is no one other than me who is distinct [from me]. Having thus renounced, he is then sky-clad (*digambara*) and a wanderer everywhere.

(88) With a heart entirely filled by the singular experience of his own universal bliss, having attained a state far removed from ritual action, he sustains his life-breath while remembering the Tāraka.
If he is a *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsī*, having traveled the hundred-path (*śatapatha*), he is met by the preceptor and other Brahmins who say: "Stop, stop, O illustrious one!
Take the staff, the cloth, and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). [Receive] the *praṇava* and the great maxims (*mahāvākya*).
[Take] a single cotton cloth (*śāṭī*) and a water-pot; [take] a staff that is flawless, even, and equal in length from the feet to the head."

He should take up the staff with the mantra: "O gentle one, without a crow’s back, endowed with auspicious marks, made of bamboo—protect me as a friend, O strength! You who are the friend of Indra, you are the thunderbolt of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; be my protection, ward off whatever is evil. [And he should think: "O Mother, protect me, the life of the world, the support of life!"
Addressing him with "Be ever gentle toward all," he takes up the water-pot preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*;
the waist-thread that supports the loincloth with *Oṃ*; the loincloth that covers the private parts with *Oṃ*;
and the garment that protects the body from cold, wind, and heat with *Oṃ*—thus [he consecrates] the waist-thread, the loincloth, and the garment.
One should be devoted to the conduct appropriate to one's own stage of life. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 39.

Thus instructed by Brahmā, Nārada, desiring to know the rules for gradual renunciation (*krama-saṃnyāsa*), questioned the Grandfather; this is introduced with the word "atha" (now). The Grandfather, having accepted Nārada’s question, gave his reply with the word "tathā" (so be it).
One should perform the eight śrāddhas preceded by penances such as the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra. Regarding the question "What are the eight śrāddhas?", [the text says] "Devarṣi," etc.
He states the sequence for the selection of the Viśvedevas and others in the śrāddhas for the gods and so forth, beginning with "First," etc.

For the sake of accomplishing the remaining rites such as the evening twilight prayer (*sāyaṃsandhyā*), he states that one should perform the internal installation (*samāropaṇa*) of the fire currently under discussion into oneself by means of the two mantras to be mentioned, beginning with "May they sprinkle me" (*saṃ mā siñcantu*). These are the two mantras beginning with "I am the tree" (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya*).

Having recited [the verses], one should utter the *preṣa* (the formal dismissal); thus he says: "I" (*aham*). Having recited the two *mandra* chants—"I [am the tree]" (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya*)—and then "Now, from the desire for a wife" (*atha dāreṣaṇāyāśca*), if, as before, he is a renunciant through knowledge (*vidvatsaṃnyāsī*).

"Then, from the Guru [it is said]: 'I alone am the Supreme Self; there is nothing whatsoever other than or separate from Me. What follows from this?—[the seeker] becomes a sky-clad ascetic (digambara), casting off that delusion of wandering through all the worlds, always abiding in his own nature which is bliss, finding joy in the renunciation of all actions, intent solely on the maintenance of life-breath, and thereby liberated."
Regarding this, it is said: "Uttering the single syllable 'Om', which is Brahman, and remembering Me, he who departs,
casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal."

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. If this person is a *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsī*, he should take up the staff with the mantra, "O friend, protect me. Having accepted the waist-thread, the loincloth, and the garment after performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and having gone into the presence of the Guru, he receives the instruction on the *praṇava* and the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) from his mouth.

Performing the conduct appropriate for his own stage of life, he brings about the cessation of the five defects beginning with doubt; this concludes the teaching on all the Vedāntas, and thus the word *upaniṣad* signifies the completion of the fourth instruction. (37–39)
Thus ends the fourth instruction;
the fifth instruction concerns the non-contradiction between the renunciation of action and the performance of duties according to one's own stage of life (*āśrama*).

Then Nārada questioned the Grandfather (Brahmā): "O Blessed One, you yourself have stated that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the cessation of all actions; yet it is further said that one should remain devoted to the conduct of one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). Thereupon the Grandfather replied: "For the embodied being possessing a body, there exist the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*)."

"O Lord, you ought to tell us in truth: what are those various types of persons— beings who are dependent on Him and who initiate action, knowledge, and dispassion— and what are the corresponding varieties of their practices that conform to Him?"
Having agreed to that with "So be it," by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thinking there to be a contradiction between the renunciation of action and the performance of action, Nārada asks; thus it is said: "Now," etc.

Nārada questioned the Grandfather (Brahmā). What did he ask? "O Blessed One," etc. Being thus questioned by Nārada, the Blessed One spoke the answer to the question: "Then," etc. Then the Grandfather said.

What is meant here by "of one possessing a body"? It refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) as delimited by the three bodies, because in its possession of the four states—waking and so forth—the occurrence of karma, devotion, detachment, and knowledge is possible.
Thus, for a living being delimited by these four states, there arise practices conducive to them.

It has been stated that one should be intent upon the conduct of one’s own stage of life (*āśrama*). The fulfillment of the conduct of one’s own stage of life means the attainment of the common Śrauta and Smārta rites to be performed by those in the stages of the student and the householder, preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), as well as the acquisition of the means for sustaining life, such as the hearing of scripture (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. This applies to one and the same person.

It is appropriate that devotion to the conduct of one's own stage of life (āśrama) follows the renunciation of all ritual actions; having accepted as "so it is" what was asked by Nārada, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke thus to him. || 1 ||
Regarding the fourfold nature of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*):
if it is asked how there can be a difference in conduct based on the different types of renunciation, in reality there is only one renunciation;
however, through ignorance, the influence of incapacity, and the omission of ritual duties, it becomes threefold, namely, renunciation through dispassion (*vairāgya-saṃnyāsa*).
It has attained a fourfold nature: renunciation through knowledge, renunciation through wisdom and dispassion, and renunciation of action. || 2 ||

If you think, "What is the reason for the difference in conduct based on the different types of renunciation?"—then listen to this. As to how it is divided: it is by means of ignorance (*ajñāna*). It exists having attained a threefold state due to the distinction between the knower (*vidvat*), the seeker of knowledge (*vidiṣu*), and the one afflicted by desire (*ātura*). Furthermore, he says that it has reached a fourfold state:
"Regarding detachment," thus [ends verse] 2.

Renunciation through dispassion (*vairāgyasaṃnyāsa*) is as follows: having attained freedom from craving for sense objects due to the absence of corrupt passion, one who has renounced by the power of prior meritorious karma is a renunciant through dispassion (*vairāgyasaṃnyāsī*). || 3 ||

It is explained in exactly that way: "And because of the absence of the wicked passion (*mada*) which is the cause of all misfortune. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the other types of renunciation] are included.

He who has renounced [all] through the intellect that perceives everything as perishable and as something to be abandoned apart from Himself—that is the renunciant of dispassion (*vairāgya-saṃnyāsī*). That which is the abandonment of everything by means of the intellect that regards what is other than oneself as perishable and fit for rejection—[that is this renunciation].
This means that it is the renunciation born of dispassion. || 3 ||
The renunciation of knowledge consists in ceasing from the phenomenal world through the study of the scriptures and hearing of the experience of the worlds resulting from merit and demerit;
it involves bringing to an end the entire cycle of transmigratory existence characterized by anger, envy, malice, egoism, and self-conceit.

Having abandoned the desire for wife, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worldly status— along with the latent impressions of the body, the latent impressions of the scriptures, and the latent impressions of the world— and considering all this as something to be discarded like vomited food, he who, endowed with the fourfold qualifications, renounces is alone a renunciant through knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsī). || 4 ||
He states the nature of the renunciation of knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsa) [in the verse beginning] with "śāstra": || 4 ||

The renunciant of knowledge and dispassion (jñānavairāgyasaṃnyāsī) is one who, having practiced everything in due order and experienced everything, becomes a wearer of the "golden form" (jātarūpadhara) through knowledge, dispassion, and the contemplation of his own true nature; he is this very renunciant of knowledge and dispassion. || 5 ||

He describes the renunciation characterized by distinguished knowledge and dispassion, beginning with the words "in sequence" (*krameṇa*). Having practiced the entire corpus of Vedānta in sequence and having experienced everything, one realizes Brahman—which is established through the negation of all else and is non-dual and without a counterpart—by means of both that knowledge and dispassion. Through the contemplation of one's own true nature, one forgets everything; he who [does this]...
"He becomes one who wears the 'gold'"—the meaning is that he is a renunciant endowed with knowledge and dispassion. || 5 ||

The renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*) consists in completing the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), becoming a householder, and then entering the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprasthāśrama*), provided there is an absence of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Having renounced through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya), one who wears gold [as a sign] after renunciation is a renunciant through dispassion (vairāgyasaṃnyāsī).

The renunciant through knowledge (vidvatsaṃnyāsī) is the renunciant through wisdom (jñānasaṃnyāsī). The renunciant through the desire to know (vividiṣāsaṃnyāsī) is the renunciant through action (karmasaṃnyāsī). || 7 ||

He clarifies the true nature of the renunciation of action (karmasaṃnyāsa) with the words "brahmacarya" and so forth. [The phrase] "having duly completed the stage of studenthood" refers to one who has renounced through studenthood due to a lack of acquaintance with sense objects; he praises such renunciation with the words "by means of studenthood. Because that person has ascended to the state of being the Self of all, there arises a variety of perspectives for one who perceives.
The meaning is that the state of possessing all forms is established. || 6-7 ||
The renunciation of action (karma-saṃnyāsa) is twofold by way of the distinction between "with cause" (nimitta) and "without cause" (animitta).

Renunciation of action is also of two kinds: renunciation with cause and renunciation without cause. That which is "with cause" is the renunciation of one who is afflicted (ātura); that which is "without cause" is the gradual renunciation (krama-saṃnyāsa). One who is afflicted is one for whom all ritual actions have ceased.

Renunciation at the time of the departure of the vital breath is renunciation with a specific cause. Having become firm in limb and having realized that everything conditioned is perishable, one should attain [the state where] the body and all else are to be abandoned. || 8 ||
The Haṃsa (the Swan) dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house;
dwelling among men, dwelling in the best, dwelling in Truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the cows, born of Truth, born of the mountains—He is the Great Truth. 9.
Having ascertained that everything other than Brahman is perishable, he who gradually renounces is one whose renunciation is "without cause" (animitta-saṃnyāsa). || 10 ||

He states the twofold nature of the renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*) through the distinction between the "caused" (*nimitta*) and the "uncaused" (*animitta*) in the verse beginning with "action" (*karma*). He explains the meaning of the terms "caused" and "uncaused" as follows: "The caused is the one who is afflicted (*ātura*); the uncaused is the sequential renunciation. He clarifies the purpose of the "caused" renunciation with the word "afflicted" (*ātura*).

He states the essential nature of the signless (*animitta*) with the words "of firm limbs. In accordance with the mantra "The Great Truth" (*ṛtaṃ bṛhat*), Brahman alone is the Truth (*ṛta*); everything other than Brahman is perishable. (8–10)

Renunciation is of six kinds according to the divisions of Kuṭīcaka and so forth; renunciation is sixfold: the Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, the Paramahaṃsa, the Turiyatīta, and the Avadhūta. || 11 ||
(p. 93) Regarding the question "How many kinds of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) are there?", he says that it is of six kinds through the distinctions of the *kuṭīcaka* and so forth—thus: "Renunciation.
To the question "In what way is that so?", he says: "The *kuṭīcaka*," etc. (verse 11).
The characteristics of the *kuṭīcaka*:
the *kuṭīcaka* wears a topknot and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), carries a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), wears a loincloth and a patched garment (*kanthā*),
is devoted to the service of his father, mother, and guru, and is intent on the practice of mantras using a cooking pot, a shovel, a sling, and other such implements.
Devoted to eating food in only one place, he wears a white vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and carries a triple staff (tridaṇḍa). || 12 ||
The characteristics of the Bahūdaka:

the Bahūdaka has his topknot and so forth hanging down below his throat, wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), is equal toward all like a *kuṭīcaka*, and eats eight mouthfuls according to the "bee-like" mode of subsistence (*madhukaravṛtti*). 13.

The characteristic of a *haṃsa* is as follows: he is a *haṃsa*, wears matted hair, bears the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), eats unprepared food obtained by begging, and wears a loincloth and a patched garment. || 14 ||
The characteristic of the Paramahaṃsa is as follows:
the Paramahaṃsa is devoid of the topknot and the sacrificial thread; he subsists on food obtained from five houses in a single night;
he uses his hands as a bowl; he wears a single loincloth, or a single garment, and carries a single bamboo staff, or he may wear only a single garment.
Devoted to smearing himself with ashes, he has renounced everything. || 15 ||
He clarifies their characteristics in sequence, beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*:

"One who wears the *tripuṇḍra* or the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*" means that he wears either the *tripuṇḍra* or the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* as may be appropriate, but not both. He eats unprepared food obtained by begging (*mādhūkara*) from the house of someone today...
Free from the mental resolve, "May there be for me the honey-gathering [of alms]," [he should wander]. || 12-15 ||
The definition of the state beyond the fourth (turīyātīta):
One who has transcended the fourth is Gomukha; he subsists on fruit or on food, and within three houses, nothing remains of him but his physical body.
Clad in the directions as his garment, he subsists upon a corpse-like body.
The characteristic of the *avadhūta* is as follows:
the *avadhūta* is free from fixed rules (*aniyama*), having first avoided those who are outcasted or fallen; he subsists among all castes with the behavior of a python (*ajagaravṛtti*).
He is "cow-mouthed" (*gomukha*) because, like a cow, he swallows whatever food is obtained by chance. And so it will be said:

"When the sage seeks food with his mouth like a cow," [it means] he subsists on a body like a corpse; just as a corpse is motionless, so too is he because his activity has been overwhelmed by the power of non-conceptual samādhi. 16.
The gradual renunciation for one who is living and afflicted.
If the afflicted person survives, the gradual renunciation (kramasaṃnyāsa) should be performed. || 18 ||

If the sick person survives, what should be done? To this he says: "The sick person. The renunciation of succession (*krama-saṃnyāsa*) consists precisely in receiving the *praṇava*, the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), and so forth from the mouth of the Guru; it does not consist of the eight *śrāddhas* and the like, because those are performed at the same time as the utterance of the funeral summons (*preṣa*). || 18 ||
The procedure for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) for the Kuṭīcaka and others;
the procedure for the renunciation of the Kuṭīcakas, Bahūdakas, and Haṃsas, which begins from the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya) up to the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama). || 19 ||

To explain how the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) applies to the *kuṭīcaka* and the others, he says: "Of the *kuṭīcaka*s, etc. The procedure for renunciation is the same for the *kuṭīcaka*s. || 19 ||
p. 95) The procedure for renunciation for the three [classes] beginning with the Paramahaṃsa:
for the three beginning with the Paramahaṃsa, there is no waist-thread, no loincloth, no garment, and no water-pot.
The staff, the practice of wandering for alms from members of all castes, and wearing the natural form (nakedness) constitute the rule.

At the time of renunciation, having studied until the attainment of contentment (*alam-buddhi*), one should thereafter discard the waist-thread, the loincloth, the staff, the garment, and the water-pot into the waters; then, if one is not to wear the natural form...

One should not study even a fragment of a patched garment (kanthāleśa), nor should one speak or listen to anything else. One should not recite any reasoning other than the *praṇava*, nor even any word other than it. One should not teach many words, nor engage in the exhaustion of great speech through vocalization. One should not converse with hands or other gestures, nor with any specific foreign language.

He shall not converse with Śūdra women, outcasts, or women in their courses; nor shall there be for the ascetic the practice of visiting temples, witnessing festivals, or undertaking pilgrimages. || 20 ||

Regarding the three classes beginning with the Paramahaṃsa— namely the Paramahaṃsa, the Turyātīta, and the Avadhūta— if the Paramahaṃsa is desirous of hearing [the scriptures], then he should accept the staff and other emblems; and having first pacified the five defects such as doubt, until direct realization of Brahman arises, even at the time of renouncing all ritual actions (sarvakarma-saṃnyāsa), [he should maintain these].
Even in the state of *saṃnyāsa*, according to the Vedic injunction, "Let those who do not know the truth listen;
knowing it, why should I listen?", one should study until the attainment of the sense of sufficiency (*alaṃbuddhi*).
Once the knowledge born of hearing and other means is established, [the text says] "thereafter. Even in the *avadhūta* stage, there is the patched garment (*kanthā*) and so forth.

To the objection that [something] must indeed be grasped, he says: "No. Not even the slightest thing should be studied. "With speech" means idle boasting; "with the hand and so forth" means conversing by means of gestures of the hands and such; the meaning is that one should not be intent on activity. For an ascetic (*yati*), there is no worship of deities nor witnessing festivals with a mind distinct from his own Self; for the ascetic, even in those matters—
The meaning is that the very realization of one's own self is the task to be accomplished; likewise, there is the practice of pilgrimage to sacred sites. || 20 ||

Furthermore, the specific types of alms-gathering for the Kuṭīcaka and others constitute the specific distinctions among the ascetics. For the Kuṭīcaka, alms are collected in one place; for the Bahūdaka, they are collected from five houses without prior appointment.

(96) One who uses his hands as a bowl, subsists on fruits, has a cow-like face, and follows the lifestyle of a python (ajagara-vṛtti) belongs to the Avadhūta who has transcended the fourth state (turīyātīta) among all castes.
A renunciant (yati) should not dwell for even a single night [in one place], nor should he bow down to anyone. This does not apply to the Avadhūta who has transcended the fourth state.

The Eldest: He who does not know his true nature is the youngest, even if he be the eldest. One should not cross a river with one's hands, nor climb a tree, nor mount a vehicle, nor be intent on buying or selling, nor be intent on bartering anything, nor be hypocritical, nor a speaker of untruth. For the ascetic, there is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done.
If there were such a confusion [of stages], then there would be no distinction; therefore, renunciants have the right to engage in reflection and the other [stages]. || 21 ||
Furthermore, there is a distinction regarding the types of ascetics (*yati*). The specific manner of alms-gathering for the *kuṭīcaka* and others is stated: "for the *kuṭīcaka*" [it is as follows].

An ascetic should not dwell anywhere for more than one night, nor should he bow to anyone. If it is asked whether salutation to the guru, elders, and so forth must be performed, the answer is: "for one who has transcended the fourth state" (*turīyātīta*). This is because such a person is senior by virtue of their knowledge. Regarding him...

By stating "with the two hands," he expresses that there is nothing whatsoever to be done due to being turned away from both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). At no time does a mendicant have anything to be done; if there were, then confusion (*sāṃkarya*) would arise.
Since such confusion with those bound by vows (*vratin*) and others occurs through performing what has been thus described, [therefore...]
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is indicated the state of remaining silent after having swallowed both worldly activity and its cessation through the attainment of the nature of Brahman. || 21 ||
The places to be reached by them are as follows:
for the Ātura and the Kuṭīcaka, they are the Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka; for the Bahūdaka, the Svargaloka; for the Haṃsa, the Tapoloka;
for the Paramahaṃsa, the Satyaloka; and for the Turīyātīta and the Avadhūta, there is liberation (kaivalya) within their own self alone.
Through the contemplation of one's own true nature, according to the analogy of the bumblebee and the caterpillar. || 22 ||
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, that very state one attains; it is not otherwise—such is the teaching of the Vedas.

The goal to be attained by those such as the *kuṭīcaka* who possess unimpaired knowledge is stated as "the world of the afflicted" (*ātura*) and so forth. If he is a *paramahaṃsa* possessing knowledge of the qualified Brahman (*saviśeṣajñānī*), then his destination is Satyaloka. If, however, they are knowers of the unqualified Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmajñānin*), namely the *turyātīta* and the *avadhūta*, [then their destination is different].
p.
97) At that time, for you—those two, the *turyātīta* and the *avadhūta*—there is isolation (*kaivalya*) within your very own self.
Since, through such contemplation of one's true nature, the attainment of the state of Brahman occurs according to the analogy of the bee and the worm, for this very reason:

The meaning is that one must always practice the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svasvarūpānusaṃdhāna*). In response to the inquiry as to why this contemplation of one's own nature must be performed at all times: although for one who possesses knowledge of the non-dual (*nirviśeṣajñānin*) liberation occurs simultaneously with that knowledge, for one who possesses knowledge of the qualified (*saviśeṣajñānin*) it does not; therefore, [it must be practiced] always.

He says that one must practice the contemplation of one's own true nature (svarūpānusaṃdhāna) with the words "whomsoever" (yam). This refers to the teaching: "At the final stage, whomever [one remembers]" and so forth. Likewise, the Smṛti also states:
"And at the time of death, remembering Me alone, having cast off the body..."
He who departs, casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal.
Thus [ends the section]. 22–23.
One must practice the contemplation of Brahman alone and nothing else;
having understood this, one should not be intent on any other conduct apart from the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).
Through the power of such conduct, one attains various respective worlds. For one who is endowed with knowledge and dispassion, [liberation occurs] in this very life.

Liberation does not imply that one must engage in all [worldly] practices; rather, it refers to the practice [of the Self] therein. Within a single body throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep:
during the waking state, it is Viśva; during the dreaming state, Taijasa; and during the state of deep sleep, Prājña.
Due to the difference in states, there is a difference in the lords of those states. Due to the difference in effects, there is a difference in causes. Among these...
The external and internal functions of the fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*) have these as their material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

The functions (*vṛtti*) are fourfold: mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). Due to the differences in the operations of those respective functions, there is a distinction in their respective modes of conduct. || 24 ||
One should know that the waking state resides in the eyes; one enters the dreaming state in the throat;
the deep sleep state resides in the heart; and the fourth state (turiya) is situated in the head.

Having realized that the fourth is the Imperishable, if one should dwell even while in the waking state as if having entered the state of deep sleep—such that whatever is heard or seen is all experienced as if unknown—even for such a person, this remains true even in the state of dreaming.

Such is his state; they call him one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Even the exposition of the meaning of all the scriptures is liberation for him alone. A mendicant has no expectation regarding this world or the next; if there were such an expectation, he would become like it. [He does not attain it] through the practice of other treatises apart from the contemplation of his own true nature.

It is as futile as carrying a load of saffron on a camel; there is no engagement with the Yoga scriptures, no practice of the Sāṃkhya scriptures, and no application of mantras and tantras. If a renunciant engages in other scriptures, it is like an ornament upon a corpse, or like a leather-worker whose actions and conduct are utterly remote from the true science.

Devoted to the chanting of the *praṇava*, whatever action he performs, he experiences that very fruit. Therefore, having abandoned everything like the froth of castor oil, and seeing that the mind is the staff, the hand is the bowl, and the quarters of space are the garment, the mendicant should wander forth. Like a child, a madman, or a ghost, [he regards] death and life as equal.
Or he should not long for anything else, but should simply await his time, like a servant waiting for instructions; such is the rule for the wandering mendicant. || 26 ||

Having understood that which is thus declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, one who possesses knowledge of the qualified [Brahman] should not, in the absence of contemplation on his own true nature, be intent on any other mode of conduct; the meaning is that he should always maintain the contemplation, "I am Brahman.
He states the obstacle to being intent on any other mode of conduct:
It is by virtue of one's conduct that one attains those respective worlds. If it is argued that this would also apply to the knower of non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣajñānin*), we say no;

for such a person has attained the state of Brahman alone, which is devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika-brahmamātra*). Consequently, there is no possibility of activity or cessation directed toward anything other than oneself, nor is there any possibility of perceiving the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of waking and so forth as something separate from oneself. This is because of the constant contemplation of Brahman.
He says "jñāna... [and so forth] to show that one should not become intent on improper conduct otherwise.
For one who is endowed with knowledge and dispassion directed toward the lower Brahman (aparabrahman), liberation occurs within oneself;
thus, there is no necessity for conduct in all matters. If there were a necessity for conduct in all matters, then such conduct would lead to misfortune.

The meaning is "it would be so. To the question "How so?"—it is because, for one whose vision is obscured by the delusion of states such as waking that are distinct from oneself, the name, function, and so forth of the single body and its delimited jīva differ according to the distinctions between the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; this is expressed as "the time of waking" and so on. Within those states of waking and the rest...

The fourteen instruments, beginning with speech, possess both external and internal functions—four of each. As to what these are, they are referred to here as "the mind" (*manas*). Therein lies their distinct difference in conduct. How then can it be said that [the mind] resides in the eye?

I, who manifest the three states— waking and the others— which are divided as the eyes and so forth, in the form of Viśva and the rest, am established in the head in the form of the Fourth (turya); knowing myself thus as the Fourth, the Imperishable (akṣara), I [am that].

By the majesty of that knowledge, I become one who has accomplished all that was to be done. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even while awake": just as one who has entered the state of deep sleep does not perceive the multitude of objects, so too, even while awake, he who exists as if everything heard through the ears and other organs and everything seen were unperceived—of such a person [it is said].
