They say that he who, even in the state of dreaming, does not perceive the diversity of objects as if in deep sleep, is one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
And so it will be said:
"For he who, even in a dream, remains composed just as when awake, especially [in his conduct]."
One whose conduct is such as this is considered the best and most excellent among the exponents of Brahman.

Thus it is said. Even for one of such a nature, if there should be a longing for objects other than his own self, then at that time—according to the scriptural statement, "At that time he is bodiless, devoid of memory of the body; if even a slight thing is remembered, then he is joined with everything"—there would be a fall from his true nature. Therefore, he says "the mendicant" (bhikṣuḥ), implying: if there is any expectation [of external things].

It becomes conformable to that; through the study of other scriptures, there arises the study of other scriptures. Since such great harm arises from the activity of [perceiving] the existence of anything apart from oneself, one should at some point renounce as a mendicant after seeing the non-conceptual Brahman—according to the maxim of the "child, the madman, and the hired girl."
"The wandering mendicant," [so it is said]. 24–26.
If he fails to maintain continuity [in his practice], he falls; one who is devoid of the qualities of forbearance, knowledge, dispassion, tranquility, and so forth,
and who subsists merely on alms, is a mendicant who has abandoned the conduct of an ascetic.
Liberation is not attained by the wielding of a staff, nor by shaving the head, nor by outward appearance, nor by hypocritical conduct. || 28 ||
He who has taken up the staff of knowledge is called a single-staffed ascetic (ekadaṇḍin);
he who has taken up a wooden staff, eats all things, and is devoid of knowledge [is not].
He goes to the terrible hells known as Mahāraurava. || 29 ||
(100) The great seers have declared that a dwelling place is equal to the dung of a sow;
therefore, having abandoned it, the ascetic should wander like an insect. (30)

He says that one who possesses knowledge of distinctions, failing to practice the means for attaining non-dual knowledge, becomes a destroyer of the conduct of the virtuous through mere outward appearance alone and perishes himself: "One devoid of the qualities of forbearance, knowledge, dispassion, tranquility, and so forth"— forbearance being the primary means for non-dual knowledge.
And it is not by the mere act of renunciation that one attains perfection, according to the Smṛti.

This supremely compassionate Śruti, although it has already expounded the multitude of duties for the wandering mendicant in many ways, speaks again with the avoidance of repetition (jāmitā), beginning with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*), etc., as follows: [and] in the opposite of that—
Regarding the phrase "wooden staff": this is the most excellent of all. || 27–30 ||
For those who have transcended the fourth state (turyātīta), their food and other necessities should be obtained unasked according to what is available, solely through the will of others;
and by the will of others, they should remain naked and perform their bathing.
He says that bathing and other rites for those beyond the fourth state (turyātīta) may be performed at the will of another: "unsolicited" (ayācita). || 31 ||
He who is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, who remains disciplined even in dream as if he were awake— especially so—
one whose conduct is such is considered the best and the most eminent among the exponents of Brahman.

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence; one should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material requisites. || 33 ||
One should utterly despise gains obtained through honor;
for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains obtained through honor.

Regarding the question, "Who is this one established in Brahman?"—the answer is: "Even in a dream. Regarding the question, "How can there be establishment in Brahman when joy and other emotions are seen upon gaining [objects] and so forth?"—the answer is: "In the absence [of gain]. [Such a person is] "free from attachment to the objects of the senses," such as sound and the rest.

Regarding the question of why there is non-attachment toward those who are objects of the devotees' love, [the text says]: "abhipūjitā" (honored). "Lābhaskaḥ" means one who possesses gain; that is, one who is wealthy. || 32–34 ||

For ascetics, there are rules regarding food and other matters for the sake of sustaining life; one should wander from house to house for alms at the proper time, when the embers have been extinguished and the people have finished their meals, among those of commendable appearance.
A yogi who uses his hands as a bowl should not practice begging repeatedly;
he should eat while standing, eat while walking, and likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in the midst of these acts.
Those of pure intent remain steadfast in their boundaries like the oceans;
like the suns, the great do not abandon their fixed course.
When the sage seeks food with his mouth like a cow, then he shall be equal toward all things; he is thus fit for immortality.
One should indeed go to a blameless house and avoid a blameworthy house;
one should enter a door that is unobstructed, and never go through one that is obstructed.
Taking shelter in an empty dwelling concealed by dust, or making his home at the foot of a tree, he has abandoned all that is pleasant and unpleasant. (40)
He describes the manner of food intake—using a honeycomb-like collection from the palms as a bowl—for the Paramahaṃsas and others, beginning with the word "prāṇa":

having stayed at the foot of a tree outside the village, he should enter the village at the prescribed time for the sake of alms to sustain his life, and wander for alms according to the rules. Thereafter...
He states the rule regarding the bowl of the hands: "the bowl of the hands" (pāṇipātra). To the question, "What is the restriction for those who have already achieved their purpose?
he replies, "as in the ocean. Regarding the three modes of livelihood beginning with *mādhūkarā*, he says they must be "blameless. He describes their dwelling place: "in the dust," and so forth.
The state of a renunciant who has conquered the senses is such that he sleeps wherever sunset finds him, being without sacred fires and without a fixed dwelling.
A sage who has subdued his senses and conquered his organs should subsist on whatever he obtains. || 41 ||
Having departed from home and resorted to the forest, performing the sacrifice of knowledge with senses subdued,
he who wanders awaiting his time is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings never experiences fear from any being anywhere. (43)
Free from pride and without egoism, beyond dualities and with doubts severed,
he neither becomes angry nor feels hatred, and he does not speak an untruthful word.
Practicing in the abodes of merit and non-violent toward living beings, when the proper time has arrived, he may seek alms; this is conducive to becoming one with Brahman.
He should never associate with forest-dwellers or householders;
he should seek to live incognito, and joy should not take possession of him.
His path is indicated by the sun; he should wander the earth like an insect.

Having departed from the cities and villages that are human dwellings, desiring the time when his commenced karma is exhausted, not harming any living being by regarding them as himself, and moreover, free from pride toward others— he is rendered capable of attaining *brahmabhūya*,
which means the state of becoming Brahman. (41–46)
The renunciation of all actions is for the ascetic;

indeed, those actions which are associated with worldly desires, those joined with violence, and even those intended for the maintenance of the world, he should neither perform nor cause others to perform. (47)

One should not become attached to false treatises, nor should one make a livelihood from them; one should abandon contentious arguments and logical speculations, and should not rely upon any partisan position whatsoever. (48)
One should not bind oneself to disciples, nor should one study many books;
one should not employ oneself in exegesis, nor should one undertake any new undertakings anywhere. (49)
With unmanifest signs and unmanifest purpose, the sage should show himself to men like one who is insane or a child, and like a mute, through his vision of the Self.
He should do nothing, say nothing, and meditate on neither the good nor the bad;
delighting in the Self through this mode of conduct, the sage should wander like one who is dull-witted.
One should wander this earth alone, free from attachment, with senses restrained, sporting in the self, delighting in the self, possessed of the self, and possessing equal vision toward all. (52)
The wise man should play like a child, act skillfully like one who is dull-witted,
speak like a madman, and the learned man should conduct himself in the world according to the ways of common folk.
Whether insulted or humiliated by the wicked, mocked or even envied; beaten or imprisoned, or distressed by the lack of livelihood; || 54 ||
Defecated upon, urinated upon, or shaken in many ways by those who know not better, one who desires his own welfare and has fallen into distress should uplift himself by means of his own self. (55)
Since honor causes the supreme ruin of the power of yoga,
the yogi who is disregarded by people attains the perfection of yoga.
In that manner, the yogi should indeed conduct himself without violating the dharma of the virtuous,
so that people might hold him in contempt and not seek his company.
One who is disciplined should not harbor malice toward those born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth, through actions of speech, mind, or body; and one should avoid all attachments. (58)
Having abandoned those defects— namely desire and anger, as well as pride, greed, delusion, and the rest— the wandering mendicant becomes free from fear.

For that reason as well, one must perform action for the sake of gathering the world; thus he says: "The blessing," etc. Nor should one cause others to do it. If the sage seeks what is beneficial, then [he should avoid] "untrue scriptures. He himself should abandon excessive speech, yet he should not fail to attend to his disciples. He should not employ exposition for the purpose of teaching non-self-scriptures.

The meaning is that one should not undertake any undertakings anywhere and should be free from all volitional constructions (niḥsaṃkalpa). Even though he is omniscient and a seer (kavi), and a sage (muni) who should move about with companions, [the text] says "alone" (eka) to address this. One who knows the true nature of everything apart from Brahman should act like a child at play, be skillful in all matters like an insentient being, and speak like a madman.

Even one who knows the true meaning of the scriptures (nigama) should not, while practicing his course of conduct, manifest the thought, "Let this be," or "Let this not be. For he may be reviled by others due to the conjunction of time and karma. He who brings about either honor or supreme humiliation for one who is absorbed in the contemplation of the true nature of Brahman experiences a fruit corresponding to his own action.

Since this is so, he says "by people" (janena) to show that by enduring honor, beating, and so forth from others, the yogi becomes worthy of the fruit of yoga. He should conduct himself in such a way that the perfection of yoga arises through endurance. This means that one should not personally fail to perform one's own duties, which constitutes an abuse of the true dharma. "Virtuous people" (santaḥ janāḥ) refers to those who, even if they do not personally consider him to be good...

He says that one should not be a hater of living beings in general—starting with "jarāyuja" (viviparous)—and furthermore, that desire and anger should not be directed toward the class of living beings as such. (Verses 47–59)
Eating alms, silence, austerity, and especially meditation, along with right knowledge and detachment— this is considered the specific duty of a mendicant.
Constantly clad in saffron robes and devoted to the practice of meditation,
he should dwell at the edge of a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a temple;
he should always subsist on alms and never eat food from a single source.
As long as purity of mind has not been attained, one should constantly practice purification;
having entered the mendicant life therein, the pure-souled one may wander wherever he pleases. (62)
Perceiving Janārdana everywhere, both outside and within,
wandering everywhere in silence, he is free from stain like the wind.
Equanimous in pain and pleasure, patient, and consuming whatever came into his hands, he looked with equal regard— free from enmity— at birds, cows, horses, deer, and other creatures.
Meditating upon Viṣṇu with the mind as the Supreme Self and the Lord, contemplating supreme bliss, and remembering "I am indeed Brahman. (65)

Having understood this, having maintained the restraint of the mind, having become free from worldly expectations, and having donned the garment of space (the sky-clad state), one should always abandon the entire cycle of existence through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
turning away from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of the constant contemplation of one's true nature, one becomes liberated according to the analogy of the bee and the insect.
"It comes to be"—this is the secret teaching (Upaniṣad). || 66 ||

The specific duty (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the ascetic (*yati*), however, is subsisting on alms and so forth. Until the purification of the mind is achieved, one should perform the hearing of Vedānta and other practices preceded by the observance of vows and duties appropriate to one's own stage of life (*āśrama*).
Thereafter, having renounced (*saṃnyasya*), whether wandering everywhere or staying in one place, one should engage in the constant contemplation of Brahman.
He says that one should act thus: "by means of the mind. Having become steady in a single posture, "contemplating" means passing the time while recollecting [the truth].

By this much of the text, he states that through the knowledge of the meaning expressed therein, having become an Avadhūta, one becomes free from the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself—saying, "having known thus. Having known in this way...

Having taken up the mental staff (*manodaṇḍa*), by which the outward-turned mind is disciplined— that [mind] being the Brahman non-different from the inner self— one becomes free from false knowledge, realizing that nothing exists apart from one's own self even as a mere appearance, because the mind is the locus for its own dissolution; thus, having become an Avadhūta clothed only in space.

Having become free from the delusion that asks whether this world—which is turned away from one’s own self—exists or does not exist, one becomes liberated through the contemplation of one's true nature (svarūpa) by means of the "bee-and-worm" analogy. This is in accordance with the statement of the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda: "The worm, meditating upon the bee, is transformed into a bee."
The meaning is that,
at the very moment of awakening to the realization that Brahman— which is established through the negation of everything else— is one's own non-dual self alone,
one becomes liberated from the delusion of anything other than oneself. Thus ends the word "Upaniṣad."
This marks the conclusion of the fifth instruction. || 60–66 ||
Thus ends the fifth instruction.
The Sixth Instruction:
Inquiry into the Means for Attaining Liberation.
Then Nārada said to the Grandfather: "O Blessed One, through the practice of that [means], according to the analogy of the bee and the worm..."

Regarding how that practice is performed, the Grandfather (Brahmā) said: "One should dwell with speech devoted to truth, distinguished by knowledge and dispassion, remaining only as the residual body. (1)

It has been stated that one becomes liberated through the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*). With the desire to know the means for that, Nārada questions the Grandfather (Brahmā); this is introduced with the word "atha" (now). Being thus questioned by Nārada, the Blessed One accepts his inquiry and delivers the reply; this is expressed by the words "tam āha pitāmahaḥ" (the Grandfather said to him).
In all circumstances, he is characterized by speech that is pleasant, beneficial, and truthful to all living beings, as well as by knowledge and dispassion. || 1 ||
Know that knowledge is the body, dispassion is the life-force, tranquility and self-restraint are the eyes, the mind is the mouth, the intellect is the faculty,
the twenty-five principles are the limbs, and the five states are the five great elements.

Action, devotion, knowledge, and dispassion are the branches; waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state are the four states of consciousness; and the fourteen organs are like the pillars of a boat.

Thus, having brought this boat under one's own control by means of one's own intellect—just as a helmsman controls a boat or a driver controls an elephant—one realizes that everything other than oneself is a mere creation.

Thinking that all is transitory, the dispassionate person should always proclaim, "I am Brahman," and nothing else whatsoever should be known apart from himself; having become liberated while living, he should dwell thus.

One becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. One should not conduct oneself with the thought "I am not Brahman," but rather, constantly realizing "I am Brahman" throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, one should attain the fourth state (turiya) and proceed to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 2 ||

In response to the inquiry as to what the body of the wise (vidvad-deha) is like, he describes that body: "Knowledge," etc. Know that the knowledge of the lower Brahman (aparabrahma-jñāna) is its body; dispassion toward the phenomenal world of non-Brahman (abrahma-prapañca) is its life-force, which is the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa); tranquility (śānti) and self-restraint (dānti) are its eyes; and the principle of the mind (manas-tattva) is its mouth.

The meaning is that the face is the inward-facing consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*). Intellect (*buddhi*) is the sixteen-fold set of *kalās*, beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *nāman*; for intellect alone is the *kalā*, since it is by intellect that the *kalās* are conceptualized. These consist of the ten faculties of speech, hearing, and the organs of action and cognition;
the five objects, sound and so forth; the five vital breaths, *prāṇa* and so forth; the fourfold internal organ; and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

The twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are the constituent parts (*avayava*). The states (*avasthā*)—waking (*jāgrat*), dreaming (*svapna*), deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turīyātīta*)—as well as the five gross elements beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*), action (*karman*), devotion (*bhakti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and dispassion (*vairāgya*), constitute the branches (*śākhā*).
The arms, which stand in the place of branches, are likewise included. Furthermore, the fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*) consist of the waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fourth states.
The fourteen instruments— namely, the ten faculties of action, knowledge, and the senses, together with the fourfold internal organ—
are like pillars set in soft mud. Even so, even in this state,
[he remains steady] like a helmsman, a steersman who guides a boat, even when that boat has touched the mud.

It leads one onto the true path. Through the direct realization that nothing exists apart from oneself and that one is indeed Brahman itself, one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and dwells having accomplished all that was to be done. Even in the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), one does not behave as "I am not Brahman," but rather constantly maintains the realization: "I am Brahman."

The meaning is that one should meditate [upon this]. To the question "What follows from that?", it is said: "In the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states as they occur through the perspective of one's own ignorance.

One who constantly contemplates "I am Brahman" reaches the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), which is accomplished through *jīvanmukti*—liberation while living—regardless of whether the three states of waking and so forth exist or not; and from that, one attains the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītatva*), which is liberation after death (*videhamukti*).
The meaning is that one should worship. || 2 ||
The means for attaining the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is as follows:

day is waking, night is dreaming, midnight is deep sleep; thus, within a single state, there are four states. These depend upon the fourteen organs, each of which is governed by one of the [five] instruments.
The functions of the eye and the other [senses] are as follows: the grasping of visible form by the eye, the grasping of sound by the two ears, and [the grasping of taste] by the tongue. (p.

The tasting of flavors belongs to the tongue; the grasping of odors to the nose; the activity of speech to the voice; the grasping of objects to the hands; the movement of locomotion to the feet; the evacuation of waste to the anus; the grasping of pleasure to the generative organ; and the grasping of touch to the skin. And the intellect (*buddhi*) is dependent upon these for the apprehension of objects. One perceives through the intellect (*buddhi*), and through the mind (*citta*).
It wills; it acts with the sense of "I" through the ego. Having cast off these [notions], the individual soul (jīva) becomes a living being through identification with the body.

Like a householder through identification with a house, the jīva moves about within the body. In the eastern petal is the occurrence of merit; in the southeast, sleep and laziness; in the south, a cruel intellect; in the southwest—

Having thus understood the face [of the deity], one should know that peace is in the northeast, knowledge in the pericarp, detachment in the filaments, and contemplation of the self likewise [in the other directions]. || 3 ||

What is that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta)? What is the means for its attainment? To this he says: "The sky," and so forth. Within Brahman, which transcends the fourth, those ignorant of their own true nature (svājña) have conceptualized the state of the fourth (turyāvasthā) as the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya). Therein, that which transcends the fourth alone shines as the non-attached fourth. In that context, day and night are conceptualized within the fourth. Therein...

Waking during the day, dreaming at night, and deep sleep occurring at midnight—thus the three states are established. Within each of these states, four further states will subsequently be explained. In accordance with that, [the following concerns] those [states] dependent upon each respective organ, such as the mind and so forth.

The functions of the fourteen instruments, beginning with speech and including the eyes and so forth, are now described— from "the eye's grasping of form" up to "I act through the ego. Having emitted these— that is, having specifically created them— the individual soul (*jīva*), by means of the conceit of identity with the body as a composite of those [instruments], becomes as if it has attained the state of a living being (*jīvabhāva*) while being nothing other than the Fourth Consciousness (*turyacaitanya*).

It occurs as follows: within the body, in the eight-petaled, adorned heart-lotus delimited by that [subtle body], the individual soul (*jīva*) moves about like a householder who, out of attachment to his home, wanders among the petals starting from the east in successive order.
There, having been characterized by mental states such as merit and so forth in the eight petals beginning with the east, as he enters the northeast petal—

Through the movement through the pericarp, one attains detachment from the phenomenal world that is other than oneself; then, by knowing the true nature of the face of consciousness within its filaments, the wise person, simultaneously with that knowledge, remains as nothing but the Brahman beyond the fourth state (turyātīta). || 3 ||
The nature of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta) consists of the states of the living being: first, waking; second, dreaming; third, deep sleep; and fourth, [the state beyond].

The Fourth (Turiya) is devoid of the four states; it is beyond the Fourth. It is one alone, distinct from the divisions of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and the Witness (Taṭastha). "I am that Brahman—the one God, the Witness, and devoid of attributes"—thus one should declare. Otherwise, there would be the four states beginning with waking in the waking state, the four states beginning with dreaming in the dream state, and [the four] in deep sleep.

There are four states beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*) in the fourth (*turīya*), and four states beginning with the fourth in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). However, it is not so for the one who is beyond the fourth and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Through the gross, subtle, and causal forms—namely Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Īśvara—the Witness (*sākṣin*) alone remains constant throughout all states. Furthermore, is He a detached observer? He is neither detached nor an observer.
Because it is the seer, it is not the seer itself [in its own nature]. The individual soul (*jīva*) is touched by agency, enjoyership, egoism, and so forth;

that which is other than the *jīva* is not touched. If it is argued that the *jīva* is also not touched, we say no. Through the conceit of being the *jīva*, there arises the conceit of being the field (*kṣetra*); through the conceit of the body, there is the state of being a *jīva*. This state of being a *jīva*—

The space within a jar is not distinct from the [great] space; it is only due to this separation that one performs the contemplation through the mantra "I am He" (so 'ham) by means of the designation of inhalation and exhalation. Having realized this, one should abandon the conceit of the body; he who no longer possesses the conceit of the body is called Brahman itself. || 4 ||

Furthermore, as to what the nature of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta) is, he says: "the state like that of the individual soul" (jīvavadavasthā). Among the four states presided over by the individual soul—namely, the first state being waking (jāgrat), the second the dreaming state (svapna), the third the deep sleep state (suṣupti), and the fourth the state of the fourth (turya)—[this refers to the state beyond them].

That which is devoid of the four states beginning with waking— the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta)— is so called because the attainment of that state beyond the fourth is preceded by the negation of the fourfold states of waking and the rest. The meaning is that whether the delusion of one's own ignorance and other such perceptions exists or not,
only the non-dual, absolute Self, the state beyond the fourth, remains.
Because the single Self alone is associated with states such as waking and so forth, it becomes characterized by the distinctions of Viśva and the others, but not inherently;

inherently, it is one alone. He says "Viśva," etc., [to show] that through the knowledge of that [Self], there occurs the attainment of its state, by means of the distinctions of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña, which arise from association with states such as waking and so forth, as well as the distinction of the "neutral" (taṭastha).
The Self that is experienced is indeed one alone.

110) The one God is the witness and devoid of qualities; He is the one self-luminous essence of consciousness, the God who [is distinct from] the three qualities which are His own objects of witnessing.

This is for the purpose of proclaiming the state of being without attributes (nirguṇatva) that is devoid of all counter-correlates (niṣpratiyogika). One should utter: "I am that Brahman which is thus devoid of attributes and without counter-correlates. One should then maintain the contemplation (anusaṃdhāna) that "That is my own Self alone" (tat svamātram).
The meaning is that from this, there occurs the attainment of that very state (tadbhāvāpatti). He states another alternative: "If not," and so forth.

It should be understood that the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*) is that which is free from the conceptualization of the four states beginning with waking. Otherwise, that in which the divisions of waking-waking and so forth—distinguished by the four states—are not perceived, but rather the manifestation of the portion of the fourth-of-the-fourth (*turyaturyāṃśa*), is the fourth-of-the-fourth (*turyaturya*), which is Brahman beyond the fourth and nothing else. Of this state beyond the fourth...

Because there is an absence of any conceptualization of division in that which is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and is the fourth-of-the-fourth (turyaturya), it is said—through its association with the gross and so forth—that it possesses the nature of Viśva and the rest, its state as the witness of all, and its being untouched by any conceptualization.

This is expressed in the verse beginning with "sthūla. The "witness" (sākṣī) is the seer (draṣṭā). If it is argued that the Lord (Īśvara) is merely an external bystander (taṭastha), [the response is: one who is a bystander is not a witness-seer.

It must be so, because [the Self] is perceived by the indifferent witness as the Lord conditioned by the seed (bīja). Therefore, this [Self] is not merely a seer; rather, the meaning is that it is devoid of the conceit of agency and the like. Otherwise, the individual soul (jīva) alone would have to be the seer; hence he says: "by the notion of agency," etc. The individual soul is touched by the conceptualization of agency and so forth.

The Witness, however, is untouched by that [conditioning], because it is entirely devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding everything; thus he says, "the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*)," indicating that there is a great difference between these two. The meaning is that there is a distinction between the living soul and the Witness, like that between the space within a jar and the great cosmic space. Having abandoned the notion of being a living soul, [one realizes] "I am the Witness of all."

He states that through knowledge one becomes Brahman itself: "Due to the separation... etc. Due to the separation between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Witness (*sākṣin*), the *jīva*—under the guise of inhalation and exhalation—attained the state of being a *jīva* during its own state of ignorance. Through self-knowledge, upon the removal of that ignorance, it realizes: "I am that very same [Self]."

"I shall be the witness of all; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), [the distinctions of] being a living soul (*jīvatva*) or being a witness (*sākṣitva*) and so forth—by that alone [the soul] remains. Having thus realized that the living soul is indeed Brahman, [the text] says "in this way" (*evam*).
As long as there is the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, so long does one remain a living soul (*jīvatva*); when this [person]...
The meaning is that when one completely abandons the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, there is no dispute that he himself is Brahman. || 4 ||
Abandoning false conduct and practicing true conduct, having renounced attachment, conquered anger, eating light food, and subdued the senses,
one should close the doors [of the senses] with the intellect and fix the mind in meditation. || 5 ||
In empty spaces, in caves, and in forests,
the yogi, ever-disciplined, should always properly undertake meditation. (6)
A knower of yoga who seeks success should never go to a guest-offering, a śrāddha, a sacrifice, a divine procession, a festival, or among great crowds.
In such a way that people despise him and treat him with contempt, so should the yogi conduct himself; he must not defile the path of the virtuous.
The staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind—these three are his;
he whose staffs are thus restrained is a great ascetic, a *tridaṇḍin*.
That ascetic who, when the smoke has ceased and the fire is extinguished,
goes to the houses of the foremost brahmins to collect honey-like alms, is considered the most excellent of all.
He who accepts alms with a staff while remaining within his own dharma without cause for distress,
and who persists therein without falling into world-weariness— he is indeed a lowly ascetic.
He who does not go again to that house from which he specifically received alms due to its habitual impression is known as a true ascetic (yati), and no other. || 12 ||
[He who knows] that which is devoid of body, senses, and so forth; the witness of all; ultimate consciousness; whose nature is bliss; and self-luminous. || 13 ||
He who knows the supreme reality becomes truly one who has transcended the castes and stages of life;
for caste, stage of life, and the like are merely imagined within the body through Māyā.
"Those [attributes] never belong to me, who am of the nature of consciousness";
he who knows this through the Vedāntas becomes one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramī). || 15 ||
He whose conduct regarding caste and stage of life has dissolved through the vision of his own Self,
having transcended all castes and stages of life, abides in his own Self. (16)

The man who, having transcended his own stages of life (āśramas) and social classes (varṇas), abides in the Self alone, is declared by those who know the meaning of all the Vedas to be one who has gone beyond both class and stage (ativarṇāśramī). || 17 ||
Therefore, O Nārada, all the castes and stages of life belonging to others are superimposed upon the Self through delusion by one who does not know the Self. (18)

For those who have realized Brahman, O Nārada, there is neither injunction nor prohibition, nor any conceptualization of what is to be avoided and what is not; such is the case, or otherwise, it is not so.

He proceeds to enumerate the entirety of the true conduct (*saccaryā*) of ascetics who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), preceded by the abandonment of false conduct, beginning with the words "having abandoned," and so forth.

The meaning is: having closed the doors—the gates through which objects are perceived—with the intellect (*buddhi*), that is, having covered them with the mind (*dhi*), one should fix the mind upon the meditation on Brahman. He concludes the section on the place of meditation:

"Regarding the phrase 'in empty [places]': he states his inaccessible location with the words 'as a guest. He describes his triple staff with the words 'speech,' etc., referring to silence, fasting, and breath control. Regarding the rules for the mendicant's begging, the obstacles to their violation are also stated: 'free from smoke,' and so forth."
He states the definitions of the primary, the secondary, and the discarded [meanings] with the words "ya" (who): "svayaṃprabham" means the self-luminous element of consciousness. || 5-19 ||
For one who desires to know [the Self], there is the injunction for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth,
provided that he has become dispassionate toward all beings, even up to the station of Brahmā (Viriñci),
and has torn away his affection for everything, including children, wealth, and the like. (20)
Possessing faith in the paths to liberation and desiring to obtain knowledge of Vedānta, one should approach a teacher who knows Brahman, carrying an offering in hand. (21)
Having fully satisfied him with services for a long time with a concentrated mind,
he should always listen to the meaning of the Vedānta texts with great composure.
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, and devoid of all attachments, being always endowed with tranquility and other virtues, he beholds the Self within the self. (23)
Dispassion always arises solely through the vision of the defects of saṃsāra;
for one who is dispassionate toward saṃsāra, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) follows—of this there is no doubt. (24)
The seeker of liberation known as a *parahaṃsa* should practice the knowledge of Brahman—the direct and sole means to liberation—by means of hearing the Vedānta and other such methods. (25)

For the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, one who is called a "supreme swan" (parahaṃsa) should be endowed with all the means of practice, such as tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. || 26 ||
Devoted to the study of the Vedānta, peaceful, self-controlled, with senses conquered, fearless, free from the sense of "mine," eternally beyond dualities, and without possessions. || 27 ||
He should wear a worn-out loincloth, or he may be shaven-headed or even naked;
he should be wise, a yogi possessing the knowledge of Vedānta, free from the sense of "mine," and devoid of egoism.
One who is equal toward friends and others, friendly toward all living beings alike, being alone, a man of knowledge with a tranquil self—he alone crosses over, and no other. (29)
Devoted to the welfare of his gurus, he should dwell there for one year; remaining vigilant in the observances (niyamas), he should always abide by the restraints (yamas).
And having finally attained that unsurpassed yoga of knowledge,
he should traverse this earth in accordance with the non-contradiction of dharma.
Then, at the end of a year, having abandoned the three stages of life, he attained the supreme stage of life, the unsurpassed yoga of knowledge.
Having obtained permission from his gurus, he should indeed wander this earth,
free from attachment, having conquered anger, moderate in diet, and with senses subdued. (33)
These two do not shine by performing contrary actions:
the householder who is devoid of enterprise, and the mendicant who is preoccupied with worldly affairs. (34)
One becomes intoxicated upon seeing a woman, and one becomes intoxicated by drinking liquor;
therefore, one should avoid from afar a woman whose very glance is poison. (35)
One should avoid conversing with women, as well as addressing them or sending messages to them; one should also avoid dancing, singing, laughter, and slanderous talk. (36)

O Nārada, for this [state], there is no bathing, no recitation, no worship, no fire-oblation, no ritual practice, and no performance of rites such as the fire-sacrifice; indeed, none of these exist here.
There is no worship, no rites for the ancestors, no pilgrimages, and no vows;
there is neither merit nor demerit, nor ritual injunction, nor worldly activity. (38)
The yogi should completely renounce all ritual actions and worldly conduct in every respect,
as well as [harm to] worms, insects, moths, and likewise trees.
A wise ascetic whose mind is fixed on the supreme reality should not destroy living beings;
he is eternally inward-turned, pure, tranquil in soul, and possessed of a self-sufficient intellect. (40)
O Nārada, dwell in this world having abandoned all internal attachments;
like a sage wandering alone, move through a land that is without a king.
Free from praise, free from salutation, and indeed free from the utterance of "svadhā," the ascetic should have no fixed abode,
whether moving or stationary, and should subsist on whatever comes by chance.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
115) He states the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa) for one who desires to know: "having become detached" (virajya).
This means having turned away from all beings—from the fruits of karma that bestow sovereignty over the earth up to the state of Viriñci (Brahmā).

The meaning is that one should renounce after becoming dispassionate even toward [worldly] purposes and attaining detachment; for there is a Smṛti text stating, "Having renounced, one should engage in hearing (śravaṇa). The further meaning is that, having become one whose collection of faculties is concentrated, one should perform the hearing of all Vedānta texts in the presence of a teacher approved by oneself, until the five defects such as doubt are eliminated.

In accordance with the aphorism of Vyāsa, "There is repetition because of the repeated instruction," one should practice hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, accompanied by tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues, until the realization of the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman" becomes firmly established.

Thus, according to the statement of the venerable teacher Bhagavatpāda: "What follows from this? To this he says: "One who is free from the sense of 'mine' regarding the identification with everything from one's wife up to one's own body. Since the knowledge born of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth leads to liberation (*kaivalya*), for that very reason, having renounced those activities that obstruct hearing and the rest, and having become endowed with tranquility (*śamatha*) and other qualities—
He says—starting with the words "saṃsāra"—that one should engage in hearing alone until the attainment of the fruit of knowledge.

The meaning is that having abandoned the three stages of life, such as the *kuṭīcaka* and others, one enters the supreme stage, namely the stage of the *paramahaṃsa*. Regarding the phrase "then, having obtained permission," he explains what kind of person one should become: [he says]...

He says that one should become averse to conversation with women who cause delusion, etc., by stating "one becomes intoxicated. Because it is so, therefore [he says this]. He states that for one who has seen the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no duty such as bathing, recitation, and so forth, by saying "no.
Regarding the point that action must be performed for the sake of maintaining the world (*lokasaṃgraha*), he says "one should completely abandon," namely, injury to moving and stationary beings.
He says that one should not act [thus] with the words "kṛmi" (worms), etc. A moving place is a deserted house and the like because it is perishable;

a non-moving place is a mountain and the like because of its stability. One should be "accidental," meaning one should be content with whatever is obtained by chance. For acting according to one's own whims is not possible, because the intention to engage in or desist from action would be impossible.
Thus ends the word "Upaniṣad," signifying the conclusion of the sixth instruction. || 20-42 ||
Thus ends the sixth instruction.
The Seventh Instruction: The Observances of the Ascetic.
Now, when asked how the observance of an ascetic is to be performed, the Grandfather (Brahmā), placing Nārada at his head, spoke.
Being dispassionate, he who maintains a fixed residence during the rainy season should wander alone for eight months and not dwell in one place.
A mendicant, out of fear, should not stay in one spot like a deer; he should not allow his own movement to be obstructed by grasping at anything.

One should not cross a river with one's hands, nor climb a tree, nor attend a festival for a deity. Abandoning all such things, subsisting on food through the "bee-like" mode of life (*madhukaravṛtti*),
becoming emaciated and avoiding the increase of fat, one should reject clarified butter as if it were blood, and food from a single source as if it were minced meat.

It is like a fragrant ointment that is an impure smear, like a garment from an outcaste, like a vessel for leftovers, like anointing with oil, like the pleasure of sexual union with a woman, like urine, like desire, like the flesh of a cow,
like a region frequented by those one knows, like a settlement of Caṇḍālas, like gold that is a serpent’s hood, and like the Kālakūṭa poison.
He regarded the assembly hall as a cremation ground, the capital city as the Kumbhīpāka hell,
and food gathered in one place as a funeral offering; having abandoned worldly activity and the perception of other bodies,
he left his own country and departed from familiar lands, experiencing the joy of recovering a forgotten object.
As if recollecting his own bliss, having forgotten the locus of identification with his own body,
he should regard his body as a corpse to be abandoned; like a thief released from prison,
he should dwell far away, leaving behind his children, relatives, and place of birth, taking only what is obtained without effort.
Being intent on the contemplation and continuous application of the Brahman-praṇava, liberated from all ritual actions, having burnt away desire,

anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and the like, transcending the three qualities (guṇas), free from the six waves (ūrmi), devoid of the six transformations of being (bhāva-vikāra), truthful in speech, pure, and free from malice.
He should stay for one night in a village, five nights in a town, five nights in a field, and five nights at a sacred ford;
being homeless and firm-minded, he should not speak untruths. He may dwell alone in mountain caves, or he may wander with two companions;
he may visit a village with three, and a city with four.
"A city has four gates; thus, a monk should wander alone. He should give no opportunity there for the fourteen causes [of distraction].
Having experienced the perfection of detachment through uninterrupted knowledge, he is not intoxicated.
Reflecting within himself that there is nothing else whatsoever distinct or separate from him, and seeing only his own true nature everywhere, he attains liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

Having understood the fourfold nature of his being until the cessation of the appearance of the *prārabdha* karma, he should remain until the fall of the body in constant contemplation of his true nature. || 1 ||
Having heard the various modes of conduct for the *kuṭīcaka* and other orders, Nārada, desiring to know the specific details once more, questioned the Grandfather (Brahmā).

[The author] says that the Grandfather, through the sequence of related topics, instructed him on everything—both what had been previously stated and what had not—beginning with the words "one who is detached" (*virakta*). If one has performed the means such as *śravaṇa* and so forth, or if one is ineligible for them, then for eight months he should remain alone.

He should wander according to the manner described as "one night in a village. However, during the four-month rainy season (*cāturmāsya*), the mendicant should dwell in one place; the meaning is that he should dwell in one place during the rains for fear that there might be harm to living beings. After the four-month period, he should never stay in one place like a *sāraṅga* deer; here, the prohibition against staying in one place refers to all other times.

One should not accept the request, "May you stay for a few days," [thinking] "if [the body] has firm limbs" or "anointing with fragrances. One should not perceive another body with a mind that considers it distinct from Brahman.
Where those who possess identification with their own bodies reside, there is the forgetting of the location of that identification with one's own body. [The sixteen...]

Freed from all actions that are other than himself, having no fixed abode anywhere, he should wander alone during his travels. When circumstances such as the *cāturmāsya* (four-month rainy season retreat) arise, he may travel through two villages, or three, or four; he may travel through a city.
The meaning is that, under the pretext of a pilgrimage to the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*), the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) should wander alone.

Having abandoned the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself regarding the fourteen instruments, beginning with speech—[the word] "from all" (sarvataḥ) refers to everything from Viśva, Virāj, and Otrā up to the end of the non-conceptual state of the fourth-turīya; this is established by the removal of the portions to be discarded within those states, such as Otrā and so forth.
There is a distinction among the Kuṭīcaka and other [orders] regarding the observances of bathing and so on.
The *kuṭīcaka* performs the ritual bath three times a day; the *bahūdaka*, twice; the *haṃsa*, once;
the *paramahaṃsa*, the mental bath; the *turyātīta*, the ash-bath; and the *avadhūta*, the wind-bath. || 2 ||

(On page 118: The vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) belongs to the *kuṭīcaka*; the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) belongs to the *bahūdaka*; both the vertical and triple marks belong to the *haṃsa*; the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*) belongs to the *paramahaṃsa*; and the sectarian mark (*tilakapuṇḍra*) belongs to the one who has transcended the fourth state (*turīyātīta*).
For the Avadhūta there is nothing; for both the Turīyātīta and the Avadhūta, there is nothing.

The Kuṭīcaka performs shaving once a season; the Bahūdaka performs shaving every two seasons; there is no shaving for the Haṃsa, nor for the Paramahaṃsa; if there is shaving, it is only at the solstices; and for the Turīyātīta and the Avadhūta, there is no shaving at all. || 4 ||

The Kuṭīcaka subsists on food from a single house; the Bahūdaka on honey-gathering (food collected from many); the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa use their hands as a bowl; the Turīyātīta uses a cow's mouth (eating only what is placed in his hand); and the Avadhūta follows the lifestyle of a python (living on whatever comes spontaneously). || 5 ||

The *kuṭīcaka* has two cloths; the *bahūdaka*, one cloth; the *haṃsa*, a fragment [of a cloth]; the *paramahaṃsa*, nakedness (*digambara*) or a single loincloth (*ekakauṣīna*); and for the *turīyātīta* and the *avadhūta*, the state of wearing only their natural form (*jātarūpadharatva*).
A deerskin (*ajina*) is prescribed for the *haṃsa* and the *paramahaṃsa*, but not for the others.

For the Kuṭīcaka and Bahūdaka, worship consists of ritual offerings to the deity; for the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, it is mental worship; for the Turīyātīta and Avadhūta, it is the contemplation of "I am He" (so'ham-bhāvanā).
The Kuṭīcaka and Bahūdaka have the authority for the recitation of mantras; the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa have the authority for meditation; no one else has the authority for instruction. || 8 ||
For the Kuṭīcaka and Bahūdaka, there is the human praṇava; for the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, there is the internal praṇava; and for the Turyātīta and Avadhūta, there is the Brahman-praṇava. || 9 ||

119) For the *kuṭīcaka* and *bahūdaka*, there is [the duty of] hearing (*śravaṇa*); for the *haṃsa* and *paramahaṃsa*, there is reflection (*manana*); and for the *turīyātīta* and *avadhūta*, there is meditation (*nididhyāsana*).
Thus, the seeker of liberation, always recollecting the *tāraka* which delivers one from *saṃsāra*, is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
According to his specific qualification, the ascetic should dwell [in this way] and seek the means for attaining absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 11.
For the *kuṭīcaka* and the others, there is a variety of practices such as bathing, the sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), shaving, eating, clothing, worship of the deity, mantras, and the *praṇava*;
however, for those two [the *kuṭīcaka* and *bahūdaka*], the sectarian mark exists because they act according to the will of another. For the *paramahaṃsa*, there is no shaving.
Furthermore, since the external *praṇava* of the collective (*samaṣṭi*) to be described hereafter consists of four morae (*mātrā*), it is a human *praṇava*.
The internal *praṇava* of the *haṃsa* and *paramahaṃsa* consists of eight *mātrās* as will be described;

it is the internal [recitation] because it pertains to the fourth state (*turya*) by virtue of consisting of sixteen *mātrās*. Recalling the *tāraka*, which is named the *brahmapraṇava* and is the savior from *saṃsāra*:

One should seek the means to liberation preceded by the performance of one's own specific duties, such as those of the *kuṭīcaka* and other orders. For the duty of the *paramahaṃsa* and others is not to be performed by them; regarding this, there is a Smṛti text: "Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed. The word "Upaniṣad" indicates the conclusion of the seventh instruction.
Thus ends the seventh instruction.
The Eighth Instruction:
Inquiry into the Nature of the Savior. Then Nārada questioned the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, regarding that which delivers one from the cycle of worldly existence.

"Be gracious; speak," [they said]. "So be it," the Supreme Lord began to speak. "Om is Brahman"—thus the *praṇava* is threefold, being internal, external, and both, according to its nature as the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), the collective (*samaṣṭi*), and the creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
These are the *brahmapraṇava*, the *antarpraṇava*, and the *vyāvahārikapraṇava*.
The external *praṇava* is the *ārṣa-praṇava*. The *virāṭ-praṇava* consists of both. The *saṃhāra-praṇava*, the *brahma-praṇava*, and the *ardhamātrā-praṇava* [are also included]. || 1 ||

Having thus received the supreme instruction from his grandfather, Nārada then asked what he desired to know regarding the true nature of Tāraka. Acknowledging that question, the Parameṣṭhin spoke the answer; this is introduced with the words "atha" (now).
The Parameṣṭhin began to speak. What was it? "Oṃ is Brahman."

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "Know that Brahman is the meaning of the Praṇava of Brahman," together with the modes such as the gross aspect (*sthūlāṃśa*) and others residing in the form of the parts of the Praṇava, which has entered into the state of individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*), along with the presiding deities (*adhyakṣa*) of those individuals and so forth. In that regard, what is the individual? What...

Regarding the term *samaṣṭi*: the Praṇava of Brahman, which consists of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), is divided into three ways from the perspective of those lacking self-knowledge (*svājña*). How so? Because of the distinctions such as the creation of the world, its end, and its exterior. What is this [distinction] beginning with the "creation-praṇava"? Regarding this:
This *saṃhārapraṇava*— in which the vowel *a* alone is predominant and the half-measures (*ardhamātrā*) of *a* and *u* are subordinate—

is presided over by Rudra, or alternatively, it is presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; it possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the *saṃhārapraṇava* endowed with the reckoning of the three measures (*trimātrā*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara, who are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, arise from that very source;
therefore, this is the Praṇava of dissolution.

Thus, from the statement regarding the *praṇava* of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). This is the *praṇava* of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), in which the vowel *a* is primary and the vowel *u* and others are subordinate. Its presiding deity is the Four-faced One;
having taken up the *tāra* consisting of a single measure (*mātrā*), he is four-faced.
Since he created the entire universe, he must therefore be its creator.

Thus it is because of the statement regarding the *sṛṣṭipraṇava*. The nature of the internal and external *praṇavas* will be explained later. Regarding the threefold nature of the *saṃhārapraṇava*: how so? This *saṃhārapraṇava* is characterized primarily by the three *mātrās*; this *sṛṣṭipraṇava* is characterized primarily by a single *mātrā*; and the internal *praṇava* consists of eight *mātrās*.

The meaning is that the external *praṇava*, consisting of four *mātrās*, together with [the internal one] becomes the *brahmapraṇava* consisting of sixteen *mātrās*. One might ask: "Is this the only division of the *brahmapraṇava*, and is there nothing beyond this?
To this he says: "Internal," etc. One...

Regarding the statement that the *brahmapraṇava* itself is divided in many ways, it is because of the Śruti which says: "The form [of the syllable Om], containing within it the fifty phonemes, becomes manifold and assumes various forms when manifested by the consonants (*sparśa*), sibilants (*ūṣman*), and so forth."
Presiding over the five Brahmans beginning with Durga, it is the cause of the manifestation of the Vaikharī speech and is known as the conventional *tāra*.
It consists of a single measure (*mātrā*), is adorned with the fifty letters,
and is declared to be the cause of the manifestation of Vaikharī for worldly transaction.
The triad of powers beginning with Durgā, the three powers beginning with action (karma) and will (icchā),
the group consisting of the Vasus, Ādityas, and Rudras, that which has the nine Brahmās as its presiding deities,
and likewise that which has the five Brahmās as its deities— this is declared to be the meaning expressed by those [terms].

Thus it is stated regarding the empirical *praṇava*. The individual *praṇava* (*vyaṣṭi-praṇava*), which consists of four measures (*mātrā*) and exists outside the collective (*samaṣṭi*), is called the external *praṇava*. It is presided over by Viśva because the individual is external to the collective, due to its connection with the portions of the *tūla* and the *turya*.
The external Praṇava is traditionally taught, and Viśva and the others have become its denotations.

Thus it is said regarding the external *praṇava*. Because it transcends the *akāra*, *ukāra*, *makāra*, *bindu*, *nāda*, *kalā*, and *kalātīta*, it consists of seven measures (*mātrā*) and is presided over by the inner ruler of the five *brahmans*.
It is called the *ārṣa-praṇava* because it is served by the circle of *ṛṣis*.
Thus it is stated in the *Ārṣa-praṇava*. Regarding the fact that the *sthitipraṇava*, which consists of both the syllables *a* and *u*, is presided over by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, [it is said]:
"Because Viṣṇu, through the material cause (*upādāna*) of the addition of two morae (*mātrā*), [is present] daily..."
Because he protects the entire universe through his abiding power, he is therefore called Viṣṇu.

Thus it is stated in the *Sthitipraṇava*. The *Virāṭ-praṇava*, consisting of the four *mātrās* beginning with the collective *akāra*, is presided over by Virāṭ and the others; in this regard, it is said: "The *Virāṭ-praṇava* is called the union of the four collective *mātrās*."
Virāṭ and the others are the denotable meaning (vācya), while the supreme syllable (paramākṣara) is their indicated meaning (lakṣya).
Thus it is because of the statement regarding the *virāṭ-praṇava*. In the preceding section, the *saṃhāra-praṇava* was explained;
however, the *brahma-praṇava* will be discussed later. [The *ardhamātrā*] consists of the four *mātrās*, beginning with the gross (*sthūla*).

The syllable *oṃ* itself is indeed fourfold; for this *oṃ* consists of the gross, the subtle, the seed, and the witness. Herein is the description of the essential nature of the internal *praṇava* and others: "Om" is Brahman. Know that "Om"—the single-syllabled internal *praṇava*—is divided into eight parts: 1. *Oṃ* is Brahman. 2. Know "Om" to be the single-syllabled internal *praṇava*. 3. And it is divided eightfold: a. *Oṃ* is the *praṇava*. b. *Oṃ* is the supreme. c. *Oṃ* is the highest. d. *Oṃ* is the most excellent. e. *Oṃ* is the best. f. *Oṃ* is the foremost. g. *Oṃ* is the greatest. h. *Oṃ* is the unsurpassed. Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is the supreme Brahman. It is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things. It is the source of all mantras and the root of all speech. It is the essence of all Vedas and the foundation of all knowledge. It is the seed of the universe and the witness of all beings. It is the door to liberation and the path to the Absolute. By meditating upon it, one attains peace, wisdom, and the state of the Infinite. It is the eternal, unchanging, and blissful reality beyond all dualities. Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is the very embodiment of the Truth.

The syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*, along with the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), the resonance (*nāda*), the point (*bindu*), the digit (*kalā*), and the Power (*śakti*)—these constitute the fourfold [Pranava].
Among them, the letter *a* is endowed with ten thousand parts; the letter *u* is endowed with a thousand parts; the letter *m* is possessed of a hundred parts;
and the half-measure *Praṇava* has the form of infinite parts. This is the *Saguṇa-virāṭ-praṇava*.

The *saṃhāra* is the *praṇava* devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*); the *utpatti* is the *praṇava* consisting of both; [the *virāṭ* is the *praṇava* consisting of both]. Just as the *pluta* is the *virāṭ*, so the *plutapluta* is the *saṃhāra*. || 2 ||
Then he states the meaning of the internal *praṇava*: "Om. It has been explained that "Om" is Brahman.
Herein, the internal *praṇava*, consisting of eight *mātrās*, is presided over by the five Brahmans, Virāṭ, Sūtra, and Īśvara.

The Praṇava is said to consist of the eight mātrās beginning with 'a' and ending with the union [of the vowels]. It is said to be the expressed meaning of the five Brahmans, the Virāṭ, the Sūtra, and the Bīja.

Thus ends the statement regarding the internal *praṇava*. As for what was said—that this *praṇava* consists of four measures (*mātrā*) primarily—it is not that it consists of four measures exclusively; rather, its constituent parts [are also included]. He states the distinction of non-difference with its parts: "The letter *A*" and so forth. This refers to the half-measure *praṇava*.

123) Because it lacks constituent parts such as those found in the *praṇava* used for creation and so forth, and because it is partless, [the text] states that it is both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*), and in reality, it is the attributeless state devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika-nirguṇatva*). This is expressed by the words "with attributes" (*saguṇa*).

The *virāṭ-praṇava* is with attributes (*saguṇa*), because it serves as the symbol (*pratīka*) for Brahman, which is the substratum for the superimposition of all things. The *saṃhāra-praṇava* is without attributes (*nirguṇa*), because it takes as its support Brahman, which is the substratum for the negation (*apavāda*) of everything other than itself. Furthermore, there is the *utpatti-praṇava*, which possesses both natures; it is of a dual nature due to its connection with the *virāṭ* (with attributes) and the Witness (*sākṣin*) (without attributes). Thus, this [praṇava] is of a dual nature.
The meaning is that, because the Self appears as having both a qualified and an unqualified nature through the perspectives of the ignorant and the wise respectively,

and because It is the cause of the origination and so forth of the phenomenal world (prapañca) which is distinct from Itself, it is logical for the Praṇava to be its designator by way of its being the "originative Praṇava" (utpatti-praṇava). Having taken the *nirguṇa*-praṇava with its counter-correlate as the illustrative example, [the following is stated] by way of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Having first elaborated upon the sixteen measures (mātrās) which constitute both the means and the attributeless state beyond all comparison, he describes the nature of Brahman as the Praṇava with the words "Just as... By the term *plutapluta*, the fourth measure (*mātrā*) and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) are expressed. That unattached conscious essence [is] the source of the letter *A* and so forth...
Likewise, the *plutapluta* consists of half-mātrās and half-mātrās; it itself is sixteen in number.
The Virāṭ-praṇava is composed of sixteen mātrās and transcends the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
The Virāṭ-praṇava is composed of sixteen mātrās and is beyond the thirty-six principles.

How is it that [the syllable *om*] consists of sixteen measures (*mātrā*)? It is said: the letter *a* is the first, the letter *u* is the second, the letter *m* is the third, the half-measure is the fourth, the point (*bindu*) is the fifth, the resonance (*nāda*) is the sixth, the digit (*kalā*) is the seventh, that which transcends the digit (*kalātītā*) is the eighth, tranquility (*śānti*) is the ninth, that which transcends tranquility (*śāntyatītā*) is the tenth, and the state beyond mind (*unmanī*) is the eleventh.
Manonmanī is the twelfth city; Madhyamā is the thirteenth; Paśyantī is the fourteenth; and Parā is the fifteenth. Furthermore, [the sixteenth] consists of sixty-four mātrās. (p. 124)
Having attained the twofold nature of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, one attains the eightfold [powers];
this is the Praṇava of Brahman.

The meaning is that this *vīrāṭ-praṇava*—in which the fifteen-fold divisions beginning with waking-within-waking (*jāgrat-jāgrat*) arise from the gross and other aspects that are distinct from one's own Self—is the *brahma-praṇava*. But how can that *vīrāṭ-praṇava* possess the nature of the *brahma-praṇava*? Because it consists of sixteen *mātrās*. What are those *mātrās*?
Therefore, he says: "consisting of sixteen measures.

Having transcended—that is, having negated—the thirty-six principles known as the elements (*tanmātra*), the great principle (*mahattattva*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*), as well as those called knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*karman*), and vital breath (*prāṇa*) as taught in the *Varāhopaniṣad*.

The meaning is that it exists and remains as that which is beyond the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) because it is without a counterpart (*niṣpratiyogika*). The rest has already been explained. He clarifies the nature of the sixteen *mātrās*: "The letter *A*," etc.
The Brahman-Pranava consists of sixteen *mātrās*. Among these:

The entire body of authoritative evidence—including the *Pañcadaśī*, its presiding authority Viśvarūpa, the *Brahmapraṇava*, the *Taddīpikā*, and so forth—is valid. The meaning is that this is not the only proof; rather, the *Nṛsiṃhatāpinī*, the *Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka*, and other Upaniṣads are also authorities.

He states that although the single Brahman-Pranava possesses multiplicity through its connection with the constituent parts of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, it remains one in its own essential nature—beginning with the word "punar" (again). Previously, the specific characteristics of the tens of thousands of constituent parts, such as the forms of the letters of the Brahman-Pranava, were described; now, however, they are described again as being distinct from itself, because they have been the subject under discussion.
Nature (*prakṛti*). How does it possess the distinction of sixty-four *mātrās*?

In this regard, there are fifteen [states] such as the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) gross *akāra* and so forth, and likewise fifteen [states] such as the collective (*samaṣṭi*) gross *akāra* and so forth; these thirty are distinguished. Likewise, there are [the states] such as the individual and collective waking-waking (*jāgrat-jāgrat*) and so forth—

The division of Prakṛti consists of sixty-four parts. Likewise, he is called Puruṣa because he fills the entire collection of ignorance, its locus, and its effects—which are distinct from himself—with his own nature as consciousness, extending from the nine Prajāpatis up to the state of non-dual oneness (Avikalpānujñaikarasa).
As to how he possesses exactly sixty-four parts, [it is explained that] having quintuplicated the five elements, there are nine Prajāpatis.
The five Brahmās who carry out [the functions] are the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas; the five immovable inner controllers (antaryāmin) are Viśvaviśva and the others;

the fifteen are Virāḍvirāḍ and the others; and the fifteen are Otrāotrā and the others—altogether, sixty-four. Thus, the essence of non-dual consciousness itself possesses sixty-four measures (mātrā) as its feet.

Having encountered the duality of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, it itself, through the perception of mere objects, assumes the state of being possessed of qualities (*saguṇatva*) by means of the perception of the natural and the personal. Through the vision of its own Knower (*svajña*), it becomes free from the affliction of the conceptualization of the distinction between the natural and the personal.

And it attains the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). Therefore, although the *brahmapraṇava* is one, it assumes both the state of having qualities (*saguṇatva*) and the state of being devoid of qualities according to the perspective of those who do not know themselves and others. || 3 ||
The wise know him as the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman, the support of all, the supreme light, and the Lord of all;
he is composed of all the gods and contains within himself the foundation of the entire phenomenal world. || 4 ||
Time consists of all syllables; Śiva consists of all scriptures;
he is the highest of all that is heard, the object of search, and consists of all the Upaniṣads.
Know that the imperishable syllable *oṃ*, which is the primordial source arising from the three times—past, present, and future—is the very bestower of liberation. (6)
That very Self is described by the word "Brahman";
having realized that One which is undecaying and immortal, one should likewise respond with "So be it."
Having superimposed [the Self] along with the body, and likewise [realizing] identity with That through the syllable "Om," determine your own self,
consisting of the three bodies, to be the Supreme Brahman.
One should contemplate the Supreme Brahman through the successive sequence of Viśva and the others.

For this very reason, it is the support of all, being the substratum for both superimposition and negation of everything. Lest it be argued that it would possess insentience by virtue of being the support of the insentient, he says: "the Supreme Light. Of its own...
Because its nature is non-inert due to being distinct from the inert phenomenal world (jaḍaprapañca), this very one is in reality the Lord of All (sarveśvara).

Since he abides as the non-dual Brahman alone—established through the negation of everything other than himself—he is the Lord by virtue of that lordship; therefore, those who possess the vision of ultimate reality know that Self through the realization that nothing remains but themselves.

The meaning is "they know. The group of mantras also reiterates the point stated by the Brahmana: "consisting of all," and so forth. It is "consisting of all deities" because its nature is that of all the deities. Since the Lord (Īśvara), who is the substratum for the superimposition of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), is produced from this [mantra], it contains within itself the substratum of that phenomenal world. It is "consisting of all syllables."

Because it consists of the nature of the fifty phonemes and their meanings; "Time" (Kāla), because it is the measurer (*kalayitṛ*) of all, or because it is the one who brings all to an end (*kālayitṛ*).
He consists of all the Āgamas, because he is the very essence of the meaning of the scriptural teachings. He is Śiva, because he devours (grasps) all that is inauspicious apart from himself.
Furthermore—regarding the word "all": "The Vedas all proclaim that state; and all ascetic practices declare what it is."
In accordance with the Śruti, "That goal which those desiring it practice as celibacy (brahmacarya), that I shall tell you in brief: 'Om'—

this [is it]," one should seek this very Self as being nothing other than the fourth-of-the-fourth (turyaturya) state, which is the meaning of the Brahman-Pranava, as declared by all the Śrutis through the word "Om."

He must be sought after, for otherwise He would be impossible to find. He consists of all the Upaniṣads beginning with the *Īśā*, because He is the primary meaning of all the Upaniṣads. Regarding Him who is delimited by the three periods of time yet transcends them, the text says "bhūta... (the past...)—meaning, "know that very one to be the means to liberation. This is stated in the *Śrī Nṛsiṃha Uttara Tāpanīya*.

The passage beginning with "The syllable *oṃ*—this is all" and ending with "that is the Self, that is to be known," should be understood here exactly as it has been explained. He explains the portion "This Self is Brahman" with the words "That alone": having experienced that one, undecaying, immortal [reality] as *oṃ*, within that [all this] is contained.

He says "that one" (tadekam) to indicate that he follows the scriptural passage: "Having superimposed the three bodies, for it is indeed identical with that; one should meditate upon this very Self, which has three bodies, as the Supreme Brahman.
This refers to the fourfold nature of Viśva and the others.
Because of its grossness, it is the enjoyer of the gross here; because of its subtlety, it is the supreme enjoyer of the subtle.
Due to its enjoyment of bliss in unity, this Self is fourfold;
indeed, the Viśva-enjoyer, whose state is waking, has four feet and possesses gross cognition.
He has nineteen mouths, possesses the eight limbs, is all-pervading, and is the Lord;
he is the enjoyer of gross objects, the fourfold self, the universal one, Vaiśvānara, and the Supreme Person.
The Viśvajit is the first quarter; the Lord has resorted to the state of dream.
He is subtle-consciousness, naturally possessed of the eight limbs, one and not another, O scorcher of foes. 12.
The consumer of the subtle, consisting of four aspects, namely Taijasa and Bhūtarāja,
as well as Hiraṇyagarbha in his gross form— this is called the second internal quarter.
(127) As long as one desires desire, and while one does not see any dream whatsoever while asleep, that state is clearly deep sleep (suṣupta). || 14 ||
Unified, abiding in deep sleep, possessing the wealth of pure consciousness, and blissful—the Self, though consisting of eternal bliss, dwells within all living beings. (15)
Nevertheless, the enjoyer of bliss, whose mouth is the mind, who is all-pervading and imperishable, the Lord consisting of four aspects—the wise one—is designated as the third foot. || 16 ||
He is the Lord of all, he is the omniscient one, the subtle contemplator; he is the inner controller, he is the source of all, and the origin and dissolution of everything.
All three of these states of beings cause the cessation of everything;
that indeed is deep sleep, while that dream is proclaimed to be mere illusion (māyāmātra). || 18 ||

Regarding how the fourfold nature of Viśva and the others is established, it is said: "Because of grossness. Since all three of these are equally described by the scriptural statement "this is deep sleep" (*suṣuptam*), the state of deep sleep—which is the substratum where all cessation occurs and which sublates [ordinary] cognition—pertains to the triad of states beginning with waking as well.

The meaning is that they are equal in being characterized by sleep, which consists in the non-apprehension of reality (*tattva*). In the statement "dream is mere illusion" (*māyāmātra*), the meaning is that both waking and dreaming are characterized by erroneous apprehension (*anyathāgrahaṇa*). (9-18)
The fourfold nature of the fourth state (turya) is as follows:
"This [Self], though consisting of the four aspects of the fourth, is indeed of the single essence of Being-Consciousness;
and because it culminates in the fourth, it follows the principle of oneness in each [aspect]. (19)
The means for realizing the knowledge that is free from the conceptualization of "permission" and "non-permission" is as follows:

even here, one should understand that these three types of conceptualization—deep sleep, dream, and the intermediate state—are merely illusion (māyāmātra). Having understood this, one indeed becomes of the singular essence of Being-Consciousness (saccidekarasa). || 20 ||

Having explained the fourfold nature of the three states beginning with waking (*jāgrad-ādyavasthā-traya*), [the text] speaks of the fourfold nature of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) as well—according to each individual [state]—with the words "following each one" (*ekaikatvānusārataḥ*). To the question, "What is the means for establishing the pervasion of the fourth state everywhere? [the text replies]: "The ear," and so forth.
Here too, the triad beginning with *otṛ* (the hearer) is indeed in deep sleep;

for, like the non-conceptual state (*avikalpa*) of *viśvaviśva* and so forth up to *anujñaikarasa*, once the perception of the differentiation of the self's veils has ceased, immediately thereafter, one remains as the single essence of Being-Consciousness (*saccidekarasa*) by oneself alone—this is the meaning. || 19-20 ||
The Brahman-Pranava is the fourth beyond the fourth;
for this instruction is indeed divided: it is not for one of gross intellect day after day, nor for one of subtle intellect to the ultimate degree, nor for the wise, nor for anyone at all, O Sage.
Neither lacking wisdom, nor possessing wisdom on both sides, nor possessing internal wisdom; neither lacking wisdom, nor a mass of wisdom, and indeed invisible. || 22 ||

That which is without characteristics, ungraspable, beyond conventional usage, inconceivable, indescribable, and whose realization is the single Self—that is Brahman, the Praṇava. It is to be known as the Fourth (Turiya), and not anything else. Like the sun, it shines everywhere for those seeking liberation because it is the Supreme Brahman. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 23.

He elaborates upon the manifold expansion (*prapañca*)— consisting of gross forms and so forth, which are conceptualized by the ignorant regarding the true nature of the Fourth-of-the-Fourth (*turyaturya*)— simultaneously, beginning with the words "divided" and ending with "that Self is to be known.
It should be understood that this has been explained through the commentary on the *Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanī*.
He concludes the discussion on the *brahmapraṇava* with the word "sa" (that).

In this teaching, that which was described as the *turyaturīya* (the fourth of the fourth) is the *brahmapraṇava*. It alone is to be known as "its own nature" (*svamātra*) in relation to the *turyaturīya*. There is no other *turīya*, because nothing beyond the *turyaturīya* is perceived; it is the *turyaturīya* itself.
From the perspective of one's own realization, [the Self] is the support for those seeking liberation because it is that which is to be attained, like the sun which illuminates everything.
It is self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*) because it is the light even of the lights such as the sun; in reality, however, there is no conceptualization of the illuminated and the illuminator.
Whether the delusion of the vision of one's own ignorance exists or not, [the Self] shines as its own measure alone. Why? Because it is the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is that its abiding as nothing but itself is logical. The word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the eighth instruction. 21–23.
Thus ends the eighth instruction.
The Ninth Instruction: A Description of the Nature of Brahman.
Then Nārada asked, "What is the nature of Brahman? To him the Grandfather (Brahmā) said: "What..."
"Regarding the phrase 'the nature of Brahman': those who perceive that 'He is one and I am another' are but cattle, not [true] beings by their own nature.
