Having known Him thus, the wise man is liberated from the jaws of death; there is no other path for the journey. (1)
Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the source, and the person—these are to be considered.
It is the conjunction of these [that produces results], and not from the self's own being; for the self is not the master over the causes of pleasure and pain.
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities—
that One who presides over all those instruments when they are joined with Time and the Self.
Within that [wheel], one [should contemplate] the wheel with three folds, sixteen spokes, and fifty radii, possessing twenty counter-spokes;
it has six sets of eight, a single noose of universal form, a division of three paths, and a single delusion caused by two factors.
[She is] the river with five currents, whose fierce mouths are the five wombs, whose waves are the five vital breaths,
whose root is the fivefold intellect and so forth; she has five whirlpools, the forceful current of the flood of the five miseries, and fifty divisions.
We study [this] which has five sections.
In that vast wheel of Brahman, which is the source of all livelihoods and the support of all things, the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) revolves.
Having perceived the Self as distinct from the Impeller, and being thus favored by Him, one attains immortality. (6)
This is indeed the supreme Brahman that has been sung; within it are the three, as well as the syllable established in itself.
Having realized the interval therein, those who know the Vedas, being devoted to that, merge into the supreme Brahman.
The Lord sustains this entire universe, which is joined together as both the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest.
Though the Self is not the master, it perceives itself as such through its state of being an enjoyer; yet, by knowing the God, one is released from all bonds.
The Knower and the Unknowing, the two unborn ones—the Lord and the Non-Lord; for the unborn Nature (Prakṛti) is indeed one, joined with the objects of enjoyment for the experiencer.
And the infinite Self is of universal form and is a non-doer. When one perceives this triad as such, that is Brahman.
The perishable is primary matter (pradhāna), and the immortal-imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self.
Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyā). 10.
Having known the God, one is released from all fetters; with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Through profound meditation upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains absolute sovereignty over all things, being solitary and having all desires fulfilled.
This should be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known beyond this.
Having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller—all this has been declared as the threefold Brahman. (12)
That supreme Upaniṣad concerning Brahman has self-knowledge and austerity as its root.
Although the true nature of Brahman had been declared by the Grandfather (Brahmā), it was [repeated] once more for the sake of the assembly of sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest:
"If you consider [the Self] to be beyond perception, then those who perceive through the sense of duality, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' are like beasts;
they are bound by the firm fetters of their own ignorance, just as the animals being slaughtered by their owner. They [are thus].
Since [it might be thought that] animals exist by their very nature, he says: "They are not animals by nature.

This is because their nature is nothing but Brahman, which is devoid of all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika*). Having known that which always remains as the non-dual residue to be one's own self alone (*svamātra*), the wise man is liberated from the jaws of death. That wise man...

The meaning is this: at the very moment of sensation, the existence of that which is other than oneself is itself death; by means of that [realization], one is liberated from one's own ignorance, and one remains as one’s own self alone. (p. 131) [This occurs] through the cessation of the perception of that which is other than oneself, which arises from one's own ignorance.
"It exists as the means of passage. Thus, having heard the Vedānta from the mouth of Brahmā along with Nārada,
the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest gathered together, presented the doctrines beginning with Time and ending with Sāṃkhya,
and then, having refuted them as prima facie views (pūrvapakṣa), [they concluded that] that which is the ultimate reality is indeed the Self alone, and nothing other than that.

It should be understood that [this work] has concluded here, as the *Śvetāśvatara-mantra-upaniṣad*— beginning with "Time, inherent nature," and ending with "That Brahman is the supreme Upaniṣad"— has been explained word by word. Thus,
the residents of the Naimiṣa forest [learned] from the mouth of Parameṣṭhin that there is indeed nothing further to be known than this.

The meaning is that, having realized that Brahman— which is established through the negation of everything other than itself— is one's own non-dual self alone, they, having accomplished all that was to be done at the very moment of that realization, remain as that alone.
This is the fruit of knowing the scripture.

For one who, having known this, contemplates its very nature—the one who perceives this oneness—what delusion can there be, what sorrow? Therefore, from that [Brahman] arises the Virāj, the past, the present, and the future, which is imperishable. Smaller than the small and greater than the great, the Self of this living being is hidden in the secret cave of the heart.
Free from sorrow, he beholds Him—the Lord of majestic power—through the clarity of his own nature, as He who possesses that sovereign will. 15.
Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears.
He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). 16.
Having realized the Self as bodiless, abiding within bodies that are themselves unstable, great, and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve. 17.

One should know Him as the sustainer of all, possessed of inconceivable power, to be known through the specific meaning at the end of all scriptures; as higher than the high, the supreme, to be known, and as the maker of an end at the conclusion of everything. || 18 ||
To the Seer, the Ancient One, the Supreme among the Supreme Persons, the Lord of All who is worshipped by all the gods;
who is without beginning, middle, or end, infinite and imperishable; the Auspicious One, the Unfailing One, the Lotus-wombed One, and the Supporter of the Earth. (19)
All this phenomenal world, consisting of five elements and existing within the five, is veiled by its own [nature];
the infinite phenomenal world of existence, though composed of quintuplicated parts, is not concealed by its own quintuplicated components.
That which is beyond the beyond, greater than the great, eternal, auspicious, and consisting of the splendor of its own nature. || 20 ||

He says—“He who thus”—that whoever knows this scripture correctly becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. Whoever, like the assembly of sages (maunipaṭala), having known from the mouth of the Guru that Brahman is to be realized solely through knowledge accompanied by renunciation as being nothing but one’s own self (svamātra), then perceives non-difference, seeing that very nature of Brahman as his own Self; for him, in that state...

In one’s own true nature (*svarūpa*), what delusion (*moha*) could there be regarding whether something other than oneself exists or does not exist? Upon the disappearance of that [delusion], what grief (*śoka*) could there be?

For the realization of Brahman alone is preceded by the negation of grief and delusion. Since this is so, that which is delimited by time—beginning with the past—and perceived as separate from oneself through the vision of the ignorant (*svājñadṛṣṭi*), is, through the vision of the knower (*svajñadṛṣṭi*), none other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

He states that it becomes its very own nature: "the past and the future. For, in reality, there is no non-existence apart from pure Being (sanmātra), according to the Śruti: "When one sees, even here, only Being, then what else could one see as other than Being?
Thus, for one who perceives the Self in this way, there is freedom from sorrow, even in the absence of the collection of the senses.
And he states that [the Self] is the cause for the operation of the collection of instruments with the words "of the atom" (*aṇoḥ*).

Both mantras have been explained in the *Śvetāśvatara*. But how can there be the transcendence of sorrow through the knowledge of the Self, given that sorrow is observed in the Self as delimited by the body? To this, he says: "bodiless" (*aśarīram*).
Because of the absence of the three bodies that are the cause of sorrow; because of the Creator who is established as the Self of Brahmā through the negation of the three bodies;

because of the Nourisher who is the Self of Viṣṇu; and because of the Lord who is the Self of Īśvara—the inconceivable accomplisher of the unaccomplished—this is the ultimate meaning of all the Agamas: "There is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman; it is Brahman alone, for the non-existent does not exist."

The ultimate conclusion (*paramasiddhānta*) alone is the specific meaning. Those knowers of Brahman who realize their own Self as being nothing but that [pure consciousness]—that which is even beyond the supreme imperishable (*parād akṣarāt*)—must understand at once, at the final end of all things, that when everything other than themselves has been sublated, it is Brahman alone, which is one's own self alone (*svamātra*). This is to be known all at once.

Because even the functioning of feeling has ceased, if one is thus unable to perceive, then who is it that, having long worshipped the Lord characterized by such attributes as "the Seer" (kavi), attains the very Brahman devoid of distinctions through the knowledge of Brahman obtained by His grace? To this he says: "The Seer" (kavi).

The Seer (*kavi*), because of his omniscience; the Ancient (*purāṇa*), because of his being from of old; without beginning, middle, or end, because he lacks birth, abiding, and dissolution for himself. Śiva, Acyuta, Ambhoruhagarbha, Hara, Hari, and Viriñci—these are their [names].

Because it is the mountain from which [all things] sprout forth. Furthermore, regarding the word "by itself" (*svena*): when it should have been stated that "this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is pervaded by that which has attained the state of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) and so forth," the change in case-ending and gender occurs in the expression "this phenomenal world" (*idaṃ prapañcam*).
"Consisting of the five elements" (*pañcātmaka*) and so forth are qualifiers of the phenomenal world. Through its pervasion, there would be its concealment (*saṃvṛtatva*).

The qualification "uncovered" (*asaṃvṛta*) is used to exclude doubt. The reason for being uncovered is that [the Self] is "higher than the high," because it is greater even than the Great One (*mahat*), the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and so forth, due to its all-pervasiveness. In reality, it is "auspicious" (*śiva*) because of the negation of anything inauspicious other than itself. The meaning is that one should know the Self as the established realization: "I am Brahman. || 14 ||
The attainment of Brahman and its cause:
neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain Him through wisdom. (21)

"One who knows that [the Self] is neither conscious of the internal nor conscious of the external, neither gross nor subtle, neither knowledge nor ignorance, nor conscious of both, which is ungraspable and beyond conventional usage, being established within itself by its own nature—he becomes liberated; he becomes liberated," so said the Blessed Grandfather. || 22 ||
Thus, it might be argued that even one who possesses a conduct such as evil deeds could attain Brahman; to this he says "no.

This is because knowledge does not arise in one whose conduct is characterized by evil deeds and the like. If it were to arise through negligence, it would be a semblance of knowledge (*tadābhāsajñāna*).
For a semblance of knowledge is not the cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. Since this is so, therefore:

The meaning is that, through the realization of Brahman alone— which is without counterpart and in which the occurrence of misconduct and so forth is impossible— one becomes established in that very state. This is the state of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) who has transcended the gross and subtle manifestations of both the internal and external worlds.
The wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) is one who knows his own true nature. The wandering mendicant wanders alone; he remains like a deer terrified by fear.
He does not create any obstacle to movement. Having renounced everything other than his own body—(p.

Abiding by way of the sixfold path and practicing the contemplation of one's own true nature, one becomes liberated within oneself alone through the realization that everything is none other than that. Such a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is the cessation of all actions and their causal agents; he is beyond the relationship of teacher and disciple, free from possessions, and happy. Possessing nothing, he transcends both knowledge and ignorance, and transcends both pleasure and pain.

"I am He—the self-luminous light, the object of all knowledge, the omniscient, the bestower of all perfections, and the Lord of all. That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, having gone to which yogis do not return. Neither the sun nor even the moon shines there. He does not return again; he does not return again. That is absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 23.
Thus he describes the state of the wandering mendicant who is a vessel for liberation: "one who knows his own true nature" (*svasvarūpajña*).

One who knows that his own true nature is nothing but his own self (*svamātra*) is "one who knows his own true nature. Having abandoned his own ignorance and its effects, he wanders as a solitary mendicant; though surrounded by a crowd of people from the perspective of those ignorant of themselves (*svājñadṛṣṭyā*), he moves alone from his own perspective (*svadṛṣṭyā*).

From the perspective of his own ignorance, he stands like a deer terrified by fear; likewise, he does not seem to offer any resistance to his own movement. Yet, from the perspective of his own realization, even in the absence of a physical body, remaining through the practice of the alms-bowl held in the mouth as attributed by others, he performs nothing but the contemplation of his true nature day and night.

Through the realization that everything is non-different from oneself, one becomes liberated within one's own self. Devoid of the duality of action and agent, and free from even the scent of distinctions such as teacher, disciple, and scripture, one is never deluded by the suffering of saṃsāra due to the state of eternal bliss within the heart. How, then, can a mendicant who possesses nothing else be happy?

For one who possesses the wealth of Brahman alone, eternal happiness arises. Being beyond both knowledge and ignorance, the state of being beyond knowledge and ignorance is established because the manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is that which is sought; for it is stated in the *Smṛti* that "the states of being a knower and being ignorant belong only to the reflection of the Self (*ātmābhāsa*), and not to the Self. This is because [the Self] is self-luminous and consists of pure light.

I am the Lord of All, who is capable of abiding as the pure Brahman established through the negation of everything else. That state which the yogis, having attained, do not return from even to this day—that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu, the wandering mendicant. For neither the sun nor the moon shines there; that state from which there is no returning again.

(135) That indeed is absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the ninth instruction. The word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the *Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad*. || 23 ||
Thus ends the ninth instruction. This clear and concise commentary on the Nāradīya [Upaniṣad] has been written by Upaniṣad-Brahma-Yogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the Parivrājakopaniṣad consists of one thousand verses.
Thus ends the Nirvāṇopaniṣad, the forty-third [treatise] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the ŚrīmadĪśa.
"May my speech be established in my mind"—thus [ends] the peace invocation.
Now we shall expound the Nirvāṇopaniṣad. 1. "I am that Supreme Swan. 2.
3. The wandering mendicants who bear the marks of the West; 4. The guardians of the field of Manmatha; 5. The established doctrine of the Sky;
6. The river of the waves of nectar; 7. The imperishable and stainless; 8. The sage free from doubt.
Nirvāṇa is the deity. || 9 || It is the activity free from lineage. || 10 || It is absolute knowledge. || 11 ||

12. The Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya). 13. The Seat of the Supportless (Nirālambapīṭha). 14. Initiation through Union (Saṃyogadīkṣā). 15. Instruction on Separation (Viyogopadeśa). 16. The Purification of Satisfaction through Initiation (Dīkṣāsaṃtoṣapāvana). 17. The Gazing upon the Twelve Suns (Dvādaśādityāvalokana). 18. The Protection of Discrimination (Vivekarakṣā).
19. Compassion as Play (Karuṇaiva keliḥ). 20. The Garland of Bliss (Ānandamālā). In the cave of the single seat (ekāsanaguhāyām).
21. One who delights in conversations that bring ease through the abandonment of formal postures; 22. One who subsists on unprepared alms-food; 23. One whose conduct is like that of a swan.

The demonstration that the *haṃsa* resides within all beings. (24) The cloak of fortitude; the loincloth of indifference; the staff of inquiry; the meditation-band of the vision of Brahman; the sandals of prosperity; and the movement according to the will of another. (p. 138)

The Kuṇḍalinī-bond; liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and free from censuring others; the yogic sleep of Śiva (śivayoganidrā), the Khecarī-mudrā, and supreme bliss. (25) The three qualities of the qualityless (nirguṇaguṇatrayam). (26) Attainable through discernment (viveka), beyond the reach of mind and speech. (27) The world is impermanent, produced by that [Brahman], and equal to a dream-world or an elephant conjured by clouds.
Likewise, the aggregate of the body and so forth, ensnared by the net of the multitude of delusions, is imagined like a snake in a rope. || 28 ||

The target of the hundreds of names beginning with Viṣṇu and Vidhi; 29. the goad is the path; 30. the void is not a convention; 31. the existence of the Supreme Lord; 32. the monastery is the yoga of the perfection of truth; 33. the station of the immortals is not its essential nature; 34. the primordial Brahman is one's own consciousness; 35. the staff, which is a modification of the Ajapā Gāyatrī, is to be meditated upon.
36. A patched garment that restrains the mind. 37. Through yoga, the constant vision of the nature of eternal bliss. 38.
He subsists on the alms-food of bliss (39). He dwells even in a great cremation ground or in a grove of bliss (40).
The monastery is a place of solitude. (41) Śāradā is the activity of the state of *unmanī*. (42) *Unmanī* is the movement.
(43) The stainless body is the supportless seat. (44) The activity is the bliss of the waves of nectar. (45)

The great established doctrine of the White Sky (Pāṇḍaragaganamahāsiddhānta). || 46 || The practice of divine powers such as tranquility and self-restraint; proficiency regarding the field and the vessel; the union of the higher and the lower; and the instruction on the Savior (Tāraka). || 47 || Non-duality and eternal bliss are the deity. || 48 || The observance (niyama) is the restraint of the internal senses within oneself. || 49 || The abandonment of fear, delusion, grief, and anger. || 50 ||

In the reality of the Self-luminous Brahman, there is the severing of the phenomenal world encapsulated by Śiva and Śakti, as well as the burning away of the existence and non-existence of the circles of the eyes, the sense organs, and the body; [the Goddess] bears this, which rests upon the support of space. || 53–54 ||
The fourth state is the auspicious sacred thread; my topknot is composed of that.

(139) Consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it is the emission (*utsṛṣṭi*) and the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), the continuous circle of the senses (*akṣika-maṇḍala*). It is the narrative of the uprooting of karma;
it is the burning away of *māyā*, the sense of "mine" (*mamata*), and egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). It is she whose limbs are unstruck (*anāhata*). (56–58)
I contemplate that which is to be known through the secret doctrine of Nirvāṇa, which is swollen with the bliss of Nirvāṇa,
the imperial sovereignty of the bliss of the three states, as being nothing but one's own self.

Indeed, here unfolds this Nirvāṇopaniṣad, which is a division of the Ṛgveda; it reveals the ultimate reality by first elucidating the collection of duties pertaining to the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya). A commentary on this [text] is now begun from its very brief composition. This is the Śruti:
Having perceived wandering mendicants who are the most excellent candidates for instruction, he teaches the Upaniṣad by means of his own name, beginning with the words "Now" (atha) and so forth.

The word "now" (atha) signifies the sequence immediately following the three stages of life (āśrama). We, the Śrutis, shall explain this Upaniṣad—the knowledge that brings about the realization of that very Nirvāṇa which is liberation in the disembodied state (videhakaivalya).
The meaning is that we shall provide an exposition. To the question, "What is that which is to be established by the knowledge (vidyā) about to be taught? he says:

"I am He"—that is, I am this very Paramātman, revealed as non-different from the immanent Self (pratyagātman), who is designated as *Haṃsa* because He destroys (*han*) the delusion of duality imagined through one's own ignorance (*svājñā*). This is the sense.

The meaning is that the subject to be established is Brahman alone, which is non-dual (niṣpratiyogika), free from all designations such as "inner" (pratyak) and so forth, and realized through right knowledge (samyagjñāna). Regarding the question of who the qualified candidates for this are, he says: "wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) bearing the external marks," meaning those who, having renounced the external world of saṃsāra, bear the staff and other such emblems.

They are called *parivrājakas* because they wander about while relying upon the manifest signs of Viṣṇu; and they possess the final internal characteristic of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) by being bearers of the unmanifest signs of Viṣṇu—
the meaning is that they wear both the manifest and unmanifest signs of Viṣṇu in order to swallow up the distractions manifested through their own external and internal activities.
"All these bear the mark of Viṣṇu, being eternally manifest and unmanifest both externally and internally," according to the Śruti.
Even though they thus possess the mark of Viṣṇu, one might ask: "Whence is their nature as Viṣṇu? To this, he says:
"They are the guardians of the field of Manmatha. [The word] *mad* refers to the object of the notion of "I" (*asmad-pratyaya*).

The meaning is that because he protects "all" through the cognition that consists solely of his own Self, his status as Viṣṇu is absolute. Since Viṣṇu is well-known for his totality (*sākalya*), one might think their own philosophical conclusion is likewise established by attaining that state; therefore, he says: "the conclusion regarding space" (*gaganasiddhānta*). Viṣṇu’s totality is dependent upon his own ignorance; when that [ignorance] is removed, it [ceases].

For those who have ascended to the state of Viṣṇu as partless (niṣkala), established by the Śruti text "This is partless and immortal" (p. 140), there is the experience of the partless Brahman, which, like the sky, is devoid of constituent parts.
The meaning is that their internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has attained the state of partless Brahman;

it is the domain of the single essence of consciousness, like the immortal waves of the state of one's own true nature, and like the river Virajā. This is because [for others], there is association with an internal organ characterized by qualities such as perishability.

Since its essential nature is also such, he says: "imperishable and stainless. Since there might be doubt regarding desire and so forth, he says: "the sage free from doubt. By the power of the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, he attains the state of non-dual Brahman alone, in a manner that is entirely free from doubt.

He who instructs or causes his disciples to understand is undoubtedly a *ṛṣi*; the meaning is that he is a teacher (*ācārya*), for the Śruti states: "The Guru is the Brahman-consciousness residing within all bodies.
To show what deity is to be served by the assembly of wandering mendicants (*parivrāj*) instructed by such a guide, he says: "Nirvāṇa..."
Regarding the word "devatā" (deity): where one should have said "nirvāṇam" (nirvāṇa), the change of gender to "nirvāṇa" is used.
The meaning is that the deity in the form of Vāsudeva is she who shines intensely as the nature of that *kaivalya*—the nirvāṇa characterized by abiding in Brahman alone.
That which is the abode of all beings and which dwells within all beings as their benefactor— that I am, Vāsudeva.

Thus it is stated in the Śruti. One might ask: "Even for those who have attained the state of the Nirvāṇa-deity, would there not still be activity (pravṛtti) according to the form of their own *kula*? To this he says: "The activity of the *niṣkula* (beyond-kula). This is because one's own *kula*, lineage (*gotra*), and so forth, being of the nature of *māyā*, are equivalent to a cause [of bondage]. Indeed, simultaneous with the knowledge of Brahman alone, there can be no activity conforming to a *kula* other than oneself.

Regarding whether there is engagement (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is stated by the venerable Pāda [Śaṅkara]: "For one who has produced the awakening to reality, there is no further transmigratory existence as before. If it is asked how the maintenance of the body is possible in the absence of all engagement, the answer is no;
for from his own perspective, there is a total absence of the delusion regarding the body and its maintenance. This is so even from the perspective of the phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*).
Then, that [knowledge] would manifest, because even the engagement in and withdrawal from the mere maintenance of the body would likewise be of that nature;

for illusory activity and so forth do not produce effects, according to the Śruti: "This is merely an appearance, not the world in the ultimate sense. Is such knowledge produced solely by the scriptures?

He says "no," [answering] "it is exclusive knowledge" (*niṣkevalajñāna*). The meaning is that although scriptural knowledge sublates the existence of anything other than itself, it does not sublate the activity that produces effects; therefore, this [knowledge in question] cannot be born of scripture, but must rather be the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which is its goal.
p.

141) Thus, those possessing knowledge should not engage in reading, teaching, and so forth; therefore, for one who has realized Brahman, there exists no other duty whatsoever, whether as something to be done or not to be done. If...

That [existence] would occur due to the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, even in the absence of the reading and teaching of the collection of scriptures pertaining to the two sections— the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) which deals with actions leading to lower states, and the section on meditation (*upāsanākāṇḍa*).
That which is taught in the collection of Upaniṣads where Brahman is situated above is this "upper scripture" (*ūrdhvāmnāya*).

The collection of one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the *Īśa* should be recited either from a teacher or by oneself, or one should cause disciples to recite them. When this is done, the lineage of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) will remain unbroken; that this occurs is what is meant here by "natural" (*sahaja*).

One should repeat the Upanishad among all the Vedas; one should constantly practice the knowledge of the Upanishad, which is the cause of liberation. Let the body perform actions, or let speech here be uttered in vain.
Let speech chant the Tāra-mantra and likewise recite the crest of the sacred tradition (Āmnāya).
Whether the intellect meditates upon Viṣṇu or dissolves into the bliss of Brahman, I am merely the witness; I do nothing here, nor do I cause anything to be done.

According to such scriptural passages as these, one might ask: "In this way, how could the maintenance of the lineage of the tradition of Brahma-vidyā have a support? To this, he says: "The seat is without support" (*nirālamba-pīṭha*). This is because of the traditional teaching: "The constant abiding in Brahman, which is devoid of any support other than itself. Regarding the question, "Where is their attachment? he says: "The initiation of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-dīkṣā*).
The meaning of *dīkṣā* is the application of devotion (*abhiniveśa*) toward bestowing the yoga of the knowledge that consists solely of Brahman through a circle of true disciples.
The sense is that even this semblance of devotion is caused by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the disciple, and not of its own accord.

As to what kind of instruction that is, it is said: "the instruction on separation" (*viyogopadeśa*). This refers to the separation from the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself that has become attached [to one]. It is not...

Indeed, the teaching is that within one’s own non-dual nature alone, there is no room for the delusion that "something other than oneself exists" or "does not exist," according to the Śruti: "There is no way to reach this [truth] unless it is taught by another. Lest one should experience suffering and the like due to being preoccupied with instructing disciples, he says: "purifying through initiation and contentment. This is because [the teacher] is not distracted by anything else.
The meaning is that it is purifying. He states that its sight is likewise so:

"the sight of the twelve suns. The meaning is that the sight of the wandering mendicants who know Brahman is just like the sight of the twelve suns, which is a cause of purification. And thus says the Śruti:
All those who move in the sky and those who move on the earth, once they come within the range of vision of one who knows Brahman,
are instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births.
Thus [it is asked]: what is the protection for those free from ego-inflation? To this he says: "The protection of discrimination.
Discrimination of Brahman alone is itself knowledge, which is the protection;
through the grace of the Śruti and the Guru, one possesses the knowledge of reality that has dispelled all doubt.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, protect the lineage of renunciants.

Thus, according to the Smṛti. To the question "Where is that play? he says: "Compassion itself is the play. That compassion which arises with the thought, "The multitude of those ignorant of their own Self must be led to my own state," is indeed the play. What is its garland? To this he says:
"In the cave of the single seat. Everywhere, there is but one seat—whether it be staying still, wandering, or moving.

Those who sit upon a single seat are "ekāsanās. Their place of dwelling is a cave; those by whom the restrictive observance (*niyama*) of adopting specific postures such as the *siddhāsana* has been relinquished and abandoned therein are "muktāsanās. The very bliss of one's own true nature (*svarūpasukha*) which is obtained by them is their "social gathering" (*goṣṭhī*), for it is not one associated with worldly people. For that purpose, why should alms be sought from others?
Regarding this, it says: "one who eats alms that are not prepared. Householders cook for their own sake and eat, remaining at ease;

when monks—who abide by rules such as staying only one night in a village and waiting for the time of milking a cow—arrive for the purpose of begging alms, there is no opportunity to cook again for them, so [the monk] takes only what remains from the meal.
One who eats alms-food without conceptualizing it as "they will give" for their own sake is called an "eater of non-conceptualized alms. And so says the Smṛti:
"Wandering through a village for only one night and entering it during the afternoon..."
Desiring only as much time as it takes to milk a cow, he should depart and not return again.

And so forth. Regarding what his conduct is like, it is said: "the conduct of a *haṃsa*. By the word *haṃsa*, what reality (*tattva*) do they indicate? To this: "dwelling within all beings. From the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge, [it refers to] the inner Self non-different from the Supreme Self; yet from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), it is Brahman, established through the negation of everything else.
They establish that [reality] is one's own nature alone, devoid of any counterpart.

As for their patched garment, loincloth, staff, yogic belt, wooden sandals, binding of the feet, liberation, sleep, and mudrās—what are they like? To this, he says, beginning with "steadfastness" (dhairya).

(143) There is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman—this mental fortitude is the patched garment (kaṇṭhā). The mind that remains indifferent toward anything distinct from itself is the loincloth (kaupīna). The investigation into the meaning of all Vedānta is the staff (daṇḍa). And the very perception of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) is [the ascetic's practice].
The *yogapaṭṭa* (the yogic cloth-band). "Prosperity" (*śrī*) refers to external abundance that is other than oneself. To avoid contact with that, there is the *pādukā* (sandals) upon it.

The mere activity of maintaining the body occurs solely through the will of another. Thus says the Śruti: "And by the will of another, one who is naked should bathe; [one should act] by the will of another. [This applies] within the *suṣumnā*.

The very intention that "the entry of Kuṇḍalinī must occur" is itself bondage. The meaning is that the contemplation of the channels and Kuṇḍalinī as being distinct from oneself constitutes bondage, because it serves as a cause for veiling Brahman.
And so says the Śruti:
O Great Sage, having liberated the self by means of the self from this human condition— which is a mere mass of channels and always insubstantial— realize it as "I am."

Thus: the Supreme Self, which is other than one's own self, is merely the delusion of the existence of something other than oneself; this is the denial of the Supreme (parāpavāda) and the veiling of the Supreme Self. Therefore, he who is liberated even while living becomes a *jīvanmukta*. And so says the Smṛti:
The delusion of the existence of that which is other than oneself is said to be the covering of one's own nature;
having severed it with the sword of the knowledge of one's own nature, the ascetic should wander.
Thus: Abiding in non-difference from Śiva is Śiva-yoga. That itself is sleep, which is the *nirvikalpaka-samādhi* (non-conceptual absorption).

From the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājñadṛṣṭi*), because the conceptualization of the plane of one's own ignorance (*svāvidyāpada*) has been set in motion, that plane of ignorance is called *khecarī*.
The notion that [anything] exists apart from its own self is expressed by the word "mū" (the root of *mūrchā*). Brahman is established through the total negation (*sarvāpahnavasiddha*) of all else.

The Khecarīmudrā is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), so called because it dissolves the joy of the sky-farer (khecarīmuda) through the cognition of one's own nature alone, which is devoid of all counterparts. By the word "and" (ca), the external Khecarīmudrā is also included. One might ask: since it is a form of mudrā, would it not be of the nature of suffering? To this he says: "the supremely blissful" (paramānandī). In the term "supremely blissful," there is a change in grammatical gender.

The meaning is that it is the *khecarīmudrā* which brings supreme bliss, because it is the cause for the attainment of bliss by those who practice it. Such a state is attained through the realization of Brahman alone, since that is preceded by the negation of the three qualities (*guṇas*) and their effects.
To the question, "By what means is the non-dual, qualityless Brahman, which has no counterpart, to be obtained? he says: "It is obtainable through discrimination (*viveka*)."

The meaning is that it is attainable by that very discriminative knowledge (*viveka*) which realizes "there is nothing beyond Brahman," for the scripture states: "There is no other path for proceeding. This is because of the use of the word "attainable" (*labhyam*).

Is that [Brahman] possessed of excellence (*sātiśaya*)? To this he says: "beyond the range of mind and speech. The meaning is that which is attainable as one's own remainder (*svāvaśeṣatayā*), being established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the entire collection of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*), is without excellence (*niratiśaya*). For, if Brahman were beyond the range of the collection of instruments, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasakti*) of the non-existence of Brahman.

Because the manifold of effects, established through the experience of one’s own ignorance, is dependent upon a cause, and since there is indeed no such cause other than Brahman, he states— with the supporting illustration— that Brahman is of the nature of non-dual existence by means of the reason that it is the cause of the universe, beginning with the words "That which is impermanent," etc. Since—

It should be understood that the Brahman which produced the world is eternal. One might argue that because the world is born from eternal Brahman, it too must be eternal; therefore, he says: "it is non-eternal. To the question, "In what way is it non-eternal? he replies: "like a dream," meaning the world, consisting of the three states characterized by dreaming and their effects, is like a city seen in the clouds.
The world, enveloped by the web of the multitude of delusions, is imagined like a snake in a rope. What is the substratum for that imagination?

To this he says: "It is that which is indicated by hundreds of names such as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and so forth. The meaning is that while Viṣṇu and others are the denotations (*vācya*) of words like "Viṣṇu," it is Brahman that is their indicated referent (*lakṣya*).

Regarding the question, "What is the cause that leads one to the path of Viṣṇu and others?"—the answer is: "The path is the goad. Just as a goad is the cause for a master of elephants to reach his desired destination, so too the path beginning with light (arcirādi) is the cause for reaching Viṣṇu and others; this is the meaning. Is the path beginning with light distinct from Viṣṇu and the others?

Regarding the statement "it is empty," he says: "empty does not mean conventional. Since the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) is non-different from Viṣṇu and the others, it is not empty; rather, the meaning is that it is real because it has that [divine] nature. And thus says the *Smṛti*:
"Because of the scriptural authority for its non-difference from itself, [it is so] despite the entire cosmic egg and so forth being superposed upon it."
Even though there is a distinction between the object to be attained and the means of attainment, the entire universe has Viṣṇu as its very self.
Thus, if one asks why it should not be called "Viṣṇu" itself, the answer is that although it is indeed Viṣṇu, it is conventionally designated as "the Path" (*mārga*);

this is a conventional designation based on common usage. Or, from a conventional perspective, while Bhū-vaikuṇṭha and Vaikuṇṭha are situated below and above [respectively], this Path is situated in the supportless intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
This is well known. In that regard, what is the power that brings about the fitness for movement in the multitude of travelers?
To this he says: "The existence of the Supreme Lord. Viṣṇu is the Lord (īśvara) of the "others," namely the individual souls (jīvas);
his "existence" (sattā) refers to his capacity (sāmarthya). The meaning is that it is potent by virtue of bestowing the power to travel upon paths without support to those who go.
Having spoken thus from *Sāṅkuśārci* onwards, he states the means for attaining Brahman alone:

"The monastery (*maṭha*) is the yoga of the realization of Truth. The yoga is precisely the contemplation, established by scripture, that "I am pure Being (*sanmātra*), and everything else is non-existent. The monastery is simply the state of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), which is the place of rest for that yoga. That indeed is...
The meaning is: the path that leads to the attainment of Brahman without distinction.
What is that immortal state to be attained by those two paths? To this he says: "the immortal state is not... (p. 145).
Regarding its essential nature: the meaning is that the state of the immortals, which is attainable through the two paths, cannot be heaven.
If that is so, what is it? To this he says: "The primordial Brahman is one's own consciousness.
Because it is the beginning of all, it is the primordial cause (ādikāraṇa), the Brahman; it is that consciousness which arises even without the status of being a cause dependent upon an effect.

That very [reality] is the Brahman of Ādibrahma; the meaning is that one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*) has the nature of knowledge consisting solely of itself, according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*). To the question, "In what form should the Self be meditated upon by those seeking liberation?
he says: "The staff, which is a modification of the *Ajapā-gāyatrī*, is to be meditated upon. This [staff] consists of the inhalation and exhalation originating from the *mūlādhāra*.

The meditation consisting of the thought "I am that Haṃsa" is called Ajapā. Because it protects (trāyate) the one who sings (gāyantaṃ), it is Gāyatrī, whose nature consists of the four parts of one's own ignorance (svāvidyā). Even the four parts—the gross and so forth—of one's own dual ignorance are its modifications;

the Supreme Self alone, established through the total negation (apahnava) of all that, is the staff (daṇḍa) of the modifications of Ajapā-Gāyatrī, [to be held] by wandering mendicants (parivrājakaiḥ).

The meaning is that [the Self] is to be meditated upon as one's own nature alone, free from all counterparts. Thus, one might ask: for the class of Paramahaṃsas who meditate in this way, what is the patched garment (kaṇṭhā) that protects against the dualities such as cold and heat? To this he says: "The patched garment is that which restrains the mind.
The mind consists of one's own ignorance and its effects; that which restrains it is the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), and that alone is the patched garment, because of the nature of knowledge.
Because one is devoured by cold and other such states imagined through one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā-vikalpita*), what is to be seen by means of knowledge (*vidyā*)? To this he says:

"By yoga, the vision of the nature of eternal bliss. Yoga is the unification of the inward-turned consciousness (*pratyak*) and the accumulated [object] (*pracita*). The meaning is that the vision of the nature of eternal bliss produced by that [yoga] is the perfection of knowledge.
To the question, "Endowed with such vision, what does he eat?", it is said: "He subsists on the alms of bliss.
This is because in the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), there is no possibility of worldly alms other than one's own bliss.
To the question, "What is the dwelling place for that?", it is said: "His residence is in the Great Cremation Ground or in the Forest of Bliss (*Ānandavana*)."

The meaning is that one should make one's dwelling or residence in the Great Cremation Ground (mahāśmaśāna), specifically in Kāśī, there in the Ānandavana forest, or in regions such as Brahmanāla; or alternatively,
it is called the Great Cremation Ground because it is the cause for reducing to ashes the entire collection of the five elements and their derivatives, beginning with Mahat.
The inner consciousness is the Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana), which is the bliss of profound density.

The meaning is that one’s dwelling—meaning one’s residence—should be in that great cremation ground, the Forest of Bliss, within the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self, in its own majesty, as nothing but itself. To the question "Where is that abode? he says:

"A solitary place, a monastery" (ekāntasthānamaṭham): a solitary place is one devoid of the crowding of people other than oneself; that very place is a "monastery," meaning a dwelling. What is its activity? To this he says:
"The state of Unmanī is the Śāradā activity. In the state of meditative absorption (samāhitadaśā), Unmanī is the non-conceptual state.

Therefore, the meaning is that during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), the activity of Śāradā—the knowledge of Brahman which illuminates the meaning of all the Vedāntas—is [the movement]. To the question "Where is its movement?", he says:
Regarding the phrase "the movement of Unmanī": at every step, there is a movement—a running—toward Unmanī, whose nature is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
To the question "What is that seat (*pīṭha*)?", he says: "The stainless body is the seat of non-support.
For the ascetic who has ascended to the state of Unmanī, the "stainless body" is non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣajñāna*).

The meaning of "the seat" (*pīṭha*) there is that it is the domain of Brahman alone and is without support. As for the question of what its activity (*kriyā*) is like, it is said: "the activity of the bliss of the waves of nectar. Just like the waves of nectar, in the ocean of bliss, its very activity is profound depth, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) it is devoid of action. What is its established doctrine (*siddhānta*)?
Regarding this, [the text states]: "The Great Siddhānta of the White Sky. By the word "white" (pāṇḷara), consciousness (cit) is expressed;
that itself is the sky, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). The certainty that "that is nothing but one's own self" is the Great Siddhānta.
Thus, he says "tranquility, self-control, and so forth," indicating that the instruction on the Siddhānta leads to the attainment of self-sovereignty (svārājya).
The mantra taught by the Guru for the sake of a disciple who possesses the aforementioned qualifications— beginning with the *praṇava*—
is called "the Savior" (*tāraka*) because it carries one across the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself. Thus, the instruction on the Savior-mantra,
preceded by the disciple's perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*), is the cause for the realization of the unity of the inner and outer consciousness.

For example, the restraint of the internal senses is tranquility (*śama*); the restraint of the external senses is self-control (*dama*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the collection of means such as cessation (*uparati*) and the rest is included. Thus, because this collection of means swallows the demonic endowment and brings about the divine endowment, it possesses divine power.

The practice of that [discipline] is its performance. The body produced by that is the "field" (*kṣetra*), because it is the ground for the growth of all means of realization. Therein, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the "vessel" (*pātra*), because it protects and saves the individual soul (*jīva*)—who would otherwise fall into the intoxicating liquor of sense-objects such as sound—by turning that soul away from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that liquor. These two [the field and the vessel]...

The cause for the proficiency—the capacity to perform the practice of the means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth—regarding both the field (kṣetra) and the vessel (pātra), is the Tāraka taught by the Ācārya; this is the meaning. To the question "Who is the deity to be realized through the Tāraka?", he says:
"The deity is non-dual, eternal bliss. Non-dual Brahman is that which swallows up all conceptualizations such as disciple, teacher, reciter, and recitation.

This bliss which constitutes its very nature is designated as "the deity" (devatā) because its form is intensely radiant; the meaning is that there is no deity superior to it. What is the rule regarding the means for attaining that? To this, it is said: "The rule is the restraint of one's own internal organ. One's own internal organ is the *antaḥkaraṇa* (the inner instrument). For example:

Just as [the mind] is not transformed into the form of the functioning of desire and so forth, so too the restraint "I am Brahman, I am indeed Brahman" is the transformation into the form of Brahman; that itself is *niyama*. And thus says the Smṛti:
"Having turned back from sense-objects, one should properly withdraw the entire collection of the senses."
Apply yourself to the form of Brahman; in that which is for his benefit, there shall be restraint.
...so it is said.
To the question, "What must be abandoned by one who possesses such discipline? he replies:
"The abandonment of fear, delusion, grief, and anger is renunciation. Fear is that which arises from the perceived distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).

Delusion is the notion of a self in the body and so forth; grief is born from the loss of a desired object; anger is produced by the non-fulfillment of desires. Renunciation is indeed the abandonment of these; by that alone, everything that obstructs knowledge is abandoned—this is the meaning. What would result from such renunciation? To this [it is said]:

He says: "The tasting of the essence of the identity of the higher and the lower. The meaning is that through the abandonment of that [duality], there occurs the tasting of the essence of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
To the question, "What results from such tasting of the essence?
he says: "The stainless power of non-restriction. That which is governed by the Lord in its respective functions is the "governed" (niyamya).

The "living-born" (jīvajāta) refers to that which is subject to the inner controller, the Lord (īśvara). Because both [the individual soul and the Lord] are of the nature of *māyā*, He is beyond them;

He is the non-controller and the witness of all, because He swallows the distinction between the controlled and the controller. That very [state] is the stainless power (*nirmala-śakti*), meaning the capacity for the illumination of everything. Thus, what [is there] from power?
How could this be? To this he says: "In the self-luminous reality of Brahman.

When the duality of one's own ignorance and its effects are sublated, what remains is the self-luminous alone, the reality of Brahman; yet, by those ignorant of it, the phenomenal world—encased within Śiva and Śakti—is superimposed upon that reality. Therein, existence, consciousness, and bliss constitute the aspect of Śiva.

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) consists of the portions of power that veil true consciousness and bliss. The union of those two—the conscious and the unconscious—which are mutually opposed like light and darkness, is encapsulated by *māyā* as the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of jars, cloths, and so forth.
Just as the destruction of that [world] may occur by means of the sword of knowledge, "I am Brahman," so too [should it be].

The meaning is that by the fire of the perfect knowledge of Brahman, there occurs the burning away of the existence and non-existence of the circles of petals, eyes, and eyes. That which, surrounding its own collection of effects, protects and sustains them—

the locus of the delusive identity arising from the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), namely the causal body consisting of both the individual and the collective— is called the "petal" (patra).

That effect— the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), both individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*), which is the locus of the innate identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) and is adorned with twenty components— is called the "organ" (*akṣa*). By virtue of being its effect, it is the locus of the identity between the individual soul and the Lord as produced by their respective karma.
The gross body, known as the individual (vyaṣṭi), the collective (samaṣṭi), the microcosm (piṇḍa), and the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa), is called "akṣī.

Thus, those who possess the three bodies designated as "patrākṣa" and "akṣi"—namely, the Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva, who are non-different from the Lord, the Sūtra, and the Virāj—are the "patrākṣākṣikas. Their circle or assembly is the "paṭala."

The meaning is that, through one's own vision (*svadṛṣṭyā*), all this collection of objects of witness (*sākṣyajāta*)—which is illuminated by the witness and which depends upon the state of being a witness—is burned away and dissolved. Then, as to what kind of form Brahman maintains, he says:
"By being the substratum of its own superstrates, namely the five great elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*), and their effects."

That which remains as the non-dual Brahman alone— established by the negation of the state of being a substratum that depends upon a superstratum— is of such a nature that it maintains this form through the vision of ultimate reality, whether the delusion of the perspective of one's own ignorance and the like exists or not. He who knows thus is this Brāhmaṇa, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman.

The intended meaning is that he becomes the primary *avadhūta*. To the question, "How can there be Brahminhood for those who have discarded the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)? he says: "Śiva is the fourth."

"The sacrificial thread and the tuft are composed of that [Śiva]. This means that the sacrificial thread and the tuft are indeed Brahman—Śiva Himself, who is the fourth (turīya) or beyond the fourth (turīyātīta), and who swallows all that is inauspicious apart from Himself; they are "composed of Śiva" (śivamayau), meaning they consist entirely of Śiva.
And so says the Śruti:
Those who know Brahman understand that he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread likewise consists of it possesses the entirety of true Brahminhood.
Thus [it is said]. He states that even the world, which is the object of the vision of such a Brahmin, is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), saying "composed of consciousness.
"Emission" (*utsṛṣṭi*) refers to the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of mountains, trees, creepers, *guñjā* shrubs, and so forth. The "egg" (*aṇḍa*) is the genus of those stationary beings.
From that, it is "well-extended" (*saṃtata*) because of its manifold forms. Those whose senses (*akṣī*) consist of the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) and so forth are [the transmigrating souls].
The living beings, such as ants and other mobile creatures, their entire circle or multitude is indeed composed of consciousness alone;
this is the meaning, according to the Vedic revelation: "The individual soul has pure consciousness as its form.
Just as a jar or similar object produced from a lump of clay is not something other than clay, so too is the world.
Likewise, the entire universe, both the stable and the moving, consists of consciousness, because it arises from consciousness.

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "Let the universe be composed of consciousness through the vision of That [the Self]. One might then ask: since that [Self] is also joined with the three bodies, would there not be worldly activity? To this he says: "The uprooting of karma. Simultaneous with the rising of the sun of the knowledge of reality—the cause for attaining the state of a true *avadhūta*—[there occurs] the destruction of one's own two-fold ignorance.
What talk can there be of "it exists" or "it does not exist" regarding the darkness of the progression and cessation of *saṃsāra*? The meaning is: what wonder is there in this?

Even so, if it is argued that the persistence of *saṃsāra* would continue until the fall of the body, we say no; for that [persistence] is rendered ineffective because it is caused by the perspective of others (*paradṛṣṭi*). Or, if it is argued that *saṃsāra* might consist merely in the maintenance of the body, we say no.

Since for one whose worldly existence consists merely in the maintenance of the body, there is an absence of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, and thus no state of transmigration,
whether the body remains for a long time or dissolves at that moment—
how could there be a return to transmigratory existence for one who is liberated at the time of self-knowledge?
Thus, according to the Smṛti. From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), since the three bodies do not exist, how could he remain?

To this, he says: "anāhatāṅgī" (she whose limbs are unstruck). By means of the knowledge of Brahman alone, which is devoid of any counter-correlate (niṣpratiyogika), that which is struck all around—namely, ignorance (avidyā)—is destroyed; hence she is "anāhatāṅgī."

The collection of words and their effects consists of negation; since even that [negation] is established through negation and exists in the form of the limb of the Unstruck (anāhata), she is the one whose limbs are the Unstruck. This occurs simultaneously with the knowledge of Brahman alone.

The meaning is that the primary Avadhūta, having attained the state of the negation of the delusion as to whether his own three bodies exist or do not exist, should wander about as one liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta). || 1.58 ||
The secondary Avadhūta: his conduct and its fruit; the contemplation of the nature of that which is beyond the three *guṇas*; the observance (*samaya*); the destruction of delusion (*bhrāntiharaṇa*);
the burning away of the fluctuations of desire and so forth; and the firm loincloth of hardness.
Clothed in old animal skins, with mantras unrecited and rituals unperformed, liberation consists in acting according to one's own will and abiding in one's own true nature. || 59 ||

Having thus described the characteristics of the primary *avadhūta*, he clarifies the secondary *avadhūta*, his conduct, and his fruit, beginning with the words "beyond the three qualities" (*nistraiguṇya*). The "three qualities" (*traiguṇya*) is the aggregate of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest.
That which is "beyond the three qualities" (*nistraiguṇya*) is Brahman—I am that Brahman—which is the substratum for the negation of one's own state of ignorance and its entire collection of effects.
The contemplation "I am Brahman" is a continuous mental connection (*anusaṃdhāna*). That too is a conventional agreement (*samaya*), meaning a common understanding.
Since such a continuous connection is a modification of knowledge (*vidyā-vṛtti*) and thus consists of the manifestation of Brahman alone, its nature as an error [is negated];
the meaning is that one should effect the burning—that is, the destruction—of that [error]. Likewise, there is the burning of modifications such as desire and volition.

And there is the dissolution [of duality]. Because it is distinct from the soft cotton loincloth that serves as the cause for the two types of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), there is the state of having the vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) remaining within, shielded by a hard and firm loincloth. It also serves as protection against cold, wind, and heat;
and it is the fourth *oṃkāra*, because the fourth *oṃkāra* is unstruck (*anāhata*) by anything due to its being the "fourth-of-the-fourth" (*turyaturya*).

The fourth state (turya) is illuminated at the tip of the syllable Om, according to the Śruti: "the fourth of the fourth" (turyaturya). The unstruck mantra (anāhatanmantra) is the Brahman that is the fourth of the fourth.
It is "served" or "resorted to" by the intellect of pure consciousness (cinmātradhī), which is established through the negation of all modifications by means of non-action (akriyā).
Alternatively, it is the "mantra"—meaning right knowledge—because it protects the one who contemplates the Brahman as the Self, who is the secondary Avadhūta.

The meaning is that it occurs through the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*). Even a secondary *avadhūta*, if thus endowed with the means of accomplishment, becomes a primary *avadhūta*.

Then, because he has transcended the engagement with injunctions and prohibitions and the inclination toward activity and cessation, this conduct according to his own will (*svecchācāra*) consists in instructing the learned.

It cannot be that which leads one onto a wrong path; for even that [path] is its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), because it devours the bondage of action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*). That very [nature] is liberation, established through the negation of all conceptualizations of "self" and "other."
The mental state that "I am indeed Brahman" is declared to be yoga itself; for those whose desires have been removed by yoga, this very realization is called the contemplation of Brahman.
Thus, according to the Smṛti. || 59 ||

The attainment of the primary means of the Avadhūta is conduct like a boat upon the Supreme Brahman; it is the embracing of celibacy and peace. Through the practice of celibacy, one attains Brahman—which is of undivided form, eternal, and the destroyer of all doubt. (60)
That which constitutes the primary state of the Avadhūta reveals both the perfection of its means and its fruit:

being endowed with the conduct of his own stage of life (*āśrama*), he possesses a boat for the shoreless, deep, and vast ocean of *saṃsāra*; having performed that practice and service toward him, he then remains in his presence.

Having lived in the teacher's household (gurukula) preceded by the two types of celibacy (brahmacarya) until the purification of one's own mind, and then having practiced tranquility, self-control, and so forth— which serve as indicators for the four means of accomplishment (sādhanacatuṣṭaya)— one should then proceed.

Having studied— that is, having performed the hearing (*śravaṇa*)— in the stage of life (*āśrama*) suited for one who is not overwhelmed by external or internal distractions and is thus unfit for the performance of rites such as hearing [the scriptures], namely in the stage of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the forest-dweller’s stage (*vānaprastha*), or the fourth stage (*turya*); and then,
having performed reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), which are the primary causes of the state of an *avadhūta*.
The meaning is that, having become Brahman, one becomes a supreme Avadhūta, liberated from the body (videhamukta). "Renunciation" (nyāsa) is Brahman; renunciation alone excels all.
Because he is imperishable, because he is most excellent, because he has shaken off the bonds of saṃsāra,
and because he is characterized by such [mahāvākya-s] as "That thou art," he is called an avadhūta.
"By knowing Brahman, one becomes Brahman itself," according to such scriptural passages. || 60 ||
(151) The determination of the qualified recipient:
This teaching on Nirvāṇa must not be given to anyone except a disciple or a son. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 61.

This scripture should not be given to one who lacks qualification; it should be given to one endowed with the aforementioned means (*sādhana*). This is established by the scriptural passage, "In the family of that man there shall be no one ignorant of Brahman," which indicates that for one born into a family of knowers of Brahman, when the aforementioned means have been perfected, he becomes a qualified disciple and thus possesses the requisite qualification. Therefore, [this teaching] is not [to be given] except to a son or a disciple.

The meaning is that this should not be given to just anyone; for there is a scriptural injunction stating, "It must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who is not a son, nor indeed to one who is not a disciple," and so forth. Thus, the two words "Upanishad" indicate the completion of the vision of Nirvana.
This commentary on the Nirvāṇopaniṣad has been written by Upa-niṣad-brahma-yogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra, for the pleasure of Hari.
The commentary on the Nirvāṇopaniṣad consists of two hundred and fifty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Nirvāṇopaniṣad, completing the forty-seventh [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the ŚrīmadĪśa.
The Parabrahmopaniṣad. Peace through the mantra: "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious... etc. (Śānti).
The supreme knowledge of Brahman.
Then, indeed, Mahāśāla Śaunaka approached the venerable Pippalāda, the descendant of Aṅgiras, according to the prescribed rule and asked:
"How does he create? What is this majesty of the Self? Having divided it, what is this pervasive majesty? To him [he said]:

He said: "This is the truth which I proclaim: the most excellent knowledge of Brahman, which shines forth stainless and pure within the city of the Supreme Brahman—devoid of passion, partless, auspicious, and imperishable.
He, free from stain like a honey-bee that has completed its work, governs it by means of the multitude of bees."

One who performs action while standing outside of non-action experiences its fruit like a farmer. One who knows the vital point of action performs action; having understood the vital point of action, one should act. Who would cast out a net? No one draws it in; [if] one draws it in, [it is lost]. || 1 ||
I worship the three-footed one who dwells everywhere— the form of indivisible bliss known through the Upanishads as the Supreme Brahman, whose home is the heart of the wandering mendicant.

Indeed, here unfolds this *Parabrahmopaniṣad*, which is a division of the *Atharvaveda*; it is intent upon revealing the turban of knowledge (*jñānaśikhā*) and the sacred thread of knowledge (*jñānopavīta*), and culminates in Brahman alone.
A brief commentary on this [text] is now commenced.

154) This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Śaunaka and Paippalāda, is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*). He introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now). He asks: what did he ask? [He asked about] those various things that are being created in the world.

All those objects are indeed already established in the divine city of Brahman, within the space of the heart of Hiraṇyagarbha. To this, he raises an objection: "How so? [The answer is: Having divided the objects situated within Himself part by part, this majesty—the Blessed Lord, endowed with the power to bring about the impossible—is [the cause].

"How does He abide while creating them from His own self? What is this all-pervading majesty?"—in response to this question of Śaunaka, Pippalāda said: "This one. To that Śaunaka who was known as Pippalāda, he (the former) spoke. What did he say? "That most excellent knowledge of Brahman which I [possess] for you..."

He declared: "This very Brahman is Truth, because it is established by the realization that the unreal cannot exist; for even here in this world, one perceives that 'only Being exists, the non-existent is other than it,' according to the Śruti: 'Brahman alone is, not the non-existent. Where is that perceived?
In the City of Brahman (brahmapura), which is free from passion (viraja) due to the absence of the three qualities such as *rajas* and the rest.
Because it is free from the sixteen kalās beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *nāmā*, it shines forth as partless (*niṣkala*), and for that very reason, as pure and imperishable (*akṣara*).

What does it do while shining? In this regard, it bestows the power to perceive their respective objects upon the deities of the senses, such as hearing, and upon the ten vital breaths, such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

The meaning is that, by not being touched by the virtues and defects pertaining to those [objects], it shines forth as stainless; thus it is always perceived by the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*) alone. To the question, "When there is an outward state (*parāgbhāva*), how can the inward vision arise?", [the answer is:
here, living beings (*jīvas*) are called "bees" (*madhukaras*) because they perform actions known as "paths" which have as their cause the fruits of objects in this world and the next.

Their collection is an aggregate. He is the "Nirmātṛ" (the Creator), because he has fashioned [the world] until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*) so that it may be fit for the conventional discourse of bondage and liberation. That very Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is such a creator, out of compassion for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), restrains—that is, he holds back and completely suppresses—the state of outward-turnedness (*parāgbhāva*) residing within them.
It seizes [the mind]. Thereupon, the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*) of those desiring liberation becomes clear;

the meaning is that Brahman is apprehended through inward vision. Having placed one's own Self before oneself, one remains through the contemplation of its true nature—this is the meaning of "standing before one's own Self" (*svapurasthita*). What is the function of inward vision? It is having placed one's own Self before oneself.
"He remains through the contemplation of that state" means he is established in his own city (svapura) with inward vision; as for what his action is,
it is the general duty of one's own performance— that action by which a living being is bound and by which, through knowledge, one is liberated.
Therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual actions.

Thus, by reflecting on the meaning of the sacred texts (śruti), it does not appear that this wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is one who performs action; for the scripture states: "Since he has accomplished all that was to be done, there remains nothing further for him to do. Conversely, one whose vision is directed outward (parāgdṛṣṭi) performs various kinds of actions with the aim of attaining fruits in this world and the next; thus, he is "one who acts" (karmaka), a performer of action.
Like a farmer (p.
155), one experiences the fruit of one's own various high and low actions, which brings about birth in diverse wombs; since this is so, therefore—

Action is the vital point; action is the cause of birth and so forth. The knower, realizing that action leads to the purification of the mind, performs action with the intent of propitiating the Supreme Lord. That sage who desires to be liberated from the delusion of anything other than his own Self, having understood the essential nature of action, performs the duties appropriate to his own stage of life with a mind free from desire.

One should act [thus]. Who indeed, being proficient in the one Brahman and possessed of discrimination, would cast aside the web of various actions and perform fruitless *kāmya* (desire-bound) action without the performance of *niṣkāma* (disinterested) action, which is the cause of mental purity that leads to the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman? The meaning is that no one at all would do so. This is with a disinterested mind.

To the objection that even the karma performed by him drags him downward, he says: "No. Karma performed by this practitioner of action with a desireless mind never at all drags him down into the realm of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

By the repetition [of the word], it is meant that through his own performance, by means of the knowledge obtained via the purification of the mind, it shall lead him to the Great State (*mahatpadam*).
Thus it is illuminated. || 1 ||

The means for attaining the three-footed Brahman are the four vital deities. All those channels are like the sky of one who has fallen into deep sleep. Just as a hawk, having taken flight from its own abode, returns to its own nest, even so is this state of deep sleep described.
And furthermore: he moves everywhere within the supreme golden sheath; for this immortal one indeed traverses the three channels.

His Brahman consists of three quarters; he moves toward it and then abides there. Speak of both this world and the beyond: everywhere within the supreme golden sheath, just as this Devadatta, when struck with a staff...

He is not tainted at all by sacrifices, charitable works, or good and evil deeds. Just as a child, free from desire, attains bliss, or just as this god rushes toward bliss in a dream, so too does the Veda itself, the supreme light, delight him with its light—just so. That which is the supreme mind...

He gladdens the Supreme Self. He is born from Īśvara with a radiant (śubhra) complexion. Again, by that very same path, he enters the state of dream. Like the nature of a leech, he is born from Īśvara with his desires rendered void.
To that extent, he gladdens himself. That which is the supreme junction is the non-supreme junction; thus, he does not abandon the supreme nor the non-supreme.
p.

156) Then, having thus joined the eight skull-bowls, that which hangs down like a breast is the source of Indra; it is the source of the Vedas—thus they awaken here. Being beyond both auspicious and inauspicious, it is not defiled even by auspicious or inauspicious karmas.

This deity who is the supreme bliss of every other deity, the inner controller, the unattached one whose nature is consciousness, the Puruṣa, the Haṃsa of Praṇava, is the Supreme Brahman; he is not the Haṃsa of Prāṇa, nor is the Praṇava the individual soul (jīva). The primordial Deity makes this known. He who knows thus—how does he make it known? He brings about the state of Brahman for the individual soul. || 2 ||
What is the means for attaining the Brahman of the three quarters, which is to be reached through the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman? To this he says:

Regarding the question of what that Brahman is which leads one to the state of Brahman, and what the means for its attainment is—in this regard, there are four deities of *praṇa*, distinguished as Viśva and so forth up to Turya, by virtue of being the support of the individual soul's vital breaths.

There are four [channels]. These channels of perception (*upalabdhi-nāḍī*) are likewise fourfold, distinguished as *ramā*, *aramā*, *icchā*, and *punarbhava*. Among them, by seizing hold of the two channels called *ramā* and *aramā*, one who is weary from the activities of waking and dreaming becomes deeply asleep (*suṣupta*), like a hawk exhausted from its flight in the sky. In this regard, the illustration is as follows: just as a hawk...

Just as a bird, having become weary from long wandering by relying upon the sky, returns to its own nest; even so, this living being (jīva), who speaks in such a manner, becomes weary from engaging in the transactions of both the waking world— which is "this" (para) relative to it— and the dream world, and thus proceeds toward its own place of rest, the two channels (nāḍīdvaya).

In accordance with such scriptural passages as, "This space is indeed as large as this space within the heart," [it is understood that] in the golden, supreme sheath— which is all-pervading everywhere— within the space of the heart, there truly exists this immortal deity in the form of the individual soul (jīva), who, having taken hold of the three channels beginning with *ramā*, [presides over] the three states beginning with waking.

And regarding the established order of bondage, liberation, and so forth, that which moves through them is, in its singular state, non-avidyic; because of the absence of any connection with it, the Vedāntins declare that Brahman remains as the "three-footed" (*traipada*)—that which protects (*trāyate*) by its own remainder—and thus only Brahman remains. In this regard:
That which is traversed and born by those at the end of the three Vedas through their own remaining essence—
that supreme Brahman consisting of the three steps remains as its own self alone.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Since this is so, this deity called the "living soul" (jīva), having reached its own true nature right here [in the Self], remains established in that alone; it becomes liberated. Therefore, it does not exist elsewhere, in any other state characterized by ignorance.

Within this manifold expansion of the three states and their effects— characterized as "this" and "the other"— the ignorant individual soul (*jīva*) wanders about, asserting that there exists something separate from itself. Although it has been moving for a long time within the supreme golden sheath, which is everywhere and at all times, it remains shrouded by the veil of its own ignorance and falls into the pit of the three states beginning with waking.
Regarding the statement that "for him too, purification occurs through the grace of the Śruti and the teacher," there is an illustration:
just as this Devadatta, being sleepy, when struck with a staff and awakened,

does not immediately fall back into sleep, so too this individual soul (jīva), by means of the knowledge of Vedānta obtained through the grace of the Śruti and the teacher, [does not return to ignorance].

Having been enlightened that "you are the *jīva* which partakes in the three states, but you are actually Brahman, the substratum for the superimposition and negation of those three states," one no longer becomes deluded regarding the three states. Therein, because there is no arising of desire-driven activity toward imagined rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, one is free from desire (*niṣkāma*) and attains bliss in whatever object is obtained by chance. Just as:

This very God of supreme serenity, who engages in activity both in the dreaming and waking states, becomes weary and enters the state of deep sleep; he who knows "I am Brahman, whose nature is solely self-bliss," having thus become the inner light— the supreme radiance beyond the external phenomenal world— becomes the illuminator of even the sun and other luminaries on all sides.
