The meaning is that it becomes transformed into the form of the Supreme Brahman; having reached that Supreme Self, it causes bliss and gratifies its own self; being under the control of that [Self], it dissolves right there. As for the question of how such clarity of mind arises, it is from the Lord that his bright-colored state—the state of non-conceptualization—is born.
By virtue of possessing the powers of non-inert action, knowledge, and will, the Lord, out of compassion for His own devotees,
leads them by that very same path to the state of dream— the reality of "That thou art" and "I am Brahman"—
and brings them to rest therein. Just as a leech, from the object it has been clinging to, such as a blade of grass, [transfers its state...].

Just as a fire moves from one blade of grass to another, so too this wise man, established in the waking state of *turiya*, relies upon the dream of *turiya* and abandons the waking state of *turiya*.

Thus, through the two types of samādhi—*savikalpa* (with mental constructs) and *nirvikalpa* (without mental constructs)—which are differentiated within the state of *turiya*, he gladdens his own Self. Thereafter, [he attains] the inward-facing...

"Sandhi" means he completely abandons. That which has thus arisen as non-distinct is itself the Supreme Brahman; there is nothing else apart from that. Or rather, it does not abandon the notion that there is something else distinct from itself.

Because Brahman alone is devoid of any counter-correlate (niṣpratiyogika), it is so when the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman does not arise through mere hearing and the like. [In that case, one should practice] *kaṃ*— the supreme bliss— which consists of the desire for the cessation of suffering, pleasure, desire, and so forth, along with the eightfold yoga comprising *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*.

The meaning is that by properly practicing the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) after having contemplated the eight skulls, and by washing away the impurities residing in the mind through its power, one attains non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣajñāna*) and becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
As for the purpose of performing yoga, meditation, and so forth, it is as follows: "This which is like a breast, like a plantain flower... [and so on].
And it always rests upon the region of the chest; at the time of yoga, rising upward, it attains expansion.

For here indeed it exists together with Brahmā, who is the source of the senses (indrayoni); thus it is "sendrayoni. That which is called the source of the senses is this very Lord, the Supreme Lord praised by all as the source of the Vedas (vedayoni), who remains awake while [the world] is awake. He who is thus...

That wise person meditates upon the Lord seated upon the lotus of his own heart; being beyond both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he is not tainted even by those occasional actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, to which he may be attached. As for the nature of that God who was meditated upon as being beyond the auspicious and the inauspicious—regarding this, [the text asks] "Who is this [Lord] even of other gods such as Brahmā? etc.
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Thus indeed is the God, the supreme deity among deities.

To express the non-difference between the meditator and the object of meditation: this very God is this state of supreme serenity (*saṃprasāda*), the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*), the unattached, conscious Puruṣa; He alone is the *Haṃsa*, the fourth-of-the-fourth (*turyāturya*) meaning of the Praṇava.

It is called the Supreme Brahman. Here, the primary vital breath (prāṇa) is not intended by the term "the swan of breath" (prāṇahaṃsa), because the context concerns the Supreme Brahman. The *praṇava* is the individual soul (*jīva*), since it is denoted by the form of the constituent parts beginning with the *praṇava*;
thus, he declares that its primordial state is the Deity. How can he who knows the true nature of the *praṇava* [be otherwise]?

How does it declare the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman? Rather, it declares the nature of the soul’s identity with Brahman—characterized by the internal and external *śikhā* (topknot) and so forth—and the state of this person as having the internal *śikhā* and sacred thread (*upavīta*). For a Brāhmaṇa seeking liberation, the internal [is the true] *śikhā* and sacred thread.
For the householder: the characteristic of the inner *upavīta* is the unmanifest internal fusion of principles (*tattva*), like a thread within [the garment]. (3 p.
159) Now, the characteristics of the inner and outer *śikhā* and *yajñopavīta* are stated—beginning with "sattva. Furthermore:

Immediately after the state of being Brahman non-different from the inner self (pratyag-abhinna-brahmabhāva), for this person who has become Brahman, that which is his very existence (sattva) is itself the internal *śikhā* and *upavīta*; the meaning is that it is non-distinctive knowledge (*nirviśeṣa-jñāna*).
To the question, "By whom is that maintained?"—here [the answer follows].

This applies only to the Brāhmaṇa seeking liberation who performs the duty of wearing the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and sacred thread (*upavīta*) consisting of the light of knowledge shining within his own self. To the question, "For whom is the wearing of the external crest-lock and sacred thread? he says, "Internal," implying that for one who does not possess the aforementioned internal characteristics, there is no external manifestation. As for the characteristic of the internal sacred thread, it is unmanifest like the inner essence (*tan-tu*) within the external.
It is evident that this does not pertain to the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman, because that transcends both mind and speech.
If the union of the inner reality were within the sphere of Brahman as qualified by one's own ignorance, then [it would be so]. (3)
The nature of Brahman is devoid of distinctions;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither different-and-non-different from existence and non-existence, nor both;
it is neither with parts nor without parts, nor even of a dual form.
It is to be abandoned through the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self, because its nature is that of falsehood.

Thus, having refuted the portion consisting of ignorance as being false through numerous logical arguments, one should establish its state of being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*). For it is not non-existent, because it appears in the form of an effect and is visible to the eye; nor is it existent, because existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single locus. What then?

It is not different from itself, because it lacks a separate existence apart from itself. Why then is it not non-different? Because it would then lack substantiality. Nor is it both different and non-different, because such a state is impossible to find. It is not with parts (sabhāga) in its causal nature, because it is partless;
nor is it without parts (nirbhāga) in its effect-nature, because it possesses parts. Nor is it of a dual form, for the reasons previously stated.
Regarding the statement "it deserves the sixfold status like Brahman," the meaning is this: as long as the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self has not arisen, it possesses existence;

however, once the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self has arisen, because its falsity is established, it attains only the status of being negated, as there is nothing apart from Brahman. || 4 ||
The capacity of action to bring about purity of mind is as follows:
in the *Pañcapāda-Brahman*, there is nothing [external]; rather, there are four stations for the inner *jīva-brahman* residing within the *catuṣpād-brahman*.
These are the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*) located in the navel, heart, throat, and head respectively.

In the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇa, and Sabhya fires, [the Lord] is Brahmā in the waking state, Viṣṇu in the dream state, and Rudra in the state of deep sleep; the fourth is the imperishable, consisting of consciousness. Therefore, there are four states and four fingers [of measurement].

Having arrived at the extraction of the thirty-two principles, purified by knowledge, and having understood the nature of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) as the state of the three forms (*trimūrti*) individually;
and having known [the Self] as endowed with the nine qualities called the nine Brahmans, measured by the number nine, and having tripled it again by three qualities,
unified it as the nature of the digits (*kalā*) of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, including even its beginning, end, and middle.

Having rotated [the breath] three times through the center, having contemplated the states of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, and having unified the beginning and the end, one should form the knot of non-duality within the knot of consciousness; then, from the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā, one should contemplate the individual connection with the twenty-seven principles, endowed with the three qualities.

Having brought about unity even that which is characterized by the marks of the three forms (trimūrti), and having contemplated [the body] from the left shoulder to the right hip, one should realize the merging of the beginning and the end; thus, the single root—the clay—would be known as the truth: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth."

By the two syllables "haṃsa," having ascertained the internal *śikhā* (topknot) and *upavīta* (sacred thread), one attains Brahminhood, the fitness for meditation on Brahman, and the state of a *yati* (renunciant) characterized by the absence of an external *śikhā* and *upavīta*. Thus, for a householder who possesses only the semblance of Brahminhood, there is the external *śikhā* of ritual action and the *upavīta* of knowledge.

The state of wearing a sacred thread (*upavīta*) made from visible cotton threads gathered from the tips of their hair; having multiplied four by four, they fashion it from threads representing the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). Because the nine principles are in fact the one supreme Brahman, they conceive of its manifestation as moving through many paths for the sake of its suitability as a counter-measure (*pratisara*). [This applies] to all [beings], beginning with Brahmā.
For celestial sages and for humans, liberation is one; Brahman is one; and Brāhmaṇahood alone is one.

The specific practices of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) are distinct; the tufts of hair (*śikhā*) belong to those in various castes and stages, yet the tuft, the sacrificial thread, and the root-syllable (*praṇava*) are said to be one for the ascetic seeking final release. He is the *Haṃsa*.
The *śikhā* (topknot) is the *praṇava*; the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is the *nāda*; and the joining (*saṃdhāna*) is this very thing. This is the true dharma, not any other dharma.
How so? The *praṇava*, the *haṃsa*, and the *nāda* constitute the threefold thread (*trivṛtsūtra*), which abides within one’s own heart in consciousness.
Know that Brahman is threefold; one should abandon the worldly topknot and sacred thread.

The delusion that there exists or does not exist anything other than oneself in the form of ignorance belongs to the five-footed Brahman; for the one who has transcended the fourth state (*turyātīta*), nothing whatsoever exists. There are four locations for the perception of the inner Brahman—the inner living self (*antarjīva*)—which resides within the four feet consisting of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*): namely, Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya, which reside within the four feet of the individual.
Regarding the question of what the locations for their perception are, [the answer is] the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head; specifically, the eyes and the throat.
And thus says the Śruti:
"One should know that the waking state resides in the eyes; one enters the dreaming state in the throat."
Deep sleep resides in the heart, while the fourth state (turiya) is situated in the crown of the head.
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, the meaning is that the Self should be meditated upon, as appropriate, within the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇa, and Sabhya fires. Regarding the distinction of the differentiated consciousness during waking and so forth, he says: "In the waking state," etc.

This is for the purpose of understanding the identity between the external sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) and the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*). Otherwise, having taken the external sacrificial thread as an illustration, he elaborates upon the sacred thread with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*):
because there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the sacrificial thread and the sacred thread, owing to their lack of distinction in being "threads."

Therefore, having visualized it as encircling the four fingers of the four states beginning with waking— just as a sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is measured at ninety-six finger-breadths according to the measurement of four fingers—
so too are there ninety-six principles (*tattva*), from the ear up to Īśvara. Thus is the sacrificial thread.

The meaning is that if action is sustained by being permeated with the meditation on the Brahmasūtra, then that action becomes a means for attaining purity of mind. To praise the Brahmasūtra, he states its nature as a mere verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇatā*)—namely, "the root" (*mūlam*). That which is the cause, like clay and so forth, is the real (*satyam*).

Whatever effect is manifested by that ignorance is a mere modification of speech (*vācārambhaṇa*), because there is no jar or other such object apart from the clay; thus, the cause alone—Brahman—is real. Having ascertained the internal state of the *śikhā* (topknot) and the sacred thread through the two syllables "Haṃ," one should always [meditate] preceded by the contemplation: "I am He" (*so 'haṃ*).

"Being intent on that" means having the inner tuft (*śikhā*) and the inner sacred thread (*upavīta*). What would result from that? To this [the text] says: one attains the state of a *brāhmaṇa*, the fitness for meditation upon Brahman, the state of a *yati* (ascetic), and the unmanifested inner tuft and sacred thread.
But for the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) other than him, it is as follows, and so forth. The single Brahma-thread [is divided] by way of the distinctions of Viśva, Virāṭ, Otr, and so on.
"Having quadrupled four times" means that because Brahman is without distinction at the beginning and the end, it is likewise one and without distinction even during its intermediate state.
He says "that" (*tad*) to show that even though [Brahman] is devoid of any counterpart (*niṣpratiyogika*), those ignorant of their own nature (*svājña*) imagine many means for its attainment.

This is because that Brahman is capable of being resorted to (*pratisaraṇa-yogyatva*) according to the respective intellects of individuals. "Resorting" (*pratisaraṇa*) refers to the basis for conceptualization; having taken hold of that [Brahman], there are many paths such as Sāṅkhya and others, which serve as the means for attaining it.
"Only one's own nature, free from all correlates" means: simultaneous with knowledge,
liberation characterized by abiding in that alone occurs for all— whether they be gods beginning with Brahmā,
celestial sages, or human beings— if the knowledge of Brahman as the non-differentiated Absolute alone arises.

Simultaneous with that is the one disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*); there is only one Brahman, and only one true Brāhmaṇahood arising from steadfastness in Brahman. Of liberation and the recipient of liberation:
know that the *haṃsa* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and the *praṇava* is the sacred thread (*upavīta*); the resonance (*nāda*) of both the *haṃsa* and the *praṇava* is their union.

The *praṇava* is the fourth *oṃkāra*, which is its referent. The meaning of the mantra "the *haṃsa* is Brahman beyond the fourth" is established as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the unity of the internal and the external. That very same [Self] is the support for the dissolution of sound (*nāda*); thus, these three—the *praṇava*, the *haṃsa*, and the *nāda*—are called the "threefold thread" (*trivṛtsūtra*). Where, then, does this deserve to have its seat? To this [question]:

The meaning is that one abides in one's own heart within consciousness, abiding by oneself in one's own glory. Know that Brahman is twofold, distinguished as the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā). If, due to the delusion of regarding anything as separate from oneself, one desires to enjoy [the fruits of action], then the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) should renounce the worldly tuft of hair and sacred thread. || 5 ||
One who desires liberation, having performed a tonsure including the top-knot, should discard the external thread;
the wise one should maintain that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman as his sacred thread.
One should remember liberation day and night for the sake of ceasing rebirth;
it is called a "sūtra" because of its indicative nature, and the sūtra is the supreme state.
He by whom that Sūtra is known is a seeker of liberation, he is a true mendicant;
he is a knower of the Vedas, a man of right conduct, and he is a Brahmin who sanctifies the assembly at a meal.
(163) That thread by which all this is strung together like clusters of gems on a string—
that thread the yogi, the knower of yoga, the brahmin, and the ascetic should wear. 9.
A Brahmin who is devoted to the knowledge of Yoga should discard the external thread;
he who wears the thread consisting of the nature of Brahman is a partaker of liberation.
For him, there is no impurity nor any state of being "unclean" (ucchiṣṭa) regarding the wearing of that [inner] thread.
Those for whom the Sūtra is internal, who wear the sacred thread of knowledge—
they alone in this world are knowers of the Sūtra, and they alone are truly invested with the sacred thread.

For those whose crest is knowledge, who are established in knowledge, and who wear the sacred thread of knowledge, knowledge alone is their supreme purifier; knowledge is declared to be their [highest] goal.
He whose crest consists of knowledge, like the flame of a fire, is called a "crested one" (śikhin)—the wise man; not others who merely wear hair. || 13 ||
But those who are authorized to perform rites, whether Vedic or worldly,
yet live merely as semblances of Brahmins, filling only their own bellies—
they go to hell birth after birth, life after life. (14)

The wise one should maintain the Brahma-sūtra on the left side, extending from the left shoulder to the right hip; it should be positioned internally along the spine, endowed with the thread of reality (tattva-tantu), and serve as the standard of measurement from the navel up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahma-randhra). || 15 ||
By them this Sūtra is to be worn, fashioned from threads as a limb of ritual action;
he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread is likewise composed of that [knowledge], possesses the entirety of Brahminhood, but others possess nothing at all. (16)
(164) This, however, is the supreme sacred thread (yajñopavīta), which is the ultimate refuge;
the wise man who wears it as his sacred thread is a partaker of liberation. 17.
A Brahmin who wears the sacred thread both outside and inside is fit to renounce; however, one who wears only a single sacred thread is not at all fit to renounce. 18.
Therefore, with every effort, an ascetic who seeks liberation should abandon the external thread and wear the internal thread within his own heart. (19)

Disregarding the external proliferation of the tuft and sacred thread, one should perform the means to liberation by relying on the tuft and sacred thread consisting of the *praṇava* and the *haṃsa*; thus said the blessed Śaunaka—so ends the Upaniṣad. 20.

It is called a *sūtra* because it indicates [the truth] by way of being the basis for all refutations. The meaning is that Śaunaka, having understood the reality of Brahman from the mouth of Pippalāda, spoke thus to his own disciples. The word "Upaniṣad" signifies the completion of the *Parabrahmopaniṣad*. || 6–20 ||
By Upaṇiṣad-Brahma-Yogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra,
this brief commentary on the Parabrahmopaniṣad has been written;
the total extent of this commentary on the present Upaniṣad is one hundred and thirty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Parabrahma Upaniṣad, completing the seventy-eighth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
The Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Upaniṣad.
"May there be well-being through our ears"— thus [ends] the Peace invocation (śānti).
The Inquiry into the Characteristics of a Wandering Ascetic:
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), having approached his own father Ādinārāyaṇa and prostrated before him, asked:
"O Blessed One, from your mouth I have heard, known, and understood the entire sequence of duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life."

"Now I wish to know the characteristics of the wandering mendicant who is a supreme sage (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka). Who is qualified for the life of a wandering mendicant? What are the characteristics of a wandering mendicant?
Who is a supreme sage? How does one become a wandering mendicant? Tell me all that. He replied:
The Blessed One is Ādinārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
I worship Hari, the Turyaturya, whose single meaning is the Praṇava of Brahman— that knowledge through which those possessing the dharma of wandering mendicancy attained the state of Brahman.

Now, this Paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka Upaniṣad, which is a branch of the Atharvaveda, unfolds the supreme knowledge. A brief commentary on it is now commenced. It begins with the question of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa:
"What is the nature of the reality that has manifested from those two, the creator and the protector of the universe?"
He introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now).
Now, after hearing the dharma concerning the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others, as well as the students and householders,
the nine Prajāpatis beginning with Kāśyapa— the fathers of all the worlds— who were even superior to them...
That father, the grandfather of all the worlds, [worships] his own father, Ādinārāyaṇa, who is himself the primordial cause (*kāraṇa*) when there is the existence of effects (*kārya*).

Because there is no "ara" (non-existence), it is "nāra"— the non-dual reality established by the awakening to the impossibility of the conceptualization of cause and effect, which is free from all opposition (*niṣpratiyogika*).

Thus, this very Ādinārāyaṇa— who exists in embodied form through the vision of those ignorant of His own nature— those of small intellect perceive me as having attained manifestation from the unmanifest,
failing to recognize my supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed state.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Having approached him and prostrated like a staff, he asked: "What is it, O Blessed One? [The reply was:
"Everything has been heard exactly as it is. Now, I wish to know correctly the characteristics of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka"—this is the definition of the qualified seeker.

Having become a learned man who has mastered all branches of knowledge in the presence of a true guru, and having recognized that everything pertaining to this world and the next is to be abandoned like food vomited up, he—making liberation his sole goal—should complete his period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and become a householder; from the state of a householder he becomes a forest-dweller and then renounce the world (*pravrajeta*). Or otherwise, he may renounce directly from the stage of celibacy itself.

One should go forth from the home or from the forest. Now, whether one is without vows or possesses vows, whether one is a graduate (*snātaka*) or not a graduate, whether one has extinguished the sacred fires or maintains no fires—if on that very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth. Thus, one who is detached from all worldly existence—whether a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller—having abandoned father, mother, wife, and trusted kinsmen...
By this [verse], he indeed effects the taking of breath. One should perform the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice; by this very [sacrifice], one obtains the three elements, namely:
*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
This is your seasonal womb, from which once born you shone forth;
knowing that, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth.

With this mantra, he should inhale the fire. "This indeed is the womb of Agni; go to the breath, go to your own womb, svāhā"—thus he says this very thing. Having brought fire from a village or from the house of a *śrotriya*, he should inhale the fire as before according to the sequence prescribed by his own ritual rules. If he is ill, or if he cannot find fire, [he should do so] in water.
He should offer an oblation. Having offered it with the formula, "The waters are indeed all the deities; I offer to all the deities, svāhā!

he should take out [the remainder] and eat it—this sacrificial food, accompanied by clarified butter, leads to freedom from disease. This is the rule for one on a journey, or during a fast, or when entering the waters, or entering the fire, or setting out on the Great Journey, or if he is afflicted by illness.
One may renounce it either with the mind or with speech; this is the path. 2.

In response to his questions, [the author] first defines the qualified candidate for the life of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) with the word "one who is" (*sat*): having realized that there is never even a trace of happiness within the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*), and having understood that the three types of desire— beginning with wife and children—
and the body and so forth are to be rejected like vomited food, he becomes one whose sole means for attaining liberation is the dispelling of the delusion that anything other than the Self exists.

Having completed the student life (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; this has the same meaning as stated in the *Jābāla Upaniṣad*. He says "the father" to indicate that one should renounce only after obtaining the consent of all, beginning with the father; the sense is that one should go forth after having obtained such permission. If one has personally maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), then there must be the completion of the final oblation (*carameṣṭi*) and other such rites.

Regarding the phrase "it should be done" (*kāryā*), there is the passage beginning with "Now, some... (*taddhaika*). This and the subsequent sections have been explained word by word in the Jābāla Upaniṣad.

For one who is free from affliction and established in self-possession, renunciation should be performed according to the prescribed sequence; having performed the *virajā* oblation for the purification of the self and having internalized the sacred fires within oneself (*agnim ātmani āropya*).

Having entrusted his worldly and Vedic capacities, as well as the functioning of his fourteen organs, to his son—or in his absence, to a disciple; or in the absence of even that, to himself alone—the father addresses him, saying, "You are Brahmā; you are the sacrifice. (p. 168)
Having sequentially dissolved the Mother of the Vedas— who is the very essence of all knowledge and meaning and the support of Brahman—
into the three *vyāhṛtis*, and having dissolved those three *vyāhṛtis* into the syllables *a*,
*u*, and *m*, one should attentively sip water, loosen the top-knot with the *praṇava*, and cut the sacred thread.

Having cast even his garment upon the ground or into the water, reciting "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā, Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā, Oṃ suvaḥ svāhā," and having assumed the state of one possessing the natural luster (of gold), while meditating on his true nature, he should again, preceded by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, renounce mentally and verbally: "I have renounced; I have renounced."

Having uttered the *praiṣa* three times, tripled by means of deep, middle, and high-pitched sounds, saying "I have renounced," and being solely intent on meditation upon the *praṇava*, [he should grant] fearlessness to all beings from himself.
Having raised his arms and uttered "Svāhā," he should contemplate the great Upanishadic truth, "I am Brahman" (Aham Brahmāsmi), beginning with "That thou art" (Tattvamasi).
If he is not qualified for that, then preceded by the request of householders, he should recite: "Fearlessness to all beings;
from me everything proceeds; O Friend, protect me! You are the vigor; you are the thunderbolt of Indra."

With the mantra, "O slayer of Vṛtra, be my refuge; ward off whatever sin there may be," one should take a single discolored garment, approach a true guru, and bow down. Having received from the mouth of the guru the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), preceded by the *praṇava* (Om), one should then don worn-out clothes, bark garments, or an antelope skin.

Then, having abandoned descending into water, ascending, and accepting alms from only one person, and practicing bathing at the three times of day while performing the practice of the *praṇava* preceded by the hearing of the Vedānta, he became fully perfected on the path of Brahman; concealing his own desires within himself, he was free from possessiveness and established in the supreme self (*adhyātma*).

Having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, envy, hypocrisy, pride, egoism, malice, arrogance, longing, and aversion— as well as intolerance, the sense of "mine," and so forth— one who is endowed with knowledge and dispassion turns away from wealth and women.

With a pure mind, having reflected upon the meaning of all the Upaniṣads, diligently guarding celibacy, non-possessiveness, non-violence, and truthfulness, with senses conquered and devoid of internal or external attachment, he who subsists on alms— avoiding those accused of crimes or fallen from their status— and who is harmless toward animals even for the sake of maintaining his body, becomes one with Brahman.
At all times, remaining equanimous toward gain and loss, eating food with his hands as a bowl by means of alms-gathering (*ādhukara*),

not allowing an increase in fat, becoming emaciated, and contemplating "I am Brahman," he should enter a village for the sake of the teacher and wander alone for eight months, firm in his conduct; or he may wander even with two others.

When the realization of "enough" (alam-buddhi) arises, then—whether one is a Kuṭīcaka, a Bahūdaka, a Haṃsa, or a Paramahaṃsa—one should, preceded by the respective mantra, cast away the waist-thread, the loincloth, the staff, and the water-pot into the waters; thereafter, wearing only the naked form (jātarūpa-dhara), one should wander. One may stay for one night in a village and three nights at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in a town.

Staying for five nights in a sacred field and seven nights without a fixed abode, with a steady mind, not maintaining a sacrificial fire, free from perturbation, having abandoned both rules and non-rules, subsisting merely for the maintenance of life, regarding gain and loss as equal, practicing mendicancy by the "cow's way" (moving like a cow), carrying a water-pot for land and water, and dwelling in secret places free from disturbance— [he should live thus].
Sleeping on the bare ground, having abandoned the rite of shaving, having relinquished the observances and rules of the four-month vow (*cāturmāsya-vrata*),
devoted solely to pure meditation (*śukla-dhyāna*), turned away from wealth, women, and cities, though not insane he appeared like one insane,
and intent upon the path of meditation on the *praṇava* as Brahman through the contemplation of his own true nature, he lived by means of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
He abandons his body and becomes a wandering mendicant who is a supreme ascetic (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka). || 3 ||
If one who is free from disease desires to renounce, then, according to the fourth instruction of the *Nāradaparivrājakopaniṣad* (p.
[the renunciation] should be performed either before a disciple or a son— since the father and others possess the right of ownership over them— or, in their absence, within one's own self.

Having dissolved [the world], one should take up a bamboo staff (*vaiṇava-daṇḍa*) originating from a sacred place, preceded by the *praṇava*, possessing the proper characteristics, with its bark intact, and having even joints; and so forth. Then, descending into water with both hands while making a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should ascend upward through the kingdom of the mind, renouncing even a single alms-meal. Brahman is beyond all opposition (*niṣpratiyogika*).
The realization that nothing exists apart from Brahman is itself the path of Brahman. Having become perfected in this,
concealing the supreme conclusion within oneself alone, and being established in one's own self,
one should wander for alms like a beast among those who do not revile their husbands, remaining free from malice, for the sake of becoming Brahman.
He becomes one with the nature of Brahman. According to the Vedic revelation, "He who ordained Brahmā in the beginning," the Guru is Viṣṇu.

In accordance with the Smṛti text, "For the sake of the Great Viṣṇu, honey is pure and delicious as an offering," he approaches the village for the sake of the Guru; though his character is fixed and his nature is immovable, [he performs] the eight [observances].

He should wander alone, or he may wander in pairs. If he is not qualified for hearing [the scriptures] and meditation, then he should follow the manner previously described: staying in one place during the four months of the rainy season and spending only one night in a village during the remaining months;
this twofold practice alone is to be observed by ascetics. This applies when he is in the *kuṭīcaka* or other stages of life.
The thought "enough" should arise; for according to the Smṛti, one should eat what has fallen into the vessel and not think of anything else therein.
It should be understood that this entire Upaniṣad has been explained for the most part by means of the commentary on the Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad. || 3 ||
The inquiry into the nature of the Brahman-Praṇava:
"O Blessed One, what is the Brahman-Praṇava like? Thus Brahmā asks. He, Nārāyaṇa, said:
"The Brahman-Praṇava consists of sixteen mātrās; it is the sphere of the fourfold set of four states."
In the waking state, there are four states beginning with waking; in the dream state, four states beginning with dreaming;

in the deep sleep state, four states beginning with deep sleep; and in the fourth state (turiya), there are four states beginning with the fourth. Thus, within the individual waking state, there is a fourfold nature of the Viśva: the Viśva-Viśva, the Viśva-Taijasa, [the Viśva-Prājña, and the Viśva-Turya].
"Viśvaprājña, Viśvatūrya. Thus, in the state of individual dream (vyaṣṭi-svapna), there is a fourfold division of Taijasa:
Taijasa-Viśva, Taijasa-Taijasa, Taijasa-Prājña, and Taijasa-Tūrya.

In the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is a fourfold division of the *prājña*: the *prājña-viśva*, the *prājña-taijasa*, the *prājña-prājña*, and the *prājña-turīya*. In the state of the fourth (*turīya*), there is likewise a fourfold division of the *turīya*:
the *turīya-viśva*, the *turīya-taijasa*, and the *turīya-prājña*. These, in their respective order, are mounted upon the sixteen *mātrās*.

In the letter *a* is the waking Viśva; in the letter *u* is the waking Taijasa; in the letter *m* is the waking Prājña; in the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is the waking Turya. In the Bindu is the dreaming Viśva; in the Nāda is the dreaming Taijasa; in the Kalā is the dreaming Prājña; beyond the Kalā is the dreaming Turya. In the Śānti is the deep sleep Viśva; beyond the Śānti is the deep sleep Taijasa.

In *unmanī* one is the *suṣupta-prājña*; in *manonmanī*, the *suṣupta-turīya*; in the *puryaṣṭakī*, the *turīya-viśva*; in *madhyamā*, the *turīya-tejasa*; in *paśyantī*, the *turīya-prājña*; and in *parā*, the *turyaturīya*.
The four measures (*mātrā*) of the waking state constitute the portion of the letter *a*; the four measures of the dreaming state constitute the portion of the letter *u*.

The four measures of deep sleep constitute the portion of the letter *ma*, while the four measures of the fourth state (*turya*) constitute the portion of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*). This indeed is the Brahman-Pranava. It is to be practiced by the Paramahamsas, those who have transcended the fourth state, and the Avadhutas. Through this alone, Brahman is revealed.
Liberation while disembodied. || 4 ||
Having grasped the seed of the question—"By way of meditation on the Brahman-Praṇava"—[the disciple asks] regarding the extent of the Brahman-Praṇava:
"O Blessed One! He, Nārāyaṇa, said: "What is that? To this [he replied]: "The Brahman-Praṇava.
To the question "How is that so?", [he replied]: "In the waking state, there are four states, beginning with the waking."

"Waking-waking" and so forth: in the state of waking, there are four states beginning with "waking-dreaming," such as "waking-waking. In deep sleep, there are four states beginning with "deep-sleep-waking," such as "deep-sleep-waking. In the fourth state (*turiya*), there are four states beginning with "fourth-waking," such as "fourth-waking. Thus, there are sixteen states consisting of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) aspects of waking-waking and the rest.

"In the state of individual dream," and likewise "in the state of individual deep sleep. Similarly, regarding the fourfold nature of the Fourth (*turya*) in the passage "the fourfold nature of the Fourth," one should understand the threefold division as the Viśva of the Fourth, the Taijasa of the Fourth, and the Prājña of the Fourth. This is done by unifying the qualified and the unqualified.

The statement regarding the fourfold nature is for the purpose of correctly discerning the distinction between the non-dual (nirviśeṣa), fourth-of-the-fourth (turyaturīya)— which is established through the negation of the phenomenal world along with its specific attributes— and [the other states]. Likewise, there is the collective waking-waking and so forth, up to the collective fourth.

One should know that the state beyond conceptualization—the fourth of the fourth (*turyaturīya*)—is that which is reached when the fifteen states, beginning with waking-waking (*jāgrajjāgrat*), established through the unity of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), are transcended by the seer who is free from the functions of hearing and so forth. Regarding this meaning, the remainder [of the instruction] is: "Know that the four measures (*mātrā*) of waking belong to the portion of the letter *A*," as stated in the *Brahmapraṇava*. Likewise:

The meaning is: know that the four measures of dream constitute the portion of the letter *U*, the four measures of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) constitute the portion of the letter *M*, and the four measures of the fourth state (*turiya*) constitute the portion of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*). Since this is so, therefore, the entire conceptualization beginning from "waking-within-waking" and ending with "the sleep of the fourth" is established through the unity of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), the collective (*samaṣṭi*), and their combination.

In this regard, according to the Śruti, "all expressible objects are of the nature of the Praṇava," the fourteen states beginning with waking-waking (jāgraj-jāgrat) remain as nothing but one's own Self due to their lack of any counter-correlate. That wherein such a meaning is understood is indeed the Brahman-Praṇava. It is to be meditated upon by the Paramahaṃsas, those who have transcended the fourth state (turīyātīta), and the Avadhūtas; it is the Brahman-Praṇava.

The meaning of this section is that liberation while in the disembodied state (videhamukti)—characterized by abiding as Brahman alone—occurs through that very awakening to Brahman alone, which has as its sole object the fourth-of-the-fourth (turyaturya) that is devoid of all counter-correlates. || 4 ||

"O Blessed One, how can one who lacks the sacrificial thread possess the status of a Brahmin? How can one who is without the sacrificial thread, without the topknot, and has abandoned all ritual actions [be so]? How can he be Brahmā or Viṣṇu? "O child, for him who possesses the non-dual knowledge of the Self, that very knowledge is the sacrificial thread. For him—"

The very culmination of meditation is the tuft of hair; its ritual action is the sacred thread. He is the performer of all rites, he is the Brāhmaṇa, he is devoted to the supreme Brahman, he is the god, he is the seer, he is the ascetic, he is the most excellent, and he alone is the eldest of all—know him to be me. In this world, a wandering mendicant who is a Paramahaṃsa is exceedingly rare; if there is even one such person, he is [the true Brāhmaṇa].

(173) He alone is eternally pure; he alone is the Veda-Purusha. That Great Purusha whose mind abides in Me alone, and in whom I likewise abide—he alone is eternally satisfied. He [is indifferent] to cold and heat, pleasure and pain...

He is devoid of the six modifications of existence. He is free from the distinction between the elder and the younger. There is no seer other than himself. He is clothed in space; he performs neither salutation, nor the utterance of *svāhā*, nor the utterance of *svadhā*, nor is he intent on ritual dismissal.
He is beyond praise and blame, not a practitioner of mantras or tantras, and empty of meditation upon any other deity.

He who has turned away from both the perceptible and the imperceptible, who is stilled in all things, who is the non-dual mass of consciousness consisting of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, who is perfectly fulfilled—he is a Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicant; such is the Upaniṣad.

Because the Brahman-Praṇava is intended for those such as the Paramahaṃsas and others, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is heard of everywhere in scripture with respect to the Paramahaṃsas and others: "He who is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) is a Paramahaṃsa; he is an Avadhūta;

he is a Brāhmaṇa. However, common worldly usage applies the term only to those performers of ritual action (karmaṭhas) who are distinguished by the tuft of hair (śikhā) and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).

Regarding the term "brahminhood": Brahmā asks the Blessed One how one who is a rare ascetic (yati) can possess brahminhood; thus he says, "O Blessed One. Viṣṇu spoke this answer to the question: "In this world, such a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) who has attained my state—the Paramahaṃsa—is exceedingly difficult to find. He alone is eternally satisfied."

Because it brings about the attainment of my own nature and bestows eternal satisfaction; because it transcends cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor, hunger and so forth; because it is devoid of the six modifications of being (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*) and is subtler than the gross body which is the locus of those six states—according to the Śruti; and because there is no other seer apart from it, nor anything else to be seen.

Because it is to be sought; because there is an absence of the *visarjanīya* (the final visarga), it is not followed by a *visarjana*. One who is a practitioner of mantra and tantra is not devoid of meditation on other deities, for there is no purpose to be achieved through the worship of deities other than those of mantra and tantra.

That which turns away from the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the non-indicated (*alakṣya*): the "indicated" is that which is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), while the "non-indicated" is its opposite.

It must be stated that, apart from itself, neither of those two exists; rather, it is the negator [of duality] through the realization: "I alone am all this," and "I am nothing but the fourth-of-the-fourth (turyaturya), which is the very self of the meaning of the Brahman-Pranava."
The meaning is that the wise one remains as the form of the "fourth of the fourth" (turyaturya) and becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta).
The word "Upaniṣad" indicates the completion of the present Upaniṣad. || 5 ||
The commentary on the *Prakṛtopaniṣad* leading to the Fourth-of-the-Fourth (*turyaturya*) has been written by Upaṇiṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
It is recorded that the total extent of this collection of texts comprising the commentary on the *Prakṛtopaniṣad* is one hundred [verses].
Thus ends the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad, the sixty-sixth [treatise] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
"Full is that"—thus [ends] the Peace (Śānti).
Now, regarding the path of the wandering mendicants who are supreme swans (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas):
what is this path of those yogins who are supreme swans, and what is their state? Thus [asked] Nārada.

Having approached the Blessed One, he spoke. The Blessed One said to him: "This path of the Paramahaṃsa is extremely rare in the world and not common; if there is even one such person, he alone is eternally pure, and the wise consider him to be the Veda-Purusha himself. The mind of that Great Being always abides in Me alone; therefore, I am [He]."

And he remains fixed in that very state. Having abandoned his own sons, friends, wife, kinsmen, and so forth, as well as the entire universe, he takes up only a loincloth, a staff, and a covering for his body—this is the primary [ascetic], if this indeed is the primary one. || 1 ||
I contemplate the reality of the glorious three-stepped Rāma— the form of supreme bliss known through the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*— as being nothing other than my own self.

Indeed, since this Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad is a branch of the Śukla Yajurveda, beginning with the verse "Īśāvāsyam," it has been composed in the form of a narrative for the sake of the ultimate liberation of those qualified aspirants who are encountered here.

Now, with the words beginning with "atha" [the text continues]: Then, following his own acts of devotion, faith, and austerity, after the Lord had become manifest, the sage Nārada—renowned as a divine seer (devarṣi)—approached that Blessed One, in whom the perfection of the sixfold sovereign powers culminates, with humility and spoke. What did he say? [He asked: "O Supreme Swan among Yogins... [and so forth].
"What is it like?"—being thus questioned by Nārada, the Blessed Lord Hari spoke to him as follows: "Tat" (That).
To Nārada, who had questioned Him in this manner, the Blessed Lord Hari spoke thus. What was that? He said:
"In this world, even the path of the Kuṭīcaka, Bahūdaka, and Haṃsa ascetics, distinguished by the aforementioned conduct, is difficult to find."

To that extent, the path of the Paramahaṃsa is even more difficult to attain. Regarding this rarer goal, the Śruti itself says, "but not in abundance. If, by some chance, such a one exists, then he alone is a Paramahaṃsa. He is called "nityapūtastha" because he abides in his own greatness—the eternally pure and purified Self. He...

Thus, those who know that the Person of the Veda is the meaning of the Veda and the Supreme Self (paramātman) consider themselves to be the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. For this very reason, one becomes a Paramahaṃsa, a Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), whose mind abides in Me alone—Nārāyaṇa—having been transformed into My own form. Since this is so, therefore, I too...

He remains established in that very state: in the Supreme Self, the innermost Self; having become established through non-difference from the innermost Self as the Supreme Self, he regards as his own his son, friend, wife, kinsmen, and so forth, as well as the tuft of hair and the sacred thread perceived externally, and the entire collection of Vedic scriptures studied by himself.

Having renounced all actions performed under its impulsion during his state of ignorance, and having abandoned— through the realization that they are not distinct from himself— the fourteen-fold universe adorned with the cosmic egg which appeared as his own dwelling,
he retains only a loincloth, a staff, a covering garment, and the clothes required for his daily duties such as wandering for alms.
One should accept [these things]. To the question, "For what purpose is that acceptance? the answer is: for the sake of the enjoyment of one's own body.

For the sake of enjoyment—meaning for the sake of warding off cold, mosquitoes, and so forth—and for the sake of benefiting the world itself, as well as for the sake of removing the world from the wrong path, one should accept such things as a loincloth; this is the meaning. Since the acceptance of a loincloth and so forth is his primary [requirement], he says:
If it is asked, "In that case, what is their primary [duty]? he says, "This is the primary one," namely, the very abandonment of even one's loincloth. || 1 ||
The state of the wandering mendicants who are supreme swans (paramahaṃsa-parivrājakas) is as follows:
the supreme swan moves about without a staff, without a topknot, without a sacred thread, and without clothing;
he experiences neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor pain, and neither honor nor dishonor. He is free from the six waves [of worldly existence].

Because that body is the cause of those things— blame, pride, envy, hypocrisy, arrogance, desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, lust, anger, greed, delusion, and so forth— for which doubt and false knowledge have been utterly destroyed.

I am eternally withdrawn from that [world], possessed of eternal awakening to it, and established in that very state myself; I am indeed that peaceful, immovable, non-dual bliss, a mass of consciousness. That alone is my supreme abode, that alone is my crest-lock, and that alone is my sacred thread. Through the knowledge of the oneness of the Supreme Self and the individual self, their distinction indeed ceases.
That twilight has passed away.
Having renounced all desires, one who abides in supreme non-duality and wields the staff of knowledge is called a single-staffed ascetic (ekadaṇḍin).
He who merely holds a wooden staff, eats all kinds of food, and is devoid of knowledge— bereft of the qualities of forbearance, wisdom, dispassion, tranquility, and so forth.
He who lives by mere alms is a sinner who destroys the livelihood of an ascetic;
he goes to the terrible hells known as Mahāraurava.
Having understood this distinction, he is a Paramahaṃsa. || 3 ||
He has no concern for clothing; he offers neither salutation nor the utterances of *svāhā* or *svadhā*; he is free from blame and praise, as well as from ritual worship.
He perceives neither the marked nor the unmarked, neither the separate nor the non-separate, neither day nor the whole [of time].
With a mind fixed on the homeless state, such a mendicant must not accept gold or other valuables, nor even look at them.

And there is no looking [at it]. If it is asked, "What is the obstacle?", there is indeed an obstacle. Because if a monk should look at gold with a sense of attachment (*rasena*), he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). Because if a monk should touch gold with a sense of attachment, he becomes a *paulkasa*. Because if a monk should take hold of gold with a sense of attachment...
He would be a destroyer of himself. Therefore, a monk [should] not, out of greed, look at gold, nor touch it, nor take hold of it;
[this applies to] all [forms of it].

Desires arising in the mind turn away; one is not agitated by suffering and is free from longing for pleasure. There is renunciation regarding passion toward all things, neither attachment to the auspicious nor aversion to the inauspicious. One neither hates nor rejoices.
The movement of all the senses ceases for one who abides in the Self alone.

"I am indeed that Brahman, which is the singular consciousness of full bliss"—having realized this, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; one has accomplished all that was to be done. Thus ends the Upanishad. || 4 ||

Indeed, a Paramahaṃsa does not wander about having taken up the staff, top-knot, sacred thread, and clothing appropriate for the householder's stage of life. For him, there is no reckoning of cold and heat, or honor and dishonor; such reckoning is rooted in the body. Since the Paramahaṃsa has ascended to the state of Brahman non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), the three bodies [have ceased to exist].

Smaya is pride regarding wealth, learning, and so forth; matsara is a firm anger fixed in the heart; dambha is the flaunting of religious hypocrisy; darpa is a mind that perceives neither itself nor others; icchā is the longing for objects to be obtained;
dveṣa is aversion toward that which causes one's own harm; sukha is pleasure born from desired objects; and duḥkha is pain born from undesired objects.
Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for a desired object; anger (*krodha*) is that which causes its obstruction;

greed (*lobha*) is the lack of desire to relinquish one’s own possessions; delusion (*moha*) is the perception of something as what it is not; joy (*harṣa*) is born from the attainment of an object dear to oneself; envy (*asūyā*) is intolerance of another’s excellence; egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is an arrogant disposition; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the attachment] to one's own things is included.

The sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*) and so forth is grasped. Having abandoned all this through the intellect that transcends itself, one who strives for abiding in one's own true nature perceives one's own body as if it were a corpse from that perspective. For, by means of the knowledge of Brahman, for those whose doubts and false cognitions have been utterly destroyed, their own body is seen thus.

That which is seen as the cause for the manifestation of knowledge regarding such Brahman— the Supreme Self who is eternally awakened, whose own ignorance has been eternally removed by means of the inner self (pratyak), through the state of being the Brahman non-different from the inner self, and who is the substratum for the cessation of that very ignorance— is this very one.

That which is of the nature of eternal consciousness is itself the state of abiding; its remaining as nothing but its own self is liberation. He who is called "liberated" is that very one in whom the state of ignorance distinct from himself, along with its effects, has been stilled—a full state beyond all opposition. That alone is the tuft (*śikhā*) and that alone is the sacred thread (*upavīta*), because, like the hair, cotton, or threads of a tuft, it is distinct from the body. What [is there] for him? *Note: The final sentence fragment "tasya kā" appears to be incomplete in the source text.*
Regarding the question "What is *saṃdhyā*?", he says: "The Supreme Self" (*paramātman*).

Through the knowledge of oneness—that "I am indeed Brahman, and Brahman is indeed I"—the very distinction between those two, the inner consciousness (*pratyak-cit*) and the supreme consciousness (*paracit*), which are the individual self (*ātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [is dissolved]. (p. 179)
The distinction between the principles has been shattered because their true nature is one; that state of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is itself the *saṃdhyā*.
This *saṃdhyā* is not produced by ritual waters, nor by the recitation of mantras.
The unification of the individual soul and the Self at the point of junction—that is called *saṃdhyā* by the wise.

Thus says the Smṛti. In this way, having renounced and negated all desires other than oneself, one's abiding in supreme non-duality—that is, remaining in that very form—is the "staff of knowledge" (jñānadaṇḍa), which consists solely in the realization of one's own Self.
He who, lacking even the scent of such knowledge, merely holds a wooden staff is indeed a consumer of everything (sarvāśī).
He becomes merely one who fills his belly, devoid of specific knowledge; moreover,
he lacks the qualities of forbearance toward cold, heat, and so forth, as well as specific knowledge, dispassion toward objects other than that [knowledge], tranquility, and the like.

If one who is active both internally and externally should live solely on alms, he becomes a sinner and the worst of evildoers; he would even become a destroyer of the livelihood of virtuous ascetics. Furthermore, people might regard even true renunciants as mere semblances of renunciants, and upon seeing them, they would treat them with indifference.

Due to that fault, he causes [others] to appear as such and goes to the hells known as Mahāraurava. Having understood this difference between the one who perceives the ultimate reality (paramārthika) and the renunciant (saṃnyāsī), the naked one (āśāmbara/digambara) offers no salutation, because of the absence of the distinction between elder and younger; there is no utterance of *svāhā*, nor any utterance of *svadhā*.

Because the common duties toward the gods and ancestors have been renounced; there is neither censure nor praise, due to the absence of qualities that would warrant either blame or commendation. One may act according to whim, provided it is for the mere maintenance of the body;
however, since acting according to desire is prescribed [only for this purpose], any conduct beyond that, being motivated by personal desire, would lead only to downfall. In this regard—
For one endowed with knowledge and dispassion, liberation occurs within oneself alone; thus, there is no obligation to follow conduct in all respects.

This is because of the Śruti: "By virtue of that conduct, one attains those respective worlds. Therefore, for a mendicant who maintains only the body and is devoid of engagement in or withdrawal from anything else, [there is indeed no such obligation].

He says that for others there exist invocation (*āvāhana*), dismissal (*visarjana*), mantra-meditation (*mantradhyāna*), worship (*upāsana*), and so forth, whether with or without a specific object (*lakṣya-alakṣya*);

however, regarding the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), he says: "Of the mendicant... For one characterized by the aforementioned qualifications, there exists no object whatsoever apart from the Self—whether as distinct (*pṛthaktvena*) or non-distinct (*apṛthaktvena*)—that falls within the scope of the words "thou," "I," or "it. If...

If there is the delusion that [the self] exists as something empirical or as something illusory, then one whose mind is steady and homeless, having cast off the conceit of "mine" regarding a dwelling—whether in one's own body or elsewhere—is free from egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).

One should not at all accept gold and such things, nor even look at them, nor gaze upon them. If it is asked, "What is the obstacle [to doing so]?"—it is because there is no ground for accepting gold and the like; having accepted that such a ground exists, one should never indeed look at gold and so forth. If it is asked, "What is the obstacle if one acts in this way?"—[the answer is: none whatsoever.

There is indeed an obstacle. How so? Because if a monk, out of a desire for enjoyment, should look upon gold, precious gems, and the like with *rasa*—that is, with affection—he would become a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*).
The phrase "because" and so forth is the same [as before]. If it is touched by that *rasa*, then he becomes a *paulkasa*, a leather-worker.

It would be so; if the object to be grasped were actually grasped, then he would be a destroyer of his own self. Therefore, a monk [should regard] gold neither with taste nor as seen, nor touched, nor grasped. By "taste," it means that seeing gold upon the road—provided there is no attachment—is not a fault, just like [seeing] grass on the path.
Because touching and grasping are not applicable here,

in accordance with the Vedic text, "Do not covet the wealth of anyone," all desires imagined in the mind— though they have become attached to the mind through the perspective of one's own ignorance— are [renounced] by the Paramahaṃsa who has no longing for gold and other such things.

From the perspective of one's own realization, they turn away; they cease because they are seen to be of a false nature. Since this is so, the Paramahaṃsa does not become agitated even when painful *prārabdha* arises; likewise, he remains free from longing even when pleasant *prārabdha* arises. Even when attachment and aversion present themselves, there is their renunciation.
It is so. In every respect, the path of cessation (*nivṛtti-mārga*) is auspicious, while the path of engagement (*pravṛtti-mārga*) is inauspicious.

One who is without attachment to these two, turning away from both the paths of engagement and cessation, feels no aversion toward the path of engagement and experiences no delight in the path of cessation. [This applies] to all the organs of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karmendriya*).
And by the word "ca" (and), the movement of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—its capacity to grasp various objects—is brought to rest within the Self alone.

That which remains as the substratum, abiding as nothing but its own essence, is this very one whose nature is full bliss and singular consciousness. For the Śruti declares: "Having abandoned the state of cause and effect, pure consciousness alone remains. Thus, full consciousness remains after casting off causality.

That which remains as full awakening—that "I am indeed that Brahman," and "that Brahman is my own self alone"—at the very moment of such knowledge, one has accomplished all that was to be done and becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*). The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
"Thus the Upanishad" marks the conclusion of the present Upanishad. || 4 ||

This clear commentary on the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad* has been written by Upa-niṣad-brahma-yogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra. This work, the commentary on the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*, is recorded as consisting of one hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad, completing the nineteenth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
The Brahmopaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"— thus the peace invocation.
The Four-Footed Brahman.
Śaunaka, the great householder, indeed questioned the venerable Pippalāda, the descendant of Aṅgiras:
"How do those who are firmly established in the divine city of Brahman create? Whose is this greatness?"
"Who indeed was he who became this greatness? Who is he? To him he spoke the most excellent knowledge of Brahman: "This Prāṇa is indeed the Self. He became the greatness of the Self.
He is the life-span of the gods; he is the death and the non-death of the gods. Stainless in the divine city of Brahman,"
That Brahman which shines forth as partless, pure, and imperishable—he controls [them], just like the king of honey-bees.
Just as all the bees fly up when the king of the honey-bees flies up, even so all those gods fly up after him as he departs. He...

It emits and draws back like honey-comb. Just as a spider spreads out its web with a single thread and withdraws it by that same means, even so this vital breath (prāṇa), when it comes, draws back everything that has been emitted.
All those deities of the vital breaths, known as the "nāḍīs," slept [in him] like a hawk in the sky; just as a hawk rests in the sky.

Relying [on this], it goes to its own abode while in the state of deep sleep; just as this Devadatta, even when struck with a staff, does not perceive [the pain], so too he is not tainted by desired sacrifices or charitable works, whether auspicious or inauspicious. Just as a child, free from desire, attains bliss, even so this Devadatta attains bliss in the dream state. This is known from the Veda.

The supreme light. Desiring light, he causes the light to rejoice. Again, by that very same [process], he goes toward dream, like a leech. Just as a leech draws itself from point to point, so does the Self lead itself; it leads the higher and joins it to the lower, yet it does not abandon the lower. This is designated as the waking state. Just as this—

He brings together eight skull-bowls... That which hangs down like a breast is the womb of the gods; therein one perceives the auspicious and inauspicious while awake. This serene state of this god is the inner controller, the sky-goer, the crab, the lotus, the person, the vital breath, the swan, Brahmā, the Self, and the deity; it makes [all] known. He who knows thus—he [attains it].
He attains the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the supreme abode of Brahman. [First Section:
Now, this person has four stations: the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head.
Therein, the four-footed Brahman shines forth: as Brahmā in the waking state, as Viṣṇu in the dream state, and as Rudra in deep sleep.
The fourth is the Imperishable. It is Āditya, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara himself—the light that is known as being without mind, without ears, and without hands or feet. || 1 ||
I contemplate that which is the radiant heart, manifesting as sparks from the *Brahmopaniṣad*,
the imperial sovereignty of the bliss of the three states, as being nothing but my own self.

Indeed, within this Brahma-branch belonging to the Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda, three sections (kāṇḍas) have been revealed; therein, for one possessed of desire, through the performance of the mere ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), [the path of] smoke and so forth [is attained],
and [there is] the meditation on action (karmopāsanā).

There is an attainment of that state together with Him. For those in whom detachment arises toward both paths due to an abundance of purity of mind, this Brahmopaniṣad, consisting of the Jñānakāṇḍa, has been set forth for the sake of the immediate realization of Brahman alone, which is free from all correlates (niṣpratiyogika). This is because it conforms to the meaning of the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *upa*.
For one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is the attainment of Brahman alone, which is devoid of all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika*), preceded by the dissolution of one's own ignorance.
Thus, a brief commentary on this *Brahmopaniṣad*, characterized as described above, is now commenced with the word "atha" (now).
"Atha" means: after the completion of the aforementioned means for the knowledge of Brahman, for the seeker of liberation.

Because one who possesses a mind ascended upon that which is other than the Self is unfit for the instruction regarding Brahman alone—which is without a counter-correlate—it is necessary to teach the means of Brahma-vidyā so that the mind may ascend to That alone. Since the Śruti, being supremely compassionate, has proceeded [to teach] in this way, it is therefore appropriate to conceive of a locus for the realization of Brahman. He who...

"Only the Full remains," and "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal"—thus, by these scriptural statements, it is established that the Puruṣa remains. Regarding this Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, there are four places of realization. What are they? In response to the inquiry as to whether they exist in some other location:

He states that these reside within one's own body with the words "the navel. By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that there are other locations such as the right eye and so forth. To the question, "What kind of Brahman is there therein?
he says: "Therein..."

"Brahman shines as four-footed" (p. 183). Because it rests upon four locations, Brahman—which is in reality devoid of all limitation—shines as four-footed; this is the meaning. [This refers to] the four-footedness as it appears through the perspective of those who lack self-knowledge.

The perception of those objects is the waking state. Therein, in the waking state, Brahmā, presiding over the circle of the navel, fashions the conceptualization of the waking world; for he is the four-faced creator of the universe. When the dream born from the dissolution of the waking state is perceived, then Viṣṇu, presiding over the heart, becomes engaged in the fashioning of that dream. When...

When the activity of waking and the other states dissolves, that is deep sleep (*suṣupti*). At that time, Rudra, presiding over the throat, withdraws the phenomenal world of waking and dreaming as conceptualized by his own ignorance.
That state wherein the triad of waking and the other two states dissolves is this fourth state (*turīyāvasthā*). At that time—
That which, by presiding over the head, reveals the existence and non-existence of the conceptualizations of waking and so forth,

is called the *turya* (the fourth) situated at the crown of the head. Although he will later state that the waking and other states reside in the eyes, throat, heart, and head, nevertheless, because the navel and other locations have already been mentioned here, this [description] is for the sake of comprehension.

This is to be reflected upon: or else, having omitted [the stages] starting from the navel in their respective order, one should contemplate the "waking-of-waking" by combining the navel and the eyes. The throat is the place of dreaming; the heart is the place of deep sleep, as before;
and the fourth state (*turya*) is situated in the head—that which, presiding over the head, becomes the self of the fourth.
Therefore, because [it might be thought that] the sun and so forth are distinct [from Him], he says: "He is the sun. This is because there is no existence of the sun and so forth apart from Him.
By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that nothing whatsoever exists apart from Him. To the question, "What is His true nature? he says:
"The state of being the Imperishable (akṣaratva) of the Supreme Brahman."
Where there are no worlds, yet not no worlds; no gods, yet not no gods; no Vedas, yet not no Vedas; no sacrifices, yet not no sacrifices; no mother, yet not no mother; no father, yet not no father;

no daughter-in-law, yet not no daughter-in-law; no outcaste, yet not no outcaste; no Pulkasa, yet not no Pulkasa; no ascetic, yet not no ascetic; no forest-dweller, yet not no forest-dweller—there that one alone, the Supreme Brahman, shines forth.

In the space of the heart, that consciousness is space; that cavity is space. One should know that as the space in the heart wherein this [world] moves together and apart, and wherein all this is woven like warp and woof.
He who knows that through meditation among living beings becomes that pervasive Supreme Brahman—this is Nirvāṇa. || 2 ||

The impossibility of the existence of one's own internal organs, such as the mind (*manas*) and the rest, as well as the external organs, such as the ears and the rest—which are distinct from oneself—[is established] because [they do not exist] apart from oneself;
[this applies to] the worlds and so forth.
The destruction of the ascetic is not possible; rather, in the form of his liberation (*nirvāṇa*), only his own true nature remains. Thus he says:

"One. When the delusion of the vision of one's own ignorance exists or does not exist, the Supreme Brahman alone—which is the non-dual Brahman-only devoid of all counterparts—shines forth in the form of liberation while still in the physical body (*vikalebara-nirvāṇa*).
The meaning is that liberation shines forth in a single, uniform form. || 2 ||
Nirvāṇa is a unity;
therein neither gods, nor seers, nor ancestors have power, for it is awakened by all-encompassing knowledge. || 3 ||

How is it that Nirvāṇa alone is without a counterpart? Since there exists a controller such as the gods and so forth, [the author] says: "Not there. That which remains as its own self alone—indeed, in that state, the gods, sages, and ancestors do not exist. In that state of abiding as the *tanmātra* (pure essence), they have not attained their own nature and cannot exist in the relationship of controller and controlled.

How do they exercise power or become capable? Rather, it means that when the one Self alone—Brahman, which is devoid of the distinctions of gods, sages, ancestors, and so forth—is realized as being nothing but itself, then even through the forms of gods, sages, and ancestors, one becomes awakened to the realization "I am Brahman," and not through the vision of duality. Whatever is imagined by one's own ignorance, all that is indeed this very Self.

That which is established by the Śruti as "all" is the knowledge of all; by that [knowledge], one should contemplate all the deities imagined by oneself as being within the thread of the triad (trivṛtsūtra).
All the deities reside in the heart, and all the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established in the heart.
They know that in the heart reside the vital breaths, the light, and the threefold thread.
And it abides in consciousness within the heart. || 4 ||

With the intention of prescribing renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) as an auxiliary means for the awakening to Brahman alone, [the author] prepares the ground with the verse beginning, "The deity residing in the heart" (*hṛdisthā devatā*). By the word "heart" (*hṛd*), the inward-facing consciousness (*pratyakcaitanya*) is meant, because it "takes away" (*harati*) everything other than itself into its own nature. In that heart, or in the lotus of the heart which is governed by it, reside Agni and the other deities.

All the deities are established [therein]. Likewise, in the heart, the five vital breaths—such as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth—as well as speech and the other [organs], have been established by the Creator according to their distinctions. Thus, in the heart characterized as described above, [are located] the two nostrils...
By means of the two *cakāra*s (the letter 'ca'), it is illuminated that whatever is conceptualized as "it exists" or "it does not exist," all of that is established within the heart.

Those who have abandoned external threads know this very thing as the "threefold thread" (*trivṛtsūtra*). To the question, "Where is the external thread established? he says: "in the heart," because everything is established in the heart. || 4 ||
The sacred thread is outside; it is the supreme purifier, that which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning.
Put on this foremost, life-prolonging, bright sacred thread; may there be strength and splendor for you. 5.

To the question, "Of what nature is the external thread? he says: "The *yajñopavīta*. The *yajñopavīta* is the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which has come specifically near to, or approached, Viṣṇu, who is the sacrifice (*yajña*). It is inherent—meaning it is the innate cause of one's worldly activity—or else it is innate like the body, senses, and so forth. It is "in front," that is, prior.

Knowing the self to be the foremost and most excellent longevity, direct your mind toward that which is other than yourself; or rather, the meaning is: taking hold of that bright, luminous inner *yajñopavīta*, cast off the external *yajñopavīta*. Since this [inner thread] abides in the consciousness of the heart, therefore—this.

The threefold sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of cotton should be worn by those of the three higher castes. The meaning is: may that cotton thread be strength and vigor for you, the cause of successful action, and may it bring about the increase of splendor, Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and so forth. 5.
The Brahma-thread.
Having shaved his head including the top-knot, the wise man should discard the external thread;
he should maintain that which is the imperishable Supreme Brahman as his [true] thread.
They say it is called a *sūtra* because it provides instruction (*sūcana*); the *sūtra* is indeed the supreme state.
He by whom that *sūtra* is known is a true Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
The yogi who knows yoga and perceives reality should wear that thread by which all this is strung together like clusters of gems on a string.
The wise man, established in the supreme yoga, should cast aside the external thread;
that conscious person who wears this thread of the nature of Brahman is truly enlightened.
By upholding that Sūtra, one shall neither be defiled by food remnants nor impure. || 9 ||

Having established that for the three social classes (traivarṇika) the means for performing Vedic and Smārta rites [is the external sacred thread], he now states that for wandering mendicants (parivrājaka), after first renouncing the external sacrificial thread, the primary topknot and sacrificial thread must be worn—thus he says: "together with the topknot" (saśikham). This refers to the shaving of the hair, beard, and so forth, while keeping the topknot intact.

Having performed the external threefold thread (*trivṛtsūtra*) which is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*), one should abandon it, as it pertains to the obligatory rites (*nityādi*) and so forth. To the question "What then?", he says:

"That which..."—that which is the supreme, incomparable, and most excellent Imperishable (*akṣara*), established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the perishable phenomenal world (*prapañca*) distinct from itself.

One should maintain the conviction that Brahman is one's own self alone, because it expands [all] through its own remaining [as the substrate]. What is that? How is it to be maintained? And what is the fruit of such maintenance? To this, he says: "Because of being indicated" (*sūcanāt*).
This is because it is indicated by such scriptural passages as: "Being alone is real, the other is unreal; Brahman alone is real, for the other does not exist."
The knowers of Brahman say that Brahman alone is the Sūtra, which is the swallowing of that which appears as other than itself. To the question "What is this so-called Sūtra?", he says:
"the Supreme State" (paraṃ padam). The meaning is that it is the Supreme, unsurpassed, and it is called a "State" (pada) because it is reached (padyate) in its own form;
thus, it is nothing but Brahman. He who has known this very Sūtra as his own true nature is a Vipra.

The meaning is that one who is most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, by way of negating what has been superimposed upon it, reaches that which is the supreme Brahman alone— the goal where the Vedas culminate— and thus becomes Brahman itself.
Anticipating the doubt as to how such a state can be accessible to those of dull intellect:

He describes the nature of the *sūtra* as the means for ascending to that state (*tatpadāroha*) with the words "by which" (*yena*). That which is threaded like a string of pearls upon the *sūtra* as the substratum for the superimposition of the world distinct from itself—
that by which all this collection of the sphere of ignorance (*avidyāpada*) and its effects is strung together and pervaded— is this very *sūtra*, the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvaracaitanya*).
The knower of Yoga has shown that very reality as either the substratum for all negations or as being without a substratum;
