one should maintain the firm conviction, "I am that very [reality]. But how, then, should it be maintained? To this he says—starting with the word "outside"—that it should be maintained by first discarding the portions to be abandoned within it, while retaining the remaining portion.

The meaning is this: that conscious, wise person who abandons the entire realm of ignorance and its effects—which are characterized by external threads and tufts of hair—this very yogi should then wear this thread, which is the state of Brahman remaining after such renunciation; he who wears it thus becomes established in the yoga of Brahman alone.
Anticipating the objection that even one who knows thus might still possess such a state due to association with specific limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa),

[the author] states "because of holding" (dhāraṇāt) to show that for one who has attained the state of the Sūtra, there is an absence of those limiting adjuncts and their effects, such as being leftover.

The meaning is that because there is no contact with the entry and exit through the nine gates, there is no "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa); because there is no association with the untouchable, there is no "impurity" (aśuci); and because there is no connection with the limiting adjuncts that cause those states, there is indeed no such thing as being "leftover" and so forth. || 6–9 ||
For those whose sacrificial thread is knowledge, Jñānaśikha and others possess the primary mark of Brahminhood;
they alone in this world are knowers of the thread, and they are the true wearers of the sacrificial thread.

For those whose crest is knowledge, who are established in knowledge, and for whom the sacred thread is knowledge—knowledge alone is their supreme purifier; knowledge is said to be their [highest] goal.
He whose crest consists of knowledge, like the flame of a fire, is called a "crested one" (śikhin)—the wise man—and not others who merely wear hair. || 12 ||
Fearing that the absence of the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) would imply a loss of Brahminhood, [the text speaks of] the knowledge-topknot and knowledge-sacred-thread:

"Those who possess the knowledge-sacred-thread of 'I am Brahman'—who are free from the conceptualization of anything other than themselves and have ascended to the state of actionlessness—for them, the sacred thread shines forth as if internalized within the world. They indeed [are the true Brahmins].

They are knowers of the true nature of the Sūtra and they wear the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta). For this very reason, these wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) have knowledge as their crest-lock (jñānaśikhin) and knowledge as their sacrificial thread (jñānopavītin); they are established in the knowledge of the Sūtra. Indeed, the knowledge of the Sūtra is said to be their purifier.
Therefore, it has been stated that for them there is neither "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) nor impurity; for their crest-lock consists of knowledge, like a flame of fire.
He who possesses this knowledge is called a "wise one" (vidvān) and a "crested one" (śikhin); others who merely wear hair do not become "crested ones.
[10]—The *Kriyāṅgasūtra* states: "Those Brāhmaṇas and others who are entitled to perform Vedic rites..."
This sutra is to be upheld by them, for it is indeed remembered as a constituent part of ritual action. || 13 ||
If this were so, then everyone would have to renounce the topknot (*śikhā*), the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth; therefore, he says: "In [regard to] action.
Those of the three higher castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, who—preceded by their own ignorance—think, "This must be performed by me," (p.
188) [are the ones referred to].

Those who are entitled to Vedic rites must wear this sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), made from cotton threads, as a constituent part of those very rituals. Thus says the Śruti: "One should study, officiate at sacrifices, or sacrifice only while wearing the sacrificial thread; [it is] for the sake of the sacrifice. In this way, the sacrificial thread is remembered in the Smṛtis as a constituent part of the ritual acts of the three social classes (*traivarṇika*).
The word "hi" indicates well-known fact. || 13 ||

Those who know Brahman understand that he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread likewise consists of it possesses the entirety of true Brahminhood in its non-figurative sense. (14)
To the question of whose among the three social classes (varṇas) possesses unqualified Brahminhood, he says: "The tuft of hair consists of knowledge.

Since the rule for wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is prescribed only for the Brāhmaṇa caste among the three classes, those who know Brahman understand that the one among them who possesses such a tuft of hair—consisting of knowledge—possesses the entirety of unqualified Brahminhood; the meaning is that they know this. || 14 ||

This is the true nature of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*): this sacred thread is indeed the supreme goal. He who possesses this knowledge is truly invested with the sacred thread; he is the sacrifice, and they know him as a sacrificer. (15)
To the question, "What is the true nature of this sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) which brings about such Brahminhood? he says:

"This... This sacred thread is the knowledge that leads to the station of Viṣṇu; it is that which, by removing the superimposition of the notions of action, agent, and so forth—along with their inherent parts to be discarded—is left over as pure consciousness alone, for whoever [possesses it].
"One who knows 'I am this' is indeed one who wears the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītī*) and is a knower of Brahman alone.

Even the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices would be that very person. Those who know him—who has thus become Brahman—know him as a performer of sacrifice, a performer of the *Agnihotra*; he alone is the true *Agnihotrī*, and no other. In this regard:
The ascetic who offers the entirety of conceptual proliferation as an oblation into the fire of knowledge,
having internalized the sacred fires within his own self— he is a true performer of the Agnihotra, a great ascetic.
According to this scriptural statement, the meaning is that the wise person, having offered everything other than himself into the fire of his own Self, remains as the Self alone.
The wise one who has become Brahman is indeed one alone—the one God hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
the supervisor of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities. 16.
The one Controller, the inner Self of all beings, who makes his single form manifold—those wise ones who perceive him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. 17.

To the question, "Is this wise one who has become Brahman manifold? he says: "He is one. This sage who has become Brahman is indeed one alone, because he has attained the state of being nothing but Brahman, which is devoid of any counterpart. To the question, "Of what nature is he? he says: "He is divine," because he is the self-luminous essence of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*). One might ask: "Why is he not seen as pure light?"

To this he says: "hidden in all beings. Although He appears as non-different from the inner self known by the wise, He is "hidden" because He does not appear to those whose vision is veiled by their own three-fold covering within the four classes of beings imagined through the perspective of the ignorant. If this is so, then there would be the state of being limited.

To this he says: "all-pervading," because it is woven through everything like space. Since it would follow that [the Self] is not so by virtue of being connected with everything as its non-self, he says: "the inner self of all beings.

This is because it shines forth as the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the objective support for the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) manifesting within the fourfold classes of beings; therefore, it is not [non-existent].

The meaning is that [the Self] is not connected with non-selfhood. One might object that if [the Self] were the inner self (*pratyak*) of all beings, it would possess the transmigratory state (*saṃsāritā*) consisting of agency and so forth belonging to those [beings]; therefore, he says "the supervisor of actions" (*karmādhyakṣa*).
This is because the inner self, by virtue of not being touched by the agency and other attributes produced by all beings, is the bestower of the fruits of all actions performed by them.
If that were so, there would be a state of mere aloofness; therefore, he says: "the abode of all beings.

This means that because He dwells presiding over all beings as their very Self, He is the form of the Self of all. [An objection: Since He is the abode of all beings, He might be permeated by the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) belonging to those respective beings. To this [he replies]:...

He says: "The witness. Because the witness is distinct from everything due to its non-contact with its own objects of witnessing (*sākṣya*), it cannot be permeated by the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*); this is the meaning. For there is a scriptural statement: "The witness of all is therefore other than all and distinct from all. To address the objection that if witnesshood is dependent upon an object of witnessing, then it would follow that "this [Self] possesses that [object]," he says:
[The Self] thinks; for it is not insentient, as it is the witness and the thinker. Indeed, the modification of the witness does not touch it.
He states the reason for this: "isolated" (kevala). This means devoid of all particularities. [It is distinct] from the possessor of qualities by virtue of its connection with qualities.

To the question "Whence is this absolute oneness (kevalatā)? he says: "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa). Because the qualities born of ignorance (āvidyaka-guṇa) are identical with their cause [Māyā], their association [with the Self] is impossible; therefore, He is "devoid of qualities. The word "and" (ca) signifies that His absolute oneness is without a counter-correlative (niṣpratiyogika), because His essential nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra-svarūpa). Such is the Supreme Self (paramātman) who is thus devoid of qualities.

Although He is of a single form without any counterpart, He appears as if manifold through the vision of those ignorant of their own Self, yet in reality He is not so. For those who know this, there arises a state of abiding in the Self alone, preceded by the peace that comes from the cessation of everything other than the Self. Thus it is said: "The One. Although the Supreme Self is in reality one, He is the controller of all because He governs everything, and He is the witness within all beings due to His pervasive presence through the vision of those ignorant of their own Self.

The meaning is that he who acts is in reality nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). While situated in his own ignorance, he sings of that [consciousness] as being manifold; however, those wise ones—the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman—who perceive Him abiding within themselves as their own non-dual self alone, for them the bliss of liberation, characterized by the remainder of nothing but one's own nature, is established.
It occurs for [the Buddhas], but not for others, because their vision is obscured by their own veils. || 16-17 ||
The means for attaining Brahman:
having made the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill, one shall behold the God hidden within, through the practice of churning with meditation. 18.

As oil is in sesame seeds, as clarified butter is in curds, as water is in riverbeds, and as fire is in wood—so does this Self arise within the self; he who perceives it through truth and austerity beholds it.
Just as a spider emits threads and also withdraws them,
so the individual soul goes forth and returns again during waking and dreaming.
One should know that the waking state resides in the eyes; one enters the dream state in the throat;
the deep sleep state resides in the heart; and the fourth state (turīya) is situated in the head—this is the Self.
Through wisdom, one unites the self with the Supreme Self;
therefore, *saṃdhyā* is indeed meditation, and for that reason, it is the salutation of *saṃdhyā*.
The twilight of meditation is without water, free from the afflictions of speech and body; it is the union of all beings—that indeed is the twilight of the single-staffed ascetics. || 21 ||
From which words turn back, along with the mind, unable to reach it—this is the bliss of the living soul, knowing which the wise man is liberated. 22.

The Self, which pervades all, is inherent like ghee in milk; it has self-knowledge and austerity as its root. That is the state of the Brahma-Upaniṣad; that is the state of the Brahma-Upaniṣad. || 23 ||

To the question, "What is the means for attaining that? he says: "The self," etc. Having made the self—the internal organ—the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi), and having made the Praṇava, the syllable *oṃ*, the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi), one should then utter the Praṇava like the resonance of a long-sounding bell.
Through the practice of churning meditation upon the *praṇava*, which serves as the position for the lower and upper friction-sticks (*araṇi*) of the internal organ;

regarding the question "What is this meaning of the *praṇava*?", the practice of churning meditation consists in the continuous contemplation of the meaning of the *praṇava* as it appears from the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge. From that practice...
Like fire hidden within wood that becomes manifest through friction,

one should perceive the Turyaturya— established by the negation of the fourteen-fold divisions beginning with waking-within-waking— by means of the realization that only it remains. Regarding the fact that its essence manifests from such friction, much has been said.

He states an illustration: "In sesame seeds," etc. Just as oil is clearly perceived in sesame seeds by means of pressing with a sesame-press and churning; just as clarified butter (*sarpiḥ-ghṛtam*) is perceived in the curd produced from churned milk when it is processed with fire; and just as water [is obtained] from streams or the earth's channels by means of digging.

They are perceived, just as fire is perceived from the friction of fire-sticks; by the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that fire is also perceived in sun-crystals and the like through contact with the rays of the sun. Just as in this series of examples, so too is this Self—the Turyaturya—within the Self, that is, within the internal organ (antahkarana).

Having swallowed the fifteen-fold conceptualization—beginning with the waking-within-waking state and so forth—which is other than itself, by means of the refinement [brought about] through scripture and the teacher, one remains as one's own self alone.
It is born; that is to say, it is perceived. This is the meaning of "that" (tad), referring to the Fourth State (turya). Regarding the means for attaining that, he says: "by truth" (satyena).

The meaning is that it is attainable by one who, being qualified, perceives it through truthful speech, through ascetic practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, through the realization "I am the Truth, Brahman," or through the ascetic practice of hearing and so forth regarding the means to that [realization].
He refutes the argument that there would be a plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) even across the three states by means of an illustration:

"The spider" (*ūrṇanābhi*). Just as a spider—a silkworm—produces threads from its own body and likewise reabsorbs them, so too are creation and dissolution appropriate, given that the threads are like saliva in their moisture.

This is the meaning. Likewise, this individual soul (jīva), while creating and withdrawing the states of waking and dreaming like a silkworm, remains one and the same. Due to the diversity of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of many people, the lack of recollection that "I am one" is not contradictory; for there is recollection in dreams and other states of both what was experienced and what was not experienced.

Because of being perceived: like a child moving from one house to another, this [Self] repeatedly goes and comes from one state, such as waking, to another state. Therefore, the meaning is that the Self is indeed one, though it moves through a multitude of states. Previously, the navel and other parts were mentioned as the locations for the waking state and so forth; now, he speaks more clearly.
The Universal-Universal. One should know that Self as the waking state, situated in the condition of wakefulness.

In the region of the throat, one should enter the Taijasa, which is distinguished from the Viśva and has entered the state of dream, which is distinguished from the waking state. [One should enter] the Prājña, which is distinguished from the Viśva and has entered the state of deep sleep, which is distinguished from the waking state.

One should know that [the Turiya] resides indeed in the heart; one should know the Turiya, which is differentiated from the universe, as situated at the tenth door, the head—this is supplied from the context. He clarifies the true nature of the Turiya with the word "yataḥ" (from which):
from which Turiya the words of the Vedas, along with the mind and its functions such as volition, turn back.

The meaning is: "not having reached that" means "not having manifested that. This very state of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the bliss of the Fourth (*turyānanda*), is that by knowing which the wise man is liberated;

this is the meaning of "the true nature of the Fourth," which consists of the bliss of the Fourth. Anticipating the objection that there might be a sense of limitation based on the statement "the Fourth is situated at the crown of the head," he refutes that [as follows]:
He concludes the meaning of the treatise with the words, "pervading all. Although the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is false,
and according to the Vedic scripture that "the Self is everything," the Self is indeed non-dual pure consciousness devoid of any counter-correlate,
it cannot be attained without a means, even though it pervades the entire phenomenal world— which appears as something separate from itself due to the vision of one's own ignorance.

Thus he states an illustration: "In milk," and so forth. Just as ghee, though inherently present in milk, cannot be obtained without means such as churning, so too this Self cannot be attained without a means;
this is the meaning. To the question, "What is this means for its realization? he says: "The Self," and so forth.

Knowledge (*vidyā*), the Upanishads, austerity (*tapas*), hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*), and so forth, are the causes for the realization of the pure Self (*ātman-mātra*) by way of the negation of the non-Self (*anātma-apahnava*);
and the root and locus of even those two is that Brahman which remains as its own nature alone.
That indeed is the "Upanishad-word," because it is to be known solely through the Upanishads. By "Upanishad" is meant the knowledge of Brahman alone;
that "word," however, is Brahman alone. The words "repetition" (abhyāsa) and "end" (iti) serve to indicate the completion of the Upanishad and its meaning.
This brief commentary on the Brahmopaniṣad was written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
this explanatory work on the Brahmopaniṣad is recorded as being two hundred [verses] in length.
Thus ends the commentary on the Brahmopaniṣad, completing the eleventh [treatise] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad Īśa.
The Bhikṣuko paniṣad.
"That is full"— thus [ends] the peace invocation.
There are four kinds of mendicants; now, for those mendicants seeking liberation, there are four types: the Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa. || 1 ||

The *kuṭīcakas*—so called because they dwell in huts—are eight [sages] such as Gautama, Bharadvāja, Yājñavalkya, Vasiṣṭha, and others; consuming only eight morsels of food, they seek liberation alone through the path of yoga. || 2 ||
May that three-worded Brahman-reality, wherein the chapter on the monks has always found its rest, make me Brahman alone.

Now, indeed, this *Bhikṣukopaniṣad*, which is a division of the White Yajurveda, begins with the exposition of the duties of the *kuṭīcaka* and other [orders of mendicants]. Having perceived the qualified seeker as described, the Śruti [proceeds] with the duties of the *kuṭīcaka* and others.
Then there are those called Bahūdakas, who carry a triple staff, a water-pot, a topknot, a sacred thread, and saffron-colored garments;
having practiced the life of a mendicant, they seek liberation alone through the path of yoga. || 3 ||
He speaks of the Bahūdaka dharma: "Now, as for those called Bahūdakas... (3)
Regarding the Haṃsas:

now, those known as Haṃsas should stay for one night in a village, five nights in a city, and seven nights in a field; beyond that, they should not dwell. They should subsist on cow urine and cow dung, be constantly devoted to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and follow the path of Yoga.
They pray for liberation alone. || 4 ||
He speaks of the qualities of the swans: "Now, as for those called swans... (4).
The Paramahaṃsas:
Now, those known as Paramahaṃsas—such as Saṃvartaka, Āruṇi, Śvetaketu, Jaḍabharata, Dattātreya, Śuka, and others—do not seek anything.
They dwell at the roots of trees, in empty houses, or in cremation grounds; they may wear clothes or remain unclothed.
Or they may be naked (digambara). For them, there is neither merit nor demerit, for they have no reckoning of gain or loss.

Free from the duality of pure and impure, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, they wander for alms among all castes and perceive the Self alone everywhere. Thus, wearing only their natural form, they are beyond the pairs of opposites.
Free from possessions, devoted to pure meditation, and established solely in the Self,

they practice begging for alms at the prescribed times for the sake of sustaining life; remaining in empty houses, temples, caves, mountain clefts, hollows, pits, waterfalls, or on open ground, they are correctly [established] there in the path of Brahman.
(197) Having attained perfection and being pure in mind, they cast off the body through the renunciation that is the practice of the Paramahaṃsas.
This is the Upaniṣad known as "The Paramahaṃsas. 5.
He elucidates the duties of the Paramahaṃsas: "Now, as for those called Paramahaṃsas. He describes their dwelling and conduct:

"At the root of a tree," and so forth. Neither merit nor demerit accrues to them, because they are turned away from both engagement and withdrawal, and because there is an absence of joy or dejection in all circumstances. Indeed, for them—

There is no reckoning of gain or loss. Those for whom qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), pure non-duality (*śuddhadvaita*), absolute non-duality (*kevaladvaita*), and impure non-duality (*aśuddhadvaita*) are not accepted are those who are devoid of both pure and impure non-duality;
the meaning is that they are proponents of non-duality without a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogikādvaitin*). Therefore, they regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal in all respects.
Because they have attained the vision of Brahman characterized by equanimity,

and because they rely upon the duties of the four castes among all the social orders distinguished by birth— such as Brāhmaṇas and others— they practice begging for alms at the prescribed times among Brāhmaṇas, non-Brāhmaṇas, and so forth, and perceive the Self alone everywhere within their own self.
Because it is the substratum of the manifold of both the individual and the collective, its nature is that of Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Now, [the sages] are those who wear golden ornaments (*jātarūpadhara*), free from dualities (*nirdvandva*), devoid of possessions (*niṣparigraha*), and devoted to pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*);
for, in accordance with the Śruti, Brahman is "that which consists of pure radiance" (*śuklatejorūpa*).

The meaning is that they have attained the state of being nothing but Brahman. For this very reason, the meaning is that they are established solely in the Self, which is realized through the negation of the non-Self. If their minds are directed outward, then, for the sake of sustaining the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they practice begging for alms at the prescribed times; by the word *haṃsa*—
The Supreme Self (paramātman) is said to be non-different from the inner self (pratyak).
That which is established by the removal of all distinctions through the realization of the non-difference of the inner self—which is dependent upon the "other" (parāk)—is the "Supreme" (parama);
and that is also the "Hamsa" (the Swan), thus he is the Paramahaṃsa, the Supreme Self devoid of any counter-correlative (niṣpratiyogika). His conduct is as follows:
Abiding in that alone— by means of that conduct of a *paramahaṃsa*, through the renunciation of all mental constructs (*kalanā*) other than oneself,

or through the renunciation of ritual action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*)— those who effect the abandonment of the body, or the abandonment of the deluded conviction that "it exists" or "it does not exist" regarding the entire collection of the state of one's own ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects as characterized by the body, they are indeed Brahman, known as *paramahaṃsas*.
The meaning is that they come into being. Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" signifies the completion of the Bhikṣukopaniṣad. || 5 ||

This commentary on the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad, leading to Brahman, has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra; the extent of this commentary on the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad is said to be thirty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikṣukopaniṣad, completing the number sixty in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmad-Īśa.
The Maitreyopaniṣad.
"May [the worlds] swell"— thus the peace invocation.
For one who is disenchanted with saṃsāra, there arises the desire to know the Self.

King Bṛhadratha by name, having established his eldest son in the kingdom and considering this body to be impermanent, became filled with detachment and departed for the forest. There, he performed supreme austerity.

Standing with his arms raised, he remained gazing at the sun. At the end of a thousand years, [the sage] approached the king and said, "Arise, arise, choose a boon. Having paid homage to him, the king said:
"O Blessed One, I am not a knower of the Self; we hear of one who knows that reality. May you tell it to us. This—
"What occurred previously cannot be told; do not ask this question. Choose other desires, O descendant of Ikṣvāku," said the king as he touched the feet of Śākāyanya, reciting this verse.
Verses on Worldly Disenchantment: Now,
what need have these for the drying up of other great oceans, the falling of mountains, the shaking or the shifting of the Pole Star, the sinking of trees, or the removal of the earth from its place?
[This is] for the gods. In this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) characterized by "I am he," what is the use of the enjoyment of desires, which are themselves the very causes of bondage?
O Blessed One, in this transmigratory existence, you are our refuge. || 2 ||

"O Blessed One, this body has arisen from sexual union; it is devoid of consciousness, having emerged indeed from the path of urine. It is a heap of bones, smeared with flesh, covered with skin, and filled with various impurities.
For one abiding in such a body as this, O Blessed One, you are our refuge. (3)
I meditate upon Brahman, which is pure self alone, established through one's own direct experience— that state which the sages know through the instruction of the Vedas and the teacher.

Indeed, this Upaniṣad, known by the name *Maitreyī*, is a division of the Sāmaveda; therefore, its introductory section (*upoddhāta*) and so forth should be understood as being like those of the *Chāndogya* and other such texts. Now begins the exposition of the realization of one’s own experience through intense dispassion. As for the narrative concerning Bṛhadratha, Śākāyanya, and others, it will be discussed later.
The passage beginning with "King Bṛhadratha by name" and ending with "who would not be released from bondage" occurs here and there in the Maitrāyaṇīyopaniṣad with neither fewer nor more syllables.
Since this [text] would be almost entirely explained by the commentary on that [Upaniṣad], no separate commentary is provided here.
A king named Bṛhadratha, being endowed with the aforementioned means of accomplishment, renounced his own kingdom and other possessions and,

having taken up residence in a great forest region, performed austerities for a long time while gazing at the sun with his arms raised. Pleased by that austerity, the Blessed One entered the sage Śākāyanya.
Thus he urged him for the attainment of his desired goal. Then that sage went into his presence.

At the mere sight of him, the king rose up suddenly and prostrated himself like a staff. To him as he lay prostrate, the sage said, "Arise, arise; choose a boon according to your desire. Thereupon the king—

He requested the knowledge of Brahman. Although he was enticed by the sage—who said, "Let that which you have asked not be [given], for it cannot be spoken because it is the domain of the inexpressible Brahman; choose other desires"—he did not waver from the ultimate truth. (1–3)
p.
201) Then the venerable Śākāyanya, being well-pleased, spoke to the king, revealing the true nature of Brahman: "O Great King!"

"You are the banner of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the crest-jewel of the Bṛhadratha dynasty, one who knows the Self, one who has accomplished all that was to be done, and you are renowned by the name Marut;
this indeed is your Self. O Blessed One, which among these is to be described? He said to him: "4."
Those objects such as sound, touch, and the rest, which stand as if they were non-objects,
are such that when the elemental self (bhūtātman) is attached to them, it does not remember the supreme state.
Through austerity, *sattva* is attained; from *sattva*, the mind is fully attained.
Through the mind, indeed, the Self (*ātman*) is attained; and through the attainment of the Self, one ceases [from rebirth].
Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so too the mind, through the cessation of its fluctuations, is extinguished in its own source. || 7 ||
For one whose mind has become tranquil within its own source and who moves toward truth,
the objects of the senses— which follow the power of karma— are false, for he is no longer deluded by them.
The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with effort.
Whatever the mind is, that it becomes—this is the eternal secret.
For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
with a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable bliss. 10.
When the mind of a living being is attached to the sphere of sensory objects, if it were likewise so [attached] to Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? (11)
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord in the center of the lotus of the heart—He who is the witness of the dance of the intellect and the object of supreme love. (12)
(202) Beyond the range of mind and speech, transcending the surging flood [of conceptualization], its sole intrinsic nature is the manifestation of pure existence; it is beyond all cultivation. (13)
Neither to be abandoned nor to be grasped, devoid of common or specific qualities, it is eternal, motionless, and profound; it is neither light nor pervading darkness;
it is free from conceptual construction, free from appearance, and consists of the consciousness of nirvāṇa. 114.

I am that Supreme One, the ocean of bliss, who is eternal, pure, of the nature of awakened liberation, true, subtle, all-pervading, and non-dual; I am the inner witness—of this there is no doubt. (15)

How could calamity enter me, who am unattached, resting within my own internal bliss, disregarding even the mistress of the quarters (the goddess of desire), and beholding the world as a magical illusion? 16.
Those who are deluded and bound by the conduct of their caste and stage of life obtain fruits according to their actions;
however, those men who abandon the duties of caste and so forth become satisfied in their own bliss. || 17 ||

Having become free from the conceit of identifying with the bodies of sons and others— [a state] which consists of the system of castes and stages of life, possesses constituent parts, is bound by beginning and end, and is merely a source of extreme hardship— one should dwell in that which is most blissful and infinite.

Thus, considering one who has turned away from objects other than the Self to be a fit vessel for the knowledge of Brahman, the author prepares this introductory section (*bhūmikā*) to reveal the means of attaining that knowledge—namely, hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—preceded by the restraint of the external and internal organs. He begins with the verse starting with "hṛdi. The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*)...

Having performed the hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) of all the Vedāntas until the cessation of the five defects beginning with doubt, one then [realizes] that very [Self] within the lotus of one's own heart; the word "tu" (then) indicates that it is the locus of the manifestation of Brahman. Therein indeed is the supreme, unsurpassed [Brahman], existing as one's own true nature alone.

The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is one who is capable and able to abide [in all things]; [one should meditate upon] that Supreme Self (Paramātman). The meaning is that one should contemplate or meditate upon Him whose essential nature is determined by the series of qualifiers beginning with "the Witness" and ending with "consciousness consisting of liberation," as being nothing but His own non-dual self devoid of any counterpart. He states those qualifiers:

"Regarding the witness," and so forth. Just as the existence of the dance of the intellect—which, by its own ignorance, is imagined to be the form of an object witnessed—is perceived by the vision of one who knows [the Self], the witness is the object of supreme love, because it illuminates both the presence and absence of that [intellect]. (p. 203)

Because it alone is the object of supreme love even more than one's own son, wealth, and so forth, according to such scriptural passages as "dearer than all else," one might think that, by being the object of supreme love, it would fall within the range of speech and other faculties; therefore, he says: "beyond the range of mind and speech. And this state of not being an object for the collection of instruments such as speech follows from its very nature.

Because it is one's own nature alone, devoid of any counterpart. If Brahman is without a counterpart, then from where does the crossing of the ocean of worldly existence by those ignorant of themselves, or the attainment of that state, arise? To this, he says: "The great flood of the Avadhūtas. [This refers to] the boundaries of the Śruti and Smṛti of the Avadhūtas.
It is a boat for those of their own ignorance to cross the ocean of worldly existence, which is infested with aquatic creatures such as mental anguish and physical disease;

or rather, it exists beyond the form of the Supreme Brahman, which serves as a place of refuge and a means for those who have shaken off their own ignorance— the knowers of Brahman— to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus ends the immersion into the Avadhūta. The meaning is: "that [which is] the non-differentiated Supreme Self. The reason for this is stated as:

"having the single nature of manifesting pure existence (*sattāmātra-prakāśaka-eka-svabhāva*). This means that because it manifests as pure existence by swallowing all existence other than itself, its one primary nature is precisely the manifestation of pure existence; thus it is so described.

Thus, because it is the locus of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises the contingency of its being [the object of] cultivation in its entirety; to this he replies: "transcending cultivation" (*bhāvanātigam*).

Since the ignorance of the scales (*tulāvidyā*)—which is the cause of such cultivation—is possible, when that ignorance of the scales consisting of one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) is removed, what remains of that nature:
is it something to be abandoned, or is it something to be accepted, or is it a commonality, or rather...?

Regarding the term "distinction" (*viśeṣam*): therein, it is not the first [alternative], because the gross aspect of one's own state of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects is to be abandoned; since that which is established through the negation of such conceptualization is not to be abandoned, He is "the Abandonable" (*aheya*). Nor is it the second, because the subtle aspect of that [ignorance] is perceivable and thus capable of being accepted; since that which is established through the negation of that is not to be accepted, He is "the Non-acceptable" (*anupādeya*). Not the third...

The third [state] is "the non-general" (*asāmānya*), established by the negation of that [third] part, because that part, being of the nature of unmanifest *prakṛti*, is of a general nature. Nor is it the fourth, for that fourth part is of the nature of the knowledge of equality (*sāmya-vidyā*) and is thus of a specific nature; the fourth state is "the non-specific" (*aviśeṣa*), established by the negation of that [fourth] part. Thus...

Because this Self ought to be impermanent due to the negation (*apahnava*) of the state of one's own ignorance—which is established by the experience of the fixedness of one's own lack of knowledge—it says, "the Fixed" (*dhruvam*). The meaning is that the state of the realm of one's own ignorance is impermanent through the experience of one's own knowledge, whereas for that which is established by the negation thereof, its fixedness is absolute and unrestricted. For this very reason:

It is steady and profound because it has the nature of a waveless ocean of consciousness (*cid-arṇava*). Regarding its being an ocean of consciousness: is it light (*tejas*), or is it darkness (*tamas*), or is it pervasive (*tata*)? Not the first, for it is not light, since elemental light is negated. Not the second, for it is not darkness, since it swallows the darkness of one's own ignorance. Not the third either, because there is no commonality of that which is to be pervaded.

It is expanded: because of the negation of both the conceptualized and its appearance, it is non-conceptual and without appearance. If this is so, what is its true nature? To this he says: "consisting of consciousness that is of the nature of *nirvāṇa*.
"Consisting of *nirvāṇa*" means having the nature of liberation with the body (*vikalebara-kaivalya*). For here, the suffix *-maya* does not [mean "made of"].

[The word "consciousness" (saṃvit)] does not denote a modification or abundance [of something else], because it refers to its own essential nature (svarūpa). Consciousness is knowledge of one's own essential nature;
it is the nature of perfect awakening, the truth, knowledge, the infinite, and consciousness-bliss Brahman.

"Having abandoned the relationship of cause and effect, pure awakening remains"—from such scriptural passages as these. Thus, King [Brahmadatta], having attained the realization of Brahman alone through the mouth of Śākāyanya, remained for a long time established in samādhi;
then, in order that the lineage of the tradition of Brahma-vidyā might not be interrupted, he manifested his own experience, saying:

"Everlasting" (*nitya*) means being unassailable throughout the three periods of time. "Pure" (*śuddha*) means due to the removal of one's own impure ignorance. "Awakened" (*buddha*) means having the nature of perfect enlightenment. "Liberated by nature" (*muktasvabhāva*) means [liberated] from the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself. "Real" (*satya*) means having the nature of ultimate reality. "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) means due to being without distinctions.
Because its form is exceedingly subtle, like a single strand of a hair divided a billionfold; because it is all-pervasive, due to the absence of the three types of limitation;

because it is non-dual, since any duality that could serve as its counterpart is sought in vain; and the word "ca" (and) is intended to demonstrate its state of being without a counterpart; it is the waveless ocean of bliss.

Because of being an ocean of full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). He who is beyond everything, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), that am I; I am indeed that very one. To the question, "How can you be the Supreme Self while the external phenomenal world (*parāk-prapañca*) exists?", he says:

"The inward element" (*pratyag-dhātu*). Because it moves in a direction contrary to the external phenomenal world, it is "inward" (*pratyak*); and it is also the "element" (*dhātu*). Thus, it is the inward element.
Regarding this meaning—"I am the Supreme Self non-different from the inner witness"—there is indeed no doubt or uncertainty.

This is because, in reality, there is no room for the distinction between "inner" and "Supreme," as everything is nothing but Brahman alone, which is devoid of any counter-correlative (niṣpratiyogika).
To the question, "How can you be thus, given the existence of the world-appearance (prapañca) apart from yourself? he says: "Bliss."

[He is] one who constantly contemplates within his own heart his own ultimate, real form—Brahman as bliss, being-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), which is nothing but himself (svamātra). To the question, "Since there is no existence apart from himself, how can he take refuge in that?", he says: "Āśā" (Hope). The very hope that "something exists apart from himself" is a female demon (piśācī); [he destroys] that.

"To one who denies, meaning one who holds the view that 'there is nothing other than Brahman' and thus performs a repudiation [of the world]"—to the question of how such a thing can be so while there is the perception of a world distinct from oneself, he says: "beholding. What is that? The world (*jagat*) is that which goes through birth, maintenance, and destruction at every step; he beholds it as a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), as mere *māyā*.

The meaning is this: how could such an obstacle—consisting of the appearance of existence as something separate from Me, who am entirely unattached—enter into the vision of the mere Reality, even though it is established by the authority of the ignorant person's own perception?
Having raised the doubt as to how this can be established while the system of conduct for castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) exists:

Those who believe that caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth exist apart from [the Self] are themselves bound; those who hold the opposite view are liberated from that delusion—thus he says, "caste," etc. "Caste" refers to Brahmin, Kshatriya, and so on;
"stage of life" refers to studenthood (*brahmacarya*) and so on. Those who possess the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding these are the deluded.
Because of the vision rooted in one's own ignorance—which perceives the existence of things other than oneself—one follows one's own inherent nature and corresponding karma.
That which dissolves through enjoyment as something insignificant—namely, the fruits such as heaven and hell—is momentary;

indeed, they experience birth and death incessantly like a waterwheel. But those who are the opposite of that, being virtuous ones who abandon the notion of "self" and "mine" regarding caste, stage of life, and so forth—

The meaning is that, having become satisfied by the state of being the Self which is the bliss of the locus for the renunciation of that [world], they become Brahman itself as "puruṣas" because of filling everything with their own nature. Clarifying this very point once more, he concludes with the words "varṇāśrama": [they remain] characterized by caste and stage of life.

The body has the nature of having parts such as hands and feet; it is "joined with beginning and end," meaning joined with birth and destruction. For this reason, since [the body] results in nothing but extreme hardship and suffering, the wise person himself, having made his mind free from the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding his own body and even the bodies of his sons and others—

Having become the non-dual Brahman alone, established through the negation of everything else, one should dwell in one's own infinite glory—the most blissful state of unbroken bliss—due to the absence of the three types of limitation. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the first chapter. || 4-18 ||
Thus ends the first chapter.
The Instruction of Mahādeva to Maitreya:
Then the Blessed One Maitreya went to Kailāsa. Having gone there, he said: "O Blessed One, please explain the secret of the supreme reality. Mahādeva replied: 1. Thus spoke Mahādeva.
The body is declared to be a temple; that living soul is Śiva alone.
One should discard the floral offerings of ignorance and worship with the sense of "I am He."
Knowledge is the vision of non-duality; meditation is a mind free from objects;
bathing is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind; and purity is the restraint of the senses.
One should drink the nectar of Brahman, practice mendicancy for the maintenance of the body, and dwell in solitude, having become one who is entirely devoted to seclusion and free from duality;
acting thus, the wise man shall indeed attain liberation. || 4 ||

Maitreya, although he had already realized the truth from the mouth of Parāśara, went to Kailāsa in accordance with the prescribed rites, desiring to learn the secret of the supreme reality from him in order to generate conviction among all people.
He said that [the sage] asked; thus, "Now" (*atha*). Being questioned by the sage, Mahādeva spoke.

What did he say? To this, [it is replied]: he who, through the vision of Śiva and the abode of Śiva within the body and the individual soul (*deha-jīva*), worships with the sense of "I am He" (*so'ham-bhāva*) after first discarding the floral offerings of his own ignorance—he is liberated.
He says "the body" (deha) [to explain] how it comes to be; the meaning is clear. || 1-4 ||
This body, born and destined for death, consists of the impurities of the mother and father; having touched this abode of pleasure and pain, which is inherently unclean, bathing is prescribed. (5)
Having touched this unstable abode of evil, which is bound by the elements, afflicted by great disease,
and expanded with the forms of various transformations, bathing is prescribed.
Having touched that which flows as impurity from the nine gates, which is produced by one's own nature at all times,
and which is foul-smelling and possessed of filth, bathing is prescribed.
The impurity associated with birth arises together with the birth itself;
having touched a body born of death or birth-impurity, bathing is prescribed.

That which consists of removing the impurities of feces, urine, smears, odors, and so forth from the eyes and other parts, regarding "I" and "mine," is called pure ritual purification; however, that which is performed with earth and water is merely worldly.
Without viewing the body as a temple for the enjoyment of the gods and so forth, one might think that the body would become pure through the mere abandonment of the conceit of "I" and "mine.

To this he says: "Born... (jātam). The meaning here is that if at any time one touches the body out of the conceit of "I" and "mine," the very renunciation of that conceit of "I" and "mine" is the bath enjoined by the sacred injunctions; such is the meaning of "bath" (snānam).

Because it has been stated that "it is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "bound by the *dhātus*": it is bound by the *dhātus* such as wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and so forth, because it is the locus of various diseases. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "nine gates": the meaning is that it is born together with the birth-fluids (*sūtaka*); for [this is true] of one who is born.
"Death is certain," according to the Smṛti. He describes the method for that purification: "I... (5–9).
Purity of mind,
or that purity which effects the purification of the mind and destroys the threefold latent impressions (vāsanās),
is called purity because it is washed away by the nectar-water of knowledge and dispassion.

The contemplation of non-duality is the alms-food, while the contemplation of duality is what is not to be eaten; for a mendicant, alms are prescribed according to the state of mind taught by the Guru and the scriptures. (11)
Having renounced his own country immediately after taking up the life of a mendicant, the wise man should dwell far away from home, like a thief released from prison. 12.
Anticipating the question, "What would result from such purity? he states that the purification of the mind occurs preceded by the destruction of the three types of latent impressions (*vāsanā*):
"the mind... etc. He clarifies with this mantra what was stated [previously] regarding "drinking the nectar of Brahman through alms": "non-dual... etc. Such is the mendicant.
Anticipating the doubt as to where he ought to sit, the author says "the wise one," meaning that he should wander only outside of places already familiar to him.
As long as one does not abandon the son of egoism, the brother of wealth, the abode of delusion, and the wife of hope—namely, egoism itself—one is not liberated; of this there is no doubt. (13)

Anticipating the objection that liberation does not come merely from renouncing external wives and sons, but rather from the renunciation of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), [the author] states "Egoism... to show that liberation occurs only through the renunciation of egoism preceded by the renunciation of external wives and so forth, and not through the abandonment of either one alone. Both external and internal renunciations must occur for liberation to be attained.
This is the meaning.
The *liṅga* of Viṣṇu is said to be twofold: manifest (*vyakta*) and unmanifest (*avyakta*).
By abandoning even one of these two, one certainly falls; there is no doubt.
Thus says the Śruti. || 13 ||
p. 208) There is the renunciation of karma;
the mother consisting of delusion has died, and the son consisting of awakening has been born.
When two periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) coincide, how should we perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana)?
In the space of the heart, the sun of consciousness shines and shines forever;
it neither sets nor rises—how then can we perform the twilight worship?
That which is ascertained by the word of the Guru as being one alone without a second—
this is called "solitude" (ekānta), not a monastery nor another forest retreat.

Anticipating the objection that one would incur sin by abandoning rituals such as the *saṃdhyā* (twilight worship), [the author] states: because of the destruction of one's own ignorance and the arising of one's own knowledge, and because there is neither sunrise nor sunset for the sun of consciousness (*cidāditya*), ritual acts such as the *saṃdhyā* need not be performed. For one who knows this, there is no sunrise or sunset of the sun of consciousness.

Because of the scriptural statement, "There is an absence of all karma," that which was said—"becoming one who dwells in solitude"—clarifies the nature of that solitude: "It is indeed one alone. (Verses 14–16)

The primary renunciation is liberation for those free from doubt; for those whose minds are possessed by doubt, there is no liberation until the end of birth after birth. Therefore, one should attain firm conviction.
Renunciation is not [achieved] by the abandonment of action, nor indeed by the utterance of the *praiṣa* formulas;
rather, renunciation is proclaimed to be the unification of the individual self (*jīvātman*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) at the point of union. (18)

Regarding what I have stated, such as "the body is a temple," liberation belongs to those who are free from doubt, and certainly not to those who possess doubt; thus he says: "For one whose mind is full of doubt, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness" (Gītā 4.40), according to the Smṛti. For one who has renounced [worldly life], the abandonment of ritual action is indeed the primary form of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).

Anticipating this objection, he states that the abandonment of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para) alone constitutes primary renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), beginning with the verse "Karma...
[The one qualified for renunciation...]
For one to whom all seeking and the like appear like vomited food, who has abandoned the conceit of "I am the body," he possesses the qualification for renunciation. (19)
When detachment toward all objects has arisen in the mind, at that very moment the wise man should renounce; otherwise, he becomes fallen.
He who renounces for the sake of wealth, food, clothing, or even for the sake of fame, falls from both paths and is not fit to attain liberation.

Anticipating the question of what kind of person is qualified for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he states— beginning with the word "vomiting"— that only one for whom external objects arise as things to be discarded, like vomit, food, urine, feces, and so forth, is qualified for renunciation. Then, anticipating the question of what is the root of renunciation, he states that it is indeed the intense dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward objects other than the Self.
Regarding the phrase "yadā": since renunciation may also be performed for some other motive, he says "dravyārtham" (for the sake of wealth).
Regarding liberation, other means are as follows:
reflection on reality is the best; reflection on the scriptures is middling;
reflection on mantras is inferior; and wandering to sacred fords is the lowest of the low. (22)
Since reflection on the principles of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), mantras, and scriptures is a means equal [to other practices] for liberation, he says:

"The highest," etc. The meaning is that these four are not equal as means to liberation, because they stand in a relationship of mutual means and ends (*upāya-upeyatā*). In the phrase "the lowest of the low due to delusion regarding sacred fords," the elision of the *visarga* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). || 22 ||
Without direct experience, the fool rejoices in vain regarding Brahman,
like one who rejoices at the imagined taste of fruit on the tip of a branch reflected in a mirror. (23)

If a liberated ascetic does not abandon that internal practice of gathering alms— which generates dispassion, has faith as its consort, and is the delight of knowledge— then he remains truly free. (24)

To the objection that the attainment of Brahman occurs through the mere knowledge of the scriptures alone and what is the use of direct experience (*anubhava*), he says: "Direct experience" (*anubhūtim*).

The scriptural knowledge that "Brahman exists" is indirect (*parokṣa*); the direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) that "I am Brahman" is [experience]. Without such an experience, the mere intellectual assent to Brahman is like tasting the reflection of a fruit in water; it is not [the real thing].

The meaning is that [only] this brings about the desired result. He says, "One should not abandon," [referring to the fact] that the ascetic who performs the internal worship of the Madhūka [flower]—known as the meditation on the Non-dual (advaita-bhāvanā)—preceded by faith, devotion, knowledge, and dispassion, becomes liberated. || 23-24 ||
The supreme instruction on Dharma:
those who are advanced in wealth, advanced in age, and likewise advanced in learning—all of them are servants to one who is advanced in knowledge, as are the servants of a disciple. (25)
With their minds deluded by my māyā, they have failed to attain Me, who am their very Self;
even the wise wander like crows for the sake of filling their own bellies. 26.
For one seeking liberation, worship performed toward images made of stone, metal, gems, or clay leads only to rebirth and worldly enjoyment.
Therefore, an ascetic should perform only the worship of his own heart and abandon external worship for the sake of non-rebirth.
Full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean;
empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky.
Do not become the nature of the grasped object, and do not become the nature of the grasper. Abandoning all mental constructions, become absorbed in that which remains. 29.
Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions,
take refuge in the absolute Self, which is the primordial manifestation of pure vision.

211) He exalts one who is advanced in knowledge over those advanced in wealth and so forth—starting with the word "wealth" (dhanādi). In accordance with His own statement, "One who knows Me as the Self alone is deemed by Me to be a knower," having thus exalted the knower of the Self, he [now] describes those who are the opposite of such self-knowers.

The meaning is that birth is as useless as the nipple on the neck of a goat (*ajāgalastana*). Regarding what was stated—that one should worship with the sense of "I am He"—it was preceded by a censure of external worship performed with a notion of duality, which leads to rebirth.
Furthermore, concerning the question asked—"Please explain the secret of the supreme reality"—therein [lies the truth] of oneself and of that which is other than oneself.

It establishes, with an illustration, both the state of absolute fullness (*niṣpratiyogikapūrṇatva*) and emptiness (*śūnyatva*): "Within" (*antar*). Like a full yet empty jar situated in the midst of the ocean and the sky, it is itself full within, without, and in between as well, because of the absence of any conceptualization of internal, external, or intermediate space. Thus:

It is devoid of the conceptualization of internal, external, and intermediate states as being separate from itself, because that which is other than itself is, in reality, neither an existent nor a non-existent entity in the absence of its counterpart; for the entire collection of sense organs along with their objects exists only through the duality of the grasped and the grasper.
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing at all apart from Brahman; if, however, such a notion arises through the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge, then—

He says, "Do not be," meaning: worship Brahman as your own self alone, which is established through the negation of the various triple-fold structures (tripuṭī) such as the seer and so forth, characterized by the conceptualization of the grasped, the grasper, and the like. "The grasped" refers to the collection of objects; "the grasper" refers to the collection of instruments; and [the witness] is the inner self (pratyak), the first manifestation pervading all these triple-fold activities.

O Maitreya, become that alone—the Supreme Self which is pure consciousness, devoid of all external existence, absolute, and without any counterpart; the meaning is: become that alone, be that very thing. (25–30)
The state of one liberated while living (videhamukta) is that in which all volitions have been completely stilled; it is a condition like that of a stone,
free from both waking and sleep— that is the supreme state of one's own true nature.
Thus [it is said].
To the question, "What is the state of one who is liberated while in the body (videhamukta) and abiding in the subtle elements (tanmātra)? he says: "Completely stilled" (saṃśānta).
In that state, all volitions (saṃkalpa) directed toward various objects other than oneself have been stilled—that is, they have reached negation (apahnava).
This is that state in which all conceptual constructions have been completely stilled— a stable abiding as solid as a massive stone, which is neither waking nor sleep.

That very state which, at the moment of awakening, becomes free from negation is the supreme pinnacle, the abiding in one's own true nature, liberation while in the physical body (*vikalebaravimukti*). Whether the delusion of one's own ignorance and other such views exists or not, this alone remains as a single, uniform reality. This was realized by Maitreya through the power of the instruction of Paramaśiva.
The meaning is that he had accomplished his purpose. The word "iti" signifies the completion of Śiva’s instruction and the completion of the second chapter. || 31 ||
Thus ends the second chapter.
Maitreya’s manifestation of his own realization:
"I am He; I am the Supreme; I am Brahman; I am the Source.
I am the Teacher of all worlds; I am the entire world; I am that very Self. (1)
I alone am the perfected one; I am pure; I am the supreme.
I am that which always is; I am eternal; I am stainless. || 2 ||
I am consciousness, I am the distinct, I am Soma, I am the whole;
I am auspicious, I am free from sorrow, I am pure awareness, and I am the equanimous one. || 3 ||
I am devoid of honor and dishonor; I am without qualities; I am Śiva.
I am free from duality and non-duality; I am free from the pairs of opposites; I am that very Self.
I am devoid of existence and non-existence; I am devoid of speech; I am that which I am. I possess the power of both the void and the non-void; I am both beautiful and ugly. || 5 ||
I am devoid of the similar and the dissimilar; I am eternal, pure, and ever-auspicious (Sadāśiva).
I am devoid of all and non-all; I am the essence of goodness (Sāttvika) and I am eternally so.
I am devoid of the number one, nor do I possess the number two;
I am free from the distinction between existence and non-existence, and I am devoid of all mental construction.
I am devoid of the distinction of various selves, for I am the embodiment of indivisible bliss;
I am not this [body], nor am I another, as I am free from the body and all else. (8)
I am devoid of the support and the supported; I am without a substratum. I am devoid of bondage and liberation; I am pure Brahman, I am That.
I am devoid of everything beginning with the mind; I am supreme, higher than the highest.
I am always of the nature of inquiry, yet I am beyond inquiry; such am I.
I am the form of the syllables A and U; I am the eternal syllable M.
I am devoid of the meditator and the meditation; I am devoid of the object of meditation—I am that very Self.
I am present everywhere in my full form, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
I am the essence of all sacred fords, I am the Supreme Self, I am Śiva.
I am devoid of the perceived and the non-perceived; I am the essence free from dissolution. I am devoid of the knower and the means of knowledge; I am Śiva, free from the object of measurement.
I am not the world; I am the seer of all, yet I am devoid of eyes and other senses. I am fully grown, I am awakened, I am serene, and I am Hara.
I am devoid of all senses, yet I am the performer of all actions;
I am satisfied by all the Vedāntas, and I am always easily attained. || 15 ||
I am known as Muditāmudita; I am the fruit of all silence.
I am eternally of the nature of pure consciousness; I am always composed of existence and consciousness.
I am indeed devoid of even the slightest thing; I do not possess even the smallest fragment.
I am free from the knot of the heart, dwelling in the center of the lotus of the heart.
I am devoid of the six modifications; I am free from the six sheaths. I am liberated from the group of six internal enemies; I am the innermost within the interior. (18)
I am liberated from space and time; I am the bliss of the sky-clad (Digambara).
I am liberated from "is" and "is not"; I am devoid of the negative particle "na. || 19 ||
I am indeed of the nature of indivisible space; I am of an undivided form. My mind is liberated from the phenomenal world; I am devoid of all worldly expansion.
I am the form of all illumination; I am the light of pure consciousness alone.
I am liberated from the three periods of time; I am devoid of desire and the like. || 21 ||
I am liberated from both body and mind; I am devoid of qualities and I am absolute.
I am devoid of liberation, yet I am liberated; I am eternally devoid of even the concept of mokṣa.
I am devoid of both truth and untruth; I am never anything other than pure Being (sanmātra).
I am devoid of any destination to be reached, and I am entirely free from movement and the like.
"I am always of the same form, I am peaceful, I am the Supreme Person.
He who has such direct experience of himself is me, without a doubt;
even he who hears this but once becomes Brahman himself. (24)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad. Now, the venerable Maitreya, having correctly understood from the mouth of Paramaśiva the secret of the supreme reality—
the knowledge that Brahman alone exists without a second— and having dispelled the delusion of the existence of anything other than himself, [attained liberation].

Furthermore, because of the abundance of merit from the multitude of living beings, by the mere hearing and so forth of this [work], the world of those who do not know their own nature becomes self-knowing,

and simultaneously with the knowledge of the supreme reality, becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*). Thus, for the sake of establishing the tradition of the Brahma-vidyā, he set forth that meaning of his own experience as taught by Paramaśiva.
Or rather, he says "I am" (aham asmi) to reveal his own experience with reference to the qualified person as previously described—one who illumines the interior of the body.
The term *pratyak* (the inward) is expressed by the word *asmad* (we/us). With respect to the outward (*parāk*) manifold that resides within oneself, I am *pratyak*;
with respect to the manifold that manifests outside the body, I am *para*.
The word *ca* (and) is intended to negate the distinction between *pratyak* and *para* based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is with respect to the non-difference between *pratyak* and *para*.

I am Brahman, non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinna-brahma-asmi*). By the perspective of those lacking self-knowledge (*svājñadṛṣṭyā*), I manifest as the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), and so forth;
thus, I am the Source (*prabhava*). Furthermore—regarding the word "all" (*sarva*): in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*), I am the teacher of all the worlds.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that I am also the Witness (*sākṣin*). In the form of Virāṭ, I am the entire world of Virāṭ.

Because [the universe] has the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) as its body; in reality, I am that which is established through the negation of all mental constructs (*kalanā*), because it is devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogikatva*). Furthermore—"I"—is established in its own nature.
It is pure due to the destruction of impure self-ignorance (*svājñāna*). The remainder has been explained. Furthermore—"I am."

I am He who is eternally of one essence. Because I have abandoned the impermanent proliferation of impurities, I am eternal and I am pure. Because my nature is that of eternal consciousness, I am pure awareness (*vijñāna*). Since the relationship of part and whole has ceased to exist, I am the Absolute (*viśeṣa*). In the form of Rudra, accompanied by Umā, I am Soma. I am the Lord (*īśvara*) endowed with the sixty-four arts.
I am the Whole. Furthermore—“Auspicious” (śubha): because I am attainable through the path of cessation (nivṛtti-mārga), I am auspicious.

Because there is an absence of objects that cause grief, I am free from sorrow (śoka-hīna). Because I am distinct from the body and so forth, I am consciousness (caitanya). Even amidst various and unequal limiting adjuncts (upādhi), I am equal, as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all.
Due to the dissolution of the ignorance that consists of the fluctuations of honor and dishonor, I am devoid of honor and dishonor.
Due to the absence of qualities such as *sattva*, I am without qualities (*nirguṇa*). Due to the absence of anything inauspicious other than myself, I am the Auspicious One (*śiva*). Furthermore:
regarding "duality and non-duality"—duality is established through the path of active engagement (*pravṛtti-mārga*), while non-duality is established through the path of cessation (*nivṛtti-mārga*).

Because, apart from myself, there is an absence of my own state of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects—which are that which must be engaged with or withdrawn from—I am devoid of both duality and non-duality. Because of the absence of dualities such as cold and heat, I am devoid of pairs of opposites (*dvandva*).
Because of the lack of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of existence and non-existence within the range of the external and internal organs, I am devoid of being and non-being.

Because I am the nature of the Great Silence and Brahman, I am devoid of speech. Because I am self-luminous in nature, I am light. Furthermore—"Śūnya" (void) refers to that which is other than myself; "aśūnya" (non-void) refers to myself. That whose power establishes both of these—I am He, the power of both the void and the non-void. [I am] knowledge and its effects.

The beautiful is auspicious; the non-beautiful consists of ignorance and its effects. From the perspective of one’s own ignorance and so forth, I am both of these. Equal means the same; unequal means dissimilar. Because of the absence of both, I am devoid of the equal and the unequal. "Eternal" and "pure" have already been explained. Whether the delusion of the perspective of one’s own ignorance and so forth exists or does not exist, I am eternally Śiva.
Because it is the nature of supreme auspiciousness and absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Furthermore: "I am devoid of all and nothing, due to the absence of the conceptualization of both the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual parts (*vyaṣṭi*)."

In the form of Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world, I am characterized by sattva; yet in reality, I am eternally devoid of all qualities (nirguṇa). I am devoid of the number one, nor do I possess the number two, because of the absence of the relative pair of one and two;
for the Śruti declares: "In the absence of one, there is no second, and without a second, there is no oneness. Thus, I am free from the distinction between existence and non-existence.

I am devoid of visual perception because of the absence of objects of sight; I am free from volition because that which causes it—the mind—is sought after [as something other than myself]; and I am devoid of the distinctions of various selves because, although the various limiting adjuncts (upādhis)—which stand in the place of jars, bowls, and so forth—are divided by their differences, the inner self (pratyagātman), which stands in the place of the space delimited by them, is of a non-dual nature.

For I am indeed only myself, the embodiment of indivisible bliss, because I am the waveless ocean of bliss. I am not something other than my own self; nor am I anything else, since that which is distinct from me is as unreal as a hare’s horn. Even when there is the appearance of a body and so forth, I am devoid of body and the like. The egg of ignorance is merely a substrate.
I am without support, because the collection of worlds contained therein does not exist and both of those are absent; I am devoid of the relationship between support and supported.

I am without a substratum, either because I alone am the substratum of all things, or because I am devoid of the status of being a substratum due to the absence of anything to be supported by me. I am devoid of bondage and liberation; for bondage is the sense of "I" (egoity) regarding the body and so forth.
The absence of that sense of "I" (tad-ahaṃbhāva) is liberation, because of being liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta); devoid of that [sense of "I"], I am the pure Brahman;

I am That. This has already been explained. I am devoid of all things beginning with the mind (citta), because of the absence of the thousands of modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) such as the mind and so forth. I am supreme, higher than the highest, the Supreme Imperishable.
Therefore, I am beyond even that, because I am the nature of the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*). I am always of the nature of reflection (*vicāra*), yet I am without reflection (*nirvicāra*);
I am that very Self, due to the absence of the fourfold divisions of ignorance (*avidyā*) such as the states of knowledge, non-knowledge, mental modification (*vṛtti*), and the fourth (*turya*).
I am of the nature of the syllables *a* and *u*, and I am the eternal *m*; for, by virtue of being the meaning of the *praṇava*, I am the primordial reality.
I am devoid of the meditator and the meditation; I am that which is devoid of the object of meditation, for the triad beginning with the meditator does not exist.

Through the Self that is Brahman, non-different from the inner witness, I am of a full nature everywhere. Because of filling the world-appearance of unreality and so forth, and because my nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss, there is no room for doubt regarding my being such [as described]. I am characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, because my essential form is truth, knowledge, and bliss.
I am the embodiment of all three hundred and fifty million sacred fords (*tīrtha*), because I am the very form of the sacred fords themselves.
I am Śiva, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because I am beyond the body and its adjuncts; for the scripture declares, "Brahman alone is the Supreme Self.
I am devoid of both the perceptible and the imperceptible; the perceptible is that which is embodied or established solely through defining characteristics.

Its opposite is the characterized (lakṣya), which is either formless (amūrta) or established through secondary indication (lakṣaṇāsiddha) as the denotable (vācya). The meaning is that I am devoid of all such mental constructions. "I am the essence devoid of dissolution" (layahīnarasa); here, dissolution (laya) means destruction (nāśa).

The meaning is: "I am the essence of eternal bliss, devoid of that [duality]. I am devoid of the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge; I am Śiva, devoid of the object of knowledge. I am void of the threefold set beginning with the knower (the *mātrādi-tripuṭī*). The world does not exist; I am the seer of all. I am not the world, but rather its seer, because I am the witness of all. I am devoid of eyes and other senses; I am the state of being the leader (*netṛtva*).

The state of being an impeller; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the state of being an illuminator and so forth is meant. [I am] manifested through the conceptualization of being a leader, an illuminator, and so on—according to the Śruti: "I am indeed Brahman alone, without beginning or end, expanding like the ocean. Awakened from the sleep of my own ignorance, I am wide awake. [I am the leader] of the multitude of devotees in the form of the Blessed Lord.
I am pleased. I am Hara, for my own ignorance, its duality, and its effects have been withdrawn into what remains as myself alone.

I am devoid of all sense organs because of the absence of the three bodies. Yet, I am also the performer of all actions, having become each respective sense organ within those various organs, being the cause of the activity of each of them. Or rather:

"Though devoid of all sense organs, yet because I perform the functions of all the sense organs, I am without hands or feet and possess inconceivable power," according to such scriptural passages as, "I see without eyes; I hear without ears. "I am satisfied by all the Upanishads; I am always easily accessible; I am the Lord, the one beyond the hundred and eight [Upanishads]."

I am most easily attained by those who worship me always with undivided devotion; and because I am Śrī Rāma, I grant supreme fearlessness even to one who worships me but once, or who seeks refuge in me just once, saying, "I am yours."
"I grant fearlessness to all beings; this is my vow."

Thus, according to the teaching of Śrī Rāma: "I am known as 'the joyful and the joyless'—joyful toward the virtuous and joyless toward the wicked; I am the absolute liberation (kaivalya) free from desire and other such [afflictions] within this physical body. "I am eternally of the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra), because that which is non-eternal and not pure consciousness is merely to be sought after. "I am always composed of existence and consciousness (saccinmaya), because my essential nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda). Whatever else...

I am devoid of inferiority, for I do not exist as even the slightest thing apart from myself; I do not exist as even the slightest thing apart from myself because that which is other than self must be sought after. I am free from the knot of the heart: "heart" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and "this" refers to the witness (*sākṣin*);

the identification of these two is called the "knot of the heart," which is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), since the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*) must be sought after.
Dwelling in the center of the lotus of the heart, I am the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and the primordial source. I am devoid of the six modifications;
I am free from the six sheaths (*ṣaṭkośa*). I am liberated from the group of six enemies (*ariṣaḍvarga*) and from the six modifications such as infancy, childhood, and youth.

Because of the absence of gross bodies and the like— which are the substrata for transformations such as the six sheaths beginning with the skin, the group of six enemies beginning with desire, and so forth— I am the inner witness, more internal than the innermost Lord. I am liberated from space and time, being devoid of space and the like.

Because it is the mere existence that is without a counterpart, I am indeed of the nature of the indivisible space; for I am of the form of the indivisible, since I am of the nature of the single, undivided essence by virtue of being the space of consciousness. My mind is liberated from the phenomenal world;
I am devoid of the phenomenal world, because my nature is the non-phenomenal state that is without a counterpart.

I am the form of all illumination; I am the light of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-jyotis*), because I consist of the nature of pure consciousness through the state of mere luminosity. I am liberated from the three periods of time; I am devoid of desire and the like, because I am of the nature of the mindless (*amanaska*). I am liberated from the body and the embodied, because of the absence of the body and the individual soul (*jīva*) delimited by it. I am without attributes (*nirguṇa*).
This has been explained. I am "alone" because I am devoid of all distinctions. I am "devoid of liberation" yet "liberated";
