I am always "devoid of liberation" because of the absolute absence of bondage from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). While bondage may appear through the vision of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājña-dṛṣṭi*), I am liberated through the vision of one who possesses self-knowledge (*svajña-dṛṣṭi*).

From the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), I am devoid of liberation because I am nothing but Brahman alone, which is free from the conceptualization of bondage and liberation; thus, I am without liberation. I am devoid of both truth and untruth, for I am established as the absolute reality (*pāramārthika*) through the negation of all relative truth and untruth. I am not other than pure Being (*sanmātra*); the meaning is that I shall always be pure Being alone. I am devoid of any destination to be reached.

I am devoid of going and so forth, because my nature is ever-full. I am always of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss; though there is diversity of name and form, I remain of uniform nature. I am the Peaceful One, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), because in reality I am the supreme imperishable (*paramākṣara*), free from the conceptualization of the perishable and the imperishable as being distinct from myself. Thus, through attaining the state of being the Lord myself—
For one who possesses direct experience [of this], there is indeed no doubt regarding the realization "I am He.
Thus, whoever hears even once the glory of the self-experience of the sage Maitreya, who has attained the state of Supreme Śiva, he himself becomes Brahman. This concludes the Upaniṣad.
This marks the conclusion of the Maitreyopaniṣad. 1-24.
Thus ends the third chapter.
This commentary on the Maitreyopaniṣad was written by Upaniṣad-Brahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra, by the grace of Lord Īśa;
this commentary on the Maitreyopaniṣad consists of two hundred and sixty verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Maitreyopaniṣad, completing the twenty-ninth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the venerable Īśa.
The Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad.
"That is full"— thus the peace invocation.
The Inquiry into the Renunciation of All Actions:

Now Janaka of Videha, having approached Yājñavalkya, said: "Venerable sir, please explain renunciation to me. Yājñavalkya replied: "Having completed the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), one becomes a householder..."

[One] may [do so]. Having lived as a householder, one may become a forest-dweller and then renounce; or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the stage of studentship, or from the house, or from the forest. Furthermore, whether one has not observed the vows or has observed them, whether one is a graduate (*snātaka*) or not a graduate, whether one has maintained the sacred fires or is without fires—on the very day that one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce. || 1 ||

The procedure for the renunciation of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*): regarding this, some perform only the *prājāpatya* sacrifice; or rather, he should not perform it at all; or he should perform only the *āgneyī* sacrifice, for Agni is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by means of this [sacrifice] he indeed establishes the vital breath. Or he should perform only the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice; these are indeed the three.
The elements are indeed sattva, rajas, and tamas. This is your seasonal source from which, once born, you shone forth; knowing that, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth.
With this mantra he should inhale the fire: "This indeed is the womb of Agni, which is the breath; go to the breath, go to your own womb, svāhā!"—this is what he says thereby. || 2 ||

The procedure for the fireless renunciation (*niragnika-saṃnyāsa*): Having brought fire from a village, one should have [the disciple] smell the fire as before. If one should not find fire, one should offer oblations into water;
for "Water indeed is all the deities. Having offered with the mantra, "I offer to all the deities, svāhā," and having drawn it out...

One should consume the sacrificial oblation with clarified butter for the sake of health. Thus, one should obtain the mantra of liberation through the three Vedas. That is Brahman; that is to be worshipped.
Having cut off the top-knot and the sacred thread, one should recite three times: "I have renounced. "It is even so, O Blessed One," said Yājñavalkya. || 3 ||
The eligibility for renunciation belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone.
Then Atri questioned Yājñavalkya: "How can one be a Brāhmaṇa without the sacrificial thread?
Yājñavalkya replied: "This very Self is his sacrificial thread; having sipped water and performed the ceremonial rinsing (ācamana), [he is so]."
This is the procedure. || 4 ||
The determination of the duties for those not qualified for renunciation:

Now, the wandering mendicant (parivrāj), wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, possessing nothing, pure, non-malevolent, and subsisting on alms, becomes one with Brahman. This is the path of the wandering mendicants; or [he may attain it] on the path of heroes or through fasting unto death.
"Whether by entering water, or by entering fire, or by the Great Departure—this is the path discovered by Brahmā;
by it goes the renunciant who knows Brahman. "It is even so, O Blessed One," said Yājñavalkya.

p. 221) Regarding the supreme excellence of the community of Paramahaṃsas, those known as Paramahaṃsas are Saṃvartaka, Āruṇi, Śvetaketu, Durvāsas, Upamanyu, Nidāgha, Raivataka, Dadhīca, Dadhīci, Ṛbhu, Nimi, Vāmadeva, Datta, Atreya, Aruṇi, Śuka, Sanatkumāra, Vyāsa, Śākalya, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Śāṇḍilya, Jaḍabharata, and others like them.
Those whose conduct is unmanifest, who are not insane, yet behave as if they were insane. || 6 ||
The characteristics of the Paramahaṃsa clad in rags are as follows:

they turn their backs on the cities of other men's wives; [they carry] the triple staff, the water-pot, the water-strainer used only after eating, the topknot, and the sacred thread—all this, saying "Bhūḥ Svāhā," [they cast] into the waters.
Having renounced oneself, one should seek [the Self].
The characteristics of the Digambara Paramahaṃsa are as follows:
wearing their natural form, free from dualities, without possessions, perfectly perfected on the path of Brahman-tattva,
pure-minded, and at the prescribed time, liberated for the sake of sustaining life.
Practicing alms-gathering with his belly as a bowl, having made gain and loss equal, or with his hand as a bowl,
or subsisting on the water from his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), he practices alms-gathering while maintaining only his belly-bowl and remaining empty of other vessels;
his water-pot being for use on land or water, he dwells in a secret place that causes no disturbance, having made gain and loss equal.

One who, intent on uprooting both auspicious and inauspicious karma, abandons the body through renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in an empty house, a temple, a grass hut, an anthill, at the foot of a tree, in a potter’s workshop, or in a sacrificial fire-chamber— he is indeed named a Paramahaṃsa. || 8 ||
I worship that state of Rāmacandra— the reality of the three steps and Brahman— which those perfected in renunciation and knowledge attain as the station of Viṣṇu.
(222) Indeed, this Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad, which is a division of the Śukla-Yajurveda,
is intent on revealing the multitude of duties pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsa and culminates in the reality of the non-dual Brahman.
It unfolds. A commentary on this [text] is begun from a very brief portion of its composition.

This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Janaka and the Kṣatriya Yājñavalkya, is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*). He introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now). "Atha" means after the hearing of the duties (*dharma*) pertaining to the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

Janaka of Videha questioned Yājñavalkya. What did he ask? "O Blessed One, please explain the characteristics of renunciation. Yājñavalkya replied: "Having completed the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder," and so forth, up to the end of the section concerning the Paramahaṃsa, which is found almost word-for-word in the Jābāla Upaniṣad.
This has been explained. || 1-8 ||

The renunciant, clothed in space, who offers no salutation and has no desire for wife or son, having turned away from both the perceptible and the imperceptible, becomes the supreme Lord as a wandering mendicant (parivrāj). On this point, there are these verses: [9]
If there should be one who was previously ordained and is indeed equal in terms of dharma,
to him alone should salutation be made, and never to anyone else.
Even those who have renounced the world are seen to be negligent, with minds directed outward, malicious, eager for quarrels, and their hearts corrupted by the Vedas. (11)

If one who knows the Self is established in the non-dual plenitude (bhūman) and self-sovereignty (svārājya) beyond name and the rest, to whom then should he bow? At that time, no ritual action remains to be performed.

One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before a dog, an outcaste, a cow, or a donkey, thinking: "The Lord, the Blessed One, has entered [this body] by means of a portion of his own life-force (jīvakalā)."

He states that the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), characterized by the definition already mentioned, is indeed the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*): "The one who has attained... By means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that which is indicated is the *lakṣya*; its opposite is the *alakṣya*. The wandering mendicant, who brings both of these to cessation through the states of meditative absorption (*samāhita*) and non-absorption (*asamāhita*), becomes the Supreme Lord due to the perfection of the threefold absence of veils (*nirāvṛti-traya*). Not [otherwise].
By the statement, "Salutation [is offered], not one who desires a wife or son," it follows that even for those who have renounced with the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsins*),
since they have abandoned wife and son, they too— (p. 223)— [are eligible].

Anticipating the objection that one should not perform salutations toward those who are senior or junior [in age], he states that, according to the Dharma, only those who are equal or superior in qualification are to be saluted, and no others. Regarding this, he says, "In this regard, there are these verses," and then speaks the mantras. To the question of who are unworthy of salutation, he replies: "The negligent ones."
One who lacks the qualities of forbearance, knowledge, detachment, tranquility, and so forth,
yet lives merely on alms, is a sinner who has abandoned the true conduct of an ascetic.
Thus,
he who maintains his staff and begs for alms while remaining within his own dharma without cause for distress,
and who persists therein without falling into world-weariness— he indeed is a true ascetic, not a lowly one.

And thus: the meaning is that if those ascetics whose intentions have been corrupted by the Vedas—those whose intentions are defiled by the Vedas—are of censurable conduct, then they are not to be saluted even if they are senior. This applies to those who are devoid of the realization of the Ground (Bhūman), which is free from the conceptualization of name and so forth up to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as recited in the seventh chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*.
Because there is an absence of the distinction between "senior" and "junior" as something separate from himself, for him there is no rule regarding saluting elders or juniors.
He says "nāma" (by name) to indicate that if he so desires, he may salute; if not, he should remain silent. If he does not know this, then he is a mere "lord" (īśvara). (9–13)

What indeed is beautiful about women and the like? Within this mechanical cage of limbs, a mere puppet of flesh, there is but a framework of sinews, bones, and joints; what excellence can there be in such a woman? (14)
Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears from your eyes, look closely; if it is beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain? (15)
O Sage, in which [lake] was seen the splendor of a radiant pearl necklace, resembling the rush of the Ganges water as it flows over the slopes of Mount Meru’s peak.
In cremation grounds and at the ends of the quarters, that very same breast of a woman is devoured by dogs in due time, like a small morsel of food. (17)
Bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye, women—flames of the fire of evil deeds—burn a man like straw. (18)
Blazing even from afar, full of passion yet devoid of essence, women are indeed the beautiful and terrible fuel for the fires of hell. (19)
Women with deluded minds are the snares for binding the limbs of the bird-like men, scattered by the hunter named Desire. (20)
For men who are like fish in the pond of birth, wandering in the mud of the mind,
woman is the baited hook on a line made of the cords of evil latent impressions.
By means of this well-fashioned casket of all the jewels of faults,
may my wife be eternally free from the filth of the chains of suffering.
He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment?
By abandoning a woman, the world is abandoned; by abandoning the world, one becomes happy. (23)
A son who is not obtained causes his parents long-lasting distress;
for once obtained, he afflicts them through miscarriage and through birth.
For one who has been born, there are planetary afflictions and diseases; for a youth, there is deceitfulness;
even when initiated, there is ignorance; and for a scholar, there is the failure to marry. (25)
For the youth, there is the wife of another and so forth; for the householder, poverty;
and for the son, there is no end to suffering—if he becomes wealthy, then he dies. (26)

225) Because the general class of renunciants (*saṃnyāsī*) is adorned with the two kinds of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he disparages women in general—in the passage beginning with "flesh"—in order to prevent any lapse in that celibacy. "With a well-closed box" means in the form of a casket.

The passage beginning with "māṃsapāñcālikāyā" and ending with "jagat tyaktvā sukhī bhavet" has been explained for the most part in the *Mahopaniṣad* and the *Nāradaparivrājakopaniṣad*. Since wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*) have no attachment to wives, sons, and so forth, and because even for detached householders the desire for children (*putreṣaṇā*) is difficult to abandon, [the teaching] is directed toward them.
For the sake of detachment, he censures the state of having or not having a son, beginning with the words "alabhyamāna" (unobtainable).
The phrase "our son is unobtainable" refers to the absence of a son between us, husband and wife.
The meaning is that since the birth of a son and so forth are touched by many defects, one must simply renounce the longing for sons and the like.
The characteristic of one who has attained immediate liberation is that the ascetic is not restless with his hands or feet, nor restless with his eyes,
nor indeed restless with his speech; having become Brahman, he has conquered his senses.

For the discerning person who perceives the same identity between the enemy bound [in prison] and his own body, how could there be anger, just as one would not feel it toward the limbs of one's own body? (28)
If you feel anger toward one who does you harm, why do you not feel anger toward anger itself, which forcibly stands as an obstacle to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation? (29)
Homage be to my anger, which intensely blazes within its own locus;
homage to my anger, which bestows detachment and awakens one to one's faults. (30)
Where people are always asleep, there the self-controlled one is awake;
where they are awake, O learned one, there the king of yogis enters deep sleep.
"Whatever exists here is consciousness alone; this is composed of consciousness and is indeed consciousness itself.
Contemplate thus: 'Consciousness is this, I am consciousness, and these worlds are consciousness. (32)
O bull among sages, that state of the highest mendicancy (pārahaṃsya), which is to be adopted by ascetics as their supreme goal, exists; there is nothing higher than this. (33)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Anticipating the question of what kind of person a true ascetic (*sadyati*) is who is worthy of homage, he states that a true ascetic is one who is free from the fickleness of hands, feet, and eyes—beginning with "na pāṇī": one who lacks the desire to go to the land of Kīkaṭa to seize the wealth of others is not one with "fickle hands"; one who is eager to behold forms, thinking "this is beautiful," is one with "fickle eyes. A true ascetic is the opposite of such.

The ascetic who has ascended to the state of Brahman is not restless with his eyes. One whose speech proclaims the merits or defects of others, saying "this is delicious" or "this is not delicious," is restless in speech; one who is the opposite of that is not restless in speech. Because such a qualified ascetic has become Brahman, he is this—[the Self].

The meaning is that one who has become Brahman and has conquered the senses becomes a true ascetic (sadyati). Raising the objection—"How can one be a true ascetic when even a so-called ascetic is characterized by the three bodies and is overwhelmed by mental states such as anger?"—the author states the impossibility of such states like anger in a true ascetic with the verse beginning "ripau" (toward an enemy). [This applies] toward an enemy, toward the group of six internal foes, and toward one's own body.

Since nothing exists apart from Brahman, when one is bound by the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman— and then, for the discerning one who perceives that the non-dual identity of all things, the commonality of existence which devours diverse objects, is Brahman alone, existing without a counterpart— how could there be any room for the functioning of anger, any more than toward the limbs of one's own body?

The meaning is that there is no possibility of mental modifications such as anger arising apart from oneself. Indeed, the modification of anger arises only by depending upon someone who has done one harm. If this is so, why does anger not arise toward the person who harms you? To this he says:
"toward the one who harms. If you direct anger toward the one who harms because of the rarity of an offender equal to him in provoking anger—then [the following applies].

The meaning is that Brahman alone remains when all conceptions of anything other than itself have subsided. He says, "Salutations," to offer obeisance to such a means (upāya). Because my own anger is trivial, he offers salutations to the one who bestows dispassion (*vairāgya*) and awakens him to the fault that anger causes harm; to the one who has become his guru; and to the one upon whom his own manifesting anger plays.
The meaning is as follows: anger has its own substratum (*svāśraya*); that which intensely inflames this [substratum] is "one who inflames its own substratum" (*svāśrayajvālī*).

To that "inflamer of its own substratum," to anger itself, let there be salutation. The sense is: "I am Brahman"—thus one performs the contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) upon the anger of anger. Between the one who is angry and the one who is not angry—the ignorant self and the knowing self—there is mutual...

He states the distinction with the words "where": where, in that very [state] of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmavidyā*), ignorant people (*svājñajanāḥ*) who are prone to anger are asleep, there, in that same [state] of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman, the self-knowing one (*svajñaḥ*) who is a master of restraint (*saṃyamī*) is one who conquers anger (*kopakopī*).
p.

227) He becomes awakened and vigilant. O wise one, where these ignorant ones (kopinaḥ) become awakened within this phenomenal world that is separate from themselves, right there the king of yogis, the master of anger (kopakopī), who knows himself (svajñaḥ), enters deep sleep (suṣuptim).
Regarding the word "goes" (yāti):
that which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.

This is according to the Smṛti. Since this is so, he says "Consciousness" (cit), instructing you to contemplate that nothing exists apart from Consciousness and everything is indeed Consciousness alone.

That which is Consciousness alone, as stated in the preceding mantra, is what is to be accepted. He says "of the ascetics" (yatīnām) to indicate that apart from that, there is nothing whatsoever denoted by words such as "you," "I," or "this."

Because it is attainable through the stage of the Paramahaṃsa, the state of the Paramahaṃsa itself—the supreme state which is pure consciousness alone—is to be accepted as remaining as one's own self, being without a counterpart (niṣpratiyogika). The meaning is that, due to its being without a counterpart, there is nothing whatsoever existing apart from it. The word "Upaniṣad" indicates the conclusion of the Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad.
This brief commentary on the Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad has been written by Upaniṣad-Brahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
the total extent of this commentary on the Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad is seventy [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Yājñavalkyopaniṣad, constituting the ninety-seventh work in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the venerable Īśa.
The Śāṭyāyanīyopaniṣad. Peace: "That is full. (p. 229)
The Mind as the Cause of Bondage and Liberation:
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense objects, it is known to lead to bondage; free from sense objects, it is remembered as the means to liberation. (1)
If the mind of a living being were to be attached to Brahman in the same way that it is attached to the realm of sensory objects, who then would not be liberated from bondage? (2)
The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with diligent effort. Whatever the mind is, that one becomes; this is the eternal secret. (3)
One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One; one who does not know Brahman does not reach the supreme abode.
But the wise man, perceiving Viṣṇu—the pervader, Vāsudeva—attains the state of true wisdom as a seer of reality.
One should worship the feet of Rāmacandra, whose form is the boundless bliss of the Śāṭyāyanī-brahmavidyā section, and whose nature is the heart of the multitude of ascetics.
Indeed, this Śāṭyāyanīyopaniṣad, which is a division of the White Yajurveda, stands preeminent here, intent upon revealing the duties of the Kuṭīcaka, Bahūdaka, Haṃsa, and Paramahaṃsa [orders],
and culminating in Brahman alone. Of this [Upaniṣad], from its very brief text...
230) The commentary begins. Here, at the outset, it is stated that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation—“the mind alone.
Just as the mind is attached to sense objects, so too, if it is attached to Brahman, one who possesses it [is freed] from the delusion of anything other than the Self.

He says "is liberated" and explains: "that which is attached. Furthermore, he says "the mind itself. The meaning is that for whomsoever the mind is dissolved in something, he becomes absorbed in that, consisting of that, and having that as his essential nature. He explains this by saying "not one who knows the Veda":
one who does not know the Veda is an ignorant person; such a person does not realize, "I am the great Virāj."

One who does not know Brahman does not attain the supreme abode; the meaning is that one ignorant of the Self does not know Brahman—whether with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*)—even in an indirect manner. However, the Brahmin who perceives reality knows Viṣṇu—the all-pervading (*vyāpanaśīla*), transcendent (*krānta*), omniscient Vāsudeva, the inner controller of all and the support of all.
Or, knowing "I am this," one attains the state of a sage (*vipratva*) and liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*); the meaning is that he goes [to that state].
1. The attainment of the fourfold means:
Now, indeed, those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who are not overcome by desire, study that which is the supreme, eternal Brahman.

One who is peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, learned in the Vedas (anūcāna), wise, impartial, free from debt, and silent—having known him, one should dwell in whatever hermitage he may inhabit. || 5 ||

He says that one should become silent (maunī) after knowing, as it truly is, that Brahman which is directly perceived by those untouched by desire (*akāmahata*): because they have realized the reality of the supreme truth (*paramārthatattva*), the learned ones (*śrotriya*)—such as Sanaka and others, or Brahmā and others—are "untouched by desire" (*akāmahata*) due to their certainty that desires cannot exist apart from the Self; [they know] that Brahman which is eternal and supreme.

They would study [the truth] as "nothing but one's own self, devoid of all counterparts"; having studied and known it, simultaneously with that knowledge they would attain it and become the Supreme Self itself— any seeker of liberation whatsoever who is endowed with the aforementioned means, such as being peaceful, self-controlled, and so forth.
This is also intended as an illustration of the four means of accomplishment, such as humility and the rest.

Being born into a family of knowers of Brahman, he was an *anūcāna* (one well-versed in sacred tradition) and was equal to those seeking liberation; thus, he "fully realized" (*abhijajñau*), that is, he came to know Him. Having discharged the three debts and being free from the three desires, he was a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) who [realized] that Supreme Self.
Having understood this, the silent sage (maunī) should dwell in any hermitage, such as that of the *kuṭīcaka* and others, until the exhaustion of his past impressions (*āprārabdhakṣayam*).

The meaning illuminated by the two occurrences of the word "hi" (*hi*) is as follows: simultaneously with the knowledge of non-dual Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmajñāna*), one remains as nothing but Brahman alone, established through the realization of the impossibility of the three types of karma. || 5 ||
231) Now, having entered the final stage of life (āśrama), he observes the duties of a *kuṭīcaka*, maintaining the five-fold [set of requisites] as they may be obtained. || 6 ||
He should carry the triple staff, the sacrificial cord, the garment, the loincloth covering, the sling,
and the water-strainer for as long as he lives.
These five are the measures for an ascetic; that measure is heard as belonging to Brahman.
One should not abandon them until death; even at the end, one should be buried with them.
The emblem of Viṣṇu is said to be twofold: manifest and unmanifest.
By abandoning even one of these two, one surely falls; of this there is no doubt.
The triple staff is indeed the Vaiṣṇava emblem, the means of liberation for Brahmins;
it is the extinction of all dharmas—such is the teaching of the Vedas.
Now, first he states the duties of the *kuṭīcaka*: "atha" (now).

This means after the three stages of life beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*). Having entered the final stage of life, namely that of the *kuṭīcaka*, in comparison to the preceding stages such as studentship, [he should maintain] the five articles beginning with the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), according to his attainment and according to his strength.
The meaning is that one should wander about while maintaining [these items]. "Vāsaḥ" (garment) refers to the covering of the private parts; this is one requisite (*mātrā*).
From the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) up to the purifier (*pavitra*), these constitute five requisites.
If one is unable to ascend to the status of a Bahūdaka and so forth, the meaning is that one should maintain them for as long as life lasts.
Furthermore—these five, consisting of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and so forth, are the measures (*mātrā*) of the *kuṭīcaka* ascetic.

Through the divisions of *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*, those measures are heard as belonging to Brahman; those five measures are heard within Brahman, that is, within the *praṇava*. Thus, [there are] the five [measures] consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest.

One should not abandon the pair of the manifest and unmanifest five-measures (*pañcamātrā*) until the moment of departure from the body. Even at the end, at the time of casting off the body, one should bury the manifest five-measures along with one's own corpse.
Since the pair of the five-measures is the sign of Viṣṇu as both manifest and unmanifest, even one who abandons either of them falls downward.
He says that it "falls" by stating "the mark of Viṣṇu. He states the fruit of bearing the two aforementioned marks of Viṣṇu by saying "the triple staff" (tridaṇḍa). || 6–10 ||
232) Furthermore, O dear one, there are four types of renunciants (saṃnyāsins), and their duties are as follows:
namely, the Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa.

There are four kinds of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*). All of these bear the marks of Viṣṇu; they wear the topknot and the sacred thread, possess pure minds, and meditate upon the Self as Brahman by means of the Self. Devoted to the worship of the nature of pure consciousness, they are observant of recitation (*japa*), self-restraint (*yama*), and religious observances (*niyama*); they are well-behaved and possess meritorious reputations.
This very point has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
"The Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa—these are distinguished by their modes of life;
yet all of them constantly bear the mark of Viṣṇu, both manifest and unmanifest, externally and internally. (11)
Performing the five sacrifices, these practitioners of ritual action, having entered the core of the Vedas, take refuge in the knowledge of Brahman;
having abandoned the tree, they have taken shelter at the root of the tree.
Having renounced the flower [of worldly objects] and partaking only of the essence,
sporting in Viṣṇu, delighting in Viṣṇu, liberated, and having Viṣṇu as their very self, they merge into Viṣṇu alone.
He states the fourfold division of the stages of life (āśrama), beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*, as well as their respective duties, starting with the word "Now" (*atha*).

He declares their duties with the words "All" (*sarva*): "All these are bearers of the marks of Viṣṇu. In this regard, for the *kuṭīcaka*, that which was designated as the "mark of Viṣṇu" consists specifically of the pair—the manifest and the unmanifest, and the five measures (*mātrā*).
The Bahūdaka is also equal [to the others], for according to the scripture, "the Bahūdaka is like the Kuṭīcaka; he is equal toward all dharmas.
As for the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, the body of their own teacher is the manifest mark of Viṣṇu, while their internal organ (antahkarana) is the unmanifest mark of Viṣṇu.
The body of the supreme teacher is the manifest sign of Viṣṇu;
however, his inner organ (antahkarana) is known as the unmanifest sign of Viṣṇu.

Thus says the Smṛti. Therefore, the meaning is that all [ascetics] wear the marks of Viṣṇu. Regarding the phrase "those with tufts and sacred threads," in the case of the Kuṭīcaka and Bahūdaka, their state of possessing tufts and sacrificial threads made of hair and cotton, respectively, like those under a vow, is clearly observed; namely, a tuft (*śikhā*) consisting of a mass of hair, and a sacrificial thread (*upavīta*) made from actual cotton fibers.
According to the Śruti (p.
"The wearing of matted hair by the Haṃsa is the manifest form of the tuft (śikhā), while the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is the unmanifest."
The meaning is "the knowledge of reality. For the Paramahaṃsa, however, the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) are unmanifest.
Indeed, the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman alone constitutes his tuft and sacred thread.
Thus says the Śruti: "Those whose crest is knowledge, who are established in knowledge, and whose sacred thread is knowledge. Therefore, for this very reason—

The meaning is that for the four types of ascetics, beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*, the possession of the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is established as a matter of course through the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest. It should be understood that everything from "those of pure mind" up to "they become men of virtuous fame" applies equally to all four, beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*. This is the purpose stated by the Brāhmaṇa.

A mantra also restates this very point: "This has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the five sacrifices": in the case of the *kuṭīcaka* (the hermit living in a hut), the sacrifice of the recitation of the Gāyatrī is the specific requirement;
however, the sacrifice of the recitation of the *praṇava* is common to all four orders.
All five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) are comprised within the distinctions of the recitation of the Praṇava, yoga, austerity, self-study, and knowledge;

for they are included in the hearing of the meaning of the Vedāntas and Upaniṣads, according to the Śruti: "For the Kuṭīcaka and Bahūdaka, there is hearing [of the scriptures]; for the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, there is reflection," and so forth.

These [ascetics] are "possessed of action" (*kriyāvantaḥ*) because they are intent upon performing the duties appropriate to their own stage of life (*āśrama*). The *paramahaṃsas*, however, especially cultivate the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Having all abandoned the tree of *saṃsāra* which is fit to be cut down, they have taken refuge in—that is, they have resorted to—Brahman, the root of the tree of *saṃsāra*, exactly as it has been known.

Because they have renounced the Vedas that fall within the scope of the ritualistic *karmakāṇḍa*, they are "those who have renounced the flowers," according to the Smṛti: "That flowery speech which the ignorant proclaim. They partake only of the "rasa," the essential essence, according to the Śruti: "He is indeed rasa; for having obtained rasa, one becomes blissful."
Those who delight in Viṣṇu—whose play concerns Viṣṇu both with and without attributes according to their own corresponding knowledge of the qualified and unqualified;
who are liberated from delight in external play; who are "Viṣṇu-natured" (viṣṇvātmaka), meaning for whom Viṣṇu alone is the Self;
and who, being such, merge into Viṣṇu alone by saying "I am His servant" or "I am He"—[attain] the qualified state of Viṣṇu.
Or they attain the state of non-distinction; the meaning is that they become those who have accomplished what was to be done. || 11-12 ||

For the Kuṭīcakas, there should be the performance of japa, sacrifice, and so forth at the three junctions of the day according to one's ability; likewise, bathing, libations, sprinkling, worship, and the five great sacrifices should be performed until death.
The Gāyatrī, consisting of ten *praṇavas*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and four feet,
along with the *Śiras*, is the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) to be performed at the three junctions of the day.

234) He describes the characteristics of the *japa-yajña* (the sacrifice of recitation) for the *kuṭīcaka* alone: "At the three junctions" (*trisandhyam*). This refers to bathing at the three periods of the day: once for the *kuṭīcaka*, twice for the *bahūdaka*, once for the *haṃsa*, and [not at all] for the *paramahaṃsa*.
Regarding the "ash-bath":
since bathing and other such rites are not prescribed for those established in the stage of the Paramahaṃsa,
they should practice the total renunciation of all mental fluctuations alone.

Thus, according to the Śruti, "bathing is the abandonment of the impurities of the mind," it means that [the bath] must be performed with the fourth [Veda] encased by the Vyāhṛtis and the Śiras. However, as for the Paramahaṃsa’s sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), even during the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), only the recitation of the Praṇava should be performed, provided he is not yet qualified for [the study of] Śravaṇa.
But for one who recites the Praṇava twelve thousand times every day,
the Supreme Brahman becomes propitious within twelve months.
Thus says the Śruti:
"A renunciant should constantly recite the Upaniṣads of his own Vedic school, the Gītā, the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu, the Śrī Rudra, and the Praṇava."
And because of the Smṛti: "Having recited [the mantra] other than the Praṇava thus, when will one become liberated? (13-14).
The fourfold sacrifice beginning with the sacrifice of yoga:
the sacrifice of yoga is constant service to Hari and the Guru with one-pointed devotion;
the sacrifice of austerity is non-violence through the actions of speech, mind, and body. (15)
The practice of various Upaniṣads is declared to be the sacrifice of self-study (svādhyāya);
with an undistracted mind, one offers the self into the fire of Brahman with the syllable "Om. 16.
That is to be known as the sacrifice of knowledge, the most excellent among all sacrifices;
they have the staff of knowledge, the topknot of knowledge, and wear the sacred thread of knowledge.
"He whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread is likewise composed of that [knowledge], possesses the entirety of Brahminhood; such is the instruction of the Vedas. (18)

For this alone is the supreme sacrifice of the silent recitation (japa-yajña) of the Paramahaṃsas. He states that the fourfold group of sacrifices beginning with the yoga-sacrifice is common to all: "The yoga-sacrifice," etc. (verses 15–18).
The Determination of the Duties of the Wandering Mendicant:
Now then, my dear, these wandering mendicants become as they appear;
having crossed over desire, anger, greed, delusion, deceit, arrogance, envy, the sense of "mine," egoism, and so forth.
Having abandoned honor and dishonor, as well as blame and praise, one should stand like a tree; even when being cut down, one should not speak.
Thus, the wise become immortal even in this very world. This has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Having made his kinsmen and son rejoice, looking back no more, enduring the pairs of opposites, he is tranquil."
He should wander, turning toward either the east or the north. || 19 ||
Carrying an alms-bowl and a staff, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, wearing a topknot or shaven-headed, clad in a sacred thread and living with a family,
accepting only what is necessary for his journey— such a man [is a true ascetic].
Whether it be obtained through compassion, requested, or acquired as alms. || 20 ||
A bowl made of clay, wood, or gourd, or one of woven fibers or leaves— whatever is obtained in that manner;
as well as [robes] of hemp, linen, grass, rags, skins, or leaves.
The covering should be either unwashed or discarded. || 21 ||
At the junction of the seasons, one should shave only the crown of the head;
never the lower part, nor the armpits, nor should one ever have the top-knot (*śikhā*) shaved.
For four months he should remain firm in his conduct, until the inner self, the person of universal form, has fallen asleep.

Having described the five types of sacrifice, he next presents their collection of duties and their fruit, beginning with the word "atha" (now). The meaning is that they become possessors of the nature of gold (*jātarūpadhara*).
He states what must be performed by them with the words "kāma" (desire): by the power of the knowledge that nothing exists apart from Brahman, like a tree...

When the wise realize that Brahman—which is established through the total negation (*sarvāpahnava*) of everything, preceded by the absence of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth—is their own non-dual Self alone, then at that very moment they become immortal right here;
the meaning is that they become liberated while in the disembodied state (*videhamukta*). This is the meaning expressed by the Brāhmaṇa.

He states that this is also expressed by a mantra: "This very thing has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse. Having given his consent for his son to depart, and never again looking back at them, being capable of enduring the pairs of opposites (dvandva) and tranquil, he proceeds either eastward or northward, preceded by the performance of the duties appropriate to his own stage of life (āśrama).
One should wander about while maintaining constant contemplation of one's own true nature. Regarding the duties of the various classes such as the *kuṭīcaka* and others, [the text] says:

receiving only what is necessary for the maintenance of the body and merely sufficient for subsistence; one should take as a fruit the coconut or the *kaphala*, and as a vessel, one made from leaves tied together with thread, or whatever is obtained.

[The materials are] hemp, linen, silk, bark, or cloth made of grass. Although one should have said "rags and skins" (*kanthājine*), the change of gender in "rags and skins" (*kanthājinau*) is for metrical reasons. The meaning is that for one adorned with such clothing, there should be an upper garment (*uttarīya*) consisting of leaves—either unwashed, sewn together, or detached—as a covering. [The word] *kakṣam* means...
The two armpits are mentioned. For those other than the *haṃsa*, shaving is the same [as for others], because the *haṃsa* wears matted hair (*jaṭā*).
He states that this is the specific distinction for the *kuṭīcaka*: "He should never have his crest-lock (*śikhā*) shaved.
He states that the rule for the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*) is the same for all: "For four... as long as Virāj sleeps.

He should reside in one place for the four months of the rainy season; otherwise, as the fortnights indeed constitute months, he may stay in one place for two months. Furthermore, when this [rainy season] has passed, desiring to perform the duties appropriate to his own stage of life (āśrama), he should wander everywhere for another eight or ten months.

There is a restriction regarding the place of residence; otherwise, when this [period] has elapsed, one who desires to pursue his own livelihood may either wander or dwell elsewhere for another eight [years].
One should dwell in a temple of the gods, at the foot of a tree, or in a cave, unattached and with one's conduct and observances unobserved.
Like a flame without fuel, he is utterly tranquil; he should neither be agitated nor cause agitation in any situation whatsoever.

If one desires the foundation for hearing, meditation, and concentration, then one should dwell in a single place. To the question, "Why should he dwell in the abode of worldly people? he says: "In a temple" and so forth. He should dwell in a praiseworthy location such as a temple or the like.
Even there, having abandoned the sense of "mine" and being free from attachment, his character and conduct should remain unobserved by others.

One should become pacified like a flame without fuel due to the cessation of the delusion of anything other than oneself. Upon seeing a person who is one's equal or one's inferior, one should never feel agitation. The meaning is that wherever the mind is attached to the notion of something "other than oneself," one should agitate that [notion] and instead maintain the awareness of one's own Self everywhere. || 23 ||
The state of one who possesses self-knowledge:
"If a person were to know the Self as 'This am I,' desiring what, or for the sake of whose desire, would he suffer with this body? (24)
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should practice wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech. 25.
For one should remain in a state of childhood, having become disillusioned with the knowledge of Brahman;
and having become disillusioned with both the knowledge of Brahman and childhood, the self-possessed sage becomes a silent seer (muni).
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here.
As long as the Self is not attained, one must practice means such as the emaciation of the body; however,
once the Self is known through the realization that it alone remains, there is no purpose for either emaciating or nourishing the body.

He states what must be done: "the Self. Having thoroughly understood the knowledge of Brahman—that is, having realized the true nature of Brahman—one should desire to remain with childlike innocence regarding objects other than oneself, through detachment.

One should desire to remain [in that state]. Then, having mastered the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and childhood, and having ascertained that nothing exists apart from Brahman, the self-possessed one remains as the Self alone; this is the meaning. As for the rest of the mantra:
there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in falling from that which has been ascended.

Now then, O gentle one, he who abandons this lifelong state of wandering mendicancy, which is the very nature of the Self, becomes a slayer of heroes, he becomes a slayer of Brahmins, he becomes a slayer of embryos, and he becomes a perpetrator of a great sin. He who forsakes this Vaiṣṇava culmination becomes a thief, he becomes one who violates the teacher’s bed.
He becomes a betrayer of friends, he becomes ungrateful, and he falls away from all the worlds.
This very point has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"The thief, the drinker of spirituous liquor, and the violator of the teacher's bed..."
Those who betray their friends attain purification through atonement;
however, one who abandons the mark of Viṣṇu—whether manifest or unmanifest, whether worn externally or held within—cannot be purified by any means, even by the light of the Self. 28.
Having abandoned the emblem of Viṣṇu, whether internally or externally,
he who serves his own stage of life or one that is not a stage of life,
or who resorts to a return [to worldly life], is utterly deluded.
Their course has not been seen even in ten million eons. || 29 ||
Having abandoned all bases of attachment, the wise man should dwell for a long time in the stage of liberation;
for one who has fallen away from the stage of liberation, no higher destination exists.

"But one who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, does not abide in his own duty—him one should know as one who has fallen from his exalted state; such is the instruction of the Vedas. (31)

Having thus established the nature of Brahman, [the text] now censures one who, after remaining in the duty of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) for as long as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) persist, acts according to his own whims once those have been abandoned; this is introduced with the word "atha.
As long as there is discrimination between self and other—which is the very nature of the Self—one should follow the characteristics of the two marks of Viṣṇu. Whoever...
He abandons [the teachings] and becomes a destroyer of heroes.
As long as the limits of the aggregates (upādhi) persist, so long should one serve the guru.
Whatever has been spoken by the guru on this earth—whether auspicious, inauspicious, or otherwise—[one should accept it].
The disciple, filled with contentment, should perform that without hesitation.
Thus,
whether the body of the Lord of Teachers contains breath or is breathless,
the yogi should always pay homage to that direction in which it rests.
As long as the vital breath remains in the body, the disciple should remain vigilant;
if he follows the will of the guru, he attains the state of Viṣṇu.

Thus, he who abandons this Vaiṣṇava steadfastness—which is characterized by the imitation of the external and internal *liṅgas* of Viṣṇu established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—[is at fault]. He states that even the mantras follow what has been declared by the Brāhmaṇa: "This very thing has been declared by a *ṛc*. [This refers to] the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) through atonement (*prāyaścitta*).

Even those who have committed the five great sins, such as the theft of gold, attain purification if they bear the manifest or unmanifest sign of Viṣṇu according to the prescribed characteristics of the preeminent Guru who has ascended to the state of Brahman. At that time, the manifest sign of Viṣṇu consists of serving the gross body of the preeminent Guru.

He who does not practice that which is characterized by being under the control of knowledge—the unmanifested mark of Viṣṇu—which was maintained and performed even by the former teachers, is a perpetrator of great sins (mahāpātakin) who cannot be purified even by all means of expiation (prāyaścitta). Self-knowledge elsewhere [in other contexts] indeed swallows up all sins; however, in this case—

Even through the knowledge of the appearance of the Self, one would not be purified; the meaning is that without the grace of the supreme teacher, no one can be purified. How then can it be said that there is no expiation for one who abandons the pair of Viṣṇu’s liṅgas? [It is because] by performing the duties appropriate to one's own stage of life (āśrama) other than those two liṅgas of Viṣṇu...
Having first abandoned the mantras taught by the preceptor, which are characterized by the stage of the paramahaṃsa asceticism marked by the carrying of the staff and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)—

Thinking that one might attain purity and achieve all that is to be done either through the characteristics of the stages of life (*pattilakṣaṇa*), by adopting the teachings of other teachers, or by the performance of religious duties, he says: "Having abandoned...
He states that a mendicant (*yati*) should dwell in the stage of liberation (*mokṣāśrama*) after first renouncing all stages of life, provided he does so with vigilance (*apramāda*).

Regarding the word "having abandoned": he concludes that one who abandons their own dharma has fallen from the state of one who had ascended—this is expressed by the phrase "the wandering life" (pārivrājya).
This refers to one who does not abide in their own dharma, characterized by the imitation of the two marks of Viṣṇu. (28–31)
The Pursuit of the Two Marks of Viṣṇu:

Now then, my dear, he who, having attained this eternal dharma of the Self—the steadfast devotion to Viṣṇu—remains following it without defiling it, becomes self-controlled; he becomes one of virtuous fame; he becomes a knower of the world. He...

He becomes a knower of the Vedanta; he becomes a knower of Brahman; he becomes all-knowing; he becomes self-sovereign; he attains the Blessed Supreme Brahman; and he delivers his ancestors, kinsmen, relatives, well-wishers, and friends from worldly existence. || 32 ||

One hundred generations of ancestors and likewise three hundred future generations in their entirety become purified in this world for those families in which a wise man here renounces the world. (33)
"The most virtuous wandering mendicant delivers thirty generations before him, thirty after him, and thirty beyond those—so indeed says the Śruti. (34)
"Even one whose life-breath is still in the throat, if he should say 'I have renounced,' by him his ancestors are delivered—such is the instruction of the Vedas. (35)

Now, my dear, one should not explain this eternal nature of the Self, this Vaiṣṇava steadfastness, without having completed [one's own training], nor to one who has not studied the Vedas, nor to one who does not know the Self, nor to one who is not free from passion, nor to one who is not pure, nor to one who has not approached [the teacher] as a disciple, nor to one whose mind is not disciplined; so they have said. This very point is expressed in a Ṛgvedic verse:
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak to one who is censorious, dishonest, or deceitful; may I be thus endowed with vigor. || 36 ||
To whomever he knows to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy—
to him who has approached him properly [he should teach this].
Having examined [the recipient], one should bestow the Vaiṣṇava state centered on the Self.
Those Brahmins who, having been instructed, do not honor their teacher in word, thought, or deed—
just as that teacher would not eat with them, so too [they are not to be honored].
In that very same way, he does not eat that food, even though it has been heard.
The guru alone is the supreme dharma; the guru alone is the supreme goal.
He who does not honor the guru who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable [of the Veda], [is lost]. (39)
"He who possesses supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as he does for the Divine—he, knowing Brahman, shall reach the Supreme; such is the instruction of the Vedas. (40)
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Having thus censured one who is averse to the two marks of Viṣṇu, he now praises, by way of having accomplished his purpose, one who follows the aforementioned two marks of Viṣṇu, beginning with the word "atha": "He becomes self-controlled, that is, one whose senses are conquered. What more need be said? He attains the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord."

He says that even the mantras repeat the meaning stated by the Brāhmaṇa: "A hundred... This means that if he becomes a renunciant through knowledge (*vidvatsaṃnyāsī*), then a hundred ancestors before him and three hundred descendants after him, up to the end of their lineage, shall have fulfilled their purpose. Furthermore: "...thirty others."
He concludes that even through the renunciation of one who is afflicted by illness or lacks knowledge, his father and other relatives shall become partakers of merit, stating:
"It has been renounced.

"This Vaiṣṇava culmination (niṣṭhā) is established for one who has accomplished his purpose; it must not be spoken to one who is unqualified. It should be spoken only after having thoroughly examined [the candidate] for a long time and having ascertained that he possesses good character. With this in mind, he says, "Now" (atha). He himself states this culmination—beginning with "not to one who has not studied the Vedas" (nānanūcānāya)—in the sense already expressed by the Brāhmaṇa: "one should not speak this culmination."

He says "ha sma" to indicate that it was also stated by means of two mantras. The word "brahmavādinaḥ" (those who discourse on Brahman) is to be supplied as the subject. To the question "What [did they say]? he replies: "Vidyāha vai" (Knowledge indeed said). To the question "To whom should it be told? he replies: "Yam" (to him). He states that ascetics should not accept alms in the house of one who does not highly respect their teacher: "adhyāpitāḥ" (having been taught).

Thus: those Brahmins who are ascetics, having been taught the Great Saying of the *praṇava* and so forth by a certain Guru, yet do not honor or highly esteem their own preceptor—the Guru—with their mind, speech, body, and actions, but instead treat him with contempt or disregard; just as it is with those defilers of the Guru, together with them...

Householders seeking their own spiritual welfare should never entertain a Guru as a guest, nor should the Guru ever eat in their home; likewise, other founders of religious traditions do not accept food from those who provide alms to those who revile the Guru— even if those individuals are otherwise faultless— nor do they allow their disciples to eat in such a house.

"By the grace of the Guru, one neither eats nor is eaten until the end"—such is the power of the Guru as heard in the mantra "to the giver of the single syllable. As for the question of what kind of person such a Guru is, the answer is simply "the Guru himself. He is the giver of the single syllable established by the Śruti, "Om is the supreme Brahman. Even for those belonging to his fold, there is fruit.

The meaning is that it is the same. Showing the supreme fruit of serving a true teacher and disciple—which is the opposite of that [former case]—he concludes with the words "of whom" (*yasya*). That which is the instruction of Viṣṇu, characterized by both manifest and unmanifest signs, reaching the state of "Self alone" (*svamātra*) with excellence—that is the teaching of all the Vedāntas.
This brief commentary on the Śāṭyāyanīyopaniṣad has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
it comprises one hundred and forty verses of the Śāṭyāyanīya school.
Thus ends the commentary on the Śāṭyāyanīyopaniṣad, completing the ninety-ninth [text] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
Saṃnyāsopaniṣad.
"May they swell"— thus the Peace invocation.
The First Chapter:
The Procedure for Renunciation.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad. He who renounces in due order— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
He becomes one who has renounced (*saṃnyasta*). What is this that is called renunciation? How does one become one who has renounced?

He who protects himself by means of ritual acts, having obtained the consent of his mother, father, wife, sons, and kinsmen, and having chosen all his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as before—[he thus becomes one who has renounced].

One should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. One should give away one's entire property to the officiating priests, including the cows. Having consigned all the ritual vessels into the Āhavanīya fire, or the Gārhapatya, or the Anvāhāryapacana, or the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires, one should let down one's hair including the top-knot, cut the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), look at one's son, and say: "You are the Brahman."

He should consecrate [the food] with the mantra: "Thou art the sacrifice; thou art all. If he is sonless, having meditated upon this very Self and without looking back, he should go forth toward the east or the north. He should practice the life of a mendicant among the four castes. He should eat from his hand as a bowl and consume food like medicine.
For five nights,
or for four months of the rainy season, he may dwell either in a village or even in a city; or indeed for two months, [considering] fortnights as months.
He should dwell [thus]. He should accept tattered clothing or bark garments, and he should accept nothing else;

for if he is unable [to maintain this], he suffers through affliction, thinking, "This is austerity. Or, he who renounces in this sequence, or he who perceives thus: "What is his sacrificial thread? What is his topknot? Or how is his ritual sipping of water? [should live as such].
He said to him: "This itself is his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*): meditation on the Self. Knowledge is his topknot (*śikhā*).
Performing his duties with water that is present everywhere, he uses his stomach as a vessel. His dwelling is on the bank of a body of water.
When the sun has set, how is his ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) performed? As by day, so by night; for him there is no distinction between night and day."
Not by day. Regarding this, it has been said by the Seer: "Day indeed becomes once for all for him who, knowing thus, unites himself with this [Self]. || 1 ||

I contemplate that which is to be known through the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads, which takes refuge in the assembly of renunciants, the glory of the universal existence of Being, as being nothing but my own Self.

Herein, this *Saṃnyāsopaniṣad*, which is a division of the Sāmaveda, begins with an exposition of the duties of the six classes of renunciants, beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*. Having observed that those endowed with the means and qualifications as previously described are not found, the Śrutis themselves present the *Saṃnyāsopaniṣad*; thus he says, "Now" (*atha*). The word "now" (*atha*)— [The remainder of the text follows.]

The meaning is that [this follows] immediately after the attainment of the qualification [for renunciation]. Since the knowledge of one's own self alone, which is without a counter-correlate, does not arise without the renunciation of everything other than oneself, we shall explain the *Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad* as a means to that end; that is to say, we shall declare it clearly and speak of it.

Regarding the question of how that process occurs, the text says "he who. The meaning is that he alone becomes a true renunciant (saṃnyāsī) who, following the sequence beginning with "having completed his student life, one should become a householder," and so forth, as well as "having attained the stage of the Bahūdaka," and so forth, renounces the threefold desire. The text anticipates the questions "What is renunciation? and "Who is a renunciant? by asking "Who? (kaḥ).

They themselves provide the answer to their own doubt with the word "ya" (he who). The meaning is: he who protects himself by means of the actions to be described hereafter, and refines himself according to the procedure to be explained, such as the approval [of the rite] by his mother and others.

Regarding the question "How so?"—[he says]: "Having obtained the permission of my mother, father, wife, sons, and kinsmen, I wish to take up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*); may you grant me your command. [This is said] for the purpose of performing the final fire-sacrifice (*carameṣṭi*).

Having chosen all [the priests] as before, he should then perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice together with them. Then, whatever sons the sacrificer may have, he should divide his self-acquired wealth among them along with himself according to their respective shares; it is said that he must give away his entire share, as obtained, to the officiating priests.

"His entire property" (*sarvasvam*) means that the sacrificer himself should give his entire property to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: one should perform the ritual transfer of the fire (*agnisamāropaṇa*) from the sacrificial vessel. Then, one should practice the life of begging (*bhaikṣacaryam*); if one is unable [to do so], then [one may keep] clothing sufficient to ward off the afflictions of cold and the like.

If one does not accept [gifts], one performs austerity (*tapas*) by being tormented by the afflictions arising from cold and other such conditions. However, when accepting clothing and other items appropriate for oneself, the meaning is that one performs the austerity suitable for one’s own stage of life (*āśrama*) with ease. Since water exists everywhere, one should not make a request for it while performing the function of quenching thirst and so forth; thus, "desire" (*kāma*) and "intoxication" (*mada*) are like a watering place (*udapāna*).

This is because of the sacred scripture (*śruti*). The meaning is that one should eat from the vessel of one's stomach according to what is obtained, and if there is a dwelling place on the bank of water, one should reside there. [The question arises: "How can there be the ritual touching of water (*upasparśana*) when the sun has set?
For there is a prohibition against touching a body of water at night. Thus, for one who has attained the state of the Sun of Consciousness (*cidāditya*), it is just as it is during the day.
At night. This too has been stated by the Seer in a mantra. What is it? "By day alone it becomes for him.
The meaning is that it is always day for him. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.
He who, knowing thus, unites himself by this—meaning he who performs the continuous contemplation through the yoga of renunciation and knowledge—he [attains this].

The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*). The remainder has been fully elaborated upon in the *Āruṇika*, *Nārada*, and other such texts; this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter.
Chapter Two:
The Qualification for Renunciation (Saṃnyāsa)

In response to the inquiry, "Who is qualified to renounce," having first described the one who possesses the forty refinements (*saṃskāra*), is detached from everything, has attained purity of mind, and is free from desire, [the author] defines the candidate for renunciation;
this has been explained in the *Nāradaparivrājaka*. (1)
He who, having made a firm resolve regarding renunciation, does not carry it out, commits a transgression; he should perform merely a *kṛcchra* penance and is then fit to renounce once again.
He who causes one to fall from renunciation, he who causes one already fallen to renounce [the world],
and he who creates obstacles to renunciation— these three are known as fallen.

Furthermore, regarding those who, having made a firm resolve for renunciation by thinking "I shall practice renunciation," subsequently disparage renunciation, cast it aside as fallen, or create obstacles to renunciation—they become liable to sin;
thus he says: "Renunciation... (2–3).
Those who are ineligible for renunciation (saṃnyāsa):
now, the eunuch, the outcaste, the one with a defective limb, the womanizer, the deaf, the child, the mute, the heretic, the wheel-turner (cakrī),

the bearer of sectarian marks (liṅgī), the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), the twice-born who maintains two wives, the teacher for hire, the one afflicted by skin disease (śipiviṣṭa), and the one who maintains no sacred fires (anagnika).
Even though they possess dispassion, these people are not fit for renunciation; even if they have renounced, they are not qualified for the instruction on the Great Sayings (Mahāvākya).
One whose offspring has fallen after having ascended [to a higher stage], one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one suffering from consumption,
and likewise one who is deficient in limbs, is not at all fit to renounce the world. || 5 ||
One should never perform the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), nor for outcasts (vrātyas), nor for those accused of heinous crimes.
One should never cause a person to take up renunciation who is devoid of vows, sacrifices, austerity, charity, fire-offerings, and Vedic study, and who has fallen away from truth and purity;
these individuals do not deserve renunciation except through the prescribed sequence for one who is afflicted by illness.
He points out those who are ineligible for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) with the word "atha" [in verse 4-7]. *Śipiviṣṭaḥ* means one whose penis is exposed.
Regarding the method of undertaking renunciation:
having torn out the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) with the mantra "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā," one should not wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) externally. [It bestows] fame and strength.
Saying, "Grant me knowledge, dispassion, and intelligence," he should cut his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the mantra *oṃ svāhā* and cast it into the water;
then, having discarded his garment and waist-string, he should consecrate them three times with the mantra, "I have renounced. || 8 ||

Those who are free from the aforementioned defects become qualified for renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Following the determination of the qualified candidate, he states the method for performing it: "Om," thus [ends the section]. (8)
The Sun moves from his station upon seeing a twice-born man who has renounced;
having pierced my orb, this man attains the Supreme Brahman. (9)
The wise person who says, "I have renounced," uplifts sixty generations of his past lineage and sixty of his future lineage.
Whatever defects arise from the mental continuum and whatever defects are born of the body,
the fire of the *praiṣa* mantra consumes them all, just as the fire of chaff purifies gold. (11)
Thus, he praises the person who has duly renounced and is qualified for knowledge with the words "the renunciant" (saṃnyāsinam).
Furthermore, he says "sixty," referring to the defects born of lineage—that is, those produced by a wicked son. (9–11)
Taking up the staff with the words, "O friend, protect me," he should grasp the staff. || 12 ||
If the patient survives, then he should accept the staff and other items according to the characteristics previously described; thus it is said:
"One should take up the staff [with the mantra] 'O friend, protect me. (12)
Regarding the characteristics of the staff:
the staff should indeed be made of bamboo, pleasing, with its bark intact, having even joints, produced from a sacred place, and purified of various impurities. (13)
A mendicant should carry a staff that is not burnt or gnawed by insects, adorned with joints and knots,
reaching up to the nose, or equal in height to the head or the eyebrows.
The conjunction of the staff and the self is indeed prescribed in every respect;
a wise man should not go even three throws of an arrow's length without his staff. (15)
He states the characteristics of the staff: "The staff," etc. (13–15).

O Mother, always address me as "Sarvasaumya" (the entirely gentle one); having taken up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)—which is the sustenance of the world and the foundation of life—and having been consecrated with the *yogapaṭṭa* (yoga-band), you may dwell at your ease. || 16 ||
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them. (17)
Having taken up the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and received the instruction on the Praṇava and the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) from the mouth of his preceptor,
he became devoted to the conduct of his own stage of life (āśrama). Having performed the hearing of the Vedānta (vedānta-śravaṇa) until the cessation of the five defects such as doubt,
the sage, consecrated with the yoga-band (yogapaṭṭa), lived at ease according to his inclination until the exhaustion of his past karma (ā-prārabdha), by the permission of his guru.

He says "one should dwell" and then "the world"; therefore, he says "abandon," meaning that the intellect which discriminates between what ought and ought not to be done regarding dharma and so forth must be relinquished. (16–17)

Regarding the fourfold classification of renunciants, there are the renunciant through dispassion, the renunciant through knowledge, the renunciant through both knowledge and dispassion, and the renunciant through action; thus he has attained this fourfold division. || 18 ||
To the question "How many kinds of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) are there?", he says: "By means of dispassion" (vairāgya), etc. (18).

Regarding the renunciant through dispassion (*vairāgyasaṃnyāsī*), it is as follows: having attained freedom from craving for objects seen or heard of in tradition, he who has renounced by virtue of his prior meritorious karma is a renunciant through dispassion. (19)
Having attained freedom from craving for objects seen or heard of, and having attained cessation of thirst for enjoyment of objects pertaining to this world or the next.
The renunciant of knowledge,

through his understanding of the scriptures and his hearing of the accounts of experiencing the worlds of merit and demerit, having ceased from the phenomenal world (prapañca) and abandoned the latent impressions of the body,
the scriptures, and the world, relinquishes all worldly activity like vomited food.

One who, having recognized [the world] as something to be abandoned and being endowed with the fourfold means (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), renounces—that person alone is a renunciant through knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsī), a renunciant through knowledge and dispassion (jñāna-vairāgya-saṃnyāsī). (p. 250)

Having practiced everything in due order and experienced everything, through knowledge and dispassion and by means of constant contemplation on his true nature, he renounces while remaining only as the body and becomes one who wears only the natural form of gold;
such a person is a renunciant of knowledge and dispassion. 21.
A karma-saṃnyāsī is one who,
having completed his student life (brahmacarya), become a householder, and entered the forest-dweller stage (vānaprastha),
renounces [worldly life] according to the sequence of the stages of life even in the absence of dispassion. || 22 ||
The sixfold renunciation:
renunciation is of six kinds—namely, the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, the *paramahaṃsa*, the *turīyātīta*, and the *avadhūta*. First, the *kuṭīcaka*:

The Kuṭīcaka wears a tuft of hair and the sacred thread, carries a staff and a water-pot, and is devoted solely to the means of subsistence consisting of a loincloth, a garment, a patched cloak, a small cooking pot, a spade, and a trident; he eats his food in one place, bears white vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and carries three staffs (tridaṇḍa). || 24 ||

Having much water [for purification], wearing a tuft of hair and the like along with a sacred thread, bearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), equal toward all like a forest-dweller (kuṭīcaka), and subsisting on eight mouthfuls of food by the manner of a honey-gatherer (madhukara-vṛtti). || 25 ||

He is the Swan, the Swan, wearing matted locks, bearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), eating unprepared food obtained by begging, and wearing a loincloth and a patched garment. || 26 ||

The Paramahaṃsa is the supreme ascetic who is devoid of the topknot and the sacrificial thread, and who subsists on alms received in his cupped hands from five houses, possessing only a single loincloth.
Devoted to smearing himself with ashes, he has renounced everything. || 27 ||

Transcending the fourth state (turiyatita), transcending the fourth state, subsisting on fruits through the practice of eating from a cow’s mouth; if he subsists on grain, he may do so within three houses; with only his body remaining [as a vessel], naked, he conducts himself toward the body like a corpse. || 28 ||

The Avadhūta is one who is free from all restrictive rules; having first avoided those who have fallen from their status or are accused of crimes, he subsists among all castes by the lifestyle of a python (ajagaravṛtti), being solely intent on the realization of his own true nature. || 29 ||

The section beginning with "one who has renounced through dispassion" and ending with "intent upon the contemplation of one's own true nature" has been explained for the most part in the *Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad* [verses 19–29].
Through the contemplation of the identity of the inner self and Brahman, this entire world— including trees, grass, and mountains— is no longer "I.
Since that which is external is utterly inert, how could I, who am all-pervading, be it?
In a short time the body will dissolve; I am not insentient matter.
Sound, which has a void-like form and originates in the void, is produced by the inert ear-cavity existing for a mere moment; therefore, I am not insentient. (31)
This [Self] is attainable through the skin which perishes in a moment, yet otherwise it is unattainable;
having realized the Self through the grace of consciousness, I am not the insentient sense of touch. (32)

I am not the insentient taste, which has acquired its nature through the tongue; it is trivial, fickle due to its restless essence, characterized by slight movement, and dependent upon material objects. (33)
Dissolved in the seen and the seeing—which are perishable and subject to momentary destruction—the form [of the ego] is exhausted in the solitary Seer; thus, "I am not the insentient. (34)
I am not the insentient odor, which is imagined by the nose—insensitive to fragrance, perishable, fragile, and of indeterminate form. (35)

Free from the sense of "mine," devoid of mental constructs, peaceful, and with the delusion of the five senses gone, I am indeed pure consciousness alone, devoid of all parts and their manifestations.

I am this pure consciousness alone, devoid of any external objects, the illuminator who pervades both the internal and the external; I am partless, untainted, the manifestation of non-conceptual consciousness, one and all-pervading. (37)
By me alone, as the conscious principle, all these things— from pots and cloths up to the sun— are illumined by my own light, just as by a lamp.
These various rows of sense-faculties flash forth here by me alone,
through the internal light of my splendor, just as rows of sparks flash from fire.
This pure vision, consisting of consciousness, which possesses infinite blissful enjoyment and is characterized by supreme tranquility, triumphs among all visions. (40)
Salutations again and again to Me alone, who am the inner Self of all beings, whose nature is consciousness free from the object of thought, and whose form is inward pure awareness.

By what means does the practice of reflecting upon the true nature of the *kuṭīcaka* and other [orders] arise? To this question, one should listen to the one hundred and eight Upanishads beginning with the *Īśa*, until the five defects such as doubt are pacified;
then, having heard their meaning—
253) He states that from reflection (*manana*) arises the mental modification (*vṛtti*) known as meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), beginning with the words "the world" (*jagat*).

[The objection is: "You are the one whose body is the world, or rather, you are sound and the other objects of sense. To this he replies with the words "by time" (*kālena*). [This is] by means of a restless existence (*lolasattayā*).
[The mind] is characterized by flickering thoughts; it is perishable, having the nature of decay.

It is "insentient" (acetana) because of the absence of sense organs and their objects apart from itself. He states that when the vision consisting of consciousness (cinmayadṛṣṭi) has arisen, the identity of the inner self and Brahman occurs—beginning with the words "all. The first half [of the verse] refers to the meaning of the term *tat* (That).

The meaning of the word *tvaṃ* consists of the twelve syllables divided into the latter half; the four syllables situated above that, however, are the meaning of the word *asi*, according to the scripture which states: "One should proclaim the oneness of 'namas' and 'tvaṃ'."
The power of consciousness and its praise consist of diverse powers that are pure and equalized by the consciousness which is changeless and free from the perception of parts.
Through the non-binding of the mind—which disregards the three times and is devoid of the object of thought—only equanimity remains for that mind which has disregarded the object of thought. (43)
For she, because of being beyond the reach of words, remains as if eternally non-existent,
as if having reached the state of the established doctrine of selflessness.
Enveloped by impurities consisting of both effort and lack of effort, that consciousness is unable to rise up, like a bird bound by a snare. (45)
Through the delusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion, living beings have attained a state of equality with worms submerged in crevices of the earth. (46)
He states that everything conceptualized by consciousness (*cit*) is indeed consciousness itself with the words "variegated" (*vicitrāḥ*).

Since the various variegated powers, such as hardness and so forth, residing in the five elements and their derivatives—earth and the rest—exist within consciousness characterized by the aforementioned attributes, [consciousness], having created them, makes them equal, consisting of its own power, according to the Vedic text: "It became both *sat* (being) and *tyat* (that-which-is-manifest)."
