This is because of the sacred scripture (*śruti*). The meaning is that the powers of solidity and so forth, which are conceptualized by consciousness, are indeed consciousness itself.

Since various forms exist as objects of cognition (*cetyatva*), characterized by diverse powers determined by the reckoning of the three periods of time, consciousness is also the cause of those diverse powers.

Since it might be argued that [the world] ought to be unequal, he says: "Time" (*kāla*). The meaning is that the various cognitions delimited by the three times, being devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), remain as such. From where, then, could there be equality for a consciousness that is accessible only through unequal speech?

He said: "For that [is]... Because, in accordance with the Vedic scripture stating "from which words turn back," that consciousness (citi) is inaccessible to speech; for that consciousness, moreover, during the state of ignorance regarding one's own nature, is perceived as if having attained an eternal non-existence apart from the body and so forth; and furthermore, that which...

That from which the conceptualization of self and non-self—accompanied by its counter-correlates as imagined through the perspectives of the knower and the ignorant—has emerged and attained total negation, is the "Selfless" (nirātman); the state of being that is "selflessness" (nairātmya).
This is indeed consciousness itself; thus, it is also "I am consciousness."
For whom there is no appearance of conceptual proliferation, nor even here the form of Brahman.

In accordance with such scriptural passages as these, abiding as the non-dual Brahman alone—which is the very nature of selflessness—is as if one has attained the emptiness of intrinsic nature; for from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it cannot be said that "it is as if" so, since both instances of the word "as if" (*iva*) are intended to conform to the vision of ultimate reality. Thus it is illuminated.

From the two occurrences of the word *hi*: when the delusion of the perception of one's own ignorance and so forth exists or does not exist, only non-dual pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) remains; regarding this, [it is said]:
"That which remains in a single form during the states of both the ignorant self and the wise self."
For that is called the general existence of the doctrine of selflessness.

Thus, according to the Smṛti; for those who, failing to realize that there is only non-dual consciousness (cinmātra) devoid of any counter-correlate, engage in activity or inactivity regarding what they consider to be other than themselves, it is said:
"In this way" (īheti). That consciousness, being without attributes, is incapable of arising; such is the case for those who hold this view.
May there be for me the experience of non-duality; salutations to You, the Self whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness!
I have been touched [by realization], I am awakened, and I have arisen in a short time.
I have been lifted out from conceptual constructions; whatever I am, that I am—homage be to you! To you who are the infinite Self, to me who am the conscious Self (cidātman). (48)
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord; salutations to me, who am Śiva.
Though standing, he is not seated; though walking, he does not walk. Though peaceful, he is engaged in worldly activity; though acting, he is not defiled.
This [Self] is exceedingly easy to attain and easy to know, like a trusted kinsman;
it is the bee within the lotus-cavity of the body for everyone. (50)
I have no desire for the maintenance of enjoyments, nor do I have any desire for their relinquishment;
let that which comes come, and let that which departs depart.
When the mind has been severed within the mind and egolessness has been attained;
when existence has dissolved through [the realization of] Being—I abide as the solitary Self, established in my own nature. (52)
Free from objective manifestation, free from egoism, free from the thinking mind, and free from desire,
my enemy remains only within the pure Self of mere vibration.
Having severed the multitude of the ropes of craving from the cage of my own body,
I know not where the bird of selflessness has flown away.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not stained, and who is equal toward all beings—for him life is truly glorious. 55.
He who, with an inwardly cooled intellect free from passion and hatred, beholds this very life like a witness—his life indeed shines. 56.
For one who, having correctly understood through thorough discernment, abandons both what is to be discarded and what is to be adopted,
and has placed the mind within the mind— that person’s life is truly radiant.
When the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has been exhausted, peace arises fully;
that peace which has attained stability is designated by the name "liberation. (58)
Like parched seeds, devoid of the sprout of further birth, the pure latent impression (vāsanā) of those liberated while living resides within their hearts. (59)
Purifying, supremely noble, and following after pure beings,
she consists eternally of self-meditation and remains as if in a state of deep sleep.
For consciousness devoid of the mind is called direct consciousness; because its nature is beyond the mind, the stain of conceptualization does not exist therein. (61)
That is truth, that is auspiciousness, that is the ultimate state;
that is omniscience and perfect contentment—indeed, that wherein the mind is destroyed.
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening my eyes, or even closing them, I am solely intent upon pure consciousness, with the bliss of all mental constructions cast aside. (63)
Having cast off the impurity of the object of perception and having utterly uprooted the mind,
and having severed the fire of the noose of desire, I am devoted solely to pure consciousness.

I am free from both auspicious and inauspicious thoughts, perfectly tranquil and free from affliction; with all perceptions of the desirable and undesirable destroyed, I am devoted solely to pure consciousness.
Having abandoned both selfhood and otherness, I am firm, supporting myself like a diamond pillar within the undifferentiated state of the world.
I abide in my own self-awareness, which is stainless and free from desire; liberated from likes and dislikes, I am devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.
When shall I attain inner contentment, established in the state of self-luminosity? When, with a tranquil mind, shall I dwell in the hollow of a mountain cave? (68)
I shall attain equality with a stone through non-conceptual meditative absorption;
upon my head, which is rendered mute by resting in partless meditation, [the world shall rest].
When will the forest birds build their nests of grass?
Having cut down the forest of the mind— the tree of volition and the creeper of craving—
and having reached the vast expanse of the ground, I dwell at ease.
I have followed that path; I am alone, I am victorious.
I am extinguished, I am desireless, I am partless, and I am free from longing.
Transparency, vigor, existence, loveliness, truthfulness, and wisdom;
blissful tranquility, ever-rejoicing and ever-arising;
fullness, magnanimity, true radiance, and eternal oneness. (72)
Reflecting thus, the monk quickly attained stability in his true nature;
knowing the nature of the non-conceptual, he became free from conceptual construction. (73)

Since those who do not know this are thus deprived, he says "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*) with the realization that "I am Brahman, non-different from the inner self"—that is, "I am the non-conceptual Brahman. Thus, I have contemplated that I am Brahman, the unity of the inner and outer consciousness. He who remains in this way through non-difference from the inner self is this very one.

"Even while remaining like one who is ignorant of his own nature"—by the knowledge of which a sage becomes untainted, this very Self is easily known through the realization, "I am Brahman. As to where such a person should take his seat, it is said: "In the body.
For one who knows the Self in this way, there is no desire for the maintenance of enjoyments, whether by virtue of the conjunction of time and karma.

Let it come when it comes; thus with the mind. Previously, in the state of ignorance (*svājñā-daśā*), that which was beyond oneself—though its own nature was empty—appeared as if real within the self. Now, in the state of self-knowledge (*svajñā-daśā*), where has that gone?

Upon investigation, that which was previously experienced as separate from the self has vanished because it is devoid of objective reality (*nirbhāva*) and is non-substantial. It is free from egoism (*nirahaṃkāra*).

Because of the absence of a body; it is "without mind" because of the state of being mindless; it is "without effort" because there is nothing to be sought through effort. Nevertheless, my enemy—the delusion of something other than the Self—remains as if real, residing only in the pure Self which is mere vibration (*kevalaspanda*). The use of the present tense for the sense of a past fact ("it remains") is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Now, by means of the Śruti and the Teacher...

258) Through grace, when the knowledge of Brahman alone—devoid of all counterparts—has arisen, then this delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself, that very delusion of "otherness" which was the bird of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), where has it gone? I am alone.

The meaning is that [only this] remains. He says "of whom" (yasya) to show that the life of one for whom such a sense of "I" does not arise toward the body and so forth is fruitful. "With a cool intellect" means with an intellect free from the heat of anything other than oneself. To the question, "How can the intellect be thus when passion and the like exist?", he says "passion" (rāga). "At the end of the mind" (cittasyānte) means in Brahman, which is the cessation of the mind.

He states that liberation is precisely the non-arising of mental modifications (vṛtti) other than one's own Self— beginning with "grāhya" (the object). To the question of how there can be the cessation of objects and so forth for all living beings who are characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā),
he says "bhṛṣṭa" (fried/scorched), indicating that such cessation arises from the perspective of the jīvanmukta who possesses pure latent impressions.

Being free from the conceptualization of the grasped and so forth, she becomes pure. He says "consciousness" (cetana) to indicate that where the mind does not exist, that alone is consciousness. He says "she" (sā) to indicate that in which consciousness—being devoid of unreality—attains the state of *manonmanī*, and whose nature is pure existence (*sanmātra*). In the attenuation of mental states...
He says, "pralapan" (while prattling), meaning that whether there is activity of the body and so forth or not, he remains as pure consciousness alone (*saṃvinmātra*).

He has cast off the entire range of objects, possessing the bliss of contemplation in which everything other than himself has been eliminated. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the stainless": *tārṇa* means made of grass; this refers to the pure consciousness established through the negation of all that is non-conscious.
He says "purity" (*svacchatā*) to show that through the knowledge that non-duality alone remains as one's own nature consisting of purity and so forth, one becomes the non-conceptual Brahman itself—
having swiftly attained the state of one's own true nature as a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Thus,
at the very moment of attaining perfect knowledge arising from hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on all the Vedāntas, [one becomes Brahman].

The wise one remains as the non-dual Self, established through the negation of all conceptual constructions that are other than oneself; this is the summarized meaning of the conclusion of all Vedānta. || 47–73 ||

The renunciation of the sick (*āturasannyāsa*), the destinations attained by renunciants, and the sequential renunciation (*kramasannyāsa*) to be performed if the sick person survives. [One should not perform renunciation] for a *śūdra*, a woman, an outcaste, or a woman in her courses. [For these], there is only one world. For the sick and the *kuṭīcaka* types, there are the worlds of Bhūr and Bhuvar. For the *bahūdaka*...

The world of Svarga belongs to the Haṃsa; the world of Tapas belongs to the Paramahaṃsa; and for the Turīyātīta and Avadhūta, there is liberation (kaivalya) within their own self alone through the contemplation of their true nature, according to the analogy of the bee and the worm. 74.

259) If the sick person survives, what purpose would there be for him? To this he says: "The sick person. This applies equally to all six types of renouncers, such as the *kuṭīcaka* and others, in their gradual renunciation (*kramasaṃnyāsa*). He states that this is the specific distinction for those who have transcended the fourth state (*turīyātīta*) and so forth: "Not..."

Regarding the word "of the ascetic" (yateḥ): because it is so, therefore he says "in the case of the sick" (āture) to show that, in accordance with the various types of renunciation such as the *kuṭīcaka* and others, and in accordance with their respective levels of knowledge, a corresponding difference in the worlds to be attained is also logical;
the meaning is that the sage attains Brahman. || 74 ||

For renunciants, there is no task whatsoever other than the contemplation of one's true nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*). The study of scriptures other than that which pertains to the contemplation of one's true nature is like a camel carrying a load of saffron; it is far from true knowledge. A wandering mendicant is not one who is intent merely on the chanting of names. Whatever action he performs—
One experiences various fruits [of action]; one should abandon everything like the froth of castor oil. This is not due to the grace of a deity;

therefore, by the practice of other scriptures apart from the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*), one attains results corresponding to their respective doctrines, but does not touch the fruit of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Having studied the system of Gautama...
Because one hears of such censured births as "he shall attain the womb of a jackal" and so forth,

the study of other scriptures is as useless as a camel carrying a load of saffron; the meaning is that, like a leather-worker who is far from knowledge, he remains devoid of the supreme knowledge of reality and its fruits.
"I am such-and-such a name in another stage of life"— thus the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is intent on the proclamation of his name; in this regard,
a true ascetic should never proclaim his name, lineage, and so forth, nor his country, time, learning, family, age, conduct, vow, or character.

Thus says the Śruti. For the meaning of this statement cannot possibly be a negation of the Lord’s name. To that effect, there are both Śruti and Smṛti: "He should remain alone and free from desire; indeed, he should not converse with anyone."
The ascetic should always respond to every greeting with the words, "Nārāyaṇa."
Thus (p.
260), constantly glorifying me and striving with firm vows, they...
And bowing to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined.
And so it is said. Furthermore, O Blessed One, since it is heard that there is sin in ceasing to remember Your names,

who— save for a slaughterer of animals— would turn away from the chanting of the virtues of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), which is a medicine for worldly existence, sung by those whose thirst has ceased, and which delights both the ear and the mind?
Thus [it is said]: "Because the meaning of the Blessed One’s name is Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (pratyak), it should always be meditated upon especially by ascetics.
The syllable *rā* denotes the Lord (Īśa), and the syllable *ma* denotes the individual soul (jīva);
the supreme Brahman, which is the unity of these two, is designated as *Rāma*."
From such scriptural passages as these, because of the negation of all that is other than itself, the glorious liberation (mukti-śrī) which is established unfolds;
the Great Light (mahaḥ) shining forth in that very form is called Śrī Rāma.

This is because of the statement regarding the discrimination between the name and its referent (*nāmārthaviveka*). Without being established in such Brahman, whatever action one performs, one experiences the fruit thereof, like the foam on castor oil. Therefore, one should renounce everything.
Having performed extremely severe austerity with the desire for the means of enjoyment in this world or the next, one should not [act] in accordance with that.
The meaning is that one should perform the reception of the grace of the deity.
Since austerity performed with a desireless mind yields infinite fruit, one should not perform external worship of deities—
that which is external to the Brahman non-different from the inner self (pratyagabhinnabrahma) wherein the Brahman non-different from the inner self is not invoked.
One should never perform the worship of deities external to that [Self], for the Śruti declares: "One should worship with the sense of 'I am That'. || 75 ||

Having abandoned everything other than himself, including their conduct and so forth, he should wander about emaciated, not increasing his fat, subsisting on food according to the "bee-like" mode of life;
he should pass his time with a bowl made of honeycomb or with his own mouth as a vessel.
One should lead [it]. || 76 ||
A self-possessed ascetic should take food in a measure suited to himself;
two parts of the meal should be for food, and the third part for water.
One should leave a fourth [part] remaining for the purpose of the movement of the wind. || 77 ||
He should always subsist on alms and never eat the food of a single person;
he should diligently approach that house which they look upon with an unperturbed mind. (78)
He should seek alms from five or seven houses of those who perform religious rites; having gone out, he should wait for only as long as it takes to milk a cow, and should not go further.
Fasting is better than eating; begging for alms is better than fasting;
therefore, one should subsist on alms.
At the time of begging for alms, he should not enter houses by taking either the left or the right path;
nor, out of delusion, should he bypass a house where no fault exists. || 81 ||
One should not beg for food from a Vedic scholar if it is devoid of faith and devotion;
however, one may beg even in the house of an outcast (vrātya) provided that [the offering] is preceded by faith and devotion.

Alms are traditionally said to be of five kinds: that collected from many houses like honey (mādhūkaraka), that which is not specifically prepared for the mendicant (asaṃkḷpta), that which was prepared beforehand (prākpraṇīta), that which is obtained without asking (ayācita), and that which is spontaneously offered at the moment (tātkālika). || 83 ||
Having made three, five, or seven houses free from mental attachment—
like a honeybee— it is known as "mādhūkara" (gleaning like a bee).

And at the time of dawn on the previous day, whatever was requested repeatedly by the devotees—that alms-food (bhaikṣa) should have been prepared beforehand; even so, he should maintain his stay there.
Whether invited by anyone through the effort of wandering for alms or otherwise, that alms-food which is unasked for should be eaten by those seeking liberation. 86.
That which was declared by the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of alms through attendance is known as "for that time"; it should then be consumed by the ascetics.
When the prepared food has been brought by the Brahmin toward the monastery,
the sages who long for liberation say, "It is ready. (88)
A renunciant may collect alms like a honey-gatherer even from the families of barbarians;
however, he should never eat food from a single source, even if that person were equal to Bṛhaspati.
He should maintain his livelihood by means of both requested and unrequested alms.
The mendicant is not defiled by the air through the fault of touch, nor by fire through its act of burning, nor by water through urine and excrement, nor by food through its impurities. (90)

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers have vanished, and when the people have finished their meal— at such a time, toward the latter part of the day, one should go about for alms.
In times of distress, one may wander for alms among all social classes, excluding those who are accused of crimes, outcasts, heretics, and worshippers of deities [for profit]. 92.
Clarified butter is like dog urine, honey is equal to liquor;
oil is like pig urine, and soup is commensurate with garlic. (93)
Bean cakes and the like, as well as beef, become equal to urine when mixed with milk;
therefore, an ascetic should avoid ghee and such substances with every effort. (94)
A yogi who uses his hands as a bowl should never eat food mixed with ghee, broth, or similar condiments; nor should he go about begging for alms more than once [a day]. (95)
When the sage seeks food with his mouth like a cow, then he shall be equal toward all things; he is fit for immortality.
The Śruti itself explains the meaning already stated by [the word] "mādhūkareṇa" with the word "ātma. It describes the rule for alms-gathering:
one who is devoid of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) prescribed in the Smṛtis is a *vrātya*. Having divided the alms into five parts, one should maintain oneself with one of them.

He says "he should lead [the life]"—namely, the *mādhūkara* [gathering like bees]. Therein, he states the definition of *mādhūkara*: "with the mind. He states the previously mentioned definition: "in the morning. He states the definition of *ayācita* (unasked for): "alms. He states the definition of *tātkālika* (temporary): "by standing nearby. He states the definition of *upapanna* (obtained as it arises): * *Mādhūkara* is defined as gathering food from various houses like bees collecting honey. * *Mana* refers to the internal mental state required for such practice. * *Prātaḥ* refers to the specific time of day for the *prāk-praṇīta* (previously prepared) mode. * *Bhikṣā* defines the *ayācita* mode of begging. * *Upasthānena* defines the *tātkālika* mode of receiving food while waiting in place. * *Upapanna* is defined as accepting whatever is offered spontaneously.
"Success! [Thus it is established]. He says "one should wander" to show that, in comparison with other types of food, the *mādhūkara* (gathering alms from various houses) is indeed superior.

He provides the reasoning for why there is no fault regarding the food of ascetics (*yatis*) by saying "not so. The rule for begging alms concerns the wandering of an ascetic for one night in a village; it does not apply to one who acts out of desire, thinking, "May this belong to me."
He says that one should not eat clarified butter and other such things—“clarified butter” (ghṛta). He describes the characteristic of the hand and belly as vessels—“the hands” (pāṇi)—[verses 76–96].

For ascetics, these things are to be avoided: one should renounce clarified butter as if it were blood; food from a single house as if it were meat; perfumes and ointments as if they were impure smears;
alkaline substances as if they were outcastes; clothing as if it were a vessel for leftovers; and anointing the body as if it were sexual union with a woman.

He viewed urine as if it were a friend’s delight; he viewed beef with longing; he viewed a woman as if she were a Caṇḍāla’s garden; he viewed gold as if it were the Great Principle (Mahiman); he viewed the assembly hall as if it were Kālakūṭa poison;
he viewed the capital city as if it were a cremation ground; and he viewed food gathered together as if it were the Kumbhīpāka hell or a funeral cake. Not...
By performing the worship of the deity and abandoning worldly involvement, one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 97 ||

The Brāhmaṇa also restates the meaning of the mantra with the words "ājyam" (the clarified butter). The sense is that there is nothing such as the clarified butter and so forth that exists apart from Brahman; rather, Brahman alone is everything. Thus, the sage who has ascended to the state of being the Self of all becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
There are six transgressions for ascetics, along with the determination of the faults that lead to loss of status:
sitting [inappropriately], the loss of the alms-bowl, hoarding, gathering disciples, sleeping during the day, and idle chatter—these are the six transgressions of ascetics. (98)
Any place other than the rainy season retreat is designated as a "seat" (āsana).
Herein, one may keep even a single vessel from among those previously mentioned, such as the gourd-ladle and others. (99)
(264) For the sake of conventional practice, the loss of the alms-bowl is called *pātralopa*;
likewise, the taking up of a second [item], such as a staff (*daṇḍa*) that was previously held, [is so termed]. || 100 ||
Accumulation is proclaimed as that which is for the purpose of enjoyment at a later time;
acquisition is that which is for the sake of service, gain, honor, or fame. (101)
The gathering of disciples is not said to be out of compassion for them;
rather, knowledge (vidyā) is called day because of its luminosity, while ignorance (avidyā) is called night. 102.

Negligence in the practice of knowledge is said to be sleeping during the day. Apart from discourse on spiritual matters, talk concerning alms, and inquiries for the sake of instruction, any other idle chatter is called "vain talk. (103)
Eating alone, intoxication, envy, perfumes, flowers, ornaments, betel, ointments, play, longing for enjoyments, and elixirs; || 104 ||
Chopping wood, reviling, prosperity, light, buying and selling, ritual action, disputes over work, and transgressing against one's teacher or the scriptures. (105)
Peace, war, marching, sitting, and white clothing; the emission of semen, sleeping during the day, and a begging bowl made of metal—these are the signs of a Taijasa [yogi]. 106.
Poison, weapons, seeds, violence, harshness, and sexual intercourse— these,
along with the duties of a householder and other such vows, have been abandoned through the yoga of renunciation.
One's lineage and so forth, conduct, the entire family of one's father and mother, and wealth—all these are prohibited [for a renunciant]; by indulging in them, one shall go downwards. 108.
Even when well-worn, a wise man should not place his trust in women, however aged they may be;
for even when rags are worn out, an old garment still clings to them.
Immovable things, moving beings, seeds, fire, poison, and weapons—
these six a renunciant should not take up, just like urine and excrement. (110)
An ascetic should never take any provisions for his journey except in times of distress;
in such emergencies, he may accept cooked food only as long as no other food can be obtained.
A mendicant who is free from disease and young should not dwell in a monastery;
he should never accept gifts for the sake of others, nor should he ever give anything away.
Out of a sense of humility toward living beings, an ascetic should wander for the sake of his own good fortune;
whether seeking cooked or uncooked food, he who begs in this manner shall not fall into ruin.
A monk intent on the gift of food may accept garments and other such items, whether made of wool or not, as well as fine cloths. (114)

Having accepted these, the ascetic surely falls; of this there is no doubt. By taking refuge in the boat of non-duality (advaita), one attains the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 115 ||

One should observe silence as a punishment for verbal transgression, fasting as a punishment for physical transgression, and breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed when a mental transgression has been committed. 116.
A living being is bound by action and liberated by knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who have seen the further shore do not perform ritual action.
On the streets there are many garments, and alms are obtained everywhere; the earth provides a vast bed—why then are ascetics miserable? (118)
The ascetic who offers the entirety of conceptual proliferation as an oblation into the fire of knowledge,
having internalized the sacred fires within the Self— he is a true performer of the Agnihotra, a great ascetic.
Activity is said to be of two kinds: that of the cat and that of the monkey.
One who possesses the practice of knowledge attains the state of the monkey, which is indeed secondary. (120)
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, the wise man should behave among people like one who is dull-witted. 121.
When a collection of all sins has arisen, one should practice the twelve-thousand-verse *Tārā* mantra; for that is indeed the severance [of those sins].
But for him who recites the Praṇava twelve thousand times every day, the Supreme Brahman becomes manifest within twelve months. || 123 ||
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
He says that even for a sage, this group of six beginning with posture (*āsana*) becomes a cause of bondage—namely, "posture" (*āsana*).
The Śruti itself explains the meaning of its own sūtra: "after the rains," etc.—referring to [the practice of] eating at a single meal, and so forth.

Astrology and the profession of a fortune-teller—all this [is forbidden]. He has renounced eating food provided by a single person and other such prohibited practices. Regarding the reason why one should never look at a woman and converse with her in private, he says: "Even if well-digested... He states that one should never undertake the acquisition of fields, servants, seeds, gold, poison, or weapons: [The verse continues: kedārabhṛtyabījasuvarṇaviṣāyudhaparigraham | kadāpi naiva kurvīta yadīccheddharmasaṃgraham || 17 || One should never at any time undertake the acquisition of fields, servants, seeds, gold, poison, or weapons, if one desires the accumulation of dharma. || 17 || He also says that one should never perform the following: na kuryāddevakāryārthaṃ pitṛkāryaṃ tathaiva ca | na ca snānaṃ na homaṃ ca na ca vai devatārcanam || 18 || One should not perform rites for the gods nor likewise rites for the ancestors; nor should one perform ritual bathing, fire-oblations, or the worship of deities. || 18 || He further states: na ca kuryāttilaiḥ śrāddhaṃ na ca kuryāttilodakam | na ca kuryāttilairdānaṃ na ca kuryāttilaiḥ kriyām || 19 || One should not perform a *śrāddha* with sesame seeds, nor offer water with sesame; one should not give gifts with sesame, nor perform any ritual action with sesame. || 19 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā śaucaṃ na ca kuryājjapaṃ tathā | na ca kuryāttathā dhyānaṃ na ca kuryāttathārcanam || 20 || One should not perform purification, nor should one perform recitation (*japa*); one should not perform meditation (*dhyāna*), nor should one perform worship (*arcana*). || 20 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā pūjāṃ na ca kuryāttathā balim | na ca kuryāttathā homaṃ na ca kuryāttathā japam || 21 || One should not perform worship (*pūjā*), nor should one offer oblations (*bali*); one should not perform fire-oblations (*homa*), nor should one perform recitation (*japa*). || 21 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā dānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām | na ca kuryāttathā svādhyāyaṃ na ca kuryāttathā vratam || 22 || One should not give gifts, nor should one perform ritual acts; one should not study the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), nor should one observe vows (*vrata*). || 22 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā yogaṃ na ca kuryāttathā tapaḥ | na ca kuryāttathā dhyānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā śrutam || 23 || One should not practice yoga, nor should one perform austerity (*tapas*); one should not practice meditation (*dhyāna*), nor should one study the scriptures (*śruta*). || 23 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā jñānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā matim | na ca kuryāttathā vṛttiṃ na ca kuryāttathā sthitim || 24 || One should not cultivate knowledge (*jñāna*), nor should one form an opinion (*mati*); one should not adopt a livelihood (*vṛtti*), nor should one maintain a fixed state (*sthiti*). || 24 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā caryāṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām | na ca kuryāttathā bhikṣāṃ na ca kuryāttathā gṛham || 25 || One should not engage in conduct (*caryā*), nor should one perform ritual acts (*kriyā*); one should not beg for alms (*bhikṣā*), nor should one maintain a household (*gṛha*). || 25 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā maunaṃ na ca kuryāttathā vacaḥ | na ca kuryāttathā śayyāṃ na ca kuryāttathāsanam || 26 || One should not observe silence (*mauna*), nor should one speak words; one should not prepare a bed (*śayyā*), nor should one prepare a seat (*āsana*). || 26 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā pānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā bhojanam | na ca kuryāttathā snānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām || 27 || One should not drink, nor should one eat; one should not bathe, nor should one perform ritual acts (*kriyā*). || 27 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā dhyānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā japaḥ | na ca kuryāttathā homaṃ na ca kuryāttathā balim || 28 || One should not practice meditation (*dhyāna*), nor should one perform recitation (*japa*); one should not perform fire-oblations (*homa*), nor should one offer oblations (*bali*). || 28 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā śrāddhaṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām | na ca kuryāttathā dānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā vratam || 29 || One should not perform a *śrāddha*, nor should one perform ritual acts (*kriyā*); one should not give gifts (*dāna*), nor should one observe vows (*vrata*). || 29 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā yogaṃ na ca kuryāttathā tapaḥ | na ca kuryāttathā dhyānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā śrutam || 30 || One should not practice yoga, nor should one perform austerity (*tapas*); one should not practice meditation (*dhyāna*), nor should one study the scriptures (*śruta*). || 30 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā jñānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā matim | na ca kuryāttathā vṛttiṃ na ca kuryāttathā sthitim || 31 || One should not cultivate knowledge (*jñāna*), nor should one form an opinion (*mati*); one should not adopt a livelihood (*vṛtti*), nor should one maintain a fixed state (*sthiti*). || 31 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā caryāṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām | na ca kuryāttathā bhikṣāṃ na ca kuryāttathā gṛham || 32 || One should not engage in conduct (*caryā*), nor should one perform ritual acts (*kriyā*); one should not beg for alms (*bhikṣā*), nor should one maintain a household (*gṛha*). || 32 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā maunaṃ na ca kuryāttathā vacaḥ | na ca kuryāttathā śayyāṃ na ca kuryāttathāsanam || 33 || One should not observe silence (*mauna*), nor should one speak words; one should not prepare a bed (*śayyā*), nor should one prepare a seat (*āsana*). || 33 || He also says: na ca kuryāttathā pānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā bhojanam | na ca kuryāttathā snānaṃ na ca kuryāttathā kriyām || 34 || One should not drink, nor should one eat; one should not bathe, nor should
Regarding "immovable" (sthāvaram): he states that provisions for the journey (pātheya) should not be accepted except in times of distress—hence, "never" (naiva).

Furthermore, he describes what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted by the ascetic (yati)—starting with "one who is free from disease," etc. In "the dwelling" (āvasathe), meaning in the house of a worldly person, he who remains having abandoned all audacity, thinking "this poor man is a holy one," possesses compassion and devotion.

Or rather, just as faith toward living beings may arise, so should the ascetic act for the welfare and the ultimate good of beings out of a sense of humility and goodness; the meaning is that he should never cause them agitation.
Or else, out of a sense of humility toward living beings—having perceived their suffering—he should act for their welfare.

The meaning is that the ascetic should practice [this]. He says "matured" (pakvam) to indicate that he should never accept gifts or give alms for any purpose other than merely maintaining his own body. He says "non-duality" (advaitam) to indicate that, having crossed the river of duality by means of the boat of non-duality and having attained the state of Brahman which is its further shore, he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
To the question, "How can there be liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā) when the activities of speech, mind, and body persist?", he states the means for their restraint:
"By action" (karmaṇā).

Since this is so, therefore: he speaks of the absence of suffering for ascetics with the words "in the street" (*rathyāyām*). He speaks of the state of being an *agnihotrin* even for one without fire with the words "the phenomenal world" (*prapañcam*).
He states that activity directed toward the higher and lower Brahman is divided into two kinds with the word "activity" (*pravṛttiḥ*).

This is an illustration of the attainment of one's true nature at the very moment of realization for those who have practiced knowledge and possess the wisdom that Brahman alone is without distinction— just as a cat (*otu*),
by the mere act of a momentary meditation, seizes its prey. However, activity directed toward the lower Brahman (*apara-brahma*) is like that of a monkey.
The meaning is that even a partial [practice], by the maxim of the "monkey's handful," gradually becomes effective in accomplishing the task.
He says "not so" to indicate that the wise person should conduct himself in the world like one who is dull-witted. To the question, "Where can there be wisdom when a heap of sins exists? he replies:
when the mountain-like mass of sins has been reduced to ashes by the fire of steadfastness in the *praṇava*, then one becomes truly wise.
The scripture concludes that one comes to rest in Brahman alone, stating: "Of all...

One should practice the *tāra* twelve thousand times, preceded by a reflection on its meaning. Through that, after twelve months, by means of the knowledge obtained through the purification of the mind, [one attains] the Supreme Brahman.
"It shines forth through the intellect that remains as its own self. From the recitation of twelve thousand *praṇavas*, purification of the mind arises.
Thereafter, knowledge obtained through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher occurs. This concludes the *Nirviśeṣa-samyag-jñāna-saṃnyāsa-upaniṣad*. (Verses 98–123)
Thus ends the second chapter.
By Śrī Vāsudevendra’s disciple, Upaṇiṣadbrahmayogin,
this commentary on the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad, which has Brahman as its object, has been written.
The commentary on the Saṃnyāsopaniṣad is recorded as consisting of two hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad, completing the sixty-fifth [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
